(Surah Ta-Ha)
(Surah Ta-Ha)

It has one hundred and thirty-five verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ta-Ha﴾ ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you distressed,﴾ ﴿but as a reminder for one who fears,﴾ ﴿a revelation from the One who created the earth and the high heavens.﴾ ﴿The Most Gracious is established upon the Throne.﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens, whatever is on the earth, whatever is between them, and whatever is beneath the soil.﴾ ﴿And if you speak aloud, indeed He knows the secret and what is more hidden.﴾ ﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him. To Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ta-Ha﴾ ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you distressed,﴾ ﴿but as a reminder for one who fears,﴾ ﴿a revelation from the One who created the earth and the high heavens.﴾ ﴿The Most Gracious is established upon the Throne.﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens, whatever is on the earth, whatever is between them, and whatever is beneath the soil.﴾ ﴿And if you speak aloud, indeed He knows the secret and what is more hidden.﴾ ﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him. To Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾.

Know that His saying ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ involves two issues:

The first issue: Abu 'Amr recited it with a fatha on the ta and a kasra on the ha. The people of Madinah recited it with a sound between the fatha and the kasra. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir recited it with a fatha on both the ta and the ha. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited it with a kasra on both the ta and the ha. Al-Zajjaj said: It was also recited as Ta with a fatha on the ta and a sukun on the ha, and all of these are dialectal forms. Al-Zajjaj said: As for the one who put a fatha on the ta and the ha, it is because the letter before the alif is fatha. As for the one who put a kasra on the ta and the ha, he inclined the fatha toward kasra (imalah, the inclination of a vowel toward a following or preceding sound), because the letter is maqsur (a letter with a short alif), and the maqsur is characterized by inclination toward the kasra.

The second issue: The exegetes have two opinions about it:

One of them: It is among the disjointed letters (huruf al-tahajji, the individual letters that open certain surahs), and the other: It is a meaningful word. As for the first view, the discussion of it has already passed at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah. What they have added here are the following matters:

The first: Al-Tha'labi said: Ta is the tree of Tuba, and ha is the Hawiyah (the abyss of Hell), so it is as if He swore by Paradise and Hell.

The second: It is related from Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him): Ta is the purity of the People of the House, and ha is their guidance.

The third: O hope of intercession for the Ummah, and O guide of creation to the religion.

The fourth: Sa'id ibn Jubayr said:

It is the opening of His good, pure, and guiding name.

The fifth: Ta is from purity (taharah) and ha is from guidance (hidayah), as if it were said: O one purified from sins, and O guide to the Knower of the unseen.

The sixth: Ta is the length of the reciters, and ha is their awe in the hearts of the disbelievers. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿We shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾ [Al 'Imran: 151].

The seventh: Ta is nine in calculation, and ha is five, which makes fourteen, and its meaning is: O full moon. You have already known in what preceded that such sayings should not be relied upon.

The second opinion: the view of those who said that it is a meaningful word. On this view they mentioned two aspects:

One of them: Its meaning is "O man," and this is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, 'Ikrimah, and al-Kalbi, may Allah be pleased with them. Then Sa'id ibn Jubayr said it is in the Nabataean tongue, Qatadah said it is in the Syriac tongue, 'Ikrimah said it is in the Abyssinian tongue, and al-Kalbi said it is in the dialect of 'Akk. Al-Kalbi recited for their poet:

Indeed, foolishness, O Ta-ha, is among your traits; may Allah not sanctify the souls of the accursed.

The people have discussed this view from two aspects:

The first: That it has the meaning of "O man" in the language, and it was taken to mean that. But if this meaning is established, it is permissible only in the language of the Arabs, since the Qur'an was revealed in this language. So it is possible that the Arabic usage of this word agrees with the other languages we have mentioned. But otherwise it is neither acceptable nor valid.

The second: The author of "al-Kashshaf" said: If Ta-ha in the dialect of 'Akk means "O man," then perhaps they altered "ya hadha" (O this one) by changing the ya into a ta, so they said "Ta," and they shortened "hadha" and limited it to "ha," so His saying "Ta-ha" means "O this one." Some objected to this and said: If it were so, it would have to be written with four letters: ta, alif, ha. 

The second aspect: He (peace be upon him) used to stand in his tahajjud (night prayer) on one leg, so he was commanded to set the earth with both feet together. The original was "ta'" (step), so its hamzah was changed to ha, as they said "hiyya" in place of "iyyaka," and "harqtu" in place of "araqtu." It is also possible that the original is from "wati'a" (to tread) without the hamzah, so its original form is "ta'," meaning "O man," and then the ha was affixed to it for pausing. Both aspects were mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verses 2–3:

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an to you to make you suffer﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: If you take Ta-Ha as an enumeration of the names of the letters, then this is the beginning of a new statement. If you take it as the name of the surah, then the statement ﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an to you to make you suffer﴾ may be a predicate about it (and it is in the position of the subject), with "the Qur'an" stated explicitly in place of a pronoun, because it is the Qur'an; or it may be the answer to it, and it is an oath.

The second issue: It has been recited as "Ma nuzzila 'alayka al-Qur'anu li-tashqa" (the verb in the passive form, with al-Qur'an as its subject).

The third issue: They mentioned several views concerning the occasion of the revelation of the verse:

The first of them: Muqatil said that Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Muti' ibn 'Adi and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Indeed, you are wretched, since you have abandoned the religion of your fathers." He, peace be upon him, said: "Rather, I have been sent as a mercy to the worlds." They said: "Rather, you are wretched." So Allah, Exalted is He, revealed this verse as a refutation of them and as an informing of Muhammad (ﷺ) that the religion of Islam is peace (salam), and this Qur'an is the means of attaining every success and the cause of attaining every happiness, while what the disbelievers are upon is wretchedness itself.

The second: "He, peace be upon him, prayed at night until his feet swelled, and Jibril, peace be upon him, said to him: 'Spare yourself, for your self has a right over you.'" That is, "We did not send it down so that you would destroy yourself through worship and make it suffer great hardship; you were sent only with the tolerant, upright religion (al-hanifiyya al-samha)." It is also narrated that he, peace be upon him, "when he stood up at night, would tie his chest with a rope so that he would not sleep." Some said he would stand on one leg, and some said he would stay awake the whole night; so by His saying "to make you suffer" He meant that. Al-Qadi said: This is far-fetched, because if he, peace be upon him, did any of that, he must have done it by the command of Allah, Exalted is He; and if he did it by His command, then it is of the category of happiness, so it is not permissible to say to him: "We did not command you to that."

The third: Some said it is possible that what is meant is: do not burden yourself and do not torment it with grief over the disbelief of these people, for We have only sent down the Qur'an to you so that you may give admonition by it; whoever believes and does righteous deeds, it is for his own self, and whoever disbelieves, let not his disbelief grieve you; there is nothing upon you but conveyance. This is like His saying: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 3], and ﴿Let not their word grieve you﴾ [Yunus: 65].

The fourth: You are not blamed for the disbelief of your people, like His saying: ﴿You are not over them a controller﴾ [al-Ghashiya: 22], and ﴿You are not over them a guardian﴾ [al-Shura: 6]; that is, their disbelief is not upon you when you have conveyed, and you will not be held accountable for their sin.

The fifth: This surah is among the first of what was revealed in Makkah, and at that time he, peace be upon him, was subdued under the humiliation of his enemies. So it is as if He, glory be to Him, said to him: Do not think that you will remain in this state forever; rather your affair will rise and your standing will become manifest. For We did not send down to you the like of this Qur'an so that you would remain wretched among them; rather you will become honored and esteemed.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But as a reminder for one who fears﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: Regarding the word "illa" (except/but) here, there are two views:

One of them: It is an exceptive particle that is disconnected (istithna' munqati'), meaning "but" (lakin).

The second: The sense is: "We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would bear the hardships of conveyance, except that it be a reminder," just as one says: "We did not address you with these words so that you would be harmed, except that others may take a lesson from you."

The second issue: He singled out "one who fears" for the reminder only because they are the ones who benefit from it, although it is general to all. This is like His saying: ﴿A guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqara: 2]. And He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ [al-Furqan: 1]; and He said: ﴿That you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned, so they are heedless﴾ [Ya-Sin: 6]; and He said: ﴿And warn thereby a stubborn people﴾ [Maryam: 97]; and He said: ﴿And remind, for the reminder benefits the believers﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 55].

The third issue: The manner in which the Qur'an is a reminder is that he, peace be upon him, used to admonish them with it and with its explanation. Thus the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) falls under His saying "for one who fears," since in fear and in reminding by the Qur'an he was above all.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verses 4–7 (part 1 of 2):

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A revelation from the One who created the earth and the high heavens﴾, there are several issues.

First issue: They mentioned several possibilities regarding the grammatical case (i'rab) of "tanzilan" (revelation):
One: its underlying sense is "It was sent down as a revelation from the One who created the earth," so "tanzilan" is in the accusative by an implied verb.
Second: it is in the accusative governed by "anzalna" (We sent down), because the meaning of "We have not sent down the Qur'an to you except as a reminder" (20:2–3) is "We sent it down as a reminder."
Third: it is in the accusative by way of praise and specification (al-madh wa'l-ikhtisas).
Fourth: it is in the accusative as an object of "yakhsha" (fears), meaning "He Who sent it down" ... "a reminder for whoever fears" (20:3), the revelation of Allah. This is a good meaning and a clear grammatical analysis. It has also been read as "tanzilun" in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject.

Second issue: The benefit of shifting from the first person plural (We) to the third person (He) comprises several things:
One: these attributes cannot be mentioned except with the third person.
Two: He first said "anzalna" (We sent down), elevating the matter by attributing it to the one obeyed; then He followed it by referring to the One specified with the attributes of greatness and glorification, so the magnificence was doubled from two directions.
Three: "anzalna" may be a quotation of the words of Jibril (peace be upon him) and the angels who descended with him.

Third issue: He, Exalted is He, magnified the state of the Qur'an by attributing it to being a revelation from the One who created the earth and created the heavens on high. He said this because the magnification of Allah, Exalted is He, appears through the magnification of His creation and His blessings. He magnified the Qur'an to encourage reflection on it, contemplation of its meanings and realities. This is customary among people: the message is magnified by magnifying the state of the one who sends it, so that the recipient is more inclined to comply.

Fourth issue: It is said "samaʾ ʿulya" (a high heaven) and "samawat ʿula" (high heavens). The benefit of describing the heavens as "high" is to indicate the greatness of the power of the One who creates the like of them in their height and the remoteness of their ascent.
* * *

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Most Merciful, who established Himself upon the Throne﴾, there are several issues.

First issue: "al-Rahman" has been read in the genitive as an attribute of "man khalaqa" (the One who created), but the nominative is better, because it is either in the nominative by way of praise, the meaning being "He is the Most Merciful," or it is a subject whose reference is indicated by the "l" to "man khalaqa." If it is asked: what is the position of the clause "established Himself upon the Throne" when you read "al-Rahman" in the genitive or in the nominative by way of praise? We say: if you read it in the genitive, it is the predicate of an omitted subject and nothing else; if you read it in the nominative, it may be so, and it may also be that together with "al-Rahman" there are two predicates of the subject.

Second issue: The Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists) have clung to this verse to claim that their worshipped one sits upon the Throne. This is false by reason and by transmitted texts, for several reasons:
One: He, glory be to Him, existed when there was no Throne and no place. When He created creation, He did not need a place, but was independent of it. So He remains in the attribute He has always had, unless someone claims that a throne has always existed alongside Allah.
Two: The one who sits must have a part of him in the right side of the Throne different from the part in its left side, so he would be composed and compounded in himself, and whatever is so requires a composer and compounder, which is impossible.
Three: The one who sits upon the Throne either is able to move and shift, or is not able to do so. If the first, he becomes a locus of motion and rest, and so is necessarily originated. If the second, he is like one who is bound, or rather like a paralytic, or worse off than him, for the paralytic, if he wills motion in his head and eyeball, is able to do so, whereas this is not possible for their worshipped one.
Four: Their worshipped one either exists in every place or in one place rather than another. If he exists in every place, it follows that he exists in places of filth and refuse, which no sensible person would say. If he exists in one place rather than another, he requires something that specifies him to that place, and so is needy, and need is impossible for Allah.
Five: His saying, ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ (42:11), comprehends the negation of likeness in all respects, as shown by the validity of the exception: it is correct to say "there is nothing like Him except in sitting, except in quantity, except in colour." The validity of the exception requires that all these matters be included under it. So if He were sitting, there would be something resembling Him in sitting, and then the meaning of the verse would be nullified.
Six: His saying, ﴿And above them on that Day eight will bear the Throne of your Lord﴾ (69:17). If they are bearers of the Throne, and the Throne is the place of their worshipped one, it follows that the angels bear their Creator and Worshipped One, which is unintelligible, for the Creator is the one who preserves the created, whereas the created does not preserve the Creator nor bear Him.
Seven: If it were permissible for whoever is fixed in a place to be a god, how would it be known that the sun and the moon are not gods? For our path to denying divinity to the sun and moon is that they are described by motion and rest, and whatever is so is originated and not a god. If you invalidate this path, the door of rejecting the divinity of the sun and moon is closed to you.
Eight: The world is a sphere, so the direction that is "above" in relation to us is "below" in relation to the inhabitants of the other side of the earth, and vice versa. If the worshipped one were specific to a direction, that direction, though it would be above for some people, would be below for others. By the agreement of sensible people, it is not permissible to say the worshipped one is beneath all things.
Nine: The Ummah has agreed that His saying, ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ (112:1), is among the clear (muhkam) verses, not the ambiguous (mutashabih). If He were specific to a place, the side of Him that faces what is on His right would be different from the side that faces what is on His left; He would then be composite and divisible, and not truly one, and so His saying ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ would be nullified.
Ten: The Khalil (Friend), peace be upon him, said: ﴿I do not love those that set﴾ (6:76). If the worshipped one were a body, He would always be setting and always absent, and so would fall under His saying ﴿I do not love those that set﴾. Thus by these proofs it is established that settling upon Allah, Exalted is He, is impossible. At this point, people have two positions:

The first: We do not occupy ourselves with interpretation, but we affirm with certainty that Allah, Exalted is He, is far above place and direction, and we leave the interpretation of the verse. Al-Shaykh al-Ghazali narrated from some companions of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal that he interpreted three reports: the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, "The Black Stone is the right hand of Allah on earth," his saying, peace be upon him, "The heart of the believer is between two fingers of the fingers of the Most Merciful," and his saying, peace be upon him, "I find the breath of the Most Merciful coming from the direction of Yemen." Know that this position is weak for two reasons:
First: if one affirms with certainty that Allah, Exalted is He, is far above place and direction, one has affirmed with certainty that Allah's intended meaning by "istiwa'" is not sitting, and this is precisely interpretation.
And if one does not affirm with certainty the declaration of Allah, Exalted is He, above place and direction, but remains in doubt about it, then one is ignorant of Allah, Exalted is He. Unless one says: "I am certain that what Allah intends is not what its apparent meaning suggests, but He intends something else, though I do not specify that intended meaning, out of fear of error." This would be closer to acceptable, but it is also weak, because when Allah addressed us in the tongue of the Arabs, it is necessary that He intends by the word only its established meaning in the language of the Arabs. And since "istiwa'" in the language has no meaning except "settling" and "mastery," and its being taken as "settling" is impossible, it is necessary to take it as "mastery"; otherwise the word would be left without meaning, and that is not permissible.

The second, which is a decisive proof that one must turn to interpretation: since rational proof has established the impossibility of settling, and the apparent wording of "istiwa'" indicates the meaning of settling, we have four options: either we act upon each of the two proofs, or we abandon both together, or we prefer transmitted text over reason, or we prefer reason and interpret the transmitted text. The first is invalid, for it would require that one and the same thing be both free of place and located in place, which is impossible. The second is also impossible, for it would require raising two contradictories together, which is false. The third is invalid, because reason is the root of transmission: until the existence of the Creator, His knowledge, His power, and His sending of messengers are established by rational proofs, transmission is not established. So discrediting reason entails discrediting both reason and transmission together. Therefore nothing remains but to affirm the soundness of reason and occupy ourselves with interpreting the transmitted text, and this is a decisive proof for the purpose. Having established this, we say: some scholars said that what is meant by "istiwa'" is "mastery," as the poet said:

"Bishr has come to mastery over Iraq, without sword or spilled blood."

If it is said that this interpretation is not permissible, for several reasons:
One: "mastery" means attaining dominance after weakness, and that is impossible with respect to Allah, Exalted is He.
Two: one says "so-and-so has mastered such-and-such" only when there is a rival who contests it, and the thing mastered already existed before; this is impossible with respect to Allah, for the Throne came into being through His creating and fashioning it.
Three: mastery is attained with respect to all created things, so singling out the Throne for mention has no benefit.

The answer: when we explain "mastery" as "power," all these objections fall away entirely. The author of al-Kashshaf said: since "settling upon the Throne," which is the seat of sovereignty, is attained only together with sovereignty, they used it as a metaphor for sovereignty, and they said: "So-and-so settled upon the land," meaning he ruled it, even if he never sat on the throne at all. They expressed the attainment of sovereignty by this because it is clearer and stronger in indication than saying "so-and-so ruled." Similar is your saying: "the hand of so-and-so is outstretched" and "the hand of so-and-so is chained," meaning he is generous or miserly. There is no difference between the two expressions except what I have mentioned, so that one whose hand was never outstretched in giving, or who had no hand at all, is said to have an outstretched hand, since to them there is no difference between it and saying "generous." From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Jews say: The hand of Allah is chained; their own hands are chained﴾ (5:64), meaning He is miserly, ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched﴾ (5:64), meaning He is generous, without imagining a hand, a chain, or an outstretching. Explaining it as "blessing," and straining to name it so, comes from narrowness of disposition. I say: if we open this door, the interpretations of the Batiniyya (esotericists) would flood in, for they too say that what is meant by His saying ﴿Take off your sandals﴾ (20:12) is total absorption in the service of Allah, Exalted is He, without imagining an act; and His saying: ﴿We said: O fire, be cool and safe for Abraham﴾

The purpose of it is to rescue Ibrahim (peace be upon him) from the hand of that oppressor, without there being any fire or any address at all. The same applies to everything else that occurs in the Book of Allah, the Exalted. Rather, the governing principle is that every word that occurs in the Qur'an must be taken in its literal sense, unless there is a definitive rational indication that compels turning away from it. Would that whoever does not know something would not delve into it. This is the complete discussion of this verse. Whoever wishes a thorough study of the ambiguous (mutashabih) verses and reports should consult the book *Ta'sis al-Taqdis* (The Foundation of Sanctification). And success is from Allah.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them and whatever is beneath the soil.﴾ Know that when He, glorified is He, explained His dominion by saying, ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾, and dominion is not organized except through power and knowledge, He necessarily followed it with power and then with knowledge. As for power, it is this verse. The meaning is that He, glorified is He, possesses these four categories. He possesses whatever is in the heavens, of angels, stars and others. He possesses whatever is on the earth, of minerals and metals. He possesses whatever is between them, of air. And He possesses whatever is beneath the *thara*. If it is said: the *thara* is the final surface of the world, so there would be nothing beneath it, how then could Allah possess it? We say: *al-thara* in the language means moist soil, so it is possible that there is something beneath it, and that is either the bull, or the fish, or the rock, or the sea, or the air, according to the differing reports.

As for knowledge, it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and that which is more hidden.﴾ And in this there are two opinions.

The first: that His saying ﴿and more hidden﴾ is in the form of an intensive (superlative). According to this view, we say that He, the Exalted, divided things into three categories: the open (*jahr*), the secret (*sirr*), and the more hidden (*akhfa*).

It is possible that what is meant by the open is the speech that is uttered aloud, though something of it may be concealed in the self even when part of it appears, and something may be concealed without appearing, as some have said. It is also possible that what is meant by the secret and the more hidden is what is not speech, and this is more apparent. So it is as if He, the Exalted, made clear that He knows the secret that is not heard, and what is more hidden than it. How then would He not know the open? The purpose of this is to deter the one bound by obligation from vices, whether they are apparent or hidden, and to encourage him toward acts of obedience, whether they are apparent or hidden. On this interpretation, the secret and the more hidden should be understood as that for which there is reward or punishment. The secret is what a person keeps within himself of matters he has resolved upon, and the more hidden is what has not reached the level of resolve. It is possible to interpret the more hidden as what he has resolved upon and what has occurred to his thought without his resolving upon it. It is possible also that it is what has not yet occurred to his inner self, so it is more hidden than the secret. It is also possible that it is what will come to be from Allah, the Exalted, of matters that have not yet appeared. Although the closest meaning is what we have mentioned first, namely what falls under deterrence and encouragement.

The second opinion: that *akhfa* is a verb (in the sense of "He conceals"), meaning that He knows the secrets of the servants, and conceals from them what He knows. It is like His saying: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they encompass nothing of His knowledge.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255] If it is asked: how does the consequent correspond to the condition? We say: its meaning is that if you speak aloud in mention of Allah, the Exalted, whether in supplication or otherwise, know that He is free of need for your speaking aloud. Or it may be a prohibition against speaking aloud, like His saying: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and with fear, and without loudness of speech.﴾ [al-A'raf: 205] Or it is a teaching to the servants that raising the voice is not for Allah, the Exalted, to hear, but is for another purpose.

Know that Allah, the Exalted, is knowing by His essence, and that He knows all the known things at all times with one knowledge, and that this knowledge does not change, and that this knowledge is among the necessary attributes of His essence, without being described as originated or contingent. The servant does not share with the Lord except in the first sixth, which is the root of knowledge. Then this sixth is divided between Him and His servants into two halves. So five *dawaniq* and a half of a unit of knowledge belong to Him, and one half belongs to the whole of His servants. Then this one unit is shared among all creation: among the cherubic angels (*karubiyyun*), the spiritual angels, the bearers of the Throne, the inhabitants of the heavens, the angels of mercy and the angels of punishment. Likewise all the prophets, the first of whom is Adam and the last of whom is Muhammad (ﷺ), upon them all. Likewise all creation in their necessary and acquired knowledge, and in crafts and professions. And all animals in their perceptions and sensations, and in their guidance toward their interests, in their foods, their harms and their benefits. What falls to you from that unit is less than an atom compounded. Yet by that atom you came to know the secrets of His divinity and His attributes, the necessary, the permissible and the impossible. If by this atom you have come to know these secrets, how could His knowledge be five *dawaniq* and a half? Would He not know by that knowledge the secrets of your servitude? This is the realization of His saying: ﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and that which is more hidden.﴾ Rather, the truth is that the whole dinar belongs to Him, because what you know, you know only through His teaching, as He said: ﴿He sent it down with His knowledge.﴾ [al-Nisa': 166] And He said: ﴿Should not He who created know?﴾ [al-Mulk: 14] For this there is an example, which is the sun, whose light makes the world bright, yet nothing whatsoever is diminished from its light. Likewise here. How then would He not be knowing of the secret and the more hidden? Among His arrangements in the creation of trees and kinds of plants is that they have no mouths, nor any of the other organs of nourishment. Therefore their roots are fixed in the earth, drawing nourishment through them, and that nourishment reaches the branches, and from them to the veins, and from them to the leaves. Then He, the Exalted, made their veins like the tent-ropes by which tents may be pitched.

Just as a rope must be extended from every side so that the tent stands, likewise the veins extend from every side so that the tree stands. Then if you look at every leaf and the fine veins spread within it, so that nourishment reaches every side of the leaf, to strengthen the body of the leaf so that it does not tear quickly, these are like the veins created in the body of an animal, to serve as channels for the blood and the spirit, strengthening the body. Then look at the trees: the most beautiful of them in appearance is the poplar and the willow, though they yield no benefit. And the ugliest of them is the fig and grape tree, yet look at their benefit. These things and their like show that not even the weight of an atom in the heavens or on the earth escapes His knowledge.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verses 4–7 (part 1 of 2):

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A revelation from the One who created the earth and the high heavens﴾, there are several issues.

First issue: They mentioned several possibilities regarding the grammatical case (i'rab) of "tanzilan" (revelation):
One: its underlying sense is "It was sent down as a revelation from the One who created the earth," so "tanzilan" is in the accusative by an implied verb.
Second: it is in the accusative governed by "anzalna" (We sent down), because the meaning of "We have not sent down the Qur'an to you except as a reminder" (20:2–3) is "We sent it down as a reminder."
Third: it is in the accusative by way of praise and specification (al-madh wa'l-ikhtisas).
Fourth: it is in the accusative as an object of "yakhsha" (fears), meaning "He Who sent it down" ... "a reminder for whoever fears" (20:3), the revelation of Allah. This is a good meaning and a clear grammatical analysis. It has also been read as "tanzilun" in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject.

Second issue: The benefit of shifting from the first person plural (We) to the third person (He) comprises several things:
One: these attributes cannot be mentioned except with the third person.
Two: He first said "anzalna" (We sent down), elevating the matter by attributing it to the one obeyed; then He followed it by referring to the One specified with the attributes of greatness and glorification, so the magnificence was doubled from two directions.
Three: "anzalna" may be a quotation of the words of Jibril (peace be upon him) and the angels who descended with him.

Third issue: He, Exalted is He, magnified the state of the Qur'an by attributing it to being a revelation from the One who created the earth and created the heavens on high. He said this because the magnification of Allah, Exalted is He, appears through the magnification of His creation and His blessings. He magnified the Qur'an to encourage reflection on it, contemplation of its meanings and realities. This is customary among people: the message is magnified by magnifying the state of the one who sends it, so that the recipient is more inclined to comply.

Fourth issue: It is said "samaʾ ʿulya" (a high heaven) and "samawat ʿula" (high heavens). The benefit of describing the heavens as "high" is to indicate the greatness of the power of the One who creates the like of them in their height and the remoteness of their ascent.
* * *

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Most Merciful, who established Himself upon the Throne﴾, there are several issues.

First issue: "al-Rahman" has been read in the genitive as an attribute of "man khalaqa" (the One who created), but the nominative is better, because it is either in the nominative by way of praise, the meaning being "He is the Most Merciful," or it is a subject whose reference is indicated by the "l" to "man khalaqa." If it is asked: what is the position of the clause "established Himself upon the Throne" when you read "al-Rahman" in the genitive or in the nominative by way of praise? We say: if you read it in the genitive, it is the predicate of an omitted subject and nothing else; if you read it in the nominative, it may be so, and it may also be that together with "al-Rahman" there are two predicates of the subject.

Second issue: The Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists) have clung to this verse to claim that their worshipped one sits upon the Throne. This is false by reason and by transmitted texts, for several reasons:
One: He, glory be to Him, existed when there was no Throne and no place. When He created creation, He did not need a place, but was independent of it. So He remains in the attribute He has always had, unless someone claims that a throne has always existed alongside Allah.
Two: The one who sits must have a part of him in the right side of the Throne different from the part in its left side, so he would be composed and compounded in himself, and whatever is so requires a composer and compounder, which is impossible.
Three: The one who sits upon the Throne either is able to move and shift, or is not able to do so. If the first, he becomes a locus of motion and rest, and so is necessarily originated. If the second, he is like one who is bound, or rather like a paralytic, or worse off than him, for the paralytic, if he wills motion in his head and eyeball, is able to do so, whereas this is not possible for their worshipped one.
Four: Their worshipped one either exists in every place or in one place rather than another. If he exists in every place, it follows that he exists in places of filth and refuse, which no sensible person would say. If he exists in one place rather than another, he requires something that specifies him to that place, and so is needy, and need is impossible for Allah.
Five: His saying, ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ (42:11), comprehends the negation of likeness in all respects, as shown by the validity of the exception: it is correct to say "there is nothing like Him except in sitting, except in quantity, except in colour." The validity of the exception requires that all these matters be included under it. So if He were sitting, there would be something resembling Him in sitting, and then the meaning of the verse would be nullified.
Six: His saying, ﴿And above them on that Day eight will bear the Throne of your Lord﴾ (69:17). If they are bearers of the Throne, and the Throne is the place of their worshipped one, it follows that the angels bear their Creator and Worshipped One, which is unintelligible, for the Creator is the one who preserves the created, whereas the created does not preserve the Creator nor bear Him.
Seven: If it were permissible for whoever is fixed in a place to be a god, how would it be known that the sun and the moon are not gods? For our path to denying divinity to the sun and moon is that they are described by motion and rest, and whatever is so is originated and not a god. If you invalidate this path, the door of rejecting the divinity of the sun and moon is closed to you.
Eight: The world is a sphere, so the direction that is "above" in relation to us is "below" in relation to the inhabitants of the other side of the earth, and vice versa. If the worshipped one were specific to a direction, that direction, though it would be above for some people, would be below for others. By the agreement of sensible people, it is not permissible to say the worshipped one is beneath all things.
Nine: The Ummah has agreed that His saying, ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ (112:1), is among the clear (muhkam) verses, not the ambiguous (mutashabih). If He were specific to a place, the side of Him that faces what is on His right would be different from the side that faces what is on His left; He would then be composite and divisible, and not truly one, and so His saying ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ would be nullified.
Ten: The Khalil (Friend), peace be upon him, said: ﴿I do not love those that set﴾ (6:76). If the worshipped one were a body, He would always be setting and always absent, and so would fall under His saying ﴿I do not love those that set﴾. Thus by these proofs it is established that settling upon Allah, Exalted is He, is impossible. At this point, people have two positions:

The first: We do not occupy ourselves with interpretation, but we affirm with certainty that Allah, Exalted is He, is far above place and direction, and we leave the interpretation of the verse. Al-Shaykh al-Ghazali narrated from some companions of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal that he interpreted three reports: the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, "The Black Stone is the right hand of Allah on earth," his saying, peace be upon him, "The heart of the believer is between two fingers of the fingers of the Most Merciful," and his saying, peace be upon him, "I find the breath of the Most Merciful coming from the direction of Yemen." Know that this position is weak for two reasons:
First: if one affirms with certainty that Allah, Exalted is He, is far above place and direction, one has affirmed with certainty that Allah's intended meaning by "istiwa'" is not sitting, and this is precisely interpretation.
And if one does not affirm with certainty the declaration of Allah, Exalted is He, above place and direction, but remains in doubt about it, then one is ignorant of Allah, Exalted is He. Unless one says: "I am certain that what Allah intends is not what its apparent meaning suggests, but He intends something else, though I do not specify that intended meaning, out of fear of error." This would be closer to acceptable, but it is also weak, because when Allah addressed us in the tongue of the Arabs, it is necessary that He intends by the word only its established meaning in the language of the Arabs. And since "istiwa'" in the language has no meaning except "settling" and "mastery," and its being taken as "settling" is impossible, it is necessary to take it as "mastery"; otherwise the word would be left without meaning, and that is not permissible.

The second, which is a decisive proof that one must turn to interpretation: since rational proof has established the impossibility of settling, and the apparent wording of "istiwa'" indicates the meaning of settling, we have four options: either we act upon each of the two proofs, or we abandon both together, or we prefer transmitted text over reason, or we prefer reason and interpret the transmitted text. The first is invalid, for it would require that one and the same thing be both free of place and located in place, which is impossible. The second is also impossible, for it would require raising two contradictories together, which is false. The third is invalid, because reason is the root of transmission: until the existence of the Creator, His knowledge, His power, and His sending of messengers are established by rational proofs, transmission is not established. So discrediting reason entails discrediting both reason and transmission together. Therefore nothing remains but to affirm the soundness of reason and occupy ourselves with interpreting the transmitted text, and this is a decisive proof for the purpose. Having established this, we say: some scholars said that what is meant by "istiwa'" is "mastery," as the poet said:

"Bishr has come to mastery over Iraq, without sword or spilled blood."

If it is said that this interpretation is not permissible, for several reasons:
One: "mastery" means attaining dominance after weakness, and that is impossible with respect to Allah, Exalted is He.
Two: one says "so-and-so has mastered such-and-such" only when there is a rival who contests it, and the thing mastered already existed before; this is impossible with respect to Allah, for the Throne came into being through His creating and fashioning it.
Three: mastery is attained with respect to all created things, so singling out the Throne for mention has no benefit.

The answer: when we explain "mastery" as "power," all these objections fall away entirely. The author of al-Kashshaf said: since "settling upon the Throne," which is the seat of sovereignty, is attained only together with sovereignty, they used it as a metaphor for sovereignty, and they said: "So-and-so settled upon the land," meaning he ruled it, even if he never sat on the throne at all. They expressed the attainment of sovereignty by this because it is clearer and stronger in indication than saying "so-and-so ruled." Similar is your saying: "the hand of so-and-so is outstretched" and "the hand of so-and-so is chained," meaning he is generous or miserly. There is no difference between the two expressions except what I have mentioned, so that one whose hand was never outstretched in giving, or who had no hand at all, is said to have an outstretched hand, since to them there is no difference between it and saying "generous." From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Jews say: The hand of Allah is chained; their own hands are chained﴾ (5:64), meaning He is miserly, ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched﴾ (5:64), meaning He is generous, without imagining a hand, a chain, or an outstretching. Explaining it as "blessing," and straining to name it so, comes from narrowness of disposition. I say: if we open this door, the interpretations of the Batiniyya (esotericists) would flood in, for they too say that what is meant by His saying ﴿Take off your sandals﴾ (20:12) is total absorption in the service of Allah, Exalted is He, without imagining an act; and His saying: ﴿We said: O fire, be cool and safe for Abraham﴾

The purpose of it is to rescue Ibrahim (peace be upon him) from the hand of that oppressor, without there being any fire or any address at all. The same applies to everything else that occurs in the Book of Allah, the Exalted. Rather, the governing principle is that every word that occurs in the Qur'an must be taken in its literal sense, unless there is a definitive rational indication that compels turning away from it. Would that whoever does not know something would not delve into it. This is the complete discussion of this verse. Whoever wishes a thorough study of the ambiguous (mutashabih) verses and reports should consult the book *Ta'sis al-Taqdis* (The Foundation of Sanctification). And success is from Allah.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them and whatever is beneath the soil.﴾ Know that when He, glorified is He, explained His dominion by saying, ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾, and dominion is not organized except through power and knowledge, He necessarily followed it with power and then with knowledge. As for power, it is this verse. The meaning is that He, glorified is He, possesses these four categories. He possesses whatever is in the heavens, of angels, stars and others. He possesses whatever is on the earth, of minerals and metals. He possesses whatever is between them, of air. And He possesses whatever is beneath the *thara*. If it is said: the *thara* is the final surface of the world, so there would be nothing beneath it, how then could Allah possess it? We say: *al-thara* in the language means moist soil, so it is possible that there is something beneath it, and that is either the bull, or the fish, or the rock, or the sea, or the air, according to the differing reports.

As for knowledge, it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and that which is more hidden.﴾ And in this there are two opinions.

The first: that His saying ﴿and more hidden﴾ is in the form of an intensive (superlative). According to this view, we say that He, the Exalted, divided things into three categories: the open (*jahr*), the secret (*sirr*), and the more hidden (*akhfa*).

It is possible that what is meant by the open is the speech that is uttered aloud, though something of it may be concealed in the self even when part of it appears, and something may be concealed without appearing, as some have said. It is also possible that what is meant by the secret and the more hidden is what is not speech, and this is more apparent. So it is as if He, the Exalted, made clear that He knows the secret that is not heard, and what is more hidden than it. How then would He not know the open? The purpose of this is to deter the one bound by obligation from vices, whether they are apparent or hidden, and to encourage him toward acts of obedience, whether they are apparent or hidden. On this interpretation, the secret and the more hidden should be understood as that for which there is reward or punishment. The secret is what a person keeps within himself of matters he has resolved upon, and the more hidden is what has not reached the level of resolve. It is possible to interpret the more hidden as what he has resolved upon and what has occurred to his thought without his resolving upon it. It is possible also that it is what has not yet occurred to his inner self, so it is more hidden than the secret. It is also possible that it is what will come to be from Allah, the Exalted, of matters that have not yet appeared. Although the closest meaning is what we have mentioned first, namely what falls under deterrence and encouragement.

The second opinion: that *akhfa* is a verb (in the sense of "He conceals"), meaning that He knows the secrets of the servants, and conceals from them what He knows. It is like His saying: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they encompass nothing of His knowledge.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255] If it is asked: how does the consequent correspond to the condition? We say: its meaning is that if you speak aloud in mention of Allah, the Exalted, whether in supplication or otherwise, know that He is free of need for your speaking aloud. Or it may be a prohibition against speaking aloud, like His saying: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and with fear, and without loudness of speech.﴾ [al-A'raf: 205] Or it is a teaching to the servants that raising the voice is not for Allah, the Exalted, to hear, but is for another purpose.

Know that Allah, the Exalted, is knowing by His essence, and that He knows all the known things at all times with one knowledge, and that this knowledge does not change, and that this knowledge is among the necessary attributes of His essence, without being described as originated or contingent. The servant does not share with the Lord except in the first sixth, which is the root of knowledge. Then this sixth is divided between Him and His servants into two halves. So five *dawaniq* and a half of a unit of knowledge belong to Him, and one half belongs to the whole of His servants. Then this one unit is shared among all creation: among the cherubic angels (*karubiyyun*), the spiritual angels, the bearers of the Throne, the inhabitants of the heavens, the angels of mercy and the angels of punishment. Likewise all the prophets, the first of whom is Adam and the last of whom is Muhammad (ﷺ), upon them all. Likewise all creation in their necessary and acquired knowledge, and in crafts and professions. And all animals in their perceptions and sensations, and in their guidance toward their interests, in their foods, their harms and their benefits. What falls to you from that unit is less than an atom compounded. Yet by that atom you came to know the secrets of His divinity and His attributes, the necessary, the permissible and the impossible. If by this atom you have come to know these secrets, how could His knowledge be five *dawaniq* and a half? Would He not know by that knowledge the secrets of your servitude? This is the realization of His saying: ﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and that which is more hidden.﴾ Rather, the truth is that the whole dinar belongs to Him, because what you know, you know only through His teaching, as He said: ﴿He sent it down with His knowledge.﴾ [al-Nisa': 166] And He said: ﴿Should not He who created know?﴾ [al-Mulk: 14] For this there is an example, which is the sun, whose light makes the world bright, yet nothing whatsoever is diminished from its light. Likewise here. How then would He not be knowing of the secret and the more hidden? Therefore their roots are fixed in the earth, drawing nourishment through them, and that nourishment reaches the branches, and from them to the veins, and from them to the leaves. Then He, the Exalted, made their veins like the tent-ropes by which tents may be pitched.

Just as a rope must be extended from every side so that the tent stands, likewise the veins extend from every side so that the tree stands. Then if you look at every leaf and the fine veins spread within it, so that nourishment reaches every side of the leaf, to strengthen the body of the leaf so that it does not tear quickly, these are like the veins created in the body of an animal, to serve as channels for the blood and the spirit, strengthening the body. Then look at the trees: the most beautiful of them in appearance is the poplar and the willow, though they yield no benefit. And the ugliest of them is the fig and grape tree, yet look at their benefit. These things and their like show that not even the weight of an atom in the heavens or on the earth escapes His knowledge.

Six: His saying, ﴿And above them on that Day eight will bear the Throne of your Lord﴾ (69:17). If they are bearers of the Throne, and the Throne is the place of their worshipped one, it follows that the angels bear their Creator and Worshipped One, which is unintelligible, for the Creator is the one who preserves the created, whereas the created does not preserve the Creator nor bear Him.
Seven: If it were permissible for whoever is fixed in a place to be a god, how would it be known that the sun and the moon are not gods? For our path to denying divinity to the sun and moon is that they are described by motion and rest, and whatever is so is originated and not a god. If you invalidate this path, the door of rejecting the divinity of the sun and moon is closed to you.
Eight: The world is a sphere, so the direction that is "above" in relation to us is "below" in relation to the inhabitants of the other side of the earth, and vice versa. If the worshipped one were specific to a direction, that direction, though it would be above for some people, would be below for others. By the agreement of sensible people, it is not permissible to say the worshipped one is beneath all things.
Nine: The Ummah has agreed that His saying, ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ (112:1), is among the clear (muhkam) verses, not the ambiguous (mutashabih). If He were specific to a place, the side of Him that faces what is on His right would be different from the side that faces what is on His left; He would then be composite and divisible, and not truly one, and so His saying ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ would be nullified.
Ten: The Khalil (Friend), peace be upon him, said: ﴿I do not love those that set﴾ (6:76). If the worshipped one were a body, He would always be setting and always absent, and so would fall under His saying ﴿I do not love those that set﴾. Thus by these proofs it is established that settling upon Allah, Exalted is He, is impossible. At this point, people have two positions:

The first: We do not occupy ourselves with interpretation, but we affirm with certainty that Allah, Exalted is He, is far above place and direction, and we leave the interpretation of the verse. Al-Shaykh al-Ghazali narrated from some companions of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal that he interpreted three reports: the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, "The Black Stone is the right hand of Allah on earth," his saying, peace be upon him, "The heart of the believer is between two fingers of the fingers of the Most Merciful," and his saying, peace be upon him, "I find the breath of the Most Merciful coming from the direction of Yemen." Know that this position is weak for two reasons:
First: if one affirms with certainty that Allah, Exalted is He, is far above place and direction, one has affirmed with certainty that Allah's intended meaning by "istiwa'" is not sitting, and this is precisely interpretation.
And if one does not affirm with certainty the declaration of Allah, Exalted is He, above place and direction, but remains in doubt about it, then one is ignorant of Allah, Exalted is He. Unless one says: "I am certain that what Allah intends is not what its apparent meaning suggests, but He intends something else, though I do not specify that intended meaning, out of fear of error." This would be closer to acceptable, but it is also weak, because when Allah addressed us in the tongue of the Arabs, it is necessary that He intends by the word only its established meaning in the language of the Arabs. And since "istiwa'" in the language has no meaning except "settling" and "mastery," and its being taken as "settling" is impossible, it is necessary to take it as "mastery"; otherwise the word would be left without meaning, and that is not permissible.

The second, which is a decisive proof that one must turn to interpretation: since rational proof has established the impossibility of settling, and the apparent wording of "istiwa'" indicates the meaning of settling, we have four options: either we act upon each of the two proofs, or we abandon both together, or we prefer transmitted text over reason, or we prefer reason and interpret the transmitted text. The first is invalid, for it would require that one and the same thing be both free of place and located in place, which is impossible. The second is also impossible, for it would require raising two contradictories together, which is false. The third is invalid, because reason is the root of transmission: until the existence of the Creator, His knowledge, His power, and His sending of messengers are established by rational proofs, transmission is not established. So discrediting reason entails discrediting both reason and transmission together. Therefore nothing remains but to affirm the soundness of reason and occupy ourselves with interpreting the transmitted text, and this is a decisive proof for the purpose. Having established this, we say: some scholars said that what is meant by "istiwa'" is "mastery," as the poet said:

"Bishr has come to mastery over Iraq, without sword or spilled blood."

If it is said that this interpretation is not permissible, for several reasons:
One: "mastery" means attaining dominance after weakness, and that is impossible with respect to Allah, Exalted is He.
Two: one says "so-and-so has mastered such-and-such" only when there is a rival who contests it, and the thing mastered already existed before; this is impossible with respect to Allah, for the Throne came into being through His creating and fashioning it.
Three: mastery is attained with respect to all created things, so singling out the Throne for mention has no benefit.

The answer: when we explain "mastery" as "power," all these objections fall away entirely. The author of al-Kashshaf said: since "settling upon the Throne," which is the seat of sovereignty, is attained only together with sovereignty, they used it as a metaphor for sovereignty, and they said: "So-and-so settled upon the land," meaning he ruled it, even if he never sat on the throne at all. They expressed the attainment of sovereignty by this because it is clearer and stronger in indication than saying "so-and-so ruled." Similar is your saying: "the hand of so-and-so is outstretched" and "the hand of so-and-so is chained," meaning he is generous or miserly. There is no difference between the two expressions except what I have mentioned, so that one whose hand was never outstretched in giving, or who had no hand at all, is said to have an outstretched hand, since to them there is no difference between it and saying "generous." From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Jews say: The hand of Allah is chained; their own hands are chained﴾ (5:64), meaning He is miserly, ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched﴾ (5:64), meaning He is generous, without imagining a hand, a chain, or an outstretching. Explaining it as "blessing," and straining to name it so, comes from narrowness of disposition. I say: if we open this door, the interpretations of the Batiniyya (esotericists) would flood in, for they too say that what is meant by His saying ﴿Take off your sandals﴾ (20:12) is total absorption in the service of Allah, Exalted is He, without imagining an act; and His saying: ﴿We said: O fire, be cool and safe for Abraham﴾

The purpose of it is to rescue Ibrahim (peace be upon him) from the hand of that oppressor, without there being any fire or any address at all. The same applies to everything else that occurs in the Book of Allah, the Exalted. Rather, the governing principle is that every word that occurs in the Qur'an must be taken in its literal sense, unless there is a definitive rational indication that compels turning away from it. Would that whoever does not know something would not delve into it. This is the complete discussion of this verse. Whoever wishes a thorough study of the ambiguous (mutashabih) verses and reports should consult the book *Ta'sis al-Taqdis* (The Foundation of Sanctification). And success is from Allah.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them and whatever is beneath the soil.﴾ Know that when He, glorified is He, explained His dominion by saying, ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾, and dominion is not organized except through power and knowledge, He necessarily followed it with power and then with knowledge. As for power, it is this verse. The meaning is that He, glorified is He, possesses these four categories. He possesses whatever is in the heavens, of angels, stars and others. He possesses whatever is on the earth, of minerals and metals. He possesses whatever is between them, of air. And He possesses whatever is beneath the *thara*. If it is said: the *thara* is the final surface of the world, so there would be nothing beneath it, how then could Allah possess it? We say: *al-thara* in the language means moist soil, so it is possible that there is something beneath it, and that is either the bull, or the fish, or the rock, or the sea, or the air, according to the differing reports.

As for knowledge, it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and that which is more hidden.﴾ And in this there are two opinions.

The first: that His saying ﴿and more hidden﴾ is in the form of an intensive (superlative). According to this view, we say that He, the Exalted, divided things into three categories: the open (*jahr*), the secret (*sirr*), and the more hidden (*akhfa*).

It is possible that what is meant by the open is the speech that is uttered aloud, though something of it may be concealed in the self even when part of it appears, and something may be concealed without appearing, as some have said. It is also possible that what is meant by the secret and the more hidden is what is not speech, and this is more apparent. So it is as if He, the Exalted, made clear that He knows the secret that is not heard, and what is more hidden than it. How then would He not know the open? The purpose of this is to deter the one bound by obligation from vices, whether they are apparent or hidden, and to encourage him toward acts of obedience, whether they are apparent or hidden. On this interpretation, the secret and the more hidden should be understood as that for which there is reward or punishment. The secret is what a person keeps within himself of matters he has resolved upon, and the more hidden is what has not reached the level of resolve. It is possible to interpret the more hidden as what he has resolved upon and what has occurred to his thought without his resolving upon it. It is possible also that it is what has not yet occurred to his inner self, so it is more hidden than the secret. It is also possible that it is what will come to be from Allah, the Exalted, of matters that have not yet appeared. Although the closest meaning is what we have mentioned first, namely what falls under deterrence and encouragement.

The second opinion: that *akhfa* is a verb (in the sense of "He conceals"), meaning that He knows the secrets of the servants, and conceals from them what He knows. It is like His saying: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they encompass nothing of His knowledge.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255] If it is asked: how does the consequent correspond to the condition? We say: its meaning is that if you speak aloud in mention of Allah, the Exalted, whether in supplication or otherwise, know that He is free of need for your speaking aloud. Or it may be a prohibition against speaking aloud, like His saying: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and with fear, and without loudness of speech.﴾ [al-A'raf: 205] Or it is a teaching to the servants that raising the voice is not for Allah, the Exalted, to hear, but is for another purpose.

Know that Allah, the Exalted, is knowing by His essence, and that He knows all the known things at all times with one knowledge, and that this knowledge does not change, and that this knowledge is among the necessary attributes of His essence, without being described as originated or contingent. The servant does not share with the Lord except in the first sixth, which is the root of knowledge. Then this sixth is divided between Him and His servants into two halves. So five *dawaniq* and a half of a unit of knowledge belong to Him, and one half belongs to the whole of His servants. Then this one unit is shared among all creation: among the cherubic angels (*karubiyyun*), the spiritual angels, the bearers of the Throne, the inhabitants of the heavens, the angels of mercy and the angels of punishment. Likewise all the prophets, the first of whom is Adam and the last of whom is Muhammad (ﷺ), upon them all. Likewise all creation in their necessary and acquired knowledge, and in crafts and professions. And all animals in their perceptions and sensations, and in their guidance toward their interests, in their foods, their harms and their benefits. What falls to you from that unit is less than an atom compounded. Yet by that atom you came to know the secrets of His divinity and His attributes, the necessary, the permissible and the impossible. If by this atom you have come to know these secrets, how could His knowledge be five *dawaniq* and a half? Would He not know by that knowledge the secrets of your servitude? This is the realization of His saying: ﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and that which is more hidden.﴾ Rather, the truth is that the whole dinar belongs to Him, because what you know, you know only through His teaching, as He said: ﴿He sent it down with His knowledge.﴾ [al-Nisa': 166] And He said: ﴿Should not He who created know?﴾ [al-Mulk: 14] For this there is an example, which is the sun, whose light makes the world bright, yet nothing whatsoever is diminished from its light. Likewise here. How then would He not be knowing of the secret and the more hidden? Among His arrangements in the creation of trees and kinds of plants is that they have no mouths, nor any of the other organs of nourishment. Therefore their roots are fixed in the earth, drawing nourishment through them, and that nourishment reaches the branches, and from them to the veins, and from them to the leaves. Then He, the Exalted, made their veins like the tent-ropes by which tents may be pitched.

Just as a rope must be extended from every side so that the tent stands, likewise the veins extend from every side so that the tree stands. Then if you look at every leaf and the fine veins spread within it, so that nourishment reaches every side of the leaf, to strengthen the body of the leaf so that it does not tear quickly, these are like the veins created in the body of an animal, to serve as channels for the blood and the spirit, strengthening the body. Then look at the trees: the most beautiful of them in appearance is the poplar and the willow, though they yield no benefit. And the ugliest of them is the fig and grape tree, yet look at their benefit. These things and their like show that not even the weight of an atom in the heavens or on the earth escapes His knowledge.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verses 4–7 (part 1 of 2):

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A revelation from the One who created the earth and the high heavens﴾, there are several issues.

First issue: They mentioned several possibilities regarding the grammatical case (i'rab) of "tanzilan" (revelation):
One: its underlying sense is "It was sent down as a revelation from the One who created the earth," so "tanzilan" is in the accusative by an implied verb.
Second: it is in the accusative governed by "anzalna" (We sent down), because the meaning of "We have not sent down the Qur'an to you except as a reminder" (20:2–3) is "We sent it down as a reminder."
Third: it is in the accusative by way of praise and specification (al-madh wa'l-ikhtisas).
Fourth: it is in the accusative as an object of "yakhsha" (fears), meaning "He Who sent it down" ... "a reminder for whoever fears" (20:3), the revelation of Allah. This is a good meaning and a clear grammatical analysis. It has also been read as "tanzilun" in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject.

Second issue: The benefit of shifting from the first person plural (We) to the third person (He) comprises several things:
One: these attributes cannot be mentioned except with the third person.
Two: He first said "anzalna" (We sent down), elevating the matter by attributing it to the one obeyed; then He followed it by referring to the One specified with the attributes of greatness and glorification, so the magnificence was doubled from two directions.
Three: "anzalna" may be a quotation of the words of Jibril (peace be upon him) and the angels who descended with him.

Third issue: He, Exalted is He, magnified the state of the Qur'an by attributing it to being a revelation from the One who created the earth and created the heavens on high. He said this because the magnification of Allah, Exalted is He, appears through the magnification of His creation and His blessings. He magnified the Qur'an to encourage reflection on it, contemplation of its meanings and realities. This is customary among people: the message is magnified by magnifying the state of the one who sends it, so that the recipient is more inclined to comply.

Fourth issue: It is said "samaʾ ʿulya" (a high heaven) and "samawat ʿula" (high heavens). The benefit of describing the heavens as "high" is to indicate the greatness of the power of the One who creates the like of them in their height and the remoteness of their ascent.
* * *

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Most Merciful, who established Himself upon the Throne﴾, there are several issues.

First issue: "al-Rahman" has been read in the genitive as an attribute of "man khalaqa" (the One who created), but the nominative is better, because it is either in the nominative by way of praise, the meaning being "He is the Most Merciful," or it is a subject whose reference is indicated by the "l" to "man khalaqa." If it is asked: what is the position of the clause "established Himself upon the Throne" when you read "al-Rahman" in the genitive or in the nominative by way of praise? We say: if you read it in the genitive, it is the predicate of an omitted subject and nothing else; if you read it in the nominative, it may be so, and it may also be that together with "al-Rahman" there are two predicates of the subject.

Second issue: The Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists) have clung to this verse to claim that their worshipped one sits upon the Throne. This is false by reason and by transmitted texts, for several reasons:
One: He, glory be to Him, existed when there was no Throne and no place. When He created creation, He did not need a place, but was independent of it. So He remains in the attribute He has always had, unless someone claims that a throne has always existed alongside Allah.
Two: The one who sits must have a part of him in the right side of the Throne different from the part in its left side, so he would be composed and compounded in himself, and whatever is so requires a composer and compounder, which is impossible.
Three: The one who sits upon the Throne either is able to move and shift, or is not able to do so. If the first, he becomes a locus of motion and rest, and so is necessarily originated. If the second, he is like one who is bound, or rather like a paralytic, or worse off than him, for the paralytic, if he wills motion in his head and eyeball, is able to do so, whereas this is not possible for their worshipped one.

If he exists in every place, it follows that he exists in places of filth and refuse, which no sensible person would say. If he exists in one place rather than another, he requires something that specifies him to that place, and so is needy, and need is impossible for Allah.
