The servant does not share with the Lord except in the first sixth, which is the root of knowledge. Then this sixth is divided between Him and His servants into two halves. So five *dawaniq* and a half of a unit of knowledge belong to Him, and one half belongs to the whole of His servants. Then this one unit is shared among all creation: among the cherubic angels (*karubiyyun*), the spiritual angels, the bearers of the Throne, the inhabitants of the heavens, the angels of mercy and the angels of punishment. Likewise all the prophets, the first of whom is Adam and the last of whom is Muhammad (ﷺ), upon them all. Likewise all creation in their necessary and acquired knowledge, and in crafts and professions. And all animals in their perceptions and sensations, and in their guidance toward their interests, in their foods, their harms and their benefits. What falls to you from that unit is less than an atom compounded. Yet by that atom you came to know the secrets of His divinity and His attributes, the necessary, the permissible and the impossible. If by this atom you have come to know these secrets, how could His knowledge be five *dawaniq* and a half? Would He not know by that knowledge the secrets of your servitude? This is the realization of His saying: ﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and that which is more hidden.﴾ Rather, the truth is that the whole dinar belongs to Him, because what you know, you know only through His teaching, as He said: ﴿He sent it down with His knowledge.﴾ [al-Nisa': 166] And He said: ﴿Should not He who created know?﴾ [al-Mulk: 14] For this there is an example, which is the sun, whose light makes the world bright, yet nothing whatsoever is diminished from its light. Likewise here. How then would He not be knowing of the secret and the more hidden? Among His arrangements in the creation of trees and kinds of plants is that they have no mouths, nor any of the other organs of nourishment. Therefore their roots are fixed in the earth, drawing nourishment through them, and that nourishment reaches the branches, and from them to the veins, and from them to the leaves. Then He, the Exalted, made their veins like the tent-ropes by which tents may be pitched.

Just as a rope must be extended from every side so that the tent stands, likewise the veins extend from every side so that the tree stands. Then if you look at every leaf and the fine veins spread within it, so that nourishment reaches every side of the leaf, to strengthen the body of the leaf so that it does not tear quickly, these are like the veins created in the body of an animal, to serve as channels for the blood and the spirit, strengthening the body. Then look at the trees: the most beautiful of them in appearance is the poplar and the willow, though they yield no benefit. And the ugliest of them is the fig and grape tree, yet look at their benefit. These things and their like show that not even the weight of an atom in the heavens or on the earth escapes His knowledge.

**Al-Razi's commentary (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on Surah 20, verse 8 (part 1 of 2)**

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah, there is no god but Him. To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾, the discussion of it falls into two parts.

The first part concerns *tawhid* (affirmation of God's oneness). Know that the proofs of *tawhid* will come, God willing, in the commentary (*tafsir*, explanation) of His saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods besides Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 22]. He mentions it here only to clarify that the One described with power and knowledge in the manner already explained is one, without partner, and that He alone deserves worship to the exclusion of others. Let us mention here some subtle points related to this topic, which are the following discussions.

**The first discussion:** Know that the levels of *tawhid* are four:
1. The first is affirmation by the tongue.
2. The second is conviction in the heart.
3. The third is strengthening that conviction with evidence.
4. The fourth is that the servant becomes immersed in the sea of *tawhid* such that nothing enters his mind except the recognition of the One, the Eternal Refuge.

As for affirmation by the tongue: if it is found without conviction in the heart, that is the hypocrite (*munafiq*). As for conviction in the heart when it is found without affirmation by the tongue, there are cases:

**The first case:** One who reflects, recognizes God Exalted, and, just as he recognizes Him, dies before enough time passes for him to pronounce the words of testimony. Some say his *iman* (faith) is not complete. The truth is that it is complete, because he has fulfilled what he was obligated to do, and he was unable to pronounce it, so he is no longer addressed. I have seen in some books that the Angel of Death has written upon his forehead: *There is no god but Allah*, so that when the believer sees him, he recalls the words of testimony, and that recollection suffices him in place of the verbal remembrance.

**The second case:** One who recognizes God and then passes a period of time in which it was possible for him to pronounce the words, but he neglected to do so. Shaykh al-Ghazali said: It may be said that the tongue is the interpreter of the heart. When the intended matter is present in the heart, his refraining from pronouncing it is like his refraining from prayer and almsgiving. How could he be among the people of the Fire, when the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "One will come out of the Fire who has in his heart the weight of a mustard seed of faith"? And the heart of this man is filled with faith? Others said: *Iman* and *kufr* (disbelief) are legal matters; we know that one who refrains from this statement is a disbeliever.

**The third case:** One who affirms with the tongue and believes in the heart without evidence is a *muqallid* (one who follows by imitation, *taqlid*). The disagreement regarding the validity of his faith is well known.

As for the third level, which is establishing *tawhid* through proof and demonstration: we have already explained in the commentary on His saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods besides Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 22] that this matter can be established by rational and scriptural proofs, and we fully examined the discussion there.

As for the fourth level, which is annihilation in the sea of *tawhid* (*fana'*): the verifying scholars said: Gnosis (*irfan*) begins with separation, dissolution, abandonment, and rejection, which is possible regarding all attributes that belong to the Truth, for the souls that are sincerely seeking, attentive to the One, the Subduer. Then the standing of these words is encompassing of the highest ranks of those who journey toward God Exalted.

**The second discussion:** Concerning the reports transmitted about the *tahlil* (the saying *la ilaha illa Allah*):

First: From the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "The best remembrance is *la ilaha illa Allah*, and the best supplication is *astaghfir Allah* (I seek the forgiveness of Allah)." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿So know that there is no god but Allah, and ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women﴾ [Muhammad: 19].

Second: He, peace be upon him, said: "Allah Exalted created an angel among the angels before He created the heavens and the earth, and he is saying: 'I bear witness that there is no god but Allah,' extending his voice with it, not stopping, not taking a breath within it, and not completing it. When he completes it, He orders Israfil to blow the trumpet, and the Resurrection will occur, out of glorification of Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Third: From Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "I continued to intercede with my Lord and He would accept my intercession, and I would intercede with Him and He would accept my intercession, until I said: 'O Lord, intercede for me on behalf of whoever says *la ilaha illa Allah*.' He said: 'O Muhammad, this is not for you, nor for anyone. By My might and My majesty, I will not leave anyone in the Fire who has said *la ilaha illa Allah*.'"

Fourth: Sufyan al-Thawri said: I asked Ja'far ibn Muhammad about *Ha Mim 'Ayn Sin Qaf*. He said: The *ha* is His judgment (*hukmuhu*), the *mim* is His kingdom (*mulkuhu*), the *ayn* is His greatness (*azamatuhu*), the *sin* is His splendor (*sana'uhu*), and the *qaf* is His power (*qudratuhu*). Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, says: "By My judgment, My kingdom, My greatness, My splendor, and My power, I will not punish with the Fire whoever says *la ilaha illa Allah, Muhammad rasul Allah*."

Fifth: From Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever stands in the marketplace and says: *La ilaha illa Allah, wahdahu la sharika lahu, lahu al-mulku wa lahu al-hamd, yuhyi wa yumit, wa huwa hayyun la yamut, biyadihi al-khayr, wa huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir* (There is no god but Allah alone, with no partner; to Him belongs the dominion and to Him belongs all praise; He gives life and causes death, and He is living and does not die; in His hand is all good, and He is capable of all things), Allah will record for him one million times one million good deeds, will erase from him one million times one million bad deeds, and will build for him a house in Paradise."

**The third discussion:** On subtle points.

First: The people of *la ilaha illa Allah* should acquire four things so that they may be among the people of *la ilaha illa Allah*: sincere belief (*tasdiq*), reverence (*ta'zim*), sweetness (of its taste, *halawah*), and freedom (*hurriyyah*). Whoever lacks *tasdiq* is a hypocrite; whoever lacks *ta'zim* is an innovator (*mubtadi'*); whoever lacks *halawah* is a show-off (*murai*); and whoever lacks *hurriyyah* is a sinner (*fajir*).

Second: Some have said that His saying: ﴿Have you not considered how Allah presents an example: a good word like a good tree﴾ [Ibrahim: 24] refers to *la ilaha illa Allah*. ﴿To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deeds raise it﴾ [Fatir: 10] refers to *la ilaha illa Allah*. ﴿And advise one another to truth﴾ [Al-'Asr: 3] refers to *la ilaha illa Allah*. ﴿Say: I only advise you of one thing﴾ [Saba': 46] refers to *la ilaha illa Allah*. ﴿And stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ [Al-Saffat: 24] refers to being questioned about the statement *la ilaha illa Allah*. ﴿Rather, he has brought the truth and confirmed the messengers﴾ [Al-Saffat: 37] refers to *la ilaha illa Allah*. ﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe with the firm word in worldly life and in the Hereafter﴾ [Ibrahim: 27] refers to *la ilaha illa Allah*. ﴿And Allah causes the wrongdoers to go astray﴾ [Ibrahim: 27] refers to those who turn away from the statement *la ilaha illa Allah*.

Third: It is reported that Musa ibn 'Imran, peace be upon him, said: "O my Lord, teach me something by which I may remember You." He said: "Say: *la ilaha illa Allah*." He said: "All Your servants say *la ilaha illa Allah*!" He said: "Say: *la ilaha illa Allah*." He said: "I only wanted something special for me to be given!" He said: "O Musa, if the seven heavens and whoever is in them were placed on one pan of a scale, and *la ilaha illa Allah* on the other pan, it would outweigh them with *la ilaha illa Allah*."

**The fourth discussion:** On its grammatical analysis (*i'rab*). They said: The particle *la* (لا) here has entered upon the quiddity (*mahiyyah*), so the quiddity is negated, and when the quiddity is negated, every individual instance of the quiddity is negated. As for *Allah* (الله), it is a proper noun (*ism 'alam*) for a specific essence, since if it were a noun of meaning, it would be possible for it to apply to many, and then this phrase would not indicate *tawhid*.

They said: *la* (لا) deserved to govern like *inna* (إنّ) because of its resemblance to it in two respects: one is the constant attachment to nouns, and the other is their opposition to one another, for one of them confirms affirmation and the other confirms negation. It is among their habits to make one of two opposites resemble the other in ruling. Having established this, we say: when they said *inna Zaydan dhahib* (إنّ زيدًا ذاهبٌ, "indeed Zayd is going"), it should have been that they would say *la rajulan dhahib* (لا رجلًا ذاهبٌ). But they built *la* together with the singular noun that follows it upon the *fath* (فتح, vowel *a*). As for the building (*bina'*, fixed form), it is due to the strong attachment of the negative particle to what follows it, so that they became as one word. As for the *fath*, it is because they intended the building upon a movement (*harakah*) that is deserved, reconciling between the evidence requiring inflection (*i'rab*) and the evidence requiring fixed form (*bina'*).

Second: Its predicate (*khabar*) is omitted, and the original is: *la ilaha fi al-wujud wa la hawla wa la quwwata lana* (there is no god in existence, and there is no power or might for us). This indicates that existence is additional to the quiddity.

**The fifth discussion:** Some have said: The conception of affirmation (*thubut*) precedes the conception of negation (*salb*), for negation cannot be conceived unless it is attributed to affirmation. How, then, is negation mentioned before affirmation here? The answer: Since this negation is among the reinforcements of affirmation, it is therefore placed before it.

The second part of the discussion of the verse concerns the names of Allah Exalted, and in it are several discussions:

**The first discussion:** The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "On the Day of Resurrection a caller will call out: 'O people, I made for you a lineage, and you made for yourselves a lineage. I made the most noble among you in My sight the most God-conscious, and you made the most noble among you the richest. Now I raise My lineage and lower yours. Where are the God-conscious, on whom there is no fear and who do not grieve?'"

Know that things, in the division of the intellects, fall into three divisions: a perfect thing that does not admit imperfection; a deficient thing that does not admit perfection; and a third that admits both. As for the perfect that does not admit imperfection, it is Allah Exalted, and that is for Him by necessity of His essence. After Him are the angels, for among their perfections is that they: ﴿do not disobey Allah in what He commands them﴾ [Al-Tahrim: 6], and among their attributes is that they are: ﴿rather, honored servants﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 26], and among their attributes is that they ask forgiveness for those who believe. As for the deficient that does not admit perfection, it is inanimate matter, plants, and animals. As for the one that admits both together, it is the human being, who at times is in ascent, such that it is said of him that he is: ﴿in a seat of truth near a Sovereign, Omnipotent﴾ [Al-Qamar: 55], and at times in descent, such that it is said: ﴿Then We return him to the lowest of the low﴾ [Al-Tin: 5]. Since this is so, it is impossible for the human being to be perfect in his essence, and what is not perfect in its essence cannot become described with perfection until it becomes connected to the one perfect in essence.

But connection is of two kinds: a kind that is liable to cease, and a kind that cannot cease. As for what is liable to cease, there is no benefit in it, and its example is health, wealth, and beauty. As for what cannot cease, it is your servitude to Allah Exalted, for just as the attribute of divinity cannot cease from Him, the attribute of servitude cannot cease from you. This relation does not admit cessation, and the one to whom it is related, who is the Truth, glorified is He, does not admit departure from the attribute of perfection.

Then, if you are from a land or belong to a tribe, you continue to exaggerate in praising that land and tribe because of that accidental connection. So it is more fitting that you occupy yourself with the remembrance of Allah Exalted and the descriptions of His greatness because of the essential connection. Therefore He said: ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [Al-A'raf: 180], and He said: ﴿Allah, there is no god but Him. To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾.

**The second discussion:** On the division of the names of Allah Exalted. Know that the name of every thing is either applied to it according to its essence, or according to the parts of its essence, or according to the external matters outside its essence.

As for the first division: they differ over whether Allah Exalted has a name in this sense. This question is based on whether the reality of Allah Exalted is known to human beings or not. Whoever says that it is not known to human beings says: He has no name for His specific essence, because the purpose of a name is that it be pointed to the named, and if the specific essence is not known, rational pointing to it is impossible, so assigning a name to it is impossible. We have discussed the verification of this in the commentary on the name *Allah*.

As for a name applied to Him according to the parts of His essence, that is impossible, because He has no parts in His essence, for every composite is contingent, and the Necessary Existent cannot be contingent, so He cannot be composite.

As for a name applied according to the attributes external to His essence: attributes are either positive and real (*thubutiyyah haqiqiyyah*), or positive and relational (*thubutiyyah idafiyyah*), or negative (*salbiyyah*), or positive with relational, or positive with negative, or relational with negative, or positive, relational, and negative together. Since the possible relations are unlimited, and likewise the negations are unlimited, it is possible that the Creator Exalted has names that are distinct and not synonymous, unlimited in number. This is the indication of the basis (*ma'khadh*).

**Fifth discussion:** Some names are better paired with others. For example, you say "al-Awwal al-Akhir, al-Mubdi' al-Mu'id, al-Zahir al-Batin." An example is God's words, quoting the Messiah: ﴿If You punish them, they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:118]. The rest of the discussions have already been covered in the commentary on ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾.

**Sixth discussion: Points of subtlety.** The first: Bishr al-Hafi saw a piece of paper on which was written "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." He picked it up, perfumed it with musk, and placed it aside. He then saw someone in a dream saying: "O Bishr, you have perfumed Our name, so We will perfume your name in this world and the next."

The second: God's words, ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names﴾. The beauty of names is not intrinsic to them, since they are mere words and sounds. Rather, their beauty lies in the beauty of their meanings. Moreover, the beauty of God's names is not a beauty related to form and shape, for that is impossible for one who is not a body. Rather, it is a beauty that returns to the meaning of benevolence. For example, the names al-Sattar (the Concealer), al-Ghaffar (the Forgiving), and al-Rahim (the Merciful) are beautiful only because they indicate the meaning of benevolence. It is related that a wise man was approached by an ugly person and a handsome person, and they both asked for advice. He said to the handsome one: "You are handsome, and it does not befit the handsome to commit an ugly act." He said to the other: "You are ugly, and when the ugly commits an ugly act, its ugliness becomes greater." So we say: "Our God, Your names are beautiful and Your attributes are beautiful. From those beautiful names and beautiful attributes, there appears to us nothing but benevolence. Our God, the ugliness of our deeds and conduct is sufficient for us; so do not add to it the ugliness of punishment and the dread of torment."

The third: his (peace be upon him) saying: "Seek needs from those with beautiful faces." Our God, the beauty of the face is accidental, but the beauty of the attributes and names is essential. So do not turn us away from Your benevolence disappointed and losers.

The fourth: It is mentioned that a fisherman was catching fish. He caught a fish, and he had a daughter who took it from him and threw it into the water, saying: "It only fell into the net because of its heedlessness." Our God, that girl had mercy on the heedlessness of that fish, and she would throw it back into the sea. We, however, have been caught by the whispering of Iblis, and he has removed us from the sea of Your mercy. So have mercy on us by Your grace, free us from him, and cast us once more into the seas of Your mercy.

The fifth: You mentioned five names in al-Fatihah: Allah, al-Rabb (the Lord), al-Rahman (the Most Gracious), al-Rahim (the Most Merciful), and al-Malik (the King). You mentioned the divinity (al-Ilahiyyah), which indicates subjugation and greatness. It is known that souls cannot bear that domination and exaltedness. So after it He mentioned four names that indicate gentleness: al-Rabb, which indicates nurturing, and it is customary that whoever nurtures someone does not neglect his affairs. Then He mentioned al-Rahman al-Rahim, and that is the utmost in gentleness and kindness. Then He concluded the matter with al-Malik, and the great king does not take revenge on the weak and powerless. Also, Aisha said to Ali (peace be upon him): "You have become ruler, so be forgiving. You are more deserving of pardoning these weak ones."

The sixth: From Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: Musa (peace be upon him) said: "My God, which of Your creatures is most honored by You?" He said: "The one whose tongue is never moist with My remembrance." He said: "Which of Your creatures is most knowing?" He said: "The one who seeks the knowledge of others in addition to his own knowledge." He said: "Which of Your creatures is most just?" He said: "The one who judges against himself as he judges against people." He said: "Which of Your creatures is greatest in sin?" He said: "The one who accuses Me, and he is the one who asks Me, then is not content with what I have decreed for him." Our God, we do not accuse You, for we know that everything You bestow is grace, and everything You do is justice. So do not hold us accountable for the evil of our deeds.

The seventh: Al-Hasan said: When the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller will call out: "The assembly will know who is most deserving of honor. Where are those whose sides used to forsake their beds?" So they will stand and step over the necks of people. Then it will be said: "Where are those whom trade and commerce did not distract from the remembrance of Allah?" Then a caller will call out: "Where are those who praised Allah in every state?" Then the accounting and reckoning will fall upon those who remain. Our God, we have praised You and extolled You to the extent of our power and the limit of our capacity, so pardon us by Your grace and mercy. Whoever wishes to investigate the names and attributes thoroughly should refer to the book *Lawami' al-Bayyinat* on the names and attributes. And success is from Allah.

[p. 13]

God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ ﴿When he saw a fire and said to his family, "Stay here, for I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I will bring you a burning brand from it, or find guidance at the fire."﴾ ﴿But when he came to it, he was called, "O Moses! Indeed, I am your Lord, so take off your sandals. Indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa."﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, magnified the condition of the Qur'an and the condition of the Messenger in what He charged him with, He followed that with what strengthens the heart of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), by mentioning the circumstances of the prophets, peace be upon them, to strengthen his heart in conveying the message, as in His saying: ﴿And We relate to you the news of the messengers, by which We strengthen your heart﴾ [Hud: 120]. He began with Moses, peace be upon him, because the trial and affliction that befell him were greater, so as to console the heart of the Messenger (ﷺ) with it and to make him patient in bearing hardships. Thus He said: ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ Here there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿Has ... reached you?﴾ may mean that this is the first thing He informed him of concerning the matter of Moses, peace be upon him. The meaning would be: "It had not reached you until now, and now it has reached you, so pay attention to it." This is the view of al-Kalbi. It may also mean that it had already reached him in an earlier time, so that it is as if He said: "Has it not reached you?" This is the view of Muqatil and al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas.

The second issue: His saying ﴿Has ... reached you?﴾ is in the form of a question, which is not permissible for God, exalted is He. But the purpose of it is to establish the answer in his heart, and this form is more eloquent for that, just as a person says to his companion, "Has the news of such-and-such reached you?" and the listener becomes eager to know what is being alluded to. Had the purpose been an actual question, the answer would have come from the Prophet, peace be upon him, not from God, exalted is He.

[p. 14]

The third issue: His saying ﴿when he saw a fire﴾ means: "Has the story of him reached you at the time when he saw a fire?" The exegetes said: Moses, peace be upon him, asked Shu'ayb for permission to return to his mother, and he granted it. So he set out, and a son was born to him on the road, on a cold, snowy night, and it was a Friday night. He had strayed from the road, so Moses, peace be upon him, struck the fire-steel, but the flint produced nothing. While he was occupied with that, he saw a fire at a distance, to the left of the road. As-Suddi said: He thought it was one of the fires of shepherds. Others said: He, peace be upon him, saw it in a tree, though there is nothing in the wording of the Qur'an indicating that. They differed: some said that what he saw was not a fire but that he imagined it to be a fire. The correct view is that he truly saw a fire, so that he would be truthful in his report, since lying is not permissible for prophets. It has been said: Fire is of four kinds: fire that consumes but does not drink, which is the fire of this world; fire that drinks but does not consume, which is the fire of trees, according to His saying: ﴿He has made for you fire from the green tree﴾ [Ya-Sin: 80]; fire that both consumes and drinks, which is the fire of the stomach; and fire that neither consumes nor drinks, which is the fire of Moses, peace be upon him. It has also been said that fire is of four kinds:
First: fire that has light without burning, which is the fire of Moses, peace be upon him.
Second: burning without light, which is the fire of Hell.
Third: burning and light, which is the fire of this world.
Fourth: neither burning nor light, which is the fire of trees.

When he perceived the fire, he turned towards it. ﴿So he said to his family, "Stay here"﴾. It is possible that the address was to the woman, her child, and the servant who was with her. It is also possible that it was to the woman alone, but it came in the apparent form of the word "family," since "family" applies to a plural. Also, one may address a single person with the plural form out of respect, meaning: "Remain in your place." ﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾, that is, I have seen it. "Iyans" (perceiving) means clear seeing about which there is no doubt, and from it comes "insan al-ayn" (the pupil of the eye), since by it a thing becomes clear. "Ins" (humankind) is so called for their being visible, as "jinn" are so called for their being hidden. It has also been said that "ins" is that with which one is comforted. Since the perceiving was present in him, while in reality it was absent for them, he used the particle "inni" (indeed) to reassure their hearts. Since the perceiving through the burning brand and the finding of guidance were both awaited and expected, the matter regarding them was founded on hope and desire, so he said: ﴿Perhaps I will come to you﴾, and he did not state it definitively by saying "I will come to you," lest he promise what he was not certain he could fulfil. The point here is that some people said: "Ibrahim lied for the sake of expediency," and that is impossible, because Moses, peace be upon him, before his prophethood, guarded himself against lying, so he did not say "I will come to you," but said "perhaps I will come to you," without stating it definitively, lest he promise what he was not certain he could fulfil. A "qabas" is fire kindled at the tip of a stick, a wick, or something else. ﴿Or find guidance at the fire﴾. "Huda" (guidance) is that by which one is guided. It is a verbal noun, so it is as if he said: "I will find at the fire what I may be guided by, such as a sign or an indication." The sense of "at the fire" (ʿalā) is that the people of the fire ascend to the place nearby it, and because those who warm themselves by it, if they surround it, are standing over it.

﴿But when he came to it﴾, that is, when he came to the fire. Ibn Abbas said: He saw a green tree from its base to its top, as if it were a white fire, so he stood in wonder at the intensity of that fire's light and the intensity of that tree's greenness. The fire did not change its greenness, and the abundance of the tree's water did not change the light of the fire. He heard the glorification of the angels and saw a great light. Wahb said: Moses, peace be upon him, thought it was a fire that had been kindled, so he took some fine kindling to take a flame from it, but it inclined towards him as if it wanted him, so he drew back from it and was frightened. Then it kept enticing him and he kept being drawn to it, but it was no sooner quenched than it was as if it had never been. Then Moses cast his gaze to its branches, and behold, its greenness was rising into the sky, and behold, there was a light between heaven and earth with a radiance at which eyes are dazzled. When Moses saw that, he put his hand over his eyes, and he was called: "O Moses!"

The Qadi said, regarding what is reported that the fire-steel did not strike sparks: this is possible. As for what is reported that the fire kept receding from him: if prophethood had already been given to him, that is permissible; otherwise it is impossible, unless it was a miracle for another of the prophets, peace be upon them. In His saying ﴿And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 13] there is an indication that in this state

[p. 15]

The sixth issue: They differed about how Moses, peace be upon him, knew that the one calling him was God, exalted is He. and the view of Muqatil, al-Kalbi, al-Dahhak, Qatada, and as-Suddi.

But the purpose of it is to establish the answer in his heart, and this form is more eloquent for that, just as a person says to his companion, "Has the news of such-and-such reached you?" and the listener becomes eager to know what is being alluded to. Had the purpose been an actual question, the answer would have come from the Prophet, peace be upon him, not from God, exalted is He.

The third issue: His saying ﴿when he saw a fire﴾ means: "Has the story of him reached you at the time when he saw a fire?" He had strayed from the road, so Moses, peace be upon him, struck the fire-steel, but the flint produced nothing. While he was occupied with that, he saw a fire at a distance, to the left of the road. As-Suddi said: He thought it was one of the fires of shepherds. Others said: He, peace be upon him, saw it in a tree, though there is nothing in the wording of the Qur'an indicating that. They differed: some said that what he saw was not a fire but that he imagined it to be a fire. The correct view is that he truly saw a fire, so that he would be truthful in his report, since lying is not permissible for prophets. It has been said: Fire is of four kinds: fire that consumes but does not drink, which is the fire of this world; fire that drinks but does not consume, which is the fire of trees, according to His saying: ﴿He has made for you fire from the green tree﴾ [Ya-Sin: 80]; fire that both consumes and drinks, which is the fire of the stomach; and fire that neither consumes nor drinks, which is the fire of Moses, peace be upon him. It has also been said that fire is of four kinds:
First: fire that has light without burning, which is the fire of Moses, peace be upon him.
Second: burning without light, which is the fire of Hell.
Third: burning and light, which is the fire of this world.
Fourth: neither burning nor light, which is the fire of trees.

When he perceived the fire, he turned towards it. ﴿So he said to his family, "Stay here"﴾. It is possible that the address was to the woman, her child, and the servant who was with her. It is also possible that it was to the woman alone, but it came in the apparent form of the word "family," since "family" applies to a plural. Also, one may address a single person with the plural form out of respect, meaning: "Remain in your place." ﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾, that is, I have seen it. "Iyans" (perceiving) means clear seeing about which there is no doubt, and from it comes "insan al-ayn" (the pupil of the eye), since by it a thing becomes clear. "Ins" (humankind) is so called for their being visible, as "jinn" are so called for their being hidden. It has also been said that "ins" is that with which one is comforted. Since the perceiving was present in him, while in reality it was absent for them, he used the particle "inni" (indeed) to reassure their hearts. Since the perceiving through the burning brand and the finding of guidance were both awaited and expected, the matter regarding them was founded on hope and desire, so he said: ﴿Perhaps I will come to you﴾, and he did not state it definitively by saying "I will come to you," lest he promise what he was not certain he could fulfil. The point here is that some people said: "Ibrahim lied for the sake of expediency," and that is impossible, because Moses, peace be upon him, before his prophethood, guarded himself against lying, so he did not say "I will come to you," but said "perhaps I will come to you," without stating it definitively, lest he promise what he was not certain he could fulfil. A "qabas" is fire kindled at the tip of a stick, a wick, or something else. ﴿Or find guidance at the fire﴾. "Huda" (guidance) is that by which one is guided. It is a verbal noun, so it is as if he said: "I will find at the fire what I may be guided by, such as a sign or an indication." The sense of "at the fire" (ʿalā) is that the people of the fire ascend to the place nearby it, and because those who warm themselves by it, if they surround it, are standing over it.

﴿But when he came to it﴾, that is, when he came to the fire. Ibn Abbas said: He saw a green tree from its base to its top, as if it were a white fire, so he stood in wonder at the intensity of that fire's light and the intensity of that tree's greenness. Then it kept enticing him and he kept being drawn to it, but it was no sooner quenched than it was as if it had never been. Then Moses cast his gaze to its branches, and behold, its greenness was rising into the sky, and behold, there was a light between heaven and earth with a radiance at which eyes are dazzled. When Moses saw that, he put his hand over his eyes, and he was called: "O Moses!"

It may also mean that it had already reached him in an earlier time, so that it is as if He said: "Has it not reached you?" This is the view of Muqatil and al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas.

The second issue: His saying ﴿Has ... reached you?﴾ is in the form of a question, which is not permissible for God, exalted is He. But the purpose of it is to establish the answer in his heart, and this form is more eloquent for that, just as a person says to his companion, "Has the news of such-and-such reached you?" and the listener becomes eager to know what is being alluded to. Had the purpose been an actual question, the answer would have come from the Prophet, peace be upon him, not from God, exalted is He.

[p. 14]

The third issue: His saying ﴿when he saw a fire﴾ means: "Has the story of him reached you at the time when he saw a fire?" The exegetes said: Moses, peace be upon him, asked Shu'ayb for permission to return to his mother, and he granted it. So he set out, and a son was born to him on the road, on a cold, snowy night, and it was a Friday night. He had strayed from the road, so Moses, peace be upon him, struck the fire-steel, but the flint produced nothing. While he was occupied with that, he saw a fire at a distance, to the left of the road. As-Suddi said: He thought it was one of the fires of shepherds. Others said: He, peace be upon him, saw it in a tree, though there is nothing in the wording of the Qur'an indicating that. They differed: some said that what he saw was not a fire but that he imagined it to be a fire. The correct view is that he truly saw a fire, so that he would be truthful in his report, since lying is not permissible for prophets. It has been said: Fire is of four kinds: fire that consumes but does not drink, which is the fire of this world; fire that drinks but does not consume, which is the fire of trees, according to His saying: ﴿He has made for you fire from the green tree﴾ [Ya-Sin: 80]; fire that both consumes and drinks, which is the fire of the stomach; and fire that neither consumes nor drinks, which is the fire of Moses, peace be upon him. It has also been said that fire is of four kinds:
First: fire that has light without burning, which is the fire of Moses, peace be upon him.
Second: burning without light, which is the fire of Hell.
Third: burning and light, which is the fire of this world.
Fourth: neither burning nor light, which is the fire of trees.

When he perceived the fire, he turned towards it. ﴿So he said to his family, "Stay here"﴾. It is possible that the address was to the woman, her child, and the servant who was with her. It is also possible that it was to the woman alone, but it came in the apparent form of the word "family," since "family" applies to a plural. Also, one may address a single person with the plural form out of respect, meaning: "Remain in your place." ﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾, that is, I have seen it. "Ins" (humankind) is so called for their being visible, as "jinn" are so called for their being hidden. It has also been said that "ins" is that with which one is comforted. Since the perceiving through the burning brand and the finding of guidance were both awaited and expected, the matter regarding them was founded on hope and desire, so he said: ﴿Perhaps I will come to you﴾, and he did not state it definitively by saying "I will come to you," lest he promise what he was not certain he could fulfil. It is a verbal noun, so it is as if he said: "I will find at the fire what I may be guided by, such as a sign or an indication." The sense of "at the fire" (ʿalā) is that the people of the fire ascend to the place nearby it, and because those who warm themselves by it, if they surround it, are standing over it.

﴿But when he came to it﴾, that is, when he came to the fire. Ibn Abbas said: He saw a green tree from its base to its top, as if it were a white fire, so he stood in wonder at the intensity of that fire's light and the intensity of that tree's greenness. The fire did not change its greenness, and the abundance of the tree's water did not change the light of the fire. He heard the glorification of the angels and saw a great light. Wahb said: Moses, peace be upon him, thought it was a fire that had been kindled, so he took some fine kindling to take a flame from it, but it inclined towards him as if it wanted him, so he drew back from it and was frightened. Then it kept enticing him and he kept being drawn to it, but it was no sooner quenched than it was as if it had never been. Then Moses cast his gaze to its branches, and behold, its greenness was rising into the sky, and behold, there was a light between heaven and earth with a radiance at which eyes are dazzled. When Moses saw that, he put his hand over his eyes, and he was called: "O Moses!"

The Qadi said, regarding what is reported that the fire-steel did not strike sparks: this is possible. As for what is reported that the fire kept receding from him: if prophethood had already been given to him, that is permissible; otherwise it is impossible, unless it was a miracle for another of the prophets, peace be upon them. In His saying ﴿And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 13] there is an indication that in this state

[p. 15]

God revealed to him and made him a prophet. On this view, what they mentioned about the fire receding from him is far-fetched. And His saying ﴿But when he came to it, he was called, "O Moses!"﴾ shows the corruption of that. Even if it were receding from him moment by moment, that would not be valid, and the particle of sequence "fa" (then) would lose its meaning.

We say: The Qadi built this objection on his doctrine that irhas (prophetic foreshadowing miracles before prophethood) is not permissible, and this is false in our view, so his statement is void. The fourth issue: Abu Amr and Ibn Kathir read "annī" with a fatha, meaning: he was called with the words "that I am your Lord." The others read it with a kasra, meaning: he was called, and it is said: "O Moses," or because calling is a kind of speech, and so it is treated as speech.

The fifth issue: Al-Ash'ari said: God made him hear the eternal speech, which is neither a letter nor a sound. The Mu'tazila denied the existence of that speech and said: He, glorified is He, created that call in a body among bodies, such as a tree or something else, because calling is God's speech, and God is capable of it and does it whenever He wills. They took the verse as evidence that what was heard was a created sound. They said: He, exalted is He, linked the calling to his coming to the fire, and what is linked to what is created is created, so the calling is created.

* * *

The sixth issue: They differed about how Moses, peace be upon him, knew that the one calling him was God, exalted is He. Our companions (the Ash'aris) said: It is permissible that God create in him a necessary knowledge of this, and it is permissible that He make him know it through a miracle. The Mu'tazila said: As for necessary knowledge, it is impossible, because if necessary knowledge of this call being the speech of God had occurred, then necessary knowledge of the existence of the Creator, the Knower, the Powerful, would have occurred, since it is impossible for an attribute to be known necessarily while the essence is known only by inference. And if the existence of the Creator, exalted is He, had been known to him by necessity, Moses would have been excluded from being a mukallaf (one charged with obligations), because the occurrence of necessary knowledge contradicts being charged. By consensus Moses was not excluded from being charged, so we know that God made him know this through a miracle. Then they differed about that miracle in several respects:

The first: Some said: We know with certainty that God made him know this through a miracle, and we have no need to know what that miracle was.

The second: It is reported that when Moses witnessed the radiant light rising from the tree to the sky, and heard the glorification of the angels, he put his hands over his eyes, and he was called: "O Moses!" He said: "Here I am! Indeed, I hear your voice and do not see you. Where are you?" He said: "I am with you, before you, behind you, encompassing you, and nearer to you than yourself." Iblis cast into his mind this doubt and said: "How do you know you are hearing the speech of God?" He said: "Because I hear it from above me, from below me, from behind me, from my right, from my left, just as I hear it from in front of me, so I know it is not the speech of created beings." The meaning of his mentioning these directions is that I hear it with all my parts and limbs, until every organ of mine has become an ear.

The third: Perhaps he heard the call from an inanimate thing, such as pebbles or others, and that would be the miracle.

The fourth: He saw the fire in the green tree in such a way that the greenness did not extinguish that fire, and that fire did not harm that greenness. No one is capable of this except God, glorified is He.

The seventh issue: They said: The repetition of the pronoun in "Indeed, I am your Lord" was for emphasizing the indication and removing doubt.

The eighth issue: They mentioned several views regarding His saying ﴿so take off your sandals﴾:

First: They were made of the skin of a dead donkey, so he was commanded to remove them to protect the sacred valley, and for this reason He said right after it: "Indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa." This is the view of Ali, peace be upon him,

[p. 16]

and the view of Muqatil, al-Kalbi, al-Dahhak, Qatada, and as-Suddi.

Second: He was only commanded to remove them so that the blessing of the valley would reach his feet. This is the view of al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Mujahid.

Third: That it be understood as honouring the place, by not stepping on it except barefoot, so that he would be showing reverence for it and humility at hearing the speech of his Lord. The evidence for this is that He, exalted is He, said right after it: "Indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa," and this indicates causation, so it is as if He said: "Take off your sandals, because you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa." As for the Ahl al-Ishara (the esoteric interpreters), they mentioned several views on it:

First: In dreams, the sandal is interpreted as wife and child, so His saying ﴿so take off your sandals﴾ is an indication that his thoughts should not turn to his wife and child, and that his heart should not remain preoccupied with their affairs.

Second: What is meant by removing the two sandals is abandoning attention to both this world and the Hereafter, as if He commanded him to become wholly absorbed in the knowledge of God, exalted is He, and not to let his thoughts turn to anything other than God, exalted is He. What is meant by the sacred valley is the holiness of God's majesty and the purity of His might, meaning: when you have arrived at the sea of knowledge, do not turn to created things.

Thirdly: when a person reasons toward the Creator (al-sani'), he cannot reach Him except through two premises, such as saying: "The perceptible world is originated (muhdath) or contingent (mumkin), and whatever is like this has a manager, an effecter, and a Creator." These two premises are like the two sandals, for through them the intellect reaches its goal and moves from contemplating creation to knowing the Creator. Then, once he has reached knowledge of the Creator, he must no longer attend to those two premises, for to the degree that one is occupied with something other than Him, one remains deprived of being wholly absorbed in Him. It is as if it were said to him: "Do not let your heart and thoughts be occupied with those two premises, for you have reached the sacred valley, which is the sea of the knowledge of Allah the Exalted and the depth of His divinity."

Ninth issue: The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that held the Qur'an to be created) cited His words ﴿So take off your two sandals﴾ as evidence that the speech of Allah the Exalted is not eternal (qadim). For if it were eternal, Allah would have been speaking before Moses existed, saying: "Take off your two sandals, O Moses." It is known that this is foolishness. For if a man in an empty house says, "O Zayd, do this," and "O 'Amr, do not do that," although Zayd and 'Amr are not present, this is considered madness and foolishness. How, then, could this befit Allah, glorified and exalted is He?

Our companions (the Ash'arites) answered this in two ways:

The first: His speech, exalted is He, is indeed eternal, but in eternity it was not a command or a prohibition.

The second: It was a command in the sense that something came into existence in eternity, and when it continued into what never ceases, the person became commanded by it without any change occurring in that thing. This is like how power (qudrah) entails the validity (sihhah) of the act. Then, that power existed in eternity without this validity, and when it continued into what never ceases, the validity came about. So too here. This statement contains obscurity and subtle investigation.

Tenth issue: The verse contains no indication that prayer or circumambulation (tawaf) in sandals is disliked (makruh). The correct view is that it is not disliked. For if we ascribe the command to remove the sandals to the reverence due to the valley and to the reverence due to the speech of Allah, then the command is restricted to that particular situation. And if we ascribe it to the fact that the sandals were made of the hide of a dead donkey, then it is permissible that wearing the hide of a dead donkey was forbidden. If it was tanned, then if that is the case, it has been abrogated (mansukh, i.e., superseded by a later ruling; naskh being abrogation) by his (ﷺ) saying: "Any hide that has been tanned has become pure." The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed in his sandals, then took them off during the prayer, so the people took off their sandals. When he finished the prayer he said: "What is wrong with you that you took off your sandals?" They said: "You took yours off, so we took ours off." He said: "Jibril informed me that there is filth in them." So the Prophet (ﷺ) did not dislike praying in sandals, and he disapproved of those who removed them, and informed them that he had only removed his because of the filth in them.

Eleventh issue: The word ṭuwā (طُوًى) is read with a ḍammah and with a kasrah, both as declinable (munsarif) and as non-declinable (ghayr munsarif). Whoever reads it with tanwin (nunation) treats it as the name of the valley. Whoever does not read it with tanwin treats it as non-declinable, because it is an altered form (ma'dul) derived from ṭāwin, like 'Umar, which is altered from 'Āmir. It is also permissible that it be a name for the location.

Twelfth issue: Regarding ṭuwā there are several opinions:

The first: It is a name for the valley. This is the view of 'Ikrimah and Ibn Zayd.

The second: Its meaning is "twice," like mathnā, i.e., the valley was made holy twice, or Moses (peace be upon him) was called twice. It is said: "I called him ṭuwā," meaning "mathnā" (twice).

The third: ṭuwā means ṭayy (folding, traversing), meaning that the valley was traversed. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said that he (Moses) passed through that valley at night and folded it up (ṭawāhu), so the meaning of "the sacred valley which you folded" is that you traversed it by crossing it until you ascended to its highest point. Whoever holds this view says that ṭuwā is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that came from its own verb, as if it were said: "You folded it, a folding (ṭuwā)," just as one says hadā yahdī hudā (he guided, guidance). And Allah knows best.

Second: What is meant by removing the two sandals is abandoning attention to both this world and the Hereafter, as if He commanded him to become wholly absorbed in the knowledge of God, exalted is He, and not to let his thoughts turn to anything other than God, exalted is He. Thirdly: when a person reasons toward the Creator (al-sani'), he cannot reach Him except through two premises, such as saying: "The perceptible world is originated (muhdath) or contingent (mumkin), and whatever is like this has a manager, an effecter, and a Creator." These two premises are like the two sandals, for through them the intellect reaches its goal and moves from contemplating creation to knowing the Creator. Then, once he has reached knowledge of the Creator, he must no longer attend to those two premises, for to the degree that one is occupied with something other than Him, one remains deprived of being wholly absorbed in Him. It is as if it were said to him: "Do not let your heart and thoughts be occupied with those two premises, for you have reached the sacred valley, which is the sea of the knowledge of Allah the Exalted and the depth of His divinity."

Ninth issue: The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that held the Qur'an to be created) cited His words ﴿So take off your two sandals﴾ as evidence that the speech of Allah the Exalted is not eternal (qadim). For if it were eternal, Allah would have been speaking before Moses existed, saying: "Take off your two sandals, O Moses." It is known that this is foolishness. For if a man in an empty house says, "O Zayd, do this," and "O 'Amr, do not do that," although Zayd and 'Amr are not present, this is considered madness and foolishness. How, then, could this befit Allah, glorified and exalted is He?

Our companions (the Ash'arites) answered this in two ways:

The first: His speech, exalted is He, is indeed eternal, but in eternity it was not a command or a prohibition.

The second: It was a command in the sense that something came into existence in eternity, and when it continued into what never ceases, the person became commanded by it without any change occurring in that thing. This is like how power (qudrah) entails the validity (sihhah) of the act. Then, that power existed in eternity without this validity, and when it continued into what never ceases, the validity came about. So too here. This statement contains obscurity and subtle investigation.

Tenth issue: The verse contains no indication that prayer or circumambulation (tawaf) in sandals is disliked (makruh). The correct view is that it is not disliked. For if we ascribe the command to remove the sandals to the reverence due to the valley and to the reverence due to the speech of Allah, then the command is restricted to that particular situation. And if we ascribe it to the fact that the sandals were made of the hide of a dead donkey, then it is permissible that wearing the hide of a dead donkey was forbidden. If it was tanned, then if that is the case, it has been abrogated (mansukh, i.e., superseded by a later ruling; naskh being abrogation) by his (ﷺ) saying: "Any hide that has been tanned has become pure." The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed in his sandals, then took them off during the prayer, so the people took off their sandals. When he finished the prayer he said: "What is wrong with you that you took off your sandals?" They said: "You took yours off, so we took ours off." He said: "Jibril informed me that there is filth in them." So the Prophet (ﷺ) did not dislike praying in sandals, and he disapproved of those who removed them, and informed them that he had only removed his because of the filth in them.

Eleventh issue: The word ṭuwā (طُوًى) is read with a ḍammah and with a kasrah, both as declinable (munsarif) and as non-declinable (ghayr munsarif). Whoever reads it with tanwin (nunation) treats it as the name of the valley. Whoever does not read it with tanwin treats it as non-declinable, because it is an altered form (ma'dul) derived from ṭāwin, like 'Umar, which is altered from 'Āmir. It is also permissible that it be a name for the location.

Twelfth issue: Regarding ṭuwā there are several opinions:

The first: It is a name for the valley. This is the view of 'Ikrimah and Ibn Zayd.

The second: Its meaning is "twice," like mathnā, i.e., the valley was made holy twice, or Moses (peace be upon him) was called twice. It is said: "I called him ṭuwā," meaning "mathnā" (twice).

The third: ṭuwā means ṭayy (folding, traversing), meaning that the valley was traversed. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said that he (Moses) passed through that valley at night and folded it up (ṭawāhu), so the meaning of "the sacred valley which you folded" is that you traversed it by crossing it until you ascended to its highest point. Whoever holds this view says that ṭuwā is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that came from its own verb, as if it were said: "You folded it, a folding (ṭuwā)," just as one says hadā yahdī hudā (he guided, guidance). And Allah knows best.

[p. 17]

[p. 13]

God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ ﴿When he saw a fire and said to his family, "Stay here, for I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I will bring you a burning brand from it, or find guidance at the fire."﴾ ﴿But when he came to it, he was called, "O Moses! Indeed, I am your Lord, so take off your sandals. Indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa."﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, magnified the condition of the Qur'an and the condition of the Messenger in what He charged him with, He followed that with what strengthens the heart of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), by mentioning the circumstances of the prophets, peace be upon them, to strengthen his heart in conveying the message, as in His saying: ﴿And We relate to you the news of the messengers, by which We strengthen your heart﴾ [Hud: 120]. He began with Moses, peace be upon him, because the trial and affliction that befell him were greater, so as to console the heart of the Messenger (ﷺ) with it and to make him patient in bearing hardships. Thus He said: ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ Here there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿Has ... reached you?﴾ may mean that this is the first thing He informed him of concerning the matter of Moses, peace be upon him. The meaning would be: "It had not reached you until now, and now it has reached you, so pay attention to it." This is the view of al-Kalbi. It may also mean that it had already reached him in an earlier time, so that it is as if He said: "Has it not reached you?" This is the view of Muqatil and al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas.

The second issue: His saying ﴿Has ... reached you?﴾ is in the form of a question, which is not permissible for God, exalted is He. But the purpose of it is to establish the answer in his heart, and this form is more eloquent for that, just as a person says to his companion, "Has the news of such-and-such reached you?" and the listener becomes eager to know what is being alluded to. Had the purpose been an actual question, the answer would have come from the Prophet, peace be upon him, not from God, exalted is He.

[p. 14]

The third issue: His saying ﴿when he saw a fire﴾ means: "Has the story of him reached you at the time when he saw a fire?" The exegetes said: Moses, peace be upon him, asked Shu'ayb for permission to return to his mother, and he granted it. So he set out, and a son was born to him on the road, on a cold, snowy night, and it was a Friday night. He had strayed from the road, so Moses, peace be upon him, struck the fire-steel, but the flint produced nothing. While he was occupied with that, he saw a fire at a distance, to the left of the road. As-Suddi said: He thought it was one of the fires of shepherds. Others said: He, peace be upon him, saw it in a tree, though there is nothing in the wording of the Qur'an indicating that. They differed: some said that what he saw was not a fire but that he imagined it to be a fire. The correct view is that he truly saw a fire, so that he would be truthful in his report, since lying is not permissible for prophets. It has been said: Fire is of four kinds: fire that consumes but does not drink, which is the fire of this world; fire that drinks but does not consume, which is the fire of trees, according to His saying: ﴿He has made for you fire from the green tree﴾ [Ya-Sin: 80]; fire that both consumes and drinks, which is the fire of the stomach; and fire that neither consumes nor drinks, which is the fire of Moses, peace be upon him. It has also been said that fire is of four kinds:
First: fire that has light without burning, which is the fire of Moses, peace be upon him.
Second: burning without light, which is the fire of Hell.
Third: burning and light, which is the fire of this world.
Fourth: neither burning nor light, which is the fire of trees.

When he perceived the fire, he turned towards it. ﴿So he said to his family, "Stay here"﴾. It is possible that the address was to the woman, her child, and the servant who was with her. It is also possible that it was to the woman alone, but it came in the apparent form of the word "family," since "family" applies to a plural. Also, one may address a single person with the plural form out of respect, meaning: "Remain in your place." ﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾, that is, I have seen it. "Iyans" (perceiving) means clear seeing about which there is no doubt, and from it comes "insan al-ayn" (the pupil of the eye), since by it a thing becomes clear. "Ins" (humankind) is so called for their being visible, as "jinn" are so called for their being hidden. It has also been said that "ins" is that with which one is comforted. Since the perceiving was present in him, while in reality it was absent for them, he used the particle "inni" (indeed) to reassure their hearts. Since the perceiving through the burning brand and the finding of guidance were both awaited and expected, the matter regarding them was founded on hope and desire, so he said: ﴿Perhaps I will come to you﴾, and he did not state it definitively by saying "I will come to you," lest he promise what he was not certain he could fulfil. The point here is that some people said: "Ibrahim lied for the sake of expediency," and that is impossible, because Moses, peace be upon him, before his prophethood, guarded himself against lying, so he did not say "I will come to you," but said "perhaps I will come to you," without stating it definitively, lest he promise what he was not certain he could fulfil. A "qabas" is fire kindled at the tip of a stick, a wick, or something else. ﴿Or find guidance at the fire﴾. "Huda" (guidance) is that by which one is guided. It is a verbal noun, so it is as if he said: "I will find at the fire what I may be guided by, such as a sign or an indication." The sense of "at the fire" (ʿalā) is that the people of the fire ascend to the place nearby it, and because those who warm themselves by it, if they surround it, are standing over it.

﴿But when he came to it﴾, that is, when he came to the fire. Ibn Abbas said: He saw a green tree from its base to its top, as if it were a white fire, so he stood in wonder at the intensity of that fire's light and the intensity of that tree's greenness. The fire did not change its greenness, and the abundance of the tree's water did not change the light of the fire. He heard the glorification of the angels and saw a great light. Wahb said: Moses, peace be upon him, thought it was a fire that had been kindled, so he took some fine kindling to take a flame from it, but it inclined towards him as if it wanted him, so he drew back from it and was frightened. Then it kept enticing him and he kept being drawn to it, but it was no sooner quenched than it was as if it had never been. Then Moses cast his gaze to its branches, and behold, its greenness was rising into the sky, and behold, there was a light between heaven and earth with a radiance at which eyes are dazzled. When Moses saw that, he put his hand over his eyes, and he was called: "O Moses!"

The Qadi said, regarding what is reported that the fire-steel did not strike sparks: this is possible. As for what is reported that the fire kept receding from him: if prophethood had already been given to him, that is permissible; otherwise it is impossible, unless it was a miracle for another of the prophets, peace be upon them. In His saying ﴿And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 13] there is an indication that in this state

[p. 15]

God revealed to him and made him a prophet. On this view, what they mentioned about the fire receding from him is far-fetched. And His saying ﴿But when he came to it, he was called, "O Moses!"﴾ shows the corruption of that. Even if it were receding from him moment by moment, that would not be valid, and the particle of sequence "fa" (then) would lose its meaning.

We say: The Qadi built this objection on his doctrine that irhas (prophetic foreshadowing miracles before prophethood) is not permissible, and this is false in our view, so his statement is void. As for relying on the particle of sequence, that is weak, because a short interval of time between the coming and the calling does not undermine the particle of sequence.

The fourth issue: Abu Amr and Ibn Kathir read "annī" with a fatha, meaning: he was called with the words "that I am your Lord." The others read it with a kasra, meaning: he was called, and it is said: "O Moses," or because calling is a kind of speech, and so it is treated as speech.

The fifth issue: Al-Ash'ari said: God made him hear the eternal speech, which is neither a letter nor a sound. The Mu'tazila denied the existence of that speech and said: He, glorified is He, created that call in a body among bodies, such as a tree or something else, because calling is God's speech, and God is capable of it and does it whenever He wills. As for the Ahl al-Sunna from Transoxiania, they affirmed the eternal speech, but they claimed that what Moses, peace be upon him, heard was a sound that God created in the tree. They took the verse as evidence that what was heard was a created sound. They said: He, exalted is He, linked the calling to his coming to the fire, and what is linked to what is created is created, so the calling is created.

* * *

The sixth issue: They differed about how Moses, peace be upon him, knew that the one calling him was God, exalted is He. Our companions (the Ash'aris) said: It is permissible that God create in him a necessary knowledge of this, and it is permissible that He make him know it through a miracle. The Mu'tazila said: As for necessary knowledge, it is impossible, because if necessary knowledge of this call being the speech of God had occurred, then necessary knowledge of the existence of the Creator, the Knower, the Powerful, would have occurred, since it is impossible for an attribute to be known necessarily while the essence is known only by inference. And if the existence of the Creator, exalted is He, had been known to him by necessity, Moses would have been excluded from being a mukallaf (one charged with obligations), because the occurrence of necessary knowledge contradicts being charged. By consensus Moses was not excluded from being charged, so we know that God made him know this through a miracle. Then they differed about that miracle in several respects:

The first: Some said: We know with certainty that God made him know this through a miracle, and we have no need to know what that miracle was.

The second: It is reported that when Moses witnessed the radiant light rising from the tree to the sky, and heard the glorification of the angels, he put his hands over his eyes, and he was called: "O Moses!" He said: "Here I am! Indeed, I hear your voice and do not see you. Where are you?" He said: "I am with you, before you, behind you, encompassing you, and nearer to you than yourself." Iblis cast into his mind this doubt and said: "How do you know you are hearing the speech of God?" He said: "Because I hear it from above me, from below me, from behind me, from my right, from my left, just as I hear it from in front of me, so I know it is not the speech of created beings." The meaning of his mentioning these directions is that I hear it with all my parts and limbs, until every organ of mine has become an ear.

The third: Perhaps he heard the call from an inanimate thing, such as pebbles or others, and that would be the miracle.

The fourth: He saw the fire in the green tree in such a way that the greenness did not extinguish that fire, and that fire did not harm that greenness. No one is capable of this except God, glorified is He.

The seventh issue: They said: The repetition of the pronoun in "Indeed, I am your Lord" was for emphasizing the indication and removing doubt.

The eighth issue: They mentioned several views regarding His saying ﴿so take off your sandals﴾:

First: They were made of the skin of a dead donkey, so he was commanded to remove them to protect the sacred valley, and for this reason He said right after it: "Indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa." This is the view of Ali, peace be upon him,

[p. 16]

and the view of Muqatil, al-Kalbi, al-Dahhak, Qatada, and as-Suddi.

Second: He was only commanded to remove them so that the blessing of the valley would reach his feet. This is the view of al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Mujahid.

Third: That it be understood as honouring the place, by not stepping on it except barefoot, so that he would be showing reverence for it and humility at hearing the speech of his Lord. The evidence for this is that He, exalted is He, said right after it: "Indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa," and this indicates causation, so it is as if He said: "Take off your sandals, because you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa." As for the Ahl al-Ishara (the esoteric interpreters), they mentioned several views on it:

First: In dreams, the sandal is interpreted as wife and child, so His saying ﴿so take off your sandals﴾ is an indication that his thoughts should not turn to his wife and child, and that his heart should not remain preoccupied with their affairs.

Second: What is meant by removing the two sandals is abandoning attention to both this world and the Hereafter, as if He commanded him to become wholly absorbed in the knowledge of God, exalted is He, and not to let his thoughts turn to anything other than God, exalted is He. What is meant by the sacred valley is the holiness of God's majesty and the purity of His might, meaning: when you have arrived at the sea of knowledge, do not turn to created things.

Thirdly: when a person reasons toward the Creator (al-sani'), he cannot reach Him except through two premises, such as saying: "The perceptible world is originated (muhdath) or contingent (mumkin), and whatever is like this has a manager, an effecter, and a Creator." These two premises are like the two sandals, for through them the intellect reaches its goal and moves from contemplating creation to knowing the Creator. Then, once he has reached knowledge of the Creator, he must no longer attend to those two premises, for to the degree that one is occupied with something other than Him, one remains deprived of being wholly absorbed in Him. It is as if it were said to him: "Do not let your heart and thoughts be occupied with those two premises, for you have reached the sacred valley, which is the sea of the knowledge of Allah the Exalted and the depth of His divinity."

Ninth issue: The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that held the Qur'an to be created) cited His words ﴿So take off your two sandals﴾ as evidence that the speech of Allah the Exalted is not eternal (qadim). For if it were eternal, Allah would have been speaking before Moses existed, saying: "Take off your two sandals, O Moses." It is known that this is foolishness. For if a man in an empty house says, "O Zayd, do this," and "O 'Amr, do not do that," although Zayd and 'Amr are not present, this is considered madness and foolishness. How, then, could this befit Allah, glorified and exalted is He?

Our companions (the Ash'arites) answered this in two ways:

The first: His speech, exalted is He, is indeed eternal, but in eternity it was not a command or a prohibition.

The second: It was a command in the sense that something came into existence in eternity, and when it continued into what never ceases, the person became commanded by it without any change occurring in that thing. This is like how power (qudrah) entails the validity (sihhah) of the act. Then, that power existed in eternity without this validity, and when it continued into what never ceases, the validity came about. So too here. This statement contains obscurity and subtle investigation.

Tenth issue: The verse contains no indication that prayer or circumambulation (tawaf) in sandals is disliked (makruh). The correct view is that it is not disliked. For if we ascribe the command to remove the sandals to the reverence due to the valley and to the reverence due to the speech of Allah, then the command is restricted to that particular situation. And if we ascribe it to the fact that the sandals were made of the hide of a dead donkey, then it is permissible that wearing the hide of a dead donkey was forbidden. If it was tanned, then if that is the case, it has been abrogated (mansukh, i.e., superseded by a later ruling; naskh being abrogation) by his (ﷺ) saying: "Any hide that has been tanned has become pure." The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed in his sandals, then took them off during the prayer, so the people took off their sandals. When he finished the prayer he said: "What is wrong with you that you took off your sandals?" They said: "You took yours off, so we took ours off." He said: "Jibril informed me that there is filth in them." So the Prophet (ﷺ) did not dislike praying in sandals, and he disapproved of those who removed them, and informed them that he had only removed his because of the filth in them.

Eleventh issue: The word ṭuwā (طُوًى) is read with a ḍammah and with a kasrah, both as declinable (munsarif) and as non-declinable (ghayr munsarif). Whoever reads it with tanwin (nunation) treats it as the name of the valley. Whoever does not read it with tanwin treats it as non-declinable, because it is an altered form (ma'dul) derived from ṭāwin, like 'Umar, which is altered from 'Āmir. It is also permissible that it be a name for the location.

Twelfth issue: Regarding ṭuwā there are several opinions:

The first: It is a name for the valley. This is the view of 'Ikrimah and Ibn Zayd.

The second: Its meaning is "twice," like mathnā, i.e., the valley was made holy twice, or Moses (peace be upon him) was called twice. It is said: "I called him ṭuwā," meaning "mathnā" (twice).

The third: ṭuwā means ṭayy (folding, traversing), meaning that the valley was traversed. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said that he (Moses) passed through that valley at night and folded it up (ṭawāhu), so the meaning of "the sacred valley which you folded" is that you traversed it by crossing it until you ascended to its highest point. Whoever holds this view says that ṭuwā is a verbal noun (maṣdar) that came from its own verb, as if it were said: "You folded it, a folding (ṭuwā)," just as one says hadā yahdī hudā (he guided, guidance). And Allah knows best.

[p. 17]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verse 14:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed﴾ ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾. Hamzah recited: "wa-anna ikhtarnaka" (And We have chosen you), and Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited: "wa-inni ikhtartuka" (And I have chosen you). Here there are several issues:

The first issue: its meaning is "I have chosen you for the message (risalah) and for the speech with which I have singled you out." This verse indicates that prophethood is not attained by merit, because His saying, ﴿And I have chosen you﴾, indicates that this lofty station was attained only because Allah Exalted chose him for it from the outset, not that he deserved it from Allah Exalted.

The second issue: His saying, ﴿so listen to what is revealed﴾, contains the utmost awe and majesty. It is as if He said: "A great and terrifying matter has come to you, so prepare yourself for it, and make all your intellect and attention directed toward it." So His saying, ﴿And I have chosen you﴾, conveys the utmost gentleness and mercy, and His saying, ﴿so listen﴾, conveys the utmost awe. Thus from the first he obtains the utmost hope, and from the second the utmost fear.

The third issue: His saying, ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾, indicates that the science of the foundations (usul) takes precedence over the science of the branches (furu'), because monotheism (tawhid) belongs to the science of the foundations and worship ('ibadah) belongs to the science of the branches. Also, the fa' in His saying, ﴿so worship Me﴾, indicates that His worship became binding because of His divinity, and this is the verification of the scholars that Allah is the one deserving of worship.

The fourth issue: After commanding him first with monotheism, and then with worship second, He commanded him with prayer third. Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued from this verse that delaying clarification (ta'khir al-bayan) beyond the time of need is permissible, in two respects:

The first: He commanded him with worship without mentioning the manner of that worship, so it is established that a general (mujmal) statement may occur without accompanying clarification.

The second: He said, ﴿and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾, and did not explain the manner of the prayer. The judge (al-Qadi) said: It is not impossible that Musa (peace be upon him) already knew the prayer with which Allah had worshipped Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) and other prophets, so the address was directed to that. It is also possible that He clarified it to him immediately, even if what is transmitted in the Qur'an mentions only this much.

The answer: As for the first excuse, it does not apply to His saying, ﴿so worship Me﴾. Also, to take such a great address as conveying a new benefit is better than taking it as conveying a known matter, because Musa (peace be upon him) did not doubt the obligation of the prayer that Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) brought. If we took His saying, ﴿and establish prayer﴾ as referring to that, no additional benefit would result from this great address; but if we take it as referring to another prayer, the additional benefit results. As for the claim that perhaps Allah clarified it in that place even though He did not relate it in the Qur'an, we say: there is no doubt that clarification is more beneficial than the general statement, so if it had been mentioned, it would have been more deserving of being related.
