The fifth issue: concerning His saying, ﴿for My remembrance﴾, there are several views:

One: "for My remembrance" means "so that you remember Me," for My remembrance is that I be worshipped and prayed to.

Two: "so that you remember Me in it," because prayer includes remembrances (adhkar), according to Mujahid.

Three: "because I have mentioned it in the books and commanded it."

Four: "so that I may mention you with praise and commendation, and make for you a tongue of truthfulness."

Five: "for My remembrance specifically, which is not mixed with the remembrance of others."

Six: "for the sincere (ikhlas) remembrance of Me and seeking My face; do not show off with it, and do not intend with it any other purpose."

Seven: "so that you may be one who remembers Me, not forgetting, like the act of the sincere who keep the remembrance of their Lord in mind, as Allah Exalted said: ﴿Trade or commerce does not distract them from the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Nur: 37]."

Eight: "for the times of My remembrance, which are the appointed times of prayer, according to His saying Exalted: ﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers at specified times﴾ [al-Nisa: 103]."

Nine: "And establish prayer when you remember it," meaning that if you forget a prayer, make it up when you remember it.

Qatadah narrated from Anas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers it; there is no expiation for it except that." Then he recited: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾. Al-Khattabi said: This hadith may bear two meanings:

One: that nothing expiates it except making it up. The other: that there is no compensation or expiation required for forgetting it, as expiation is required for abandoning the fast of Ramadan without excuse, and as the muhrim who abandons some of his rites must pay a ransom (fidyah) of feeding or a sacrifice. He only prays what he missed. If it is said: the correct wording should be "establish prayer for its remembrance," as he (peace be upon him) said: "let him pray it when he remembers it," we reply: His saying, ﴿for My remembrance﴾ means for the remembrance that occurs through My creation, or by supposing an omitted genitive, i.e., for the remembrance of My prayer.

The sixth issue: If a person misses prayers, it is recommended that he make them up in the order of their performance. If he abandons the order in making them up, it is permissible according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him. If the time of an obligatory prayer enters while he remembers a missed prayer, he should consider: if there is ample time, it is recommended that he begin with the missed prayer; if he begins with the prayer of the present time, that is permissible. If the time is so constrained that if he begins with the missed prayer the time of the present prayer would pass, he must begin with the prayer of the present time so that it is not lost. If he remembers the missed prayer after he has begun the prayer of the present time, he completes it, then makes up the missed prayer, and it is recommended, though not obligatory, that he repeat the prayer of the present time after it.

Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The order in making up missed prayers is obligatory as long as they do not exceed the prayers of one day and night. He even said: if during the prayer of the present time he remembers a missed prayer that he abandoned that day, the obligatory prayer of the present time is invalidated, so he makes up the missed prayer and then repeats the prayer of the present time, unless the time is constrained, in which case it is not invalidated.

The proof of Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, consists of the verse, the report, the narration, and analogy. As for the verse, it is His saying, Exalted: ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾, i.e., for its remembering, and the lam here means "at," like His saying: ﴿Establish prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ [al-Isra: 78], i.e., at its decline. So the meaning of the verse is: establish the prayer remembered at the time of its remembrance, and this requires observing the order. As for the report, it is His saying (peace be upon him): "Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers it," and the fa' indicates sequence. Also, Jabir ibn Abd Allah narrated: "On the day of the Trench, Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and began cursing the disbelievers of Quraysh, saying: O Messenger of Allah, I did not pray the afternoon prayer until the sun was nearly setting. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: And by Allah, I have not prayed it either. He said: So he went down to al-Batha, prayed the afternoon prayer after the sun had set, and then prayed the maghrib after it." This hadith is recorded in the Two Sahihs. The Hanafis argued from it in two respects:

One: he (peace be upon him) said: "Pray as you have seen me pray." So when he prayed the missed prayers in succession, it became binding upon us.

The second: the action of the Prophet (ﷺ), when it comes as an explanation of a general statement, is a proof. This action came as an explanation of the general statement of Allah Exalted: ﴿Establish prayer﴾. For this reason we say that when missed prayers are within a small number, the order must be observed, and when they exceed the limit of abundance, the order falls away. As for the narration, it is what is related from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "Whoever misses a prayer and does not remember it except during the imam's prayer, let him continue his prayer; when he finishes his prayer with the imam, he prays what he missed, then repeats the one he prayed with the imam." This is also sometimes related as a marfu' report to the Prophet (ﷺ). As for analogy, it is that these are two obligatory prayers that share one time within the day and night, so they resemble the prayers of Arafah and Muzdalifah. Since the order is not dropped in those, the ruling for missed prayers within less than a day and night should likewise be so.

The proof of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, is that it is reported in the hadith of Abu Qatadah that when they slept through the dawn prayer and woke after sunrise, the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded them to lead their mounts away, and then he prayed it. Had the time of remembrance been specific for the prayer, this would not have been permissible. So we know that this time is a time for the obligation to become settled upon him, but not in the manner of strict restriction, rather in the manner of expansion. Given this, we say: the imposition of making up missed prayers and the imposition of performing the obligation of the present time operate like a choice between two obligations, so the one responsible must be free to begin with whichever he wishes. Also, if the order in missed prayers were a condition, it would not drop by forgetfulness. Do you not see that if someone prays the Dhuhr and Asr at Arafah on a cloudy day, and then it becomes clear that he prayed Dhuhr before midday and Asr after midday, he repeats both of them? The order did not drop by forgetfulness, because it was a condition for both. So here too, if it were a condition for them, it would not drop by forgetfulness.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verses 15–16:

The Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it, that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for.﴾ ﴿So let not one who does not believe in it and follows his desire turn you away from it, lest you perish.﴾

Know that when the Exalted addressed Musa, peace be upon him, with His words: ﴿So worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾, He followed it with His words: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it﴾. How fitting this is for the interpretation of one who interpreted His words ﴿for My remembrance﴾ as meaning: so that I may remind you of trust and honour. So He said immediately after that: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾, because it is the time of reward and the time of recompense. Then He said: ﴿I almost conceal it﴾. Regarding this there are two questions.

The first question: The negation of (kāda) is affirmation and its affirmation is negation, as evidenced by His words: ﴿and they almost did not do it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 71], meaning they did it. So His words ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ imply that He did not conceal it, and that is false for two reasons.

The first of them: His words: ﴿Indeed, with Allah is the knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34].

The second: His words ﴿that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for﴾ are fitting only with concealment, not with disclosure. The answer has several aspects.

The first: (kāda) is set for proximity only, without indicating negation or affirmation. So His words ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ mean: the matter came close to being concealed. Whether that concealment actually took place or not is not conveyed by the wording itself, but by the indication of His words ﴿that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for﴾, for that is fitting only with concealment, not with disclosure.

The second: (kāda) from Allah is obligatory, so the meaning of His words ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ is: I conceal it from the creation, like His words ﴿it may be that it is near﴾ [al-Isra': 51], meaning it is near. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: Abu Muslim said: "akādu" means "uridu" (I want), like His words ﴿Thus did We plan for Yusuf﴾ [Yusuf: 76], and from their widely circulated sayings: "I will not do that, nor do I almost (akādu)", meaning, nor do I want to do it.

The fourth: Its meaning is: ﴿I almost conceal it﴾ from myself. It is said that it is so in the codex of Ubayy, and in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "I almost conceal it from myself, so how would I announce it to you?" Al-Qadi said: this is far-fetched, because concealment is valid only regarding one to whom disclosure is possible, and that is impossible for Allah the Exalted, since every known thing is known to Him, so disclosure and concealment from Him are impossible. It can be answered that this is said on a hypothetical basis, meaning: if it were valid for me to conceal it from myself, I would have concealed it from myself. And although concealment is impossible in itself, it is not impossible to mention it on this hypothesis, as an exaggeration of the non-awareness of others of it. Qutrub said: this is according to the habit of the Arabs in addressing one another; they say, when they exaggerate in concealing a thing: "I concealed it even from myself." So Allah the Exalted exaggerated in concealing the Hour, and mentioned it in the most eloquent manner known to the Arabs in such a case.

The fifth: "akādu" is a filler in the speech, and the meaning is: "Indeed, the Hour is coming; I conceal it." Zayd al-Khayl said:

Swift to the battle, armed with his weapons, so that his opponent hardly breathes.

The meaning is: so that his opponent breathes.

The sixth: Abu al-Fath al-Mawsili said: "I almost conceal it" its interpretation is "I almost disclose it", and the summary of this wording is: "I almost remove its concealment", because af'ala may come with the meaning of removal and negation, as when you say: "a'jamtu al-kitab" and "ashkaltuhu", meaning I removed its non-clarity and its ambiguity, and "ashkaytuhu", meaning I removed his complaint.

The seventh: It was read as "akhfīhā" with an open alif, meaning: "I almost disclose it", from "khafāhu" when he disclosed it, meaning its disclosure came close, like His words ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ [al-Qamar: 1]. Imru' al-Qays said:

If you bury the disease, we will not conceal it, and if you withhold war, we will not sit idle.

Meaning: we will not disclose it. Al-Zajjaj said: this reading is clearer, because the meaning "I almost disclose it" indicates that He had concealed it.

The eighth: He intended: "Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost—" and the speech stopped, then He said: "I conceal it", then the first speech returned to: the better course is concealment: ﴿that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for﴾. This aspect is far-fetched, and Allah knows best.

The second question: What is the wisdom in concealing the Hour and concealing the time of death? The answer: because Allah the Exalted promised the acceptance of repentance, so if a person knew the time of death, he would busy himself with sin until close to that time, then repent, and thus escape the punishment of sin. So making known the time of death is like an incitement to commit sin, and that is not permissible.

As for His words ﴿that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives for﴾, there are several issues.

The first issue: When the Exalted decreed the coming of the Day of Resurrection, He mentioned the proof for it, which is that if there were no Resurrection, the obedient would not be distinguished from the disobedient, nor the good-doer from the evil-doer, and that is impermissible. This is what Allah the Exalted meant by His words: ﴿Shall We make those who believe and do righteous deeds like the corrupters on earth?﴾ [Sad: 28] ﴿Shall We make the righteous like the wicked?﴾ [Sad: 28].

The second issue: The Mu'tazilah used this verse to argue that reward is deserved for the deed, because the bā' denotes attachment, so His words ﴿for what it strives for﴾ indicate that the effective cause of that recompense is that striving.

The third issue: They used it to argue that the act of the servant is not created by Allah the Exalted, because the verse is explicit in affirming the servant's striving, and if everything were created by Allah the Exalted, the servant would have no striving at all.

* * *

As for His words ﴿So let not one who does not believe in it turn you away from it﴾, al-Sadd is prevention. Here there are issues:

The first issue: Regarding these two pronouns there are two views.

The first: Abu Muslim said: "let him not turn you away from it" means from the prayer which I commanded you to perform, "one who does not believe in it" means in the Hour. So the first pronoun refers to the prayer and the second to the Hour. Such usage is permissible in the language, for the Arabs combine two reports and then give their answer together, so that the listener returns to each report its due.

The second: Ibn 'Abbas said: "let him not turn you away from the Hour", meaning from belief in its coming, "one who does not believe in it", so both pronouns refer to the Day of Resurrection. Al-Qadi said: this is better, because the pronoun must refer to the nearer of the two mentioned, and here the nearer is the Hour; what Abu Muslim said is resorted to only out of necessity, and there is no necessity here.

The second issue: The address in His words ﴿So let not you be turned away﴾ may be to Musa, peace be upon him, and may be to Muhammad ﷺ. The closer view is that it is to Musa, because the whole discourse is addressed to him. On both views there is no sense in al-Zajjaj's statement that it is not intended, and that someone else is meant by it; for he thought that since the Prophet ﷺ, by virtue of prophethood, could not be turned away from belief in the Hour by anyone, the address could not be directed to him. The matter is not as he thought, for if he was obligated not to accept disbelief in the Hour from anyone, and was able to do so, it is permissible to address him with it while meaning both him and others. It is also possible that His words ﴿let him not turn you away from it﴾ mean a prohibition to him from inclining toward them and drawing near to them.

The third issue: The intended meaning is the prohibition of Musa, peace be upon him, from denying the Resurrection, but the apparent wording requires the prohibition of the one who does not believe from turning Musa, peace be upon him, away. There are two views on this:

The first: that the turning away of the disbeliever from belief in it is a cause of denial, so He mentioned the cause to indicate the effect.

The second: that the turning away of the disbeliever results from a man's laxity in religion, so He mentioned the result so that its implication would point to the cause, like His words "lā arayannaka hāhunā" (let me not see you here), where the intended meaning is a prohibition of his being seen and being present in his presence. Likewise here, as if it were said: do not be lax, but be strong and firm in religion.

The fourth issue: The verse indicates that learning the science of the principles (uṣūl) is obligatory, because His words ﴿let him not turn you away﴾ return in meaning to firmness in religion, and that firmness, if it is meant as taqlid (blind imitation), does not distinguish the false from the true in it. So this firmness must be taken to mean being strong in establishing proofs and removing doubts, so that the opponent cannot divert him from religion; rather he is able to remove the falsehood from its falsehood.

The fifth issue: Al-Qadi said: His words ﴿let him not turn you away﴾ indicate that the servants are the ones who turn away, and if the Exalted were the Creator of their acts, He would be the one who turns away, not them. So this shows the invalidity of the doctrine of compulsion (jabr).

The answer: a counter-argument based on the issue of knowledge and the motive, and Allah knows best. As for His words ﴿and follows his desire﴾, the meaning is that the denier of resurrection denies it only by following desire, not by evidence, and this is among the greatest proofs of the corruption of taqlid, for the one who follows taqlid follows desire, not proof. As for His words ﴿lest you perish﴾, it has the meaning: "let him not turn you away, lest you perish"; and even if they turn you away and you accept, there is nothing but destruction in the Fire.

Know that those who delve deeply into the secrets of gnosis (ma'rifa) said: the station has two stages:

The first: the station of effacement (maḥw) and annihilation (fanā') from all besides Allah the Exalted.

The second: the station of subsistence (baqā') in Allah.

The first precedes the second, because whoever wishes to write something on a tablet occupied with other writing has no way to do so except by removing the first writing; after that it is possible to inscribe the second writing. The Truth, glory be to Him, observed this fine order in this matter, for He said to Musa, peace be upon him, first: ﴿Take off your sandals﴾, which is an indication of purifying the inner self from all besides Allah the Exalted; then after that He commanded him to acquire what must be acquired. The principles of this matter go back to three: the science of the origin (mabda'), the science of the middle (wasat), and the science of the return (ma'ad).

The science of the origin is the knowledge of the Truth, glory be to Him, and that is what is meant by His words: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no god but I﴾.

As for the science of the middle, it is the science of servitude ('ubudiyya), and its meaning is the matter with which a person must occupy himself in this bodily life, and that is what is meant by His words: ﴿So worship Me and establish prayer﴾. Then in this too there is a stumbling point, for His words ﴿So worship Me﴾ refer to bodily deeds, and His words ﴿for My remembrance﴾ refer to spiritual deeds, while servitude begins with bodily deeds and ends with spiritual deeds.

As for the science of the return, it is His words: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it﴾. Then the Exalted opened these obligations with pure kindness, which is His words: ﴿Indeed, I am your Lord﴾, and concluded them with pure severity, which is His words: ﴿So let not one who does not believe in it and follows his desire turn you away from it, lest you perish﴾, as an admonition that His mercy precedes His wrath, and as an indication that the servant in servitude must have both desire and dread, hope and fear. Upon reflection on this sentence you will know that this order is the utmost in goodness and excellence, and that this cannot be achieved except by one who knows all things.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah Ta-Ha, verses 17–20 (part 1 of 2)

God Most High says: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ ﴿He said, "It is my staff; I lean upon it, and beat down (leaves) with it for my sheep, and in it I have other uses."﴾ ﴿He said, "Throw it down, O Musa."﴾ ﴿So he threw it down, and behold, it was a serpent, moving swiftly.﴾ ﴿He said, "Take hold of it and fear not. We shall restore it to its original form."﴾

Know that His saying ﴿And what is that in your right hand﴾ consists of two expressions. His saying ﴿And what is that﴾ is a reference to the staff, and His saying ﴿in your right hand﴾ is a reference to the hand. On this there are some subtle points (nukat):

The first: when He, glorified be He, pointed to both of them, He made each one of them a compelling miracle and a dazzling proof. He transferred them from the state of inanimacy (jamadiyyah) to the station of honour. Thus an inanimate object became a living creature with a single glance, and a dense body became subtle and luminous. Furthermore, He, Most High, looks upon the heart of the servant three hundred and sixty times each day. So what wonder if his heart is transformed from the death of disobedience to the happiness of obedience and the light of knowledge (ma'rifah).

The second: by a single glance the inanimate object became a serpent that swallowed the magic of the magicians. So what wonder if the heart, by the aid of the divine glance, becomes such that it swallows the magic of the soul that commands to evil.

The third: the staff was in the right hand of Musa, peace be upon him. Because of the blessing of his right hand it turned into a serpent and a proof. The heart of the believer is between two fingers of the fingers of the Most Merciful. If the right hand of Musa, peace be upon him, obtained this honour and blessing, what wonder if the heart of the believer is transformed, by means of the two fingers of the Most Merciful, from the darkness of disobedience to the light of servitude.

Then here there are some questions:

The first: His saying ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ is a question. A question is asked only to seek knowledge, and that is impossible for God Most High. So what is the purpose of it?

The answer to this contains several benefits:

The first: whoever wishes to show a noble quality in a lowly thing takes it, presents it to those present, and says to them, "What is this?" They reply, "This is such-and-such a thing." Then, after showing its outstanding quality in it, he says to them, "Take from it such-and-such." When God Most High wished to show from the staff those noble signs, such as its turning into a serpent, and His striking the sea so that it split, and (striking) the rock so that water gushed from it, He first presented it to Musa. It is as if He said to him, "O Musa, do you know the reality of this thing in your hand, that it is a piece of wood that neither harms nor benefits?" Then He turned it into a great serpent. Thus by this means He alerted the minds to the perfection of His power and the extreme of His greatness, in that He displayed these great signs from among the least of things in His sight. This is the benefit of His saying ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾.

The second: when He, glorified be He, made him witness those luminous lights rising from the tree to the sky, and made him hear the glorification of the angels, then made him hear His own speech, then He combined gentleness with majesty. He first gentled him with His saying ﴿And I have chosen you﴾, then overwhelmed him by imposing upon him difficult obligations and binding him to the knowledge of the origin, the intermediate, and the return, and then concluded all of that with a great threat. Musa became bewildered and astonished, and nearly did not know the right from the left. So he was told ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ so that Musa, peace be upon him, would know that his right hand is the one in which the staff is. Or, because when He spoke with him at first with words of divinity, and Musa was bewildered by the astonishment, He spoke with him in human speech to remove that astonishment and bewilderment. The subtle point in this is that when astonishment overcame Musa in the presence, the Lord of Might wished to remove it, so He asked him about the staff, about which he could not make an error. Likewise, the believer, when he dies and arrives at the presence of the Lord of Majesty, astonishment overcomes him and shyness prevents him from speaking. So they ask him about the matter in which he did not err in this world, which is monotheism (tawhid). When he mentions it, the astonishment and the dread leave him.

The third: when God, Most High, made Musa know the perfection of divinity, He wished to make him know the deficiency of humanity. So He asked him about the benefits of the staff, and he mentioned some of them. God Most High then informed him that there are in it benefits greater than what he mentioned, as an alert that minds fall short of knowing the attributes of the present Prophet. Were it not for divine success and protection (ismah), how could they reach the knowledge of the most sublime and greatest of things?

The fourth: the benefit of this question is to establish in his mind that it is a piece of wood, so that when He turns it into a serpent he will not fear it.

The second question: His saying ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ is an address from God Most High with Musa, peace be upon him, without intermediary, and this did not happen for Muhammad (ﷺ). Therefore it follows that Musa is superior to Muhammad. The answer is in two respects:

The first: just as He addressed Musa, He addressed Muhammad, peace be upon him, in His saying ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 10]. However, the difference between them is that what He spoke with Musa, peace be upon him, God disclosed to creation, whereas what He spoke with Muhammad (ﷺ) was a secret for which none of creation was worthy.

The second: if Musa was addressed by Him, and He is the one who addressed Musa, then the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) address God every day several times, as he (ﷺ) said: "The one who prays is conversing with his Lord." And the Lord speaks with individuals of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) on the Day of Resurrection, with greeting, honouring, and speech, in His saying ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58].

The answer: The author of al-Kashshaf said: "That in your right hand" is like His saying ﴿And this is my husband, an old man﴾ [Hud: 72] in terms of the accusative of the state (hal), in the sense of pointing. It is also permissible for "that" (tilka) to be a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), with its relative clause being "in your right hand." Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "and what is the one that is in your right hand." Al-Farra' said: its meaning is "what is this that is in your right hand?" Know that when He, glorified be He, asked Musa, peace be upon him, about that, Musa, peace be upon him, answered with four things: three in detail and one in summary.

The first: his saying ﴿It is my staff﴾. Ibn Abi Ishaq recited "hiya 'asa" (without the yā'). The same is his saying ﴿O good news﴾ [Yusuf: 19]. Al-Hasan recited "hiya 'asayy" with the yā' sukun. The points here are three:

The first: he said ﴿It is my staff﴾, and he mentioned the staff. How can one whose heart is occupied with the staff and its benefits be absorbed in the ocean of the knowledge of the Truth? But Muhammad (ﷺ) was shown Paradise and Hell and did not turn to anything: ﴿The sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾ [al-Najm: 17]. When it was said to him, "Praise us," he said: "I cannot count praise of You." Then he forgot himself and forgot his praise, and said: "You are as You have praised Yourself."

The second: when he said ﴿my staff﴾, God, glorified and exalted be He, said ﴿Throw it down﴾. When he threw it down, behold, it was ﴿a serpent, moving swiftly﴾, so that he would know that everything other than God, attention to it is distracting, and it is like a deadly serpent for you. For this reason the Friend (Khalil, Abraham), peace be upon him, said: ﴿For they are an enemy to me, except the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 77]. In a hadith: "On the Day of Resurrection, the owner of wealth who did not pay its zakat will be brought, and that wealth will be brought to him in the form of a bald, poisonous snake," and the hadith in its entirety.

The third: he said "it is my staff," and thus the answer was complete. However, he (peace be upon him) mentioned the other aspects, because he loved conversation with his Lord, so he made that as a means to achieving this aim.

The second: his saying ﴿I lean upon it﴾. Al-tawakki' and al-ittika' are one and the same, like al-tawaqqi and al-ittiqa'. Its meaning is: I rely upon it when I am weary, or when I stand at the head of the flock, or at the leaping. So Musa, peace be upon him, made himself lean upon the staff. And God Most High said to Muhammad (ﷺ): "Lean upon My mercy," by His saying ﴿O Prophet, God is sufficient for you, and for those who follow you of the believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 64], and He said: ﴿And God will protect you from the people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67]. If it is said: does not His saying ﴿and for those who follow you of the believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 64] imply that Muhammad leans upon the believers? We say: His saying ﴿and for those who follow you of the believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 64] is conjoined with the "kaf" (you) in His saying ﴿God is sufficient for you﴾ [al-Anfal: 64], and the meaning is: God is sufficient for you, and sufficient for those who follow you of the believers.

The third: his saying ﴿And I beat down (leaves) with it for my sheep﴾, that is, I strike with it and beat the branches of the tree so that its leaves fall upon my sheep and they eat them. The lexicographers said: "hashsha 'ala ghanamihi, yahushshu" with a damma on the ha' in the imperfect; "hashashtu al-rajul, ahishshu" with a fatha on the ha' in the imperfect; and "hashsha al-raghif, yahishshu" with a kasra on the ha'. This was said by Tha'lab. And Ikrimah recited "wa-ahissu" with an unpointed sin. Al-hashsh means driving away the sheep. Know that his sheep are his flock, so he began with the interests of himself in his saying ﴿I lean upon it﴾, then with the interests of his flock in his saying ﴿and I beat down (leaves) with it for my sheep﴾. Likewise on the Day of Resurrection he begins with himself and says: "Myself, myself." Yet Muhammad (ﷺ) did not occupy himself in this world except with setting right the affairs of the community: ﴿God would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33], and "O God, guide my people, for they do not know." Therefore, without doubt, on the Day of Resurrection he too begins with his community, and says: "My community, my community."

The fourth: his saying ﴿And in it I have other uses﴾, that is, needs and benefits. Its singular is ma'raba, with a fatha or damma on the ra'. Ibn al-A'rabi and Qutrub also related it with a kasra on the ra'. Al-arab with a fatha on the ra', and al-irbah with a kasra on the alif and sukun on the ra', mean need. He said "other" (ukhra) only because al-ma'arib carries the sense of a group; so it is as if he said: "a group of needs, other." Had it been "ukhar" it would have been correct, as in His saying ﴿then a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184]. Then here there are subtle points:

The first: when he heard God's saying ﴿And what is that in your right hand﴾, he knew that God has great secrets in it, so he mentioned what he knew, and referred to the rest, which he did not know in detail but only in summary, by his saying ﴿And in it I have other uses﴾.

The second: Musa, peace be upon him, sensed that He asked him about the matter of the staff only for great benefits. So Musa said: "My God, this staff is nothing but like any other, but since You asked about it, I know that there are for me in it other uses. Among them is that You spoke to me by means of it, and I found this great and noble matter by means of it."

The third: Musa, peace be upon him, hoped that his Lord would ask him about those uses, so that he would hear God's speech once more, and the matter of conversation would be prolonged on account of that.

The fourth: because of gentleness his tongue was loosened, then astonishment overcame him, his tongue was cut off, and his thoughts were disordered, so he summarized once more. Then Wahb said: it had two prongs like a crook. When the branch grew long, he bent it with the crook; when it tried to break, he twisted it with the two prongs; and when he travelled, he placed it on his shoulder, hanging from it his equipment: the bow, the quiver, and the garments. When he was in the desert, he planted it and cast a cloak over it, and it became shade. It was also said: among its miracles, he would draw water with it, and it would lengthen with the length of the well, and its two prongs would become a bucket, and they would become two candles at night. When an enemy appeared, it would fight on his behalf. When he desired a fruit, he planted it and it would put forth leaves and bear fruit. He would carry his provisions and water on it, and it would walk alongside him. When he planted it, water would spring forth, and when he lifted it, the water would recede. It would also protect him from venomous creatures.

Know that when Musa, peace be upon him, mentioned these answers, God Most High commanded him to throw down the staff, saying ﴿Throw it down, O Musa.﴾ And in this there are subtle points:

The first: when he, peace be upon him, said ﴿And in it I have other uses﴾, God wished to make him know that in it there is another use which he does not perceive or know, and that it is greater than all his other uses. So He said ﴿Throw it down, O Musa﴾ ﴿So he threw it down, and behold, it was a serpent, moving swiftly.﴾

Second: there was something on his foot, which was the sandal, and something in his hand, which was the staff. The foot is the instrument of flight and the hand is the instrument of pursuit. So He first said, ﴿So take off your sandals﴾, as a sign of abandoning flight. Then He said, "Throw it down, O Musa," which is a sign of abandoning pursuit. It is as if He, glory be to Him, said: "As long as you are in the station of fleeing and pursuing, you are occupied with yourself and seeking your own share, and so you will not be sincere in knowing Me. So abandon both fleeing and pursuing, so that you may be sincere to Me."

Third: Musa, peace be upon him, despite the loftiness of his rank and the perfection of his virtue, when he reached the Presence and had with him nothing but the two sandals and the staff, was commanded to cast them off until he could reach the Presence. So how can you, carrying a burden of a thousand sins, reach His threshold?

Fourth: Muhammad ﷺ was stripped of everything; "the gaze did not swerve" (53:17), so he found everything. As for Musa, since that staff remained with him, he was commanded to throw down the staff.

Know that al-Ka'bi (the Mu'tazili theologian) relied on this to argue that capacity (istita'a) exists before the act. He said: The power to throw the staff either exists while the staff is in his hand, or while it is outside his hand. If the power came to him while it was in his hand, that is our position, as in ﴿and Allah is not unjust to the servants﴾ (3:182). But if the power came to him while it was not in his hand, and he was able to throw from his hand what was not in his hand, that is impossible.

* * *

As for His words, ﴿So he threw it, and suddenly it was a snake, moving swiftly﴾, there are questions concerning it:

First question: What is the wisdom in turning the staff into a snake at that moment? The answer: there are several aspects.

One: He, exalted is He, turned it into a snake to be a miracle for Musa, peace be upon him, by which he would recognize his own prophethood. This is because, up to this point, he, peace be upon him, had heard only the call, and although the call was contrary to customary norms, it was not a miracle, since it could be the habit of angels or jinn. So Allah turned the staff into a snake so that this would be a decisive proof. And it is remarkable that Musa, peace be upon him, said, "I lean on it," and Allah confirmed him in this by making it a support for him through making it a miracle.

Two: The call was an honor for him, so turning the staff into a snake was an increase in honor, so that the succession of stripping away and honors would be a cause for removing the fear from his heart.

Three: He displayed it to him so that he might witness it first, and when he witnessed it in the presence of Pharaoh, he would not fear him.

Four: He had been a poor shepherd and then was appointed to a great office, so perhaps some astonishment remained in his heart about this. So He turned the staff into a snake as a reminder that since I am able to do that, how can it be deemed unlikely that I would support one like you in establishing the religion?

Five: When he said, ﴿It is my staff; I lean on it, and I have in it other uses﴾, up to His words, and He told him, "Throw it down," and when he threw it and it became a snake, Musa, peace be upon him, fled from it. It is as if it were said to him: "You claimed it is your staff and that you have other uses for it, so why do you flee from it?" This is a reminder of the secret in His words, ﴿So flee to Allah﴾ (51:50), and His words, ﴿Say, "Allah." Then leave them﴾ (6:91).

Second question: Here He says "ḥayya" (snake), while in another place He says "thu'bān" (serpent) and "jānn" (small snake). The word ḥayya is a generic noun that applies to the male and female, the young and the large. But thu'bān and jānn are contrary to each other, since the thu'bān is a large snake and the jānn is a slender one. On this there are two views:

One: At the moment of its transformation it was a small, slender snake, then it swelled and its body grew until it became a thu'bān. So jānn refers to its initial state and thu'bān to its final state.

Two: It was in the form of a thu'bān but with the swift movement of a jānn. The proof for this is His words, ﴿When he saw it moving as if it were a jānn﴾ (27:10).

Third question: What was the description of the snake? The answer: It had a mane like that of a horse, the distance between its jaws was forty cubits, and it swallowed everything it passed by, from rocks and trees, until Musa heard the grinding of the stone in its mouth and its belly.

He said "other" (ukhra) only because al-ma'arib carries the sense of a group; so it is as if he said: "a group of needs, other." Had it been "ukhar" it would have been correct, as in His saying ﴿then a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184]. Then here there are subtle points:

The first: when he heard God's saying ﴿And what is that in your right hand﴾, he knew that God has great secrets in it, so he mentioned what he knew, and referred to the rest, which he did not know in detail but only in summary, by his saying ﴿And in it I have other uses﴾.

The second: Musa, peace be upon him, sensed that He asked him about the matter of the staff only for great benefits. So Musa said: "My God, this staff is nothing but like any other, but since You asked about it, I know that there are for me in it other uses. Among them is that You spoke to me by means of it, and I found this great and noble matter by means of it."

The third: Musa, peace be upon him, hoped that his Lord would ask him about those uses, so that he would hear God's speech once more, and the matter of conversation would be prolonged on account of that.

The fourth: because of gentleness his tongue was loosened, then astonishment overcame him, his tongue was cut off, and his thoughts were disordered, so he summarized once more. Then Wahb said: it had two prongs like a crook. When the branch grew long, he bent it with the crook; when it tried to break, he twisted it with the two prongs; and when he travelled, he placed it on his shoulder, hanging from it his equipment: the bow, the quiver, and the garments. When he was in the desert, he planted it and cast a cloak over it, and it became shade. It was also said: among its miracles, he would draw water with it, and it would lengthen with the length of the well, and its two prongs would become a bucket, and they would become two candles at night. When an enemy appeared, it would fight on his behalf. When he desired a fruit, he planted it and it would put forth leaves and bear fruit. He would carry his provisions and water on it, and it would walk alongside him. When he planted it, water would spring forth, and when he lifted it, the water would recede. It would also protect him from venomous creatures.

Know that when Musa, peace be upon him, mentioned these answers, God Most High commanded him to throw down the staff, saying ﴿Throw it down, O Musa.﴾ And in this there are subtle points:

The first: when he, peace be upon him, said ﴿And in it I have other uses﴾, God wished to make him know that in it there is another use which he does not perceive or know, and that it is greater than all his other uses. So He said ﴿Throw it down, O Musa﴾ ﴿So he threw it down, and behold, it was a serpent, moving swiftly.﴾

Second: there was something on his foot, which was the sandal, and something in his hand, which was the staff. The foot is the instrument of flight and the hand is the instrument of pursuit. So He first said, ﴿So take off your sandals﴾, as a sign of abandoning flight. Then He said, "Throw it down, O Musa," which is a sign of abandoning pursuit. It is as if He, glory be to Him, said: "As long as you are in the station of fleeing and pursuing, you are occupied with yourself and seeking your own share, and so you will not be sincere in knowing Me. So abandon both fleeing and pursuing, so that you may be sincere to Me."

Third: Musa, peace be upon him, despite the loftiness of his rank and the perfection of his virtue, when he reached the Presence and had with him nothing but the two sandals and the staff, was commanded to cast them off until he could reach the Presence. So how can you, carrying a burden of a thousand sins, reach His threshold?

Fourth: Muhammad ﷺ was stripped of everything; "the gaze did not swerve" (53:17), so he found everything. As for Musa, since that staff remained with him, he was commanded to throw down the staff.

Know that al-Ka'bi (the Mu'tazili theologian) relied on this to argue that capacity (istita'a) exists before the act. He said: The power to throw the staff either exists while the staff is in his hand, or while it is outside his hand. If the power came to him while it was in his hand, that is our position, as in ﴿and Allah is not unjust to the servants﴾ (3:182). But if the power came to him while it was not in his hand, and he was able to throw from his hand what was not in his hand, that is impossible.

* * *

As for His words, ﴿So he threw it, and suddenly it was a snake, moving swiftly﴾, there are questions concerning it:

First question: What is the wisdom in turning the staff into a snake at that moment? The answer: there are several aspects.

One: He, exalted is He, turned it into a snake to be a miracle for Musa, peace be upon him, by which he would recognize his own prophethood. This is because, up to this point, he, peace be upon him, had heard only the call, and although the call was contrary to customary norms, it was not a miracle, since it could be the habit of angels or jinn. So Allah turned the staff into a snake so that this would be a decisive proof. And it is remarkable that Musa, peace be upon him, said, "I lean on it," and Allah confirmed him in this by making it a support for him through making it a miracle.

Two: The call was an honor for him, so turning the staff into a snake was an increase in honor, so that the succession of stripping away and honors would be a cause for removing the fear from his heart.

Three: He displayed it to him so that he might witness it first, and when he witnessed it in the presence of Pharaoh, he would not fear him.

Four: He had been a poor shepherd and then was appointed to a great office, so perhaps some astonishment remained in his heart about this. So He turned the staff into a snake as a reminder that since I am able to do that, how can it be deemed unlikely that I would support one like you in establishing the religion?

Five: When he said, ﴿It is my staff; I lean on it, and I have in it other uses﴾, up to His words, and He told him, "Throw it down," and when he threw it and it became a snake, Musa, peace be upon him, fled from it. It is as if it were said to him: "You claimed it is your staff and that you have other uses for it, so why do you flee from it?" This is a reminder of the secret in His words, ﴿So flee to Allah﴾ (51:50), and His words, ﴿Say, "Allah." Then leave them﴾ (6:91).

Second question: Here He says "ḥayya" (snake), while in another place He says "thu'bān" (serpent) and "jānn" (small snake). The word ḥayya is a generic noun that applies to the male and female, the young and the large. But thu'bān and jānn are contrary to each other, since the thu'bān is a large snake and the jānn is a slender one. On this there are two views:

One: At the moment of its transformation it was a small, slender snake, then it swelled and its body grew until it became a thu'bān. So jānn refers to its initial state and thu'bān to its final state.

Two: It was in the form of a thu'bān but with the swift movement of a jānn. The proof for this is His words, ﴿When he saw it moving as if it were a jānn﴾ (27:10).

Third question: What was the description of the snake? The answer: It had a mane like that of a horse, the distance between its jaws was forty cubits, and it swallowed everything it passed by, from rocks and trees, until Musa heard the grinding of the stone in its mouth and its belly.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah Ta-Ha, verses 17–20 (part 1 of 2)

God Most High says: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ ﴿He said, "It is my staff; I lean upon it, and beat down (leaves) with it for my sheep, and in it I have other uses."﴾ ﴿He said, "Throw it down, O Musa."﴾ ﴿So he threw it down, and behold, it was a serpent, moving swiftly.﴾ ﴿He said, "Take hold of it and fear not. We shall restore it to its original form."﴾

Know that His saying ﴿And what is that in your right hand﴾ consists of two expressions. His saying ﴿And what is that﴾ is a reference to the staff, and His saying ﴿in your right hand﴾ is a reference to the hand. On this there are some subtle points (nukat):

The first: when He, glorified be He, pointed to both of them, He made each one of them a compelling miracle and a dazzling proof. He transferred them from the state of inanimacy (jamadiyyah) to the station of honour. Thus an inanimate object became a living creature with a single glance, and a dense body became subtle and luminous. Furthermore, He, Most High, looks upon the heart of the servant three hundred and sixty times each day. So what wonder if his heart is transformed from the death of disobedience to the happiness of obedience and the light of knowledge (ma'rifah).

The second: by a single glance the inanimate object became a serpent that swallowed the magic of the magicians. So what wonder if the heart, by the aid of the divine glance, becomes such that it swallows the magic of the soul that commands to evil.

The third: the staff was in the right hand of Musa, peace be upon him. Because of the blessing of his right hand it turned into a serpent and a proof. The heart of the believer is between two fingers of the fingers of the Most Merciful. If the right hand of Musa, peace be upon him, obtained this honour and blessing, what wonder if the heart of the believer is transformed, by means of the two fingers of the Most Merciful, from the darkness of disobedience to the light of servitude.

Then here there are some questions:

The first: His saying ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ is a question. A question is asked only to seek knowledge, and that is impossible for God Most High. So what is the purpose of it?

The answer to this contains several benefits:

The first: whoever wishes to show a noble quality in a lowly thing takes it, presents it to those present, and says to them, "What is this?" They reply, "This is such-and-such a thing." Then, after showing its outstanding quality in it, he says to them, "Take from it such-and-such." When God Most High wished to show from the staff those noble signs, such as its turning into a serpent, and His striking the sea so that it split, and (striking) the rock so that water gushed from it, He first presented it to Musa. It is as if He said to him, "O Musa, do you know the reality of this thing in your hand, that it is a piece of wood that neither harms nor benefits?" Then He turned it into a great serpent. Thus by this means He alerted the minds to the perfection of His power and the extreme of His greatness, in that He displayed these great signs from among the least of things in His sight. This is the benefit of His saying ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾.

The second: when He, glorified be He, made him witness those luminous lights rising from the tree to the sky, and made him hear the glorification of the angels, then made him hear His own speech, then He combined gentleness with majesty. He first gentled him with His saying ﴿And I have chosen you﴾, then overwhelmed him by imposing upon him difficult obligations and binding him to the knowledge of the origin, the intermediate, and the return, and then concluded all of that with a great threat. Musa became bewildered and astonished, and nearly did not know the right from the left. So he was told ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ so that Musa, peace be upon him, would know that his right hand is the one in which the staff is. Or, because when He spoke with him at first with words of divinity, and Musa was bewildered by the astonishment, He spoke with him in human speech to remove that astonishment and bewilderment. The subtle point in this is that when astonishment overcame Musa in the presence, the Lord of Might wished to remove it, so He asked him about the staff, about which he could not make an error. Likewise, the believer, when he dies and arrives at the presence of the Lord of Majesty, astonishment overcomes him and shyness prevents him from speaking. So they ask him about the matter in which he did not err in this world, which is monotheism (tawhid). When he mentions it, the astonishment and the dread leave him.

The third: when God, Most High, made Musa know the perfection of divinity, He wished to make him know the deficiency of humanity. So He asked him about the benefits of the staff, and he mentioned some of them. God Most High then informed him that there are in it benefits greater than what he mentioned, as an alert that minds fall short of knowing the attributes of the present Prophet. Were it not for divine success and protection (ismah), how could they reach the knowledge of the most sublime and greatest of things?

The fourth: the benefit of this question is to establish in his mind that it is a piece of wood, so that when He turns it into a serpent he will not fear it.

The second question: His saying ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ is an address from God Most High with Musa, peace be upon him, without intermediary, and this did not happen for Muhammad (ﷺ). Therefore it follows that Musa is superior to Muhammad. The answer is in two respects:

The first: just as He addressed Musa, He addressed Muhammad, peace be upon him, in His saying ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 10]. However, the difference between them is that what He spoke with Musa, peace be upon him, God disclosed to creation, whereas what He spoke with Muhammad (ﷺ) was a secret for which none of creation was worthy.

The second: if Musa was addressed by Him, and He is the one who addressed Musa, then the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) address God every day several times, as he (ﷺ) said: "The one who prays is conversing with his Lord." And the Lord speaks with individuals of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) on the Day of Resurrection, with greeting, honouring, and speech, in His saying ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58].

The third question: what is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of His saying ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾? The answer: The author of al-Kashshaf said: "That in your right hand" is like His saying ﴿And this is my husband, an old man﴾ [Hud: 72] in terms of the accusative of the state (hal), in the sense of pointing. It is also permissible for "that" (tilka) to be a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), with its relative clause being "in your right hand." Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "and what is the one that is in your right hand." Al-Farra' said: its meaning is "what is this that is in your right hand?" Know that when He, glorified be He, asked Musa, peace be upon him, about that, Musa, peace be upon him, answered with four things: three in detail and one in summary.

The first: his saying ﴿It is my staff﴾. Ibn Abi Ishaq recited "hiya 'asa" (without the yā'). The same is his saying ﴿O good news﴾ [Yusuf: 19]. Al-Hasan recited "hiya 'asayy" with the yā' sukun. The points here are three:

The first: he said ﴿It is my staff﴾, and he mentioned the staff. How can one whose heart is occupied with the staff and its benefits be absorbed in the ocean of the knowledge of the Truth? But Muhammad (ﷺ) was shown Paradise and Hell and did not turn to anything: ﴿The sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾ [al-Najm: 17]. When it was said to him, "Praise us," he said: "I cannot count praise of You." Then he forgot himself and forgot his praise, and said: "You are as You have praised Yourself."

The second: when he said ﴿my staff﴾, God, glorified and exalted be He, said ﴿Throw it down﴾. When he threw it down, behold, it was ﴿a serpent, moving swiftly﴾, so that he would know that everything other than God, attention to it is distracting, and it is like a deadly serpent for you. For this reason the Friend (Khalil, Abraham), peace be upon him, said: ﴿For they are an enemy to me, except the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 77]. In a hadith: "On the Day of Resurrection, the owner of wealth who did not pay its zakat will be brought, and that wealth will be brought to him in the form of a bald, poisonous snake," and the hadith in its entirety.

The third: he said "it is my staff," and thus the answer was complete. However, he (peace be upon him) mentioned the other aspects, because he loved conversation with his Lord, so he made that as a means to achieving this aim.

The second: his saying ﴿I lean upon it﴾. Al-tawakki' and al-ittika' are one and the same, like al-tawaqqi and al-ittiqa'. Its meaning is: I rely upon it when I am weary, or when I stand at the head of the flock, or at the leaping. So Musa, peace be upon him, made himself lean upon the staff. And God Most High said to Muhammad (ﷺ): "Lean upon My mercy," by His saying ﴿O Prophet, God is sufficient for you, and for those who follow you of the believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 64], and He said: ﴿And God will protect you from the people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67]. If it is said: does not His saying ﴿and for those who follow you of the believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 64] imply that Muhammad leans upon the believers? We say: His saying ﴿and for those who follow you of the believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 64] is conjoined with the "kaf" (you) in His saying ﴿God is sufficient for you﴾ [al-Anfal: 64], and the meaning is: God is sufficient for you, and sufficient for those who follow you of the believers.

The third: his saying ﴿And I beat down (leaves) with it for my sheep﴾, that is, I strike with it and beat the branches of the tree so that its leaves fall upon my sheep and they eat them. The lexicographers said: "hashsha 'ala ghanamihi, yahushshu" with a damma on the ha' in the imperfect; "hashashtu al-rajul, ahishshu" with a fatha on the ha' in the imperfect; and "hashsha al-raghif, yahishshu" with a kasra on the ha'. This was said by Tha'lab. And Ikrimah recited "wa-ahissu" with an unpointed sin. Al-hashsh means driving away the sheep. Know that his sheep are his flock, so he began with the interests of himself in his saying ﴿I lean upon it﴾, then with the interests of his flock in his saying ﴿and I beat down (leaves) with it for my sheep﴾. Likewise on the Day of Resurrection he begins with himself and says: "Myself, myself." Yet Muhammad (ﷺ) did not occupy himself in this world except with setting right the affairs of the community: ﴿God would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33], and "O God, guide my people, for they do not know." Therefore, without doubt, on the Day of Resurrection he too begins with his community, and says: "My community, my community."

Then, after showing its outstanding quality in it, he says to them, "Take from it such-and-such." When God Most High wished to show from the staff those noble signs, such as its turning into a serpent, and His striking the sea so that it split, and (striking) the rock so that water gushed from it, He first presented it to Musa. It is as if He said to him, "O Musa, do you know the reality of this thing in your hand, that it is a piece of wood that neither harms nor benefits?" Then He turned it into a great serpent. Thus by this means He alerted the minds to the perfection of His power and the extreme of His greatness, in that He displayed these great signs from among the least of things in His sight. This is the benefit of His saying ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾.

The second: when He, glorified be He, made him witness those luminous lights rising from the tree to the sky, and made him hear the glorification of the angels, then made him hear His own speech, then He combined gentleness with majesty. He first gentled him with His saying ﴿And I have chosen you﴾, then overwhelmed him by imposing upon him difficult obligations and binding him to the knowledge of the origin, the intermediate, and the return, and then concluded all of that with a great threat. Musa became bewildered and astonished, and nearly did not know the right from the left. So he was told ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ so that Musa, peace be upon him, would know that his right hand is the one in which the staff is. Or, because when He spoke with him at first with words of divinity, and Musa was bewildered by the astonishment, He spoke with him in human speech to remove that astonishment and bewilderment. The subtle point in this is that when astonishment overcame Musa in the presence, the Lord of Might wished to remove it, so He asked him about the staff, about which he could not make an error. Likewise, the believer, when he dies and arrives at the presence of the Lord of Majesty, astonishment overcomes him and shyness prevents him from speaking. So they ask him about the matter in which he did not err in this world, which is monotheism (tawhid). When he mentions it, the astonishment and the dread leave him.

The third: when God, Most High, made Musa know the perfection of divinity, He wished to make him know the deficiency of humanity. So He asked him about the benefits of the staff, and he mentioned some of them. God Most High then informed him that there are in it benefits greater than what he mentioned, as an alert that minds fall short of knowing the attributes of the present Prophet. Were it not for divine success and protection (ismah), how could they reach the knowledge of the most sublime and greatest of things?

The fourth: the benefit of this question is to establish in his mind that it is a piece of wood, so that when He turns it into a serpent he will not fear it.

The second question: His saying ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ is an address from God Most High with Musa, peace be upon him, without intermediary, and this did not happen for Muhammad (ﷺ). Therefore it follows that Musa is superior to Muhammad. The answer is in two respects:

The first: just as He addressed Musa, He addressed Muhammad, peace be upon him, in His saying ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 10]. However, the difference between them is that what He spoke with Musa, peace be upon him, God disclosed to creation, whereas what He spoke with Muhammad (ﷺ) was a secret for which none of creation was worthy.

The second: if Musa was addressed by Him, and He is the one who addressed Musa, then the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) address God every day several times, as he (ﷺ) said: "The one who prays is conversing with his Lord." And the Lord speaks with individuals of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) on the Day of Resurrection, with greeting, honouring, and speech, in His saying ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58].

The third question: what is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of His saying ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾? The answer: The author of al-Kashshaf said: "That in your right hand" is like His saying ﴿And this is my husband, an old man﴾ [Hud: 72] in terms of the accusative of the state (hal), in the sense of pointing. It is also permissible for "that" (tilka) to be a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), with its relative clause being "in your right hand." Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is "and what is the one that is in your right hand." Al-Farra' said: its meaning is "what is this that is in your right hand?" Know that when He, glorified be He, asked Musa, peace be upon him, about that, Musa, peace be upon him, answered with four things: three in detail and one in summary.

The first: his saying ﴿It is my staff﴾. Ibn Abi Ishaq recited "hiya 'asa" (without the yā'). The same is his saying ﴿O good news﴾ [Yusuf: 19]. Al-Hasan recited "hiya 'asayy" with the yā' sukun. The points here are three:

The first: he said ﴿It is my staff﴾, and he mentioned the staff. How can one whose heart is occupied with the staff and its benefits be absorbed in the ocean of the knowledge of the Truth? But Muhammad (ﷺ) was shown Paradise and Hell and did not turn to anything: ﴿The sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾ [al-Najm: 17]. When it was said to him, "Praise us," he said: "I cannot count praise of You." Then he forgot himself and forgot his praise, and said: "You are as You have praised Yourself."

The second: when he said ﴿my staff﴾, God, glorified and exalted be He, said ﴿Throw it down﴾. When he threw it down, behold, it was ﴿a serpent, moving swiftly﴾, so that he would know that everything other than God, attention to it is distracting, and it is like a deadly serpent for you. For this reason the Friend (Khalil, Abraham), peace be upon him, said: ﴿For they are an enemy to me, except the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 77]. In a hadith: "On the Day of Resurrection, the owner of wealth who did not pay its zakat will be brought, and that wealth will be brought to him in the form of a bald, poisonous snake," and the hadith in its entirety.

The third: he said "it is my staff," and thus the answer was complete. However, he (peace be upon him) mentioned the other aspects, because he loved conversation with his Lord, so he made that as a means to achieving this aim.

The second: his saying ﴿I lean upon it﴾. Al-tawakki' and al-ittika' are one and the same, like al-tawaqqi and al-ittiqa'. Its meaning is: I rely upon it when I am weary, or when I stand at the head of the flock, or at the leaping. So Musa, peace be upon him, made himself lean upon the staff. And God Most High said to Muhammad (ﷺ): "Lean upon My mercy," by His saying ﴿O Prophet, God is sufficient for you, and for those who follow you of the believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 64], and He said: ﴿And God will protect you from the people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67]. If it is said: does not His saying ﴿and for those who follow you of the believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 64] imply that Muhammad leans upon the believers? We say: His saying ﴿and for those who follow you of the believers﴾ [al-Anfal: 64] is conjoined with the "kaf" (you) in His saying ﴿God is sufficient for you﴾ [al-Anfal: 64], and the meaning is: God is sufficient for you, and sufficient for those who follow you of the believers.

The third: his saying ﴿And I beat down (leaves) with it for my sheep﴾, that is, I strike with it and beat the branches of the tree so that its leaves fall upon my sheep and they eat them. The lexicographers said: "hashsha 'ala ghanamihi, yahushshu" with a damma on the ha' in the imperfect; "hashashtu al-rajul, ahishshu" with a fatha on the ha' in the imperfect; and "hashsha al-raghif, yahishshu" with a kasra on the ha'. This was said by Tha'lab. And Ikrimah recited "wa-ahissu" with an unpointed sin. Al-hashsh means driving away the sheep. Know that his sheep are his flock, so he began with the interests of himself in his saying ﴿I lean upon it﴾, then with the interests of his flock in his saying ﴿and I beat down (leaves) with it for my sheep﴾. Likewise on the Day of Resurrection he begins with himself and says: "Myself, myself." Yet Muhammad (ﷺ) did not occupy himself in this world except with setting right the affairs of the community: ﴿God would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33], and "O God, guide my people, for they do not know." Therefore, without doubt, on the Day of Resurrection he too begins with his community, and says: "My community, my community."

The fourth: his saying ﴿And in it I have other uses﴾, that is, needs and benefits. Its singular is ma'raba, with a fatha or damma on the ra'. Ibn al-A'rabi and Qutrub also related it with a kasra on the ra'. Al-arab with a fatha on the ra', and al-irbah with a kasra on the alif and sukun on the ra', mean need. He said "other" (ukhra) only because al-ma'arib carries the sense of a group; so it is as if he said: "a group of needs, other." Had it been "ukhar" it would have been correct, as in His saying ﴿then a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184]. Then here there are subtle points:

The first: when he heard God's saying ﴿And what is that in your right hand﴾, he knew that God has great secrets in it, so he mentioned what he knew, and referred to the rest, which he did not know in detail but only in summary, by his saying ﴿And in it I have other uses﴾.

The second: Musa, peace be upon him, sensed that He asked him about the matter of the staff only for great benefits. So Musa said: "My God, this staff is nothing but like any other, but since You asked about it, I know that there are for me in it other uses. Among them is that You spoke to me by means of it, and I found this great and noble matter by means of it."

The third: Musa, peace be upon him, hoped that his Lord would ask him about those uses, so that he would hear God's speech once more, and the matter of conversation would be prolonged on account of that.

The fourth: because of gentleness his tongue was loosened, then astonishment overcame him, his tongue was cut off, and his thoughts were disordered, so he summarized once more. Then Wahb said: it had two prongs like a crook. When the branch grew long, he bent it with the crook; when it tried to break, he twisted it with the two prongs; and when he travelled, he placed it on his shoulder, hanging from it his equipment: the bow, the quiver, and the garments. When he was in the desert, he planted it and cast a cloak over it, and it became shade. It was also said: among its miracles, he would draw water with it, and it would lengthen with the length of the well, and its two prongs would become a bucket, and they would become two candles at night. When an enemy appeared, it would fight on his behalf. When he desired a fruit, he planted it and it would put forth leaves and bear fruit. He would carry his provisions and water on it, and it would walk alongside him. When he planted it, water would spring forth, and when he lifted it, the water would recede. It would also protect him from venomous creatures.

Know that when Musa, peace be upon him, mentioned these answers, God Most High commanded him to throw down the staff, saying ﴿Throw it down, O Musa.﴾ And in this there are subtle points:

The first: when he, peace be upon him, said ﴿And in it I have other uses﴾, God wished to make him know that in it there is another use which he does not perceive or know, and that it is greater than all his other uses. So He said ﴿Throw it down, O Musa﴾ ﴿So he threw it down, and behold, it was a serpent, moving swiftly.﴾
