The fourth benefit: His saying, ﴿When your sister walked﴾. Know that the governing element for ﴿when she walked﴾ is either "I cast" or "you be brought up." It is narrated that when the news spread in Egypt that the people of Pharaoh had taken a boy from the Nile, and he would not suckle from the breast of any woman brought to him, because God had forbidden him the wet-nurses other than his mother, they were compelled to search among the women. When Moses' sister saw this, she came to them disguised and said, ﴿Shall I direct you to a household that will nurse him for you?﴾ Then she brought the mother, and he accepted her breast. Thus he returned to his mother through the subtle arrangement God had devised for him. As for His saying, ﴿So We returned you to your mother﴾, meaning "We restored you," and He said in another place, ﴿So We returned him to his mother﴾ [al-Qasas: 13]. It is like His saying, ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99], meaning, "Return me to the world." As for His saying, ﴿that her eye might be comforted and she not grieve﴾, the meaning is that the purpose of returning you to her is the attainment of joy for her and the removal of sorrow from her. If it is said: had He said, "that she not grieve and her eye be comforted," the speech would be meaningful, since the negation of grief does not necessitate the attainment of joy for her; but since He first said, "that her eye be comforted," His saying afterwards, "and she not grieve," is superfluous, for whenever joy is attained, the removal of sorrow is inevitable. We say: the meaning is that her eye is comforted by means of your arrival to her, so sorrow is removed from her because the milk of another does not reach your inner being.

The fifth benefit: His saying, ﴿And you killed a soul, and We saved you from the distress﴾. Its meaning: you killed a soul after your old age, namely the man whom he killed by mistake, by striking him, when the Israelite sought his help against him, and he was a Copt. Thus distress came to him from two directions:

One of them: from the punishment of this world, which is Pharaoh's retaliation against him, as God related: ﴿So he became in the city, fearful and watchful﴾ [al-Qasas: 18]. The other: from the punishment of God, since he killed without God's command. So God saved him from both distresses: from Pharaoh, when He enabled him to emigrate to Madyan; and from the punishment of the Hereafter, because He, glorified and exalted, forgave him for that.

The sixth benefit: His saying, ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾. Regarding it there are discussions:

The first discussion: concerning His saying ﴿with a testing (futunan)﴾ there are two views:
One: it is a verbal noun like "ukuf" and "julus," and the meaning is "We tested you truly," according to their view of emphasizing reports with verbal nouns, like His saying, ﴿And God spoke to Moses with speech﴾ [al-Nisa': 164].
The second: it is the plural of fatn or fitnah, with the feminine ta disregarded, like ḥujūz and budūr from ḥujzah and badrah, meaning: "We tested you with various kinds of trials." Here there are two questions:

Question one: God enumerated the kinds of His favors upon Moses, peace be upon him, in this context, so how does His saying ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾ fit this place? The answer to this has two parts:
One: testing (fitnah) is the intensification of an ordeal. It is said, "So-and-so was tested in his religion" when the ordeal became severe upon him until he turned away from his religion. God said: ﴿So when he is harmed for God's sake, he regards the trial of people as the punishment of God﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 10]. And God said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Do people think they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested? And We did test those before them, and God will surely make evident those who are truthful and will surely make evident the liars﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 1–3]. And He said: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed on before you? They were touched by hardship and adversity and were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of God?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214]. So the shaking mentioned in the verse, and the touching of hardship and adversity, are the fitnah and the futun. Since intensification of an ordeal is something that necessitates abundant reward, God counted it among the blessings without doubt.

Two: ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾
meaning: We purified you with purification, from the saying "fatantu al-dhahab min al-fiddah" when you wish to separate it (refine gold from silver). Sa'id ibn Jubayr asked Ibn 'Abbas about the futun, and he said: "Let us begin it for him by day, O Ibn Jubayr." Then when morning came, Ibn 'Abbas began reciting to him the verses concerning Moses, peace be upon him, from the beginning of his affair. He mentioned the story of Pharaoh and his killing of the sons of the Children of Israel, then the story of Moses, peace be upon him, being cast into the river, and the picking up of him by Pharaoh's household, and his refusal to nurse from foreign women; then the story that Moses, peace be upon him, seized Pharaoh's beard and placed the ember in his mouth; then the story of the killing of the Copt; then his flight to Madyan, and his becoming a hired man for Shu'ayb, peace be upon him; then his return to Egypt, and that he lost the way on the dark night, and his seeking comfort from the fire from the tree. And at the completion of each of these he would say, "This is among the testings, O Ibn Jubayr."

Question two: Is it valid to apply the name "al-Fattan" to Him, glorified, derived from His saying ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾? The answer: No; because it is a term of blame in common usage, and the names of God, exalted, are tawqifiyyah (fixed by revelation), especially in what gives an impression of what is not fitting.

* * *

The seventh benefit: His saying, exalted: ﴿Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan; then you came at a predestined time, O Moses﴾. Know that the implied sense is: ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾, so you went out in fear to the people of Madyan, and you stayed years among them. As for the duration of the stay, Abu Muslim said: it is explained in His saying, ﴿And when he turned toward Madyan﴾ up to His saying, ﴿When Moses had fulfilled the term﴾ [al-Qasas: 29]; and it is either ten or eight, according to His saying, ﴿On condition that you hire yourself to me for eight years, and if you complete ten, it is from you﴾ [al-Qasas: 27]. Wahb said: Moses, peace be upon him, stayed with Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, for twenty-eight years, of which ten years were the bride-price of his wife. The verse indicates that he, peace be upon him, stayed with him ten years, and there is nothing in it that negates an addition beyond the ten.

Know that His saying, ﴿Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan﴾ after His saying, ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾, is like an indication that his stay in Madyan was among the testings, and so it was. He, peace be upon him, bore, because of poverty and estrangement, many ordeals, and needed to hire himself out. As for His saying, exalted, ﴿Then you came at a predestined time, O Moses﴾, there must be an omission in the speech, because it was at a predestined measure of some matter. The commentators mentioned several possibilities for that omitted element:

One: it had preceded in My decree and My predestination that I would make you My messenger at a specified time that I had appointed for that, so you came only at that predestination, not before it nor after it. From this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, We created all things according to a measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49].

Two: at a measure of time in which revelation is sent down to the prophets, and that is at the head of forty years.

Three: that the predestination is the appointed time. If it is established that this appointment had preceded, it is valid to interpret it as such, and there is nothing to prevent that, given the possibility that Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, or other prophets had been assigned that appointed time. If it is said: how does God mention Moses' coming at that time among His favors upon him? We say: because, had it not been for His enabling him to do so, nothing of that would have been arranged.

* * *

The eighth benefit: His saying, exalted: ﴿And I have made you for Myself﴾. Istina' means taking up a craft, and it is an ifti'al form from sun'. It is said: "So-and-so made so-and-so" (iṣṭana'a fulan fulanan), i.e., took him as his protégé. If it is said: He, exalted, is independent of all; so what is the meaning of His saying ﴿for Myself﴾? The answer to this has several parts:

One: this is a figure of speech, for when He, exalted, gave him the rank of nearness, honor, and speaking, He likened his state to the state of one whom some kings see as possessing comprehensive qualities, making him fit to be the closest of people in rank to them and the nearest of them to them.

Two: the Mu'tazilah said: when He, glorified and exalted, imposes obligations on His servants, it is obligatory upon Him to show them kindness (lutf). Among the kindnesses are some that are known only through revelation. So if He had not made him a chosen one by the messengership, he would have remained under the obligation of what is required. Thus Moses, peace be upon him, became like a deputy for his Lord in carrying out what was incumbent upon God, the exalted. So it is correct for Him to say, ﴿And I have made you for Myself﴾. Al-Qaffal said: ﴿And I have made you﴾ originates from the saying of people, "So-and-so made so-and-so" when he did good to him until he was attributed to him, so it is said, "This is so-and-so's creation, so-and-so's wounded one." His saying
Page 50
﴿for Myself﴾: meaning, that I might direct you in My commands, so that you would not occupy yourself with anything other than what I commanded you, which is establishing My proof, conveying My message, and that your movements and stillnesses be for Me, not for yourself nor for others. Know that when He, glorified and exalted, enumerated for him the eight favors in return for those eight requests, He arranged upon the mention of that a command and a prohibition. As for the command, He, glorified and exalted, repeated the first command, saying: ﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs﴾. Know that when He, glorified and exalted, said, ﴿And I have made you for Myself﴾, He followed it with mention of what He made him for, which is conveyance and delivery. Then there are issues here:

First issue: the ba' here means "with"; for if they went to him without a sign with them, belief would not be binding upon him, and that is among the strongest proofs against the invalidity of taqlid (blind imitation).

Second issue: they differed about the signs mentioned here, on three views:

**[Part 2 of 2]**

The first view: they are the hand and the staff, because these are the two that are mentioned in this passage and in the other places where God related the story of Musa (peace be upon him). In none of these places does God mention that he (peace be upon him) was given a sign before he came to Pharaoh or after he came to Pharaoh and met him. Pharaoh then demanded from him a sign other than these two signs. God said about him: ﴿So bring it, if you are of the truthful﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 154], and He said: ﴿So he cast down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent﴾ [al-A'raf: 107], ﴿and he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers﴾ [al-A'raf: 108], and He said: ﴿These two are proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ [al-Qasas: 32]. If it is asked of these scholars, "How is the plural form used for two?", they answered with several explanations:

The first: the staff was not a single sign, but rather several signs. The transformation of the staff into a living creature is one sign. Then, at the beginning, it was small, as in His saying: ﴿it moved as though it were a jinn﴾ [al-Naml: 10]. Then it would grow large, and this is another sign. Then it would become a serpent, and this is another sign. Then Musa (peace be upon him) would put his hand into its mouth, and it would not harm Musa (peace be upon him), and this is another sign. Then it would turn back into a piece of wood, and this is another sign. Likewise with the hand: its whiteness is a sign, its radiance is another sign, and then their disappearance after they had appeared is another sign. Thus it is correct that the two were many signs, not two signs.

The second: suppose the staff was one matter. Nevertheless, there are many signs in it, because its transformation into a living serpent indicates the existence of a God who is capable of all things, all-knowing of all things, and wise. It also indicates the prophethood of Musa (peace be upon him), and it indicates the possibility of resurrection, since an inanimate object became a living creature. These are many signs. For this reason He said: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds. In it are clear signs: the station of Ibrahim﴾ [Al 'Imran: 96–97]. When one thing is described as containing signs, then two things are more deserving of this description.

The third: some people said: the least number of the plural is two, as you know from the discussions in *usul al-fiqh* (the principles of jurisprudence).

The second view: His saying "Go with My signs" means: I am supplying you both with My signs, and I will manifest through your hands signs by which the proofs against Pharaoh and his people are removed. So go, for My signs are with you both, just as one says, "Go, for My soldiers are with you," meaning: I will supply them to you whenever you need them.

The third view: God gave him the staff and the hand, and He loosened the knot of his tongue, and that too is a miracle. Thus the signs become three. This is the explanation of the command. As for the prohibition, it is His saying: ﴿and do not slacken in My remembrance﴾. *Al-wany* means slackness and negligence. It is recited as *wa-la tiniya* with a kasra on the letter of the present tense for harmonization (*ittiba'*). Then several views were stated about it:

The first: the meaning is, "Do not slacken; rather, take My remembrance as a means to attain your aims, and believe that no matter can be accomplished for anyone except through My remembrance." The wisdom in this is that whoever remembers the majesty of God regards everything else as insignificant, so he fears no one. Also, whoever remembers the majesty of God has his spirit strengthened by that remembrance, so he does not weaken in pursuing his aim. Also, whoever remembers God must be remembering His favor, and one who remembers His favor does not slacken in carrying out His commands.

The second: the intended meaning of "remembrance" is conveying the message, for the term "remembrance" applies to all acts of worship, and conveying the message is among the greatest of them, so it was fitting that it be called "remembrance."

The third: His saying "and do not slacken in My remembrance" refers to [remembrance] before Pharaoh. The manner of this remembrance is that they should tell Pharaoh and his people that God does not accept disbelief from them, and they should tell them about reward and punishment, and encourage and warn them.

The fourth: that they should remind Pharaoh of God's bounties, His blessings, and the various kinds of His favor toward him. Then after that He said: ﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed﴾. Here there are two questions:

The first: what is the benefit of this after His saying "Go, you and your brother, with My signs"? Al-Qaffal said: there are two answers to this:

One of them: His saying "Go, you and your brother, with My signs" may mean that each of them is commanded to go individually. So He said again, "Go," to make clear that what is intended is that they should both engage in this together, not that Harun alone should undertake it without Musa.

The second: His saying "Go, you and your brother, with My signs" is a command to go to all people, the Children of Israel and the people of Pharaoh. Then His saying "Go to Pharaoh" is a command to go to Pharaoh alone.

The second question: His saying "Go to Pharaoh" is addressed to Musa and Harun (peace be upon them both), and this is problematic, because Harun (peace be upon him) was not present there. The same applies to His saying: ﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 45]. Al-Qaffal answered this in several ways:

One of them: the speech was addressed to Musa (peace be upon him) alone, but he was the one who was followed by Harun, so the address to him was made an address to Harun as well. Harun's speech is understood by way of implication. Thus, in that situation, although the address was to Musa (peace be upon him) alone, God attributed it to both of them, as in His saying: ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72], and His saying: ﴿If we return to Medina, the more honorable will surely expel the more humble from it﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. It is related that the speaker was 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy alone.

The second: it is possible that when God said, "You have been given your request, O Musa" [Ta-Ha: 36], he remained silent until he met his brother. Then God addressed both of them with His saying: ﴿Go to Pharaoh﴾.

The third: it is related that in the codices of Ibn Mas'ud and Hafsah, the reading is: "He said, 'Our Lord, indeed we fear'", meaning that Musa said: "I and my brother fear Pharaoh."

As for His saying: ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech﴾, there are two questions:

The first question: why did God command Musa (peace be upon him) to be gentle with the disbelieving rejecter? The answer has two parts:

The first: he (peace be upon him) had been raised by Pharaoh, so he was commanded to address him gently, out of regard for those rights. This is an indication of the utmost honor due to one's parents.

The second: it is a habit of tyrants that when they are addressed harshly in admonition, they increase in arrogance and pride. The purpose of the mission is to achieve benefit, not to increase harm. For this reason God commanded gentleness.

The second question: what was that gentle speech like? They mentioned several answers:

One of them: what God related of part of it, when He said: ﴿Would you like to purify yourself? And I would guide you to your Lord, so that you would fear Him﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18–19]. He also mentioned in this surah part of it, when He said: ﴿So come to him and say, "Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord"﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And peace be upon him who follows guidance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47].

The second: that they promise him a youth that will not age after it, a kingship that will not be taken from him except by death, and that the pleasure of food, drink, and marriage remain with him until his death.

The third: they should address him with kunyas. He was one of the three people who had three kunyas: Abu al-'Abbas, Abu al-Walid, and Abu Murrah.

The fourth: it is related from 'Amr ibn Dinar that he said: "It has reached me that Pharaoh lived four hundred and nine years. Musa (peace be upon him) said to him: 'If you obey me, you will live as long as you have lived, and when you die, you will have Paradise.'" They raised objections to these last three answers.

As for the first: it was said that if these three matters were granted to him over this long period, that would amount to compulsion toward knowledge of God, and that is not valid alongside moral responsibility.

As for the second: addressing him by kunya is an easy matter, so it cannot be taken as the intended meaning of His saying ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech﴾. Rather, it may be part of what is intended.

As for the third: the objection to it is the same as to the first.

As for His saying: ﴿Perhaps he will remember or fear﴾, know that the intended meaning is not that God was in doubt about this, because doubt is impossible for God. Rather, the meaning is: "Speak to him gently, while you both hope that he may remember or fear." Know that the states of the heart are three:

One: persistence upon the truth.

Two: persistence upon falsehood.

Three: hesitation between the two matters. Pharaoh was persistent in falsehood, and this kind is the worst of the states. So God said: ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech, perhaps he will remember or fear﴾, so that he would turn from his denial to acknowledging the truth. Even if he did not move from denial to acknowledgment, fear would arise in his heart, and he would abandon denial. And even if he did not move to acknowledgment, this is better than persisting in denial.

Know that the secret of this obligation is known only to God. Since God knew that he would never believe, his belief would be the opposite of that knowledge, which cannot be reversed. Therefore He, glory be to Him, knows that such belief is impossible. And if this is so, how could He command Musa (peace be upon him) to such gentleness, and how could He insist on such a command, gently calling him to God, while knowing that this could not happen? Moreover, suppose the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) dispute this impossibility without offering any argument that undermines this question. Yet they concede that He knew he would not attain that belief, and they concede that Pharaoh gains nothing from the mission of Musa (peace be upon him) except deserving punishment. How is it fitting for the Merciful and Generous to hand a knife to one whom He knows for certain will tear open his own belly with it, and then say: "I did not intend by handing him the knife anything but kindness to him"? My brother, minds are too limited to grasp these secrets, and there is no path here except submission, leaving off objection, and silence of heart and tongue.

It is related from Ka'b that he said: "By Him by whom Ka'b swears, it is indeed written in the Torah: 'So speak to him with gentle speech, and I will harden his heart so that he will not believe.'"

[p. 52]

The third benefit (minnah): His saying, ﴿And that you might be brought up under My eye﴾. Al-Qaffal said: "That you might be seen under My eye" means according to My will. The metaphor is this: whoever makes something for a person while being present and watching him, makes it for him as he loves, and cannot do anything that contradicts his purpose. So it is here. There are two views on how the metaphor works:

The first: by "eye" is meant knowledge, "that you may be seen with knowledge from Me." Since one who knows a thing guards it from harms, just as one who watches it guards it from harms, the word "eye" was applied to knowledge because the two resemble each other in this respect.

The second: by "eye" is meant protection, because one who looks at a thing protects it from what would harm it, so the eye is like the cause of protection, and the name of the cause is applied to the effect metaphorically. This is like His saying, ﴿Indeed I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ [Taha: 46]. And it is said, "The eye of God be upon you," when one prays for someone's preservation and safeguarding. Al-Qadi said: The apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates that what is meant by His saying, ﴿And that you might be brought up under My eye﴾, is protection and safeguarding, like His saying, ﴿When your sister walked and said, "Shall I direct you to one who will nurse him?" So We returned you to your mother that her eye might be comforted and she not grieve﴾. Thus that serves as an explanation of God's safeguarding of him. Two discussions remain here:

The first: the waw in His saying, ﴿And that you might be brought up under My eye﴾ has three possible readings:
One: it is as if it were said, "And I cast upon you love from Me, that you might be brought up under My eye." Then His saying, ﴿When your sister walked﴾ is connected to the beginning of the speech, which is His saying, ﴿And We conferred favor upon you another time, when We inspired to your mother what is inspired﴾, and "when your sister walked."
Two: it is permissible that His saying ﴿And that you might be brought up under My eye﴾ is connected to what follows it, which is His saying, ﴿When [your sister] walked﴾. We mentioned similar two readings in His saying, ﴿And that he might be among the certain [in faith]﴾ [al-An'am: 75].
Three: it is permissible that the waw is superfluous, meaning, "And I cast upon you love from Me, so that you would be brought up." This is weak.

The second: it was read as "wa-li-tuṣna'a" with the lam both kasra and sukun; the jazm (jussive) reading is on the basis that it is an imperative. It was also read as "wa-li-taṣna'a" with a fatha on the ta and the subjunctive, meaning: "and that your work and conduct would be with knowledge from Me."

* * *

The fourth benefit: His saying, ﴿When your sister walked﴾. Know that the governing element for ﴿when she walked﴾ is either "I cast" or "you be brought up." It is narrated that when the news spread in Egypt that the people of Pharaoh had taken a boy from the Nile, and he would not suckle from the breast of any woman brought to him, because God had forbidden him the wet-nurses other than his mother, they were compelled to search among the women. When Moses' sister saw this, she came to them disguised and said, ﴿Shall I direct you to a household that will nurse him for you?﴾ Then she brought the mother, and he accepted her breast. Thus he returned to his mother through the subtle arrangement God had devised for him. As for His saying, ﴿So We returned you to your mother﴾, meaning "We restored you," and He said in another place, ﴿So We returned him to his mother﴾ [al-Qasas: 13]. It is like His saying, ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99], meaning, "Return me to the world." As for His saying, ﴿that her eye might be comforted and she not grieve﴾, the meaning is that the purpose of returning you to her is the attainment of joy for her and the removal of sorrow from her. If it is said: had He said, "that she not grieve and her eye be comforted," the speech would be meaningful, since the negation of grief does not necessitate the attainment of joy for her; but since He first said, "that her eye be comforted," His saying afterwards, "and she not grieve," is superfluous, for whenever joy is attained, the removal of sorrow is inevitable. We say: the meaning is that her eye is comforted by means of your arrival to her, so sorrow is removed from her because the milk of another does not reach your inner being.

The fifth benefit: His saying, ﴿And you killed a soul, and We saved you from the distress﴾. Its meaning: you killed a soul after your old age, namely the man whom he killed by mistake, by striking him, when the Israelite sought his help against him, and he was a Copt. Thus distress came to him from two directions:

One of them: from the punishment of this world, which is Pharaoh's retaliation against him, as God related: ﴿So he became in the city, fearful and watchful﴾ [al-Qasas: 18]. The other: from the punishment of God, since he killed without God's command. So God saved him from both distresses: from Pharaoh, when He enabled him to emigrate to Madyan; and from the punishment of the Hereafter, because He, glorified and exalted, forgave him for that.

meaning: We purified you with purification, from the saying "fatantu al-dhahab min al-fiddah" when you wish to separate it (refine gold from silver). The answer: No; because it is a term of blame in common usage, and the names of God, exalted, are tawqifiyyah (fixed by revelation), especially in what gives an impression of what is not fitting.

The seventh benefit: His saying, exalted: ﴿Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan; then you came at a predestined time, O Moses﴾. Know that the implied sense is: ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾, so you went out in fear to the people of Madyan, and you stayed years among them. As for the duration of the stay, Abu Muslim said: it is explained in His saying, ﴿And when he turned toward Madyan﴾ up to His saying, ﴿When Moses had fulfilled the term﴾ [al-Qasas: 29]; and it is either ten or eight, according to His saying, ﴿On condition that you hire yourself to me for eight years, and if you complete ten, it is from you﴾ [al-Qasas: 27]. Wahb said: Moses, peace be upon him, stayed with Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, for twenty-eight years, of which ten years were the bride-price of his wife. The verse indicates that he, peace be upon him, stayed with him ten years, and there is nothing in it that negates an addition beyond the ten.

Know that His saying, ﴿Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan﴾ after His saying, ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾, is like an indication that his stay in Madyan was among the testings, and so it was. He, peace be upon him, bore, because of poverty and estrangement, many ordeals, and needed to hire himself out. As for His saying, exalted, ﴿Then you came at a predestined time, O Moses﴾, there must be an omission in the speech, because it was at a predestined measure of some matter. The commentators mentioned several possibilities for that omitted element:

One: it had preceded in My decree and My predestination that I would make you My messenger at a specified time that I had appointed for that, so you came only at that predestination, not before it nor after it. From this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, We created all things according to a measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49].

Two: at a measure of time in which revelation is sent down to the prophets, and that is at the head of forty years.

Three: that the predestination is the appointed time. If it is established that this appointment had preceded, it is valid to interpret it as such, and there is nothing to prevent that, given the possibility that Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, or other prophets had been assigned that appointed time. If it is said: how does God mention Moses' coming at that time among His favors upon him? We say: because, had it not been for His enabling him to do so, nothing of that would have been arranged.

* * *

The eighth benefit: His saying, exalted: ﴿And I have made you for Myself﴾. Istina' means taking up a craft, and it is an ifti'al form from sun'. It is said: "So-and-so made so-and-so" (iṣṭana'a fulan fulanan), i.e., took him as his protégé. If it is said: He, exalted, is independent of all; so what is the meaning of His saying ﴿for Myself﴾? The answer to this has several parts:

One: this is a figure of speech, for when He, exalted, gave him the rank of nearness, honor, and speaking, He likened his state to the state of one whom some kings see as possessing comprehensive qualities, making him fit to be the closest of people in rank to them and the nearest of them to them.

Two: the Mu'tazilah said: when He, glorified and exalted, imposes obligations on His servants, it is obligatory upon Him to show them kindness (lutf). Among the kindnesses are some that are known only through revelation. So if He had not made him a chosen one by the messengership, he would have remained under the obligation of what is required. Thus Moses, peace be upon him, became like a deputy for his Lord in carrying out what was incumbent upon God, the exalted. So it is correct for Him to say, ﴿And I have made you for Myself﴾. Al-Qaffal said: ﴿And I have made you﴾ originates from the saying of people, "So-and-so made so-and-so" when he did good to him until he was attributed to him, so it is said, "This is so-and-so's creation, so-and-so's wounded one." His saying

﴿for Myself﴾: meaning, that I might direct you in My commands, so that you would not occupy yourself with anything other than what I commanded you, which is establishing My proof, conveying My message, and that your movements and stillnesses be for Me, not for yourself nor for others. Know that when He, glorified and exalted, enumerated for him the eight favors in return for those eight requests, He arranged upon the mention of that a command and a prohibition. As for the command, He, glorified and exalted, repeated the first command, saying: ﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs﴾. Know that when He, glorified and exalted, said, ﴿And I have made you for Myself﴾, He followed it with mention of what He made him for, which is conveyance and delivery. Then there are issues here:

First issue: the ba' here means "with"; for if they went to him without a sign with them, belief would not be binding upon him, and that is among the strongest proofs against the invalidity of taqlid (blind imitation).

Second issue: they differed about the signs mentioned here, on three views:

**[Part 2 of 2]**

The first view: they are the hand and the staff, because these are the two that are mentioned in this passage and in the other places where God related the story of Musa (peace be upon him). In none of these places does God mention that he (peace be upon him) was given a sign before he came to Pharaoh or after he came to Pharaoh and met him. Pharaoh then demanded from him a sign other than these two signs. God said about him: ﴿So bring it, if you are of the truthful﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 154], and He said: ﴿So he cast down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent﴾ [al-A'raf: 107], ﴿and he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers﴾ [al-A'raf: 108], and He said: ﴿These two are proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ [al-Qasas: 32]. If it is asked of these scholars, "How is the plural form used for two?", they answered with several explanations:

The first: the staff was not a single sign, but rather several signs. The transformation of the staff into a living creature is one sign. Then, at the beginning, it was small, as in His saying: ﴿it moved as though it were a jinn﴾ [al-Naml: 10]. Then it would grow large, and this is another sign. Then it would become a serpent, and this is another sign. Then Musa (peace be upon him) would put his hand into its mouth, and it would not harm Musa (peace be upon him), and this is another sign. Then it would turn back into a piece of wood, and this is another sign. Likewise with the hand: its whiteness is a sign, its radiance is another sign, and then their disappearance after they had appeared is another sign. Thus it is correct that the two were many signs, not two signs.

The second: suppose the staff was one matter. Nevertheless, there are many signs in it, because its transformation into a living serpent indicates the existence of a God who is capable of all things, all-knowing of all things, and wise. It also indicates the prophethood of Musa (peace be upon him), and it indicates the possibility of resurrection, since an inanimate object became a living creature. These are many signs. For this reason He said: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds. In it are clear signs: the station of Ibrahim﴾ [Al 'Imran: 96–97]. When one thing is described as containing signs, then two things are more deserving of this description.

The third: some people said: the least number of the plural is two, as you know from the discussions in *usul al-fiqh* (the principles of jurisprudence).

The second view: His saying "Go with My signs" means: I am supplying you both with My signs, and I will manifest through your hands signs by which the proofs against Pharaoh and his people are removed. So go, for My signs are with you both, just as one says, "Go, for My soldiers are with you," meaning: I will supply them to you whenever you need them.

The third view: God gave him the staff and the hand, and He loosened the knot of his tongue, and that too is a miracle. Thus the signs become three. This is the explanation of the command. As for the prohibition, it is His saying: ﴿and do not slacken in My remembrance﴾. *Al-wany* means slackness and negligence. It is recited as *wa-la tiniya* with a kasra on the letter of the present tense for harmonization (*ittiba'*). Then several views were stated about it:

The first: the meaning is, "Do not slacken; rather, take My remembrance as a means to attain your aims, and believe that no matter can be accomplished for anyone except through My remembrance." The wisdom in this is that whoever remembers the majesty of God regards everything else as insignificant, so he fears no one. Also, whoever remembers the majesty of God has his spirit strengthened by that remembrance, so he does not weaken in pursuing his aim. Also, whoever remembers God must be remembering His favor, and one who remembers His favor does not slacken in carrying out His commands.

The second: the intended meaning of "remembrance" is conveying the message, for the term "remembrance" applies to all acts of worship, and conveying the message is among the greatest of them, so it was fitting that it be called "remembrance."

The third: His saying "and do not slacken in My remembrance" refers to [remembrance] before Pharaoh. The manner of this remembrance is that they should tell Pharaoh and his people that God does not accept disbelief from them, and they should tell them about reward and punishment, and encourage and warn them.

The fourth: that they should remind Pharaoh of God's bounties, His blessings, and the various kinds of His favor toward him. Then after that He said: ﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed﴾. Here there are two questions:

The first: what is the benefit of this after His saying "Go, you and your brother, with My signs"? Al-Qaffal said: there are two answers to this:

One of them: His saying "Go, you and your brother, with My signs" may mean that each of them is commanded to go individually. So He said again, "Go," to make clear that what is intended is that they should both engage in this together, not that Harun alone should undertake it without Musa.

The second: His saying "Go, you and your brother, with My signs" is a command to go to all people, the Children of Israel and the people of Pharaoh. Then His saying "Go to Pharaoh" is a command to go to Pharaoh alone.

The second question: His saying "Go to Pharaoh" is addressed to Musa and Harun (peace be upon them both), and this is problematic, because Harun (peace be upon him) was not present there. The same applies to His saying: ﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 45]. Al-Qaffal answered this in several ways:

One of them: the speech was addressed to Musa (peace be upon him) alone, but he was the one who was followed by Harun, so the address to him was made an address to Harun as well. Harun's speech is understood by way of implication. Thus, in that situation, although the address was to Musa (peace be upon him) alone, God attributed it to both of them, as in His saying: ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72], and His saying: ﴿If we return to Medina, the more honorable will surely expel the more humble from it﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. It is related that the speaker was 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy alone.

The second: it is possible that when God said, "You have been given your request, O Musa" [Ta-Ha: 36], he remained silent until he met his brother. Then God addressed both of them with His saying: ﴿Go to Pharaoh﴾.

The third: it is related that in the codices of Ibn Mas'ud and Hafsah, the reading is: "He said, 'Our Lord, indeed we fear'", meaning that Musa said: "I and my brother fear Pharaoh."

As for His saying: ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech﴾, there are two questions:

The first question: why did God command Musa (peace be upon him) to be gentle with the disbelieving rejecter? The answer has two parts:

The first: he (peace be upon him) had been raised by Pharaoh, so he was commanded to address him gently, out of regard for those rights. This is an indication of the utmost honor due to one's parents.

The second: it is a habit of tyrants that when they are addressed harshly in admonition, they increase in arrogance and pride. The purpose of the mission is to achieve benefit, not to increase harm. For this reason God commanded gentleness.

The second question: what was that gentle speech like? They mentioned several answers:

One of them: what God related of part of it, when He said: ﴿Would you like to purify yourself? And I would guide you to your Lord, so that you would fear Him﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18–19]. He also mentioned in this surah part of it, when He said: ﴿So come to him and say, "Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord"﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And peace be upon him who follows guidance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47].

The second: that they promise him a youth that will not age after it, a kingship that will not be taken from him except by death, and that the pleasure of food, drink, and marriage remain with him until his death.

The third: they should address him with kunyas. He was one of the three people who had three kunyas: Abu al-'Abbas, Abu al-Walid, and Abu Murrah.

The fourth: it is related from 'Amr ibn Dinar that he said: "It has reached me that Pharaoh lived four hundred and nine years. Musa (peace be upon him) said to him: 'If you obey me, you will live as long as you have lived, and when you die, you will have Paradise.'" They raised objections to these last three answers.

As for the first: it was said that if these three matters were granted to him over this long period, that would amount to compulsion toward knowledge of God, and that is not valid alongside moral responsibility.

As for the second: addressing him by kunya is an easy matter, so it cannot be taken as the intended meaning of His saying ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech﴾. Rather, it may be part of what is intended.

As for the third: the objection to it is the same as to the first.

As for His saying: ﴿Perhaps he will remember or fear﴾, know that the intended meaning is not that God was in doubt about this, because doubt is impossible for God. Rather, the meaning is: "Speak to him gently, while you both hope that he may remember or fear." Know that the states of the heart are three:

One: persistence upon the truth.

Two: persistence upon falsehood.

Three: hesitation between the two matters. Pharaoh was persistent in falsehood, and this kind is the worst of the states. So God said: ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech, perhaps he will remember or fear﴾, so that he would turn from his denial to acknowledging the truth. Even if he did not move from denial to acknowledgment, fear would arise in his heart, and he would abandon denial. And even if he did not move to acknowledgment, this is better than persisting in denial.

Know that the secret of this obligation is known only to God. Since God knew that he would never believe, his belief would be the opposite of that knowledge, which cannot be reversed. Therefore He, glory be to Him, knows that such belief is impossible. And if this is so, how could He command Musa (peace be upon him) to such gentleness, and how could He insist on such a command, gently calling him to God, while knowing that this could not happen? Moreover, suppose the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) dispute this impossibility without offering any argument that undermines this question. Yet they concede that He knew he would not attain that belief, and they concede that Pharaoh gains nothing from the mission of Musa (peace be upon him) except deserving punishment. How is it fitting for the Merciful and Generous to hand a knife to one whom He knows for certain will tear open his own belly with it, and then say: "I did not intend by handing him the knife anything but kindness to him"? My brother, minds are too limited to grasp these secrets, and there is no path here except submission, leaving off objection, and silence of heart and tongue.

It is related from Ka'b that he said: "By Him by whom Ka'b swears, it is indeed written in the Torah: 'So speak to him with gentle speech, and I will harden his heart so that he will not believe.'"

[p. 52]

The third benefit (minnah): His saying, ﴿And that you might be brought up under My eye﴾. Al-Qaffal said: "That you might be seen under My eye" means according to My will. The metaphor is this: whoever makes something for a person while being present and watching him, makes it for him as he loves, and cannot do anything that contradicts his purpose. So it is here. There are two views on how the metaphor works:

The first: by "eye" is meant knowledge, "that you may be seen with knowledge from Me." Since one who knows a thing guards it from harms, just as one who watches it guards it from harms, the word "eye" was applied to knowledge because the two resemble each other in this respect.

The second: by "eye" is meant protection, because one who looks at a thing protects it from what would harm it, so the eye is like the cause of protection, and the name of the cause is applied to the effect metaphorically. This is like His saying, ﴿Indeed I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ [Taha: 46]. And it is said, "The eye of God be upon you," when one prays for someone's preservation and safeguarding. Al-Qadi said: The apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates that what is meant by His saying, ﴿And that you might be brought up under My eye﴾, is protection and safeguarding, like His saying, ﴿When your sister walked and said, "Shall I direct you to one who will nurse him?" So We returned you to your mother that her eye might be comforted and she not grieve﴾. Thus that serves as an explanation of God's safeguarding of him. Two discussions remain here:

The first: the waw in His saying, ﴿And that you might be brought up under My eye﴾ has three possible readings:
One: it is as if it were said, "And I cast upon you love from Me, that you might be brought up under My eye." Then His saying, ﴿When your sister walked﴾ is connected to the beginning of the speech, which is His saying, ﴿And We conferred favor upon you another time, when We inspired to your mother what is inspired﴾, and "when your sister walked."
Two: it is permissible that His saying ﴿And that you might be brought up under My eye﴾ is connected to what follows it, which is His saying, ﴿When [your sister] walked﴾. We mentioned similar two readings in His saying, ﴿And that he might be among the certain [in faith]﴾ [al-An'am: 75].
Three: it is permissible that the waw is superfluous, meaning, "And I cast upon you love from Me, so that you would be brought up." This is weak.

The second: it was read as "wa-li-tuṣna'a" with the lam both kasra and sukun; the jazm (jussive) reading is on the basis that it is an imperative. It was also read as "wa-li-taṣna'a" with a fatha on the ta and the subjunctive, meaning: "and that your work and conduct would be with knowledge from Me."

* * *

The fourth benefit: His saying, ﴿When your sister walked﴾. Know that the governing element for ﴿when she walked﴾ is either "I cast" or "you be brought up." It is narrated that when the news spread in Egypt that the people of Pharaoh had taken a boy from the Nile, and he would not suckle from the breast of any woman brought to him, because God had forbidden him the wet-nurses other than his mother, they were compelled to search among the women. When Moses' sister saw this, she came to them disguised and said, ﴿Shall I direct you to a household that will nurse him for you?﴾ Then she brought the mother, and he accepted her breast. Thus he returned to his mother through the subtle arrangement God had devised for him. As for His saying, ﴿So We returned you to your mother﴾, meaning "We restored you," and He said in another place, ﴿So We returned him to his mother﴾ [al-Qasas: 13]. It is like His saying, ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99], meaning, "Return me to the world." As for His saying, ﴿that her eye might be comforted and she not grieve﴾, the meaning is that the purpose of returning you to her is the attainment of joy for her and the removal of sorrow from her. If it is said: had He said, "that she not grieve and her eye be comforted," the speech would be meaningful, since the negation of grief does not necessitate the attainment of joy for her; but since He first said, "that her eye be comforted," His saying afterwards, "and she not grieve," is superfluous, for whenever joy is attained, the removal of sorrow is inevitable. We say: the meaning is that her eye is comforted by means of your arrival to her, so sorrow is removed from her because the milk of another does not reach your inner being.

The fifth benefit: His saying, ﴿And you killed a soul, and We saved you from the distress﴾. Its meaning: you killed a soul after your old age, namely the man whom he killed by mistake, by striking him, when the Israelite sought his help against him, and he was a Copt. Thus distress came to him from two directions:

One of them: from the punishment of this world, which is Pharaoh's retaliation against him, as God related: ﴿So he became in the city, fearful and watchful﴾ [al-Qasas: 18]. The other: from the punishment of God, since he killed without God's command. So God saved him from both distresses: from Pharaoh, when He enabled him to emigrate to Madyan; and from the punishment of the Hereafter, because He, glorified and exalted, forgave him for that.

The sixth benefit: His saying, ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾. Regarding it there are discussions:

The first discussion: concerning His saying ﴿with a testing (futunan)﴾ there are two views:
One: it is a verbal noun like "ukuf" and "julus," and the meaning is "We tested you truly," according to their view of emphasizing reports with verbal nouns, like His saying, ﴿And God spoke to Moses with speech﴾ [al-Nisa': 164].
The second: it is the plural of fatn or fitnah, with the feminine ta disregarded, like ḥujūz and budūr from ḥujzah and badrah, meaning: "We tested you with various kinds of trials." Here there are two questions:

Question one: God enumerated the kinds of His favors upon Moses, peace be upon him, in this context, so how does His saying ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾ fit this place? The answer to this has two parts:
One: testing (fitnah) is the intensification of an ordeal. It is said, "So-and-so was tested in his religion" when the ordeal became severe upon him until he turned away from his religion. God said: ﴿So when he is harmed for God's sake, he regards the trial of people as the punishment of God﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 10]. And God said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Do people think they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested? And We did test those before them, and God will surely make evident those who are truthful and will surely make evident the liars﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 1–3]. And He said: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed on before you? They were touched by hardship and adversity and were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of God?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214]. So the shaking mentioned in the verse, and the touching of hardship and adversity, are the fitnah and the futun. Since intensification of an ordeal is something that necessitates abundant reward, God counted it among the blessings without doubt.

Two: ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾
meaning: We purified you with purification, from the saying "fatantu al-dhahab min al-fiddah" when you wish to separate it (refine gold from silver). Sa'id ibn Jubayr asked Ibn 'Abbas about the futun, and he said: "Let us begin it for him by day, O Ibn Jubayr." Then when morning came, Ibn 'Abbas began reciting to him the verses concerning Moses, peace be upon him, from the beginning of his affair. He mentioned the story of Pharaoh and his killing of the sons of the Children of Israel, then the story of Moses, peace be upon him, being cast into the river, and the picking up of him by Pharaoh's household, and his refusal to nurse from foreign women; then the story that Moses, peace be upon him, seized Pharaoh's beard and placed the ember in his mouth; then the story of the killing of the Copt; then his flight to Madyan, and his becoming a hired man for Shu'ayb, peace be upon him; then his return to Egypt, and that he lost the way on the dark night, and his seeking comfort from the fire from the tree. And at the completion of each of these he would say, "This is among the testings, O Ibn Jubayr."

Question two: Is it valid to apply the name "al-Fattan" to Him, glorified, derived from His saying ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾? The answer: No; because it is a term of blame in common usage, and the names of God, exalted, are tawqifiyyah (fixed by revelation), especially in what gives an impression of what is not fitting.

**[Part 2 of 2]**

The first view: they are the hand and the staff, because these are the two that are mentioned in this passage and in the other places where God related the story of Musa (peace be upon him). In none of these places does God mention that he (peace be upon him) was given a sign before he came to Pharaoh or after he came to Pharaoh and met him. Pharaoh then demanded from him a sign other than these two signs. God said about him: ﴿So bring it, if you are of the truthful﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 154], and He said: ﴿So he cast down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent﴾ [al-A'raf: 107], ﴿and he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers﴾ [al-A'raf: 108], and He said: ﴿These two are proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ [al-Qasas: 32]. If it is asked of these scholars, "How is the plural form used for two?", they answered with several explanations:

The first: the staff was not a single sign, but rather several signs. The transformation of the staff into a living creature is one sign. Then, at the beginning, it was small, as in His saying: ﴿it moved as though it were a jinn﴾ [al-Naml: 10]. Then it would grow large, and this is another sign. Then it would become a serpent, and this is another sign. Then Musa (peace be upon him) would put his hand into its mouth, and it would not harm Musa (peace be upon him), and this is another sign. Then it would turn back into a piece of wood, and this is another sign. Likewise with the hand: its whiteness is a sign, its radiance is another sign, and then their disappearance after they had appeared is another sign. Thus it is correct that the two were many signs, not two signs.

The second: suppose the staff was one matter. Nevertheless, there are many signs in it, because its transformation into a living serpent indicates the existence of a God who is capable of all things, all-knowing of all things, and wise. It also indicates the prophethood of Musa (peace be upon him), and it indicates the possibility of resurrection, since an inanimate object became a living creature. These are many signs. For this reason He said: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds. In it are clear signs: the station of Ibrahim﴾ [Al 'Imran: 96–97]. When one thing is described as containing signs, then two things are more deserving of this description.

The third: some people said: the least number of the plural is two, as you know from the discussions in *usul al-fiqh* (the principles of jurisprudence).

The second view: His saying "Go with My signs" means: I am supplying you both with My signs, and I will manifest through your hands signs by which the proofs against Pharaoh and his people are removed. So go, for My signs are with you both, just as one says, "Go, for My soldiers are with you," meaning: I will supply them to you whenever you need them.

The third view: God gave him the staff and the hand, and He loosened the knot of his tongue, and that too is a miracle. Thus the signs become three. This is the explanation of the command. As for the prohibition, it is His saying: ﴿and do not slacken in My remembrance﴾. *Al-wany* means slackness and negligence. It is recited as *wa-la tiniya* with a kasra on the letter of the present tense for harmonization (*ittiba'*). Then several views were stated about it:

The first: the meaning is, "Do not slacken; rather, take My remembrance as a means to attain your aims, and believe that no matter can be accomplished for anyone except through My remembrance." The wisdom in this is that whoever remembers the majesty of God regards everything else as insignificant, so he fears no one. Also, whoever remembers the majesty of God has his spirit strengthened by that remembrance, so he does not weaken in pursuing his aim. Also, whoever remembers God must be remembering His favor, and one who remembers His favor does not slacken in carrying out His commands.

The second: the intended meaning of "remembrance" is conveying the message, for the term "remembrance" applies to all acts of worship, and conveying the message is among the greatest of them, so it was fitting that it be called "remembrance."

The third: His saying "and do not slacken in My remembrance" refers to [remembrance] before Pharaoh. The manner of this remembrance is that they should tell Pharaoh and his people that God does not accept disbelief from them, and they should tell them about reward and punishment, and encourage and warn them.

The fourth: that they should remind Pharaoh of God's bounties, His blessings, and the various kinds of His favor toward him. Then after that He said: ﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed﴾. Here there are two questions:

The first: what is the benefit of this after His saying "Go, you and your brother, with My signs"? Al-Qaffal said: there are two answers to this:

One of them: His saying "Go, you and your brother, with My signs" may mean that each of them is commanded to go individually. So He said again, "Go," to make clear that what is intended is that they should both engage in this together, not that Harun alone should undertake it without Musa.

The second: His saying "Go, you and your brother, with My signs" is a command to go to all people, the Children of Israel and the people of Pharaoh. Then His saying "Go to Pharaoh" is a command to go to Pharaoh alone.

The second question: His saying "Go to Pharaoh" is addressed to Musa and Harun (peace be upon them both), and this is problematic, because Harun (peace be upon him) was not present there. The same applies to His saying: ﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 45]. Al-Qaffal answered this in several ways:

One of them: the speech was addressed to Musa (peace be upon him) alone, but he was the one who was followed by Harun, so the address to him was made an address to Harun as well. Harun's speech is understood by way of implication. Thus, in that situation, although the address was to Musa (peace be upon him) alone, God attributed it to both of them, as in His saying: ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72], and His saying: ﴿If we return to Medina, the more honorable will surely expel the more humble from it﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. It is related that the speaker was 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy alone.

The second: it is possible that when God said, "You have been given your request, O Musa" [Ta-Ha: 36], he remained silent until he met his brother. Then God addressed both of them with His saying: ﴿Go to Pharaoh﴾.

The third: it is related that in the codices of Ibn Mas'ud and Hafsah, the reading is: "He said, 'Our Lord, indeed we fear'", meaning that Musa said: "I and my brother fear Pharaoh."

As for His saying: ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech﴾, there are two questions:

The first question: why did God command Musa (peace be upon him) to be gentle with the disbelieving rejecter? The answer has two parts:

The first: he (peace be upon him) had been raised by Pharaoh, so he was commanded to address him gently, out of regard for those rights. This is an indication of the utmost honor due to one's parents.

The second: it is a habit of tyrants that when they are addressed harshly in admonition, they increase in arrogance and pride. The purpose of the mission is to achieve benefit, not to increase harm. For this reason God commanded gentleness.

The second question: what was that gentle speech like? They mentioned several answers:

One of them: what God related of part of it, when He said: ﴿Would you like to purify yourself? And I would guide you to your Lord, so that you would fear Him﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18–19]. He also mentioned in this surah part of it, when He said: ﴿So come to him and say, "Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord"﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And peace be upon him who follows guidance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47].

The second: that they promise him a youth that will not age after it, a kingship that will not be taken from him except by death, and that the pleasure of food, drink, and marriage remain with him until his death.

The third: they should address him with kunyas. He was one of the three people who had three kunyas: Abu al-'Abbas, Abu al-Walid, and Abu Murrah.

The fourth: it is related from 'Amr ibn Dinar that he said: "It has reached me that Pharaoh lived four hundred and nine years. Musa (peace be upon him) said to him: 'If you obey me, you will live as long as you have lived, and when you die, you will have Paradise.'" They raised objections to these last three answers.

As for the first: it was said that if these three matters were granted to him over this long period, that would amount to compulsion toward knowledge of God, and that is not valid alongside moral responsibility.

As for the second: addressing him by kunya is an easy matter, so it cannot be taken as the intended meaning of His saying ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech﴾. Rather, it may be part of what is intended.

As for the third: the objection to it is the same as to the first.

As for His saying: ﴿Perhaps he will remember or fear﴾, know that the intended meaning is not that God was in doubt about this, because doubt is impossible for God. Rather, the meaning is: "Speak to him gently, while you both hope that he may remember or fear." Know that the states of the heart are three:

One: persistence upon the truth.

Two: persistence upon falsehood.

Three: hesitation between the two matters. Pharaoh was persistent in falsehood, and this kind is the worst of the states. So God said: ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech, perhaps he will remember or fear﴾, so that he would turn from his denial to acknowledging the truth. Even if he did not move from denial to acknowledgment, fear would arise in his heart, and he would abandon denial. And even if he did not move to acknowledgment, this is better than persisting in denial.

Know that the secret of this obligation is known only to God. Since God knew that he would never believe, his belief would be the opposite of that knowledge, which cannot be reversed. Therefore He, glory be to Him, knows that such belief is impossible. And if this is so, how could He command Musa (peace be upon him) to such gentleness, and how could He insist on such a command, gently calling him to God, while knowing that this could not happen? Moreover, suppose the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) dispute this impossibility without offering any argument that undermines this question. Yet they concede that He knew he would not attain that belief, and they concede that Pharaoh gains nothing from the mission of Musa (peace be upon him) except deserving punishment. How is it fitting for the Merciful and Generous to hand a knife to one whom He knows for certain will tear open his own belly with it, and then say: "I did not intend by handing him the knife anything but kindness to him"? My brother, minds are too limited to grasp these secrets, and there is no path here except submission, leaving off objection, and silence of heart and tongue.

It is related from Ka'b that he said: "By Him by whom Ka'b swears, it is indeed written in the Torah: 'So speak to him with gentle speech, and I will harden his heart so that he will not believe.'"

[p. 52]

The third benefit (minnah): His saying, ﴿And that you might be brought up under My eye﴾. Al-Qaffal said: "That you might be seen under My eye" means according to My will. The metaphor is this: whoever makes something for a person while being present and watching him, makes it for him as he loves, and cannot do anything that contradicts his purpose. So it is here. There are two views on how the metaphor works:

The first: by "eye" is meant knowledge, "that you may be seen with knowledge from Me." Since one who knows a thing guards it from harms, just as one who watches it guards it from harms, the word "eye" was applied to knowledge because the two resemble each other in this respect.

The second: by "eye" is meant protection, because one who looks at a thing protects it from what would harm it, so the eye is like the cause of protection, and the name of the cause is applied to the effect metaphorically. This is like His saying, ﴿Indeed I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ [Taha: 46]. And it is said, "The eye of God be upon you," when one prays for someone's preservation and safeguarding. Al-Qadi said: The apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates that what is meant by His saying, ﴿And that you might be brought up under My eye﴾, is protection and safeguarding, like His saying, ﴿When your sister walked and said, "Shall I direct you to one who will nurse him?" So We returned you to your mother that her eye might be comforted and she not grieve﴾. Thus that serves as an explanation of God's safeguarding of him. Two discussions remain here:

The first: the waw in His saying, ﴿And that you might be brought up under My eye﴾ has three possible readings:
One: it is as if it were said, "And I cast upon you love from Me, that you might be brought up under My eye." Then His saying, ﴿When your sister walked﴾ is connected to the beginning of the speech, which is His saying, ﴿And We conferred favor upon you another time, when We inspired to your mother what is inspired﴾, and "when your sister walked."
Two: it is permissible that His saying ﴿And that you might be brought up under My eye﴾ is connected to what follows it, which is His saying, ﴿When [your sister] walked﴾. We mentioned similar two readings in His saying, ﴿And that he might be among the certain [in faith]﴾ [al-An'am: 75].
Three: it is permissible that the waw is superfluous, meaning, "And I cast upon you love from Me, so that you would be brought up." This is weak.

The second: it was read as "wa-li-tuṣna'a" with the lam both kasra and sukun; the jazm (jussive) reading is on the basis that it is an imperative. It was also read as "wa-li-taṣna'a" with a fatha on the ta and the subjunctive, meaning: "and that your work and conduct would be with knowledge from Me."

* * *

The fourth benefit: His saying, ﴿When your sister walked﴾. Know that the governing element for ﴿when she walked﴾ is either "I cast" or "you be brought up." It is narrated that when the news spread in Egypt that the people of Pharaoh had taken a boy from the Nile, and he would not suckle from the breast of any woman brought to him, because God had forbidden him the wet-nurses other than his mother, they were compelled to search among the women. When Moses' sister saw this, she came to them disguised and said, ﴿Shall I direct you to a household that will nurse him for you?﴾ Then she brought the mother, and he accepted her breast. Thus he returned to his mother through the subtle arrangement God had devised for him. As for His saying, ﴿So We returned you to your mother﴾, meaning "We restored you," and He said in another place, ﴿So We returned him to his mother﴾ [al-Qasas: 13]. It is like His saying, ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99], meaning, "Return me to the world." As for His saying, ﴿that her eye might be comforted and she not grieve﴾, the meaning is that the purpose of returning you to her is the attainment of joy for her and the removal of sorrow from her. If it is said: had He said, "that she not grieve and her eye be comforted," the speech would be meaningful, since the negation of grief does not necessitate the attainment of joy for her; but since He first said, "that her eye be comforted," His saying afterwards, "and she not grieve," is superfluous, for whenever joy is attained, the removal of sorrow is inevitable. We say: the meaning is that her eye is comforted by means of your arrival to her, so sorrow is removed from her because the milk of another does not reach your inner being.

The fifth benefit: His saying, ﴿And you killed a soul, and We saved you from the distress﴾. Its meaning: you killed a soul after your old age, namely the man whom he killed by mistake, by striking him, when the Israelite sought his help against him, and he was a Copt. Thus distress came to him from two directions:

One of them: from the punishment of this world, which is Pharaoh's retaliation against him, as God related: ﴿So he became in the city, fearful and watchful﴾ [al-Qasas: 18]. The other: from the punishment of God, since he killed without God's command. So God saved him from both distresses: from Pharaoh, when He enabled him to emigrate to Madyan; and from the punishment of the Hereafter, because He, glorified and exalted, forgave him for that.

The sixth benefit: His saying, ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾. Regarding it there are discussions:

The first discussion: concerning His saying ﴿with a testing (futunan)﴾ there are two views:
One: it is a verbal noun like "ukuf" and "julus," and the meaning is "We tested you truly," according to their view of emphasizing reports with verbal nouns, like His saying, ﴿And God spoke to Moses with speech﴾ [al-Nisa': 164].
The second: it is the plural of fatn or fitnah, with the feminine ta disregarded, like ḥujūz and budūr from ḥujzah and badrah, meaning: "We tested you with various kinds of trials." Here there are two questions:

Question one: God enumerated the kinds of His favors upon Moses, peace be upon him, in this context, so how does His saying ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾ fit this place? The answer to this has two parts:
One: testing (fitnah) is the intensification of an ordeal. It is said, "So-and-so was tested in his religion" when the ordeal became severe upon him until he turned away from his religion. God said: ﴿So when he is harmed for God's sake, he regards the trial of people as the punishment of God﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 10]. And God said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Do people think they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested? And We did test those before them, and God will surely make evident those who are truthful and will surely make evident the liars﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 1–3]. And He said: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed on before you? They were touched by hardship and adversity and were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of God?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214]. So the shaking mentioned in the verse, and the touching of hardship and adversity, are the fitnah and the futun. Since intensification of an ordeal is something that necessitates abundant reward, God counted it among the blessings without doubt.

Two: ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾
meaning: We purified you with purification, from the saying "fatantu al-dhahab min al-fiddah" when you wish to separate it (refine gold from silver). Sa'id ibn Jubayr asked Ibn 'Abbas about the futun, and he said: "Let us begin it for him by day, O Ibn Jubayr." Then when morning came, Ibn 'Abbas began reciting to him the verses concerning Moses, peace be upon him, from the beginning of his affair. He mentioned the story of Pharaoh and his killing of the sons of the Children of Israel, then the story of Moses, peace be upon him, being cast into the river, and the picking up of him by Pharaoh's household, and his refusal to nurse from foreign women; then the story that Moses, peace be upon him, seized Pharaoh's beard and placed the ember in his mouth; then the story of the killing of the Copt; then his flight to Madyan, and his becoming a hired man for Shu'ayb, peace be upon him; then his return to Egypt, and that he lost the way on the dark night, and his seeking comfort from the fire from the tree. And at the completion of each of these he would say, "This is among the testings, O Ibn Jubayr."

Question two: Is it valid to apply the name "al-Fattan" to Him, glorified, derived from His saying ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾? The answer: No; because it is a term of blame in common usage, and the names of God, exalted, are tawqifiyyah (fixed by revelation), especially in what gives an impression of what is not fitting.

* * *

The seventh benefit: His saying, exalted: ﴿Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan; then you came at a predestined time, O Moses﴾. Know that the implied sense is: ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾, so you went out in fear to the people of Madyan, and you stayed years among them. As for the duration of the stay, Abu Muslim said: it is explained in His saying, ﴿And when he turned toward Madyan﴾ up to His saying, ﴿When Moses had fulfilled the term﴾ [al-Qasas: 29]; and it is either ten or eight, according to His saying, ﴿On condition that you hire yourself to me for eight years, and if you complete ten, it is from you﴾ [al-Qasas: 27]. Wahb said: Moses, peace be upon him, stayed with Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, for twenty-eight years, of which ten years were the bride-price of his wife. The verse indicates that he, peace be upon him, stayed with him ten years, and there is nothing in it that negates an addition beyond the ten.

Know that His saying, ﴿Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan﴾ after His saying, ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾, is like an indication that his stay in Madyan was among the testings, and so it was. He, peace be upon him, bore, because of poverty and estrangement, many ordeals, and needed to hire himself out. As for His saying, exalted, ﴿Then you came at a predestined time, O Moses﴾, there must be an omission in the speech, because it was at a predestined measure of some matter. The commentators mentioned several possibilities for that omitted element:

One: it had preceded in My decree and My predestination that I would make you My messenger at a specified time that I had appointed for that, so you came only at that predestination, not before it nor after it. From this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, We created all things according to a measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49].

Two: at a measure of time in which revelation is sent down to the prophets, and that is at the head of forty years.

Three: that the predestination is the appointed time. If it is established that this appointment had preceded, it is valid to interpret it as such, and there is nothing to prevent that, given the possibility that Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, or other prophets had been assigned that appointed time. If it is said: how does God mention Moses' coming at that time among His favors upon him? We say: because, had it not been for His enabling him to do so, nothing of that would have been arranged.

* * *

The eighth benefit: His saying, exalted: ﴿And I have made you for Myself﴾. Istina' means taking up a craft, and it is an ifti'al form from sun'. It is said: "So-and-so made so-and-so" (iṣṭana'a fulan fulanan), i.e., took him as his protégé. If it is said: He, exalted, is independent of all; so what is the meaning of His saying ﴿for Myself﴾? The answer to this has several parts:

One: this is a figure of speech, for when He, exalted, gave him the rank of nearness, honor, and speaking, He likened his state to the state of one whom some kings see as possessing comprehensive qualities, making him fit to be the closest of people in rank to them and the nearest of them to them.

Two: the Mu'tazilah said: when He, glorified and exalted, imposes obligations on His servants, it is obligatory upon Him to show them kindness (lutf). Among the kindnesses are some that are known only through revelation. So if He had not made him a chosen one by the messengership, he would have remained under the obligation of what is required. Thus Moses, peace be upon him, became like a deputy for his Lord in carrying out what was incumbent upon God, the exalted. So it is correct for Him to say, ﴿And I have made you for Myself﴾. Al-Qaffal said: ﴿And I have made you﴾ originates from the saying of people, "So-and-so made so-and-so" when he did good to him until he was attributed to him, so it is said, "This is so-and-so's creation, so-and-so's wounded one." His saying
