﴿for Myself﴾: meaning, that I might direct you in My commands, so that you would not occupy yourself with anything other than what I commanded you, which is establishing My proof, conveying My message, and that your movements and stillnesses be for Me, not for yourself nor for others. Know that when He, glorified and exalted, enumerated for him the eight favors in return for those eight requests, He arranged upon the mention of that a command and a prohibition. As for the command, He, glorified and exalted, repeated the first command, saying: ﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs﴾. Know that when He, glorified and exalted, said, ﴿And I have made you for Myself﴾, He followed it with mention of what He made him for, which is conveyance and delivery. Then there are issues here:

First issue: the ba' here means "with"; for if they went to him without a sign with them, belief would not be binding upon him, and that is among the strongest proofs against the invalidity of taqlid (blind imitation).

Second issue: they differed about the signs mentioned here, on three views:

**[Part 2 of 2]**

The first view: they are the hand and the staff, because these are the two that are mentioned in this passage and in the other places where God related the story of Musa (peace be upon him). In none of these places does God mention that he (peace be upon him) was given a sign before he came to Pharaoh or after he came to Pharaoh and met him. Pharaoh then demanded from him a sign other than these two signs. God said about him: ﴿So bring it, if you are of the truthful﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 154], and He said: ﴿So he cast down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent﴾ [al-A'raf: 107], ﴿and he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers﴾ [al-A'raf: 108], and He said: ﴿These two are proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ [al-Qasas: 32]. If it is asked of these scholars, "How is the plural form used for two?", they answered with several explanations:

The first: the staff was not a single sign, but rather several signs. The transformation of the staff into a living creature is one sign. Then, at the beginning, it was small, as in His saying: ﴿it moved as though it were a jinn﴾ [al-Naml: 10]. Then it would grow large, and this is another sign. Then it would become a serpent, and this is another sign. Then Musa (peace be upon him) would put his hand into its mouth, and it would not harm Musa (peace be upon him), and this is another sign. Then it would turn back into a piece of wood, and this is another sign. Likewise with the hand: its whiteness is a sign, its radiance is another sign, and then their disappearance after they had appeared is another sign. Thus it is correct that the two were many signs, not two signs.

The second: suppose the staff was one matter. Nevertheless, there are many signs in it, because its transformation into a living serpent indicates the existence of a God who is capable of all things, all-knowing of all things, and wise. It also indicates the prophethood of Musa (peace be upon him), and it indicates the possibility of resurrection, since an inanimate object became a living creature. These are many signs. For this reason He said: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds. In it are clear signs: the station of Ibrahim﴾ [Al 'Imran: 96–97]. When one thing is described as containing signs, then two things are more deserving of this description.

The third: some people said: the least number of the plural is two, as you know from the discussions in *usul al-fiqh* (the principles of jurisprudence).

The second view: His saying "Go with My signs" means: I am supplying you both with My signs, and I will manifest through your hands signs by which the proofs against Pharaoh and his people are removed. So go, for My signs are with you both, just as one says, "Go, for My soldiers are with you," meaning: I will supply them to you whenever you need them.

The third view: God gave him the staff and the hand, and He loosened the knot of his tongue, and that too is a miracle. Thus the signs become three. This is the explanation of the command. As for the prohibition, it is His saying: ﴿and do not slacken in My remembrance﴾. *Al-wany* means slackness and negligence. It is recited as *wa-la tiniya* with a kasra on the letter of the present tense for harmonization (*ittiba'*). Then several views were stated about it:

The first: the meaning is, "Do not slacken; rather, take My remembrance as a means to attain your aims, and believe that no matter can be accomplished for anyone except through My remembrance." The wisdom in this is that whoever remembers the majesty of God regards everything else as insignificant, so he fears no one. Also, whoever remembers the majesty of God has his spirit strengthened by that remembrance, so he does not weaken in pursuing his aim. Also, whoever remembers God must be remembering His favor, and one who remembers His favor does not slacken in carrying out His commands.

The second: the intended meaning of "remembrance" is conveying the message, for the term "remembrance" applies to all acts of worship, and conveying the message is among the greatest of them, so it was fitting that it be called "remembrance."

The third: His saying "and do not slacken in My remembrance" refers to [remembrance] before Pharaoh. The manner of this remembrance is that they should tell Pharaoh and his people that God does not accept disbelief from them, and they should tell them about reward and punishment, and encourage and warn them.

The fourth: that they should remind Pharaoh of God's bounties, His blessings, and the various kinds of His favor toward him. Then after that He said: ﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed﴾. Here there are two questions:

The first: what is the benefit of this after His saying "Go, you and your brother, with My signs"? Al-Qaffal said: there are two answers to this:

One of them: His saying "Go, you and your brother, with My signs" may mean that each of them is commanded to go individually. So He said again, "Go," to make clear that what is intended is that they should both engage in this together, not that Harun alone should undertake it without Musa.

The second: His saying "Go, you and your brother, with My signs" is a command to go to all people, the Children of Israel and the people of Pharaoh. Then His saying "Go to Pharaoh" is a command to go to Pharaoh alone.

The second question: His saying "Go to Pharaoh" is addressed to Musa and Harun (peace be upon them both), and this is problematic, because Harun (peace be upon him) was not present there. The same applies to His saying: ﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 45]. Al-Qaffal answered this in several ways:

One of them: the speech was addressed to Musa (peace be upon him) alone, but he was the one who was followed by Harun, so the address to him was made an address to Harun as well. Harun's speech is understood by way of implication. Thus, in that situation, although the address was to Musa (peace be upon him) alone, God attributed it to both of them, as in His saying: ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72], and His saying: ﴿If we return to Medina, the more honorable will surely expel the more humble from it﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. It is related that the speaker was 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy alone.

The second: it is possible that when God said, "You have been given your request, O Musa" [Ta-Ha: 36], he remained silent until he met his brother. Then God addressed both of them with His saying: ﴿Go to Pharaoh﴾.

The third: it is related that in the codices of Ibn Mas'ud and Hafsah, the reading is: "He said, 'Our Lord, indeed we fear'", meaning that Musa said: "I and my brother fear Pharaoh."

As for His saying: ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech﴾, there are two questions:

The first question: why did God command Musa (peace be upon him) to be gentle with the disbelieving rejecter? The answer has two parts:

The first: he (peace be upon him) had been raised by Pharaoh, so he was commanded to address him gently, out of regard for those rights. This is an indication of the utmost honor due to one's parents.

The second: it is a habit of tyrants that when they are addressed harshly in admonition, they increase in arrogance and pride. The purpose of the mission is to achieve benefit, not to increase harm. For this reason God commanded gentleness.

The second question: what was that gentle speech like? They mentioned several answers:

One of them: what God related of part of it, when He said: ﴿Would you like to purify yourself? And I would guide you to your Lord, so that you would fear Him﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18–19]. He also mentioned in this surah part of it, when He said: ﴿So come to him and say, "Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord"﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And peace be upon him who follows guidance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47].

The second: that they promise him a youth that will not age after it, a kingship that will not be taken from him except by death, and that the pleasure of food, drink, and marriage remain with him until his death.

The third: they should address him with kunyas. He was one of the three people who had three kunyas: Abu al-'Abbas, Abu al-Walid, and Abu Murrah.

The fourth: it is related from 'Amr ibn Dinar that he said: "It has reached me that Pharaoh lived four hundred and nine years. Musa (peace be upon him) said to him: 'If you obey me, you will live as long as you have lived, and when you die, you will have Paradise.'" They raised objections to these last three answers.

As for the first: it was said that if these three matters were granted to him over this long period, that would amount to compulsion toward knowledge of God, and that is not valid alongside moral responsibility.

As for the second: addressing him by kunya is an easy matter, so it cannot be taken as the intended meaning of His saying ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech﴾. Rather, it may be part of what is intended.

As for the third: the objection to it is the same as to the first.

As for His saying: ﴿Perhaps he will remember or fear﴾, know that the intended meaning is not that God was in doubt about this, because doubt is impossible for God. Rather, the meaning is: "Speak to him gently, while you both hope that he may remember or fear." Know that the states of the heart are three:

One: persistence upon the truth.

Two: persistence upon falsehood.

Three: hesitation between the two matters. Pharaoh was persistent in falsehood, and this kind is the worst of the states. So God said: ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech, perhaps he will remember or fear﴾, so that he would turn from his denial to acknowledging the truth. Even if he did not move from denial to acknowledgment, fear would arise in his heart, and he would abandon denial. And even if he did not move to acknowledgment, this is better than persisting in denial.

Know that the secret of this obligation is known only to God. Since God knew that he would never believe, his belief would be the opposite of that knowledge, which cannot be reversed. Therefore He, glory be to Him, knows that such belief is impossible. And if this is so, how could He command Musa (peace be upon him) to such gentleness, and how could He insist on such a command, gently calling him to God, while knowing that this could not happen? Moreover, suppose the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) dispute this impossibility without offering any argument that undermines this question. Yet they concede that He knew he would not attain that belief, and they concede that Pharaoh gains nothing from the mission of Musa (peace be upon him) except deserving punishment. How is it fitting for the Merciful and Generous to hand a knife to one whom He knows for certain will tear open his own belly with it, and then say: "I did not intend by handing him the knife anything but kindness to him"? My brother, minds are too limited to grasp these secrets, and there is no path here except submission, leaving off objection, and silence of heart and tongue.

It is related from Ka'b that he said: "By Him by whom Ka'b swears, it is indeed written in the Torah: 'So speak to him with gentle speech, and I will harden his heart so that he will not believe.'"

[p. 52]

The third benefit (minnah): His saying, ﴿And that you might be brought up under My eye﴾. Al-Qaffal said: "That you might be seen under My eye" means according to My will. The metaphor is this: whoever makes something for a person while being present and watching him, makes it for him as he loves, and cannot do anything that contradicts his purpose. So it is here. There are two views on how the metaphor works:

The first: by "eye" is meant knowledge, "that you may be seen with knowledge from Me." Since one who knows a thing guards it from harms, just as one who watches it guards it from harms, the word "eye" was applied to knowledge because the two resemble each other in this respect.

The second: by "eye" is meant protection, because one who looks at a thing protects it from what would harm it, so the eye is like the cause of protection, and the name of the cause is applied to the effect metaphorically. This is like His saying, ﴿Indeed I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾ [Taha: 46]. And it is said, "The eye of God be upon you," when one prays for someone's preservation and safeguarding. Al-Qadi said: The apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates that what is meant by His saying, ﴿And that you might be brought up under My eye﴾, is protection and safeguarding, like His saying, ﴿When your sister walked and said, "Shall I direct you to one who will nurse him?" So We returned you to your mother that her eye might be comforted and she not grieve﴾. Thus that serves as an explanation of God's safeguarding of him. Two discussions remain here:

The first: the waw in His saying, ﴿And that you might be brought up under My eye﴾ has three possible readings:
One: it is as if it were said, "And I cast upon you love from Me, that you might be brought up under My eye." Then His saying, ﴿When your sister walked﴾ is connected to the beginning of the speech, which is His saying, ﴿And We conferred favor upon you another time, when We inspired to your mother what is inspired﴾, and "when your sister walked."
Two: it is permissible that His saying ﴿And that you might be brought up under My eye﴾ is connected to what follows it, which is His saying, ﴿When [your sister] walked﴾. We mentioned similar two readings in His saying, ﴿And that he might be among the certain [in faith]﴾ [al-An'am: 75].
Three: it is permissible that the waw is superfluous, meaning, "And I cast upon you love from Me, so that you would be brought up." This is weak.

The second: it was read as "wa-li-tuṣna'a" with the lam both kasra and sukun; the jazm (jussive) reading is on the basis that it is an imperative. It was also read as "wa-li-taṣna'a" with a fatha on the ta and the subjunctive, meaning: "and that your work and conduct would be with knowledge from Me."

* * *

The fourth benefit: His saying, ﴿When your sister walked﴾. Know that the governing element for ﴿when she walked﴾ is either "I cast" or "you be brought up." It is narrated that when the news spread in Egypt that the people of Pharaoh had taken a boy from the Nile, and he would not suckle from the breast of any woman brought to him, because God had forbidden him the wet-nurses other than his mother, they were compelled to search among the women. When Moses' sister saw this, she came to them disguised and said, ﴿Shall I direct you to a household that will nurse him for you?﴾ Then she brought the mother, and he accepted her breast. Thus he returned to his mother through the subtle arrangement God had devised for him. As for His saying, ﴿So We returned you to your mother﴾, meaning "We restored you," and He said in another place, ﴿So We returned him to his mother﴾ [al-Qasas: 13]. It is like His saying, ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 99], meaning, "Return me to the world." As for His saying, ﴿that her eye might be comforted and she not grieve﴾, the meaning is that the purpose of returning you to her is the attainment of joy for her and the removal of sorrow from her. If it is said: had He said, "that she not grieve and her eye be comforted," the speech would be meaningful, since the negation of grief does not necessitate the attainment of joy for her; but since He first said, "that her eye be comforted," His saying afterwards, "and she not grieve," is superfluous, for whenever joy is attained, the removal of sorrow is inevitable. We say: the meaning is that her eye is comforted by means of your arrival to her, so sorrow is removed from her because the milk of another does not reach your inner being.

The fifth benefit: His saying, ﴿And you killed a soul, and We saved you from the distress﴾. Its meaning: you killed a soul after your old age, namely the man whom he killed by mistake, by striking him, when the Israelite sought his help against him, and he was a Copt. Thus distress came to him from two directions:

One of them: from the punishment of this world, which is Pharaoh's retaliation against him, as God related: ﴿So he became in the city, fearful and watchful﴾ [al-Qasas: 18]. The other: from the punishment of God, since he killed without God's command. So God saved him from both distresses: from Pharaoh, when He enabled him to emigrate to Madyan; and from the punishment of the Hereafter, because He, glorified and exalted, forgave him for that.

The sixth benefit: His saying, ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾. Regarding it there are discussions:

The first discussion: concerning His saying ﴿with a testing (futunan)﴾ there are two views:
One: it is a verbal noun like "ukuf" and "julus," and the meaning is "We tested you truly," according to their view of emphasizing reports with verbal nouns, like His saying, ﴿And God spoke to Moses with speech﴾ [al-Nisa': 164].
The second: it is the plural of fatn or fitnah, with the feminine ta disregarded, like ḥujūz and budūr from ḥujzah and badrah, meaning: "We tested you with various kinds of trials." Here there are two questions:

Question one: God enumerated the kinds of His favors upon Moses, peace be upon him, in this context, so how does His saying ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾ fit this place? The answer to this has two parts:
One: testing (fitnah) is the intensification of an ordeal. It is said, "So-and-so was tested in his religion" when the ordeal became severe upon him until he turned away from his religion. God said: ﴿So when he is harmed for God's sake, he regards the trial of people as the punishment of God﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 10]. And God said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Do people think they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested? And We did test those before them, and God will surely make evident those who are truthful and will surely make evident the liars﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 1–3]. And He said: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed on before you? They were touched by hardship and adversity and were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of God?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214]. So the shaking mentioned in the verse, and the touching of hardship and adversity, are the fitnah and the futun. Since intensification of an ordeal is something that necessitates abundant reward, God counted it among the blessings without doubt.

Two: ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾
meaning: We purified you with purification, from the saying "fatantu al-dhahab min al-fiddah" when you wish to separate it (refine gold from silver). Sa'id ibn Jubayr asked Ibn 'Abbas about the futun, and he said: "Let us begin it for him by day, O Ibn Jubayr." Then when morning came, Ibn 'Abbas began reciting to him the verses concerning Moses, peace be upon him, from the beginning of his affair. He mentioned the story of Pharaoh and his killing of the sons of the Children of Israel, then the story of Moses, peace be upon him, being cast into the river, and the picking up of him by Pharaoh's household, and his refusal to nurse from foreign women; then the story that Moses, peace be upon him, seized Pharaoh's beard and placed the ember in his mouth; then the story of the killing of the Copt; then his flight to Madyan, and his becoming a hired man for Shu'ayb, peace be upon him; then his return to Egypt, and that he lost the way on the dark night, and his seeking comfort from the fire from the tree. And at the completion of each of these he would say, "This is among the testings, O Ibn Jubayr."

Question two: Is it valid to apply the name "al-Fattan" to Him, glorified, derived from His saying ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾? The answer: No; because it is a term of blame in common usage, and the names of God, exalted, are tawqifiyyah (fixed by revelation), especially in what gives an impression of what is not fitting.

* * *

The seventh benefit: His saying, exalted: ﴿Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan; then you came at a predestined time, O Moses﴾. Know that the implied sense is: ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾, so you went out in fear to the people of Madyan, and you stayed years among them. As for the duration of the stay, Abu Muslim said: it is explained in His saying, ﴿And when he turned toward Madyan﴾ up to His saying, ﴿When Moses had fulfilled the term﴾ [al-Qasas: 29]; and it is either ten or eight, according to His saying, ﴿On condition that you hire yourself to me for eight years, and if you complete ten, it is from you﴾ [al-Qasas: 27]. Wahb said: Moses, peace be upon him, stayed with Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, for twenty-eight years, of which ten years were the bride-price of his wife. The verse indicates that he, peace be upon him, stayed with him ten years, and there is nothing in it that negates an addition beyond the ten.

Know that His saying, ﴿Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan﴾ after His saying, ﴿And We tested you with a testing﴾, is like an indication that his stay in Madyan was among the testings, and so it was. He, peace be upon him, bore, because of poverty and estrangement, many ordeals, and needed to hire himself out. As for His saying, exalted, ﴿Then you came at a predestined time, O Moses﴾, there must be an omission in the speech, because it was at a predestined measure of some matter. The commentators mentioned several possibilities for that omitted element:

One: it had preceded in My decree and My predestination that I would make you My messenger at a specified time that I had appointed for that, so you came only at that predestination, not before it nor after it. From this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, We created all things according to a measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49].

Two: at a measure of time in which revelation is sent down to the prophets, and that is at the head of forty years.

Three: that the predestination is the appointed time. If it is established that this appointment had preceded, it is valid to interpret it as such, and there is nothing to prevent that, given the possibility that Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, or other prophets had been assigned that appointed time. If it is said: how does God mention Moses' coming at that time among His favors upon him? We say: because, had it not been for His enabling him to do so, nothing of that would have been arranged.

* * *

The eighth benefit: His saying, exalted: ﴿And I have made you for Myself﴾. Istina' means taking up a craft, and it is an ifti'al form from sun'. It is said: "So-and-so made so-and-so" (iṣṭana'a fulan fulanan), i.e., took him as his protégé. If it is said: He, exalted, is independent of all; so what is the meaning of His saying ﴿for Myself﴾? The answer to this has several parts:

One: this is a figure of speech, for when He, exalted, gave him the rank of nearness, honor, and speaking, He likened his state to the state of one whom some kings see as possessing comprehensive qualities, making him fit to be the closest of people in rank to them and the nearest of them to them.

Two: the Mu'tazilah said: when He, glorified and exalted, imposes obligations on His servants, it is obligatory upon Him to show them kindness (lutf). Among the kindnesses are some that are known only through revelation. So if He had not made him a chosen one by the messengership, he would have remained under the obligation of what is required. Thus Moses, peace be upon him, became like a deputy for his Lord in carrying out what was incumbent upon God, the exalted. So it is correct for Him to say, ﴿And I have made you for Myself﴾. Al-Qaffal said: ﴿And I have made you﴾ originates from the saying of people, "So-and-so made so-and-so" when he did good to him until he was attributed to him, so it is said, "This is so-and-so's creation, so-and-so's wounded one." His saying
Page 50
﴿for Myself﴾: meaning, that I might direct you in My commands, so that you would not occupy yourself with anything other than what I commanded you, which is establishing My proof, conveying My message, and that your movements and stillnesses be for Me, not for yourself nor for others. Know that when He, glorified and exalted, enumerated for him the eight favors in return for those eight requests, He arranged upon the mention of that a command and a prohibition. As for the command, He, glorified and exalted, repeated the first command, saying: ﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs﴾. Know that when He, glorified and exalted, said, ﴿And I have made you for Myself﴾, He followed it with mention of what He made him for, which is conveyance and delivery. Then there are issues here:

First issue: the ba' here means "with"; for if they went to him without a sign with them, belief would not be binding upon him, and that is among the strongest proofs against the invalidity of taqlid (blind imitation).

Second issue: they differed about the signs mentioned here, on three views:

**[Part 2 of 2]**

The first view: they are the hand and the staff, because these are the two that are mentioned in this passage and in the other places where God related the story of Musa (peace be upon him). In none of these places does God mention that he (peace be upon him) was given a sign before he came to Pharaoh or after he came to Pharaoh and met him. Pharaoh then demanded from him a sign other than these two signs. God said about him: ﴿So bring it, if you are of the truthful﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 154], and He said: ﴿So he cast down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent﴾ [al-A'raf: 107], ﴿and he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers﴾ [al-A'raf: 108], and He said: ﴿These two are proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ [al-Qasas: 32]. If it is asked of these scholars, "How is the plural form used for two?", they answered with several explanations:

The first: the staff was not a single sign, but rather several signs. The transformation of the staff into a living creature is one sign. Then, at the beginning, it was small, as in His saying: ﴿it moved as though it were a jinn﴾ [al-Naml: 10]. Then it would grow large, and this is another sign. Then it would become a serpent, and this is another sign. Then Musa (peace be upon him) would put his hand into its mouth, and it would not harm Musa (peace be upon him), and this is another sign. Then it would turn back into a piece of wood, and this is another sign. Likewise with the hand: its whiteness is a sign, its radiance is another sign, and then their disappearance after they had appeared is another sign. Thus it is correct that the two were many signs, not two signs.

The second: suppose the staff was one matter. Nevertheless, there are many signs in it, because its transformation into a living serpent indicates the existence of a God who is capable of all things, all-knowing of all things, and wise. It also indicates the prophethood of Musa (peace be upon him), and it indicates the possibility of resurrection, since an inanimate object became a living creature. These are many signs. For this reason He said: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds. In it are clear signs: the station of Ibrahim﴾ [Al 'Imran: 96–97]. When one thing is described as containing signs, then two things are more deserving of this description.

The third: some people said: the least number of the plural is two, as you know from the discussions in *usul al-fiqh* (the principles of jurisprudence).

The second view: His saying "Go with My signs" means: I am supplying you both with My signs, and I will manifest through your hands signs by which the proofs against Pharaoh and his people are removed. So go, for My signs are with you both, just as one says, "Go, for My soldiers are with you," meaning: I will supply them to you whenever you need them.

The third view: God gave him the staff and the hand, and He loosened the knot of his tongue, and that too is a miracle. Thus the signs become three. This is the explanation of the command. As for the prohibition, it is His saying: ﴿and do not slacken in My remembrance﴾. *Al-wany* means slackness and negligence. It is recited as *wa-la tiniya* with a kasra on the letter of the present tense for harmonization (*ittiba'*). Then several views were stated about it:

The first: the meaning is, "Do not slacken; rather, take My remembrance as a means to attain your aims, and believe that no matter can be accomplished for anyone except through My remembrance." The wisdom in this is that whoever remembers the majesty of God regards everything else as insignificant, so he fears no one. Also, whoever remembers the majesty of God has his spirit strengthened by that remembrance, so he does not weaken in pursuing his aim. Also, whoever remembers God must be remembering His favor, and one who remembers His favor does not slacken in carrying out His commands.

The second: the intended meaning of "remembrance" is conveying the message, for the term "remembrance" applies to all acts of worship, and conveying the message is among the greatest of them, so it was fitting that it be called "remembrance."

The third: His saying "and do not slacken in My remembrance" refers to [remembrance] before Pharaoh. The manner of this remembrance is that they should tell Pharaoh and his people that God does not accept disbelief from them, and they should tell them about reward and punishment, and encourage and warn them.

The fourth: that they should remind Pharaoh of God's bounties, His blessings, and the various kinds of His favor toward him. Then after that He said: ﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed﴾. Here there are two questions:

The first: what is the benefit of this after His saying "Go, you and your brother, with My signs"? Al-Qaffal said: there are two answers to this:

One of them: His saying "Go, you and your brother, with My signs" may mean that each of them is commanded to go individually. So He said again, "Go," to make clear that what is intended is that they should both engage in this together, not that Harun alone should undertake it without Musa.

The second: His saying "Go, you and your brother, with My signs" is a command to go to all people, the Children of Israel and the people of Pharaoh. Then His saying "Go to Pharaoh" is a command to go to Pharaoh alone.

The second question: His saying "Go to Pharaoh" is addressed to Musa and Harun (peace be upon them both), and this is problematic, because Harun (peace be upon him) was not present there. The same applies to His saying: ﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 45]. Al-Qaffal answered this in several ways:

One of them: the speech was addressed to Musa (peace be upon him) alone, but he was the one who was followed by Harun, so the address to him was made an address to Harun as well. Harun's speech is understood by way of implication. Thus, in that situation, although the address was to Musa (peace be upon him) alone, God attributed it to both of them, as in His saying: ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72], and His saying: ﴿If we return to Medina, the more honorable will surely expel the more humble from it﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. It is related that the speaker was 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy alone.

The second: it is possible that when God said, "You have been given your request, O Musa" [Ta-Ha: 36], he remained silent until he met his brother. Then God addressed both of them with His saying: ﴿Go to Pharaoh﴾.

The third: it is related that in the codices of Ibn Mas'ud and Hafsah, the reading is: "He said, 'Our Lord, indeed we fear'", meaning that Musa said: "I and my brother fear Pharaoh."

As for His saying: ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech﴾, there are two questions:

The first question: why did God command Musa (peace be upon him) to be gentle with the disbelieving rejecter? The answer has two parts:

The first: he (peace be upon him) had been raised by Pharaoh, so he was commanded to address him gently, out of regard for those rights. This is an indication of the utmost honor due to one's parents.

The second: it is a habit of tyrants that when they are addressed harshly in admonition, they increase in arrogance and pride. The purpose of the mission is to achieve benefit, not to increase harm. For this reason God commanded gentleness.

The second question: what was that gentle speech like? They mentioned several answers:

One of them: what God related of part of it, when He said: ﴿Would you like to purify yourself? And I would guide you to your Lord, so that you would fear Him﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18–19]. He also mentioned in this surah part of it, when He said: ﴿So come to him and say, "Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord"﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And peace be upon him who follows guidance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47].

The second: that they promise him a youth that will not age after it, a kingship that will not be taken from him except by death, and that the pleasure of food, drink, and marriage remain with him until his death.

The third: they should address him with kunyas. He was one of the three people who had three kunyas: Abu al-'Abbas, Abu al-Walid, and Abu Murrah.

The fourth: it is related from 'Amr ibn Dinar that he said: "It has reached me that Pharaoh lived four hundred and nine years. Musa (peace be upon him) said to him: 'If you obey me, you will live as long as you have lived, and when you die, you will have Paradise.'" They raised objections to these last three answers.

As for the first: it was said that if these three matters were granted to him over this long period, that would amount to compulsion toward knowledge of God, and that is not valid alongside moral responsibility.

As for the second: addressing him by kunya is an easy matter, so it cannot be taken as the intended meaning of His saying ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech﴾. Rather, it may be part of what is intended.

As for the third: the objection to it is the same as to the first.

As for His saying: ﴿Perhaps he will remember or fear﴾, know that the intended meaning is not that God was in doubt about this, because doubt is impossible for God. Rather, the meaning is: "Speak to him gently, while you both hope that he may remember or fear." Know that the states of the heart are three:

One: persistence upon the truth.

Two: persistence upon falsehood.

Three: hesitation between the two matters. Pharaoh was persistent in falsehood, and this kind is the worst of the states. So God said: ﴿So speak to him with gentle speech, perhaps he will remember or fear﴾, so that he would turn from his denial to acknowledging the truth. Even if he did not move from denial to acknowledgment, fear would arise in his heart, and he would abandon denial. And even if he did not move to acknowledgment, this is better than persisting in denial.

Know that the secret of this obligation is known only to God. Since God knew that he would never believe, his belief would be the opposite of that knowledge, which cannot be reversed. Therefore He, glory be to Him, knows that such belief is impossible. And if this is so, how could He command Musa (peace be upon him) to such gentleness, and how could He insist on such a command, gently calling him to God, while knowing that this could not happen? Moreover, suppose the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) dispute this impossibility without offering any argument that undermines this question. Yet they concede that He knew he would not attain that belief, and they concede that Pharaoh gains nothing from the mission of Musa (peace be upon him) except deserving punishment. How is it fitting for the Merciful and Generous to hand a knife to one whom He knows for certain will tear open his own belly with it, and then say: "I did not intend by handing him the knife anything but kindness to him"? My brother, minds are too limited to grasp these secrets, and there is no path here except submission, leaving off objection, and silence of heart and tongue.

It is related from Ka'b that he said: "By Him by whom Ka'b swears, it is indeed written in the Torah: 'So speak to him with gentle speech, and I will harden his heart so that he will not believe.'"

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verses 46–48:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress."﴾ ﴿He said, "Do not fear. Indeed, I am with you both, hearing and seeing."﴾ ﴿So go to him and say, "Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord, so send with us the Children of Israel and do not torment them. We have come to you with a sign from your Lord. And peace be upon those who follow guidance."﴾ ﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment is for whoever denies and turns away.﴾

Know that His saying, ﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear,"﴾ raises questions.

The first question: His saying ﴿They said, "Our Lord"﴾ indicates that the one speaking was Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both, yet Harun was not present at this statement. How is that? Its answer has already been given.

The second question: Musa, peace be upon him, said, ﴿"My Lord, expand for me my breast"﴾, and God answered him with His saying, ﴿"You have been given your request, O Musa."﴾ This indicates that his breast had been expanded and his affair made easy. How then does he say afterward, ﴿"Indeed, we fear"﴾? For the occurrence of fear prevents the occurrence of the expansion of the breast. The answer: the expansion of the breast means strengthening him to preserve those commands and prohibitions and to safeguard those laws in a manner that neither forgetfulness nor distortion can reach. That is something other than the removal of fear.

The third question: Did Musa and Harun not know, when God had charged them with the message, that He would secure them from being killed, which would cut off the carrying out of the message? The answer: they were secure from that, although they allowed that harm might reach them before the completion of the delivery or after it. Also, they sought support by asking their Lord for what would increase the steadfastness of their hearts, by adding the transmitted proof to the rational proof for greater tranquility, as He said: ﴿"But that my heart may be assured"﴾ (2:260).

The fourth question: Since God repeated the command to go, does non-going and the pretext of fear indicate disobedience? The answer: if the command required immediacy, that would be among the strongest indications of disobedience, especially since God had multiplied the kinds of honor, strengthening of the heart, and removal of distress. But the command is not for immediacy, so the question is resolved. This is among the strongest indications that a command does not necessarily require immediacy, when you combine it with what shows that disobedience is not permissible for the messengers.

As for His saying, ﴿"that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress"﴾, know that there are several interpretations of ﴿"that he will hasten"﴾ (yafruta):

The first: farata means to precede and go ahead; from it comes al-farit, the one who goes ahead of the watering party, and a faras farth is a horse that outruns the horses. The meaning is: "We fear that he will hasten the punishment against us."

The second: it is derived from afrata ghayrahu, meaning to drive someone to haste. So Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both, feared that some driver would push him to hasten the punishment. That driver is either Satan, or his claim to lordship, or his love of rule, or his people, namely the Copts, the rebellious ones, about whom God related: ﴿"The eminent ones of his people said"﴾ (7:60).

The third: yafrutu means to exceed in harm. As for His saying, ﴿"or that he will transgress"﴾, the meaning is that he will exceed bounds by advancing to say about you what is not fitting, because of his boldness against you. Know that whoever is commanded to do something and tries to avert it with excuses he mentions must end his speech with what is strongest. This is like the hoopoe, which ended its excuse with his saying: ﴿"I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of God"﴾ (27:24). Likewise here, Musa began with ﴿"that he will hasten against us"﴾ and ended with ﴿"or that he will transgress,"﴾ because his transgression against the right of God, exalted is He, is greater than his excess against Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both.

As for His saying, ﴿"He said, 'Do not fear. Indeed, I am with you both, hearing and seeing.'"﴾ the meaning is: do not fear what has occurred to your hearts of excess and transgression, because that is what is understood from the speech. This is shown by the fact that He did not assure them against being rejected or denied, or against the magicians' opposition to the signs. As for His saying, ﴿"Indeed, I am with you"﴾, it is an expression of protection and guarding. In this sense one says, "God is with you," as a supplication. He confirmed this with ﴿"hearing and seeing,"﴾ for one who is with another and supports and guards him may not know everything that reaches him, but protects him only in what he knows. So He, glory be to Him and exalted, declared that He is with them both by protection and knowledge in everything that reaches them, and that is the utmost in removing fear.

Al-Qaffal said: His saying ﴿"hearing and seeing"﴾ may be a counterpart to His saying ﴿"that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress."﴾ The meaning would be: "[He might] hasten against us" by not listening to us; "or transgress" by killing us. So God said: ﴿"Indeed, I am with you,"﴾ hearing his speech with you, so I will make him attentive to listen to you; and seeing his actions, so I will not leave him until he does to you what you dislike.

Know that this verse indicates that God's being Hearing and Seeing are two attributes additional to knowledge, because His saying ﴿"Indeed, I am with you"﴾ already indicates knowledge. If ﴿"hearing and seeing"﴾ also indicated knowledge, that would be repetition, which contradicts the original principle.

Then He, glory be to Him, repeated that charge, saying ﴿"So go to him"﴾ (fa'tiyahu). Because He, glory be to Him and exalted, said the first time: ﴿"That We may show you of Our greatest signs"﴾ and ﴿"Go to Pharaoh"﴾ (20:23–24); the second time: ﴿"Go, you and your brother"﴾; the third time He said: ﴿"Go, both of you, to Pharaoh"﴾; and the fourth time, here, He said: ﴿"So go to him."﴾

If it is said: He commanded them, the second time, to say to him ﴿"a gentle word"﴾ (20:44), and this fourth time He commanded them to say ﴿"Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord, so send with us the Children of Israel,"﴾ which contains severity in several respects:

The first: His saying ﴿"Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord"﴾ contains several discussions:

The first discussion: his submission to them both and his committing himself to their obedience, which is very great for a ruler who is obeyed.

The second discussion: His saying ﴿"so send with us the Children of Israel"﴾ contains a diminishing of his kingdom, because he was in need of them for what he wanted done of works, such as building or other things.

The third discussion: His saying ﴿"and do not torment them."﴾

The fourth discussion: His saying ﴿"We have come to you with a sign from your Lord."﴾ What is the benefit of gentleness first and severity second? We say: because when a person's obstinacy becomes evident, he must be met with severity. If it is said: Was it not obligatory for them to say, "Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord, we have come to you with a sign, so send with us the Children of Israel and do not torment them," because mentioning the miracle together with the claim to prophethood is better than delaying it? We say: rather, this is better than delaying it, because they mentioned the whole set of claims and then presented the miracle as proof for that whole set.

As for His saying ﴿"We have come to you with a sign from your Lord,"﴾ there is a question: God had given him two signs, the staff and the hand, and then said ﴿"Go, you and your brother, with My signs"﴾ (23:35), which indicates three signs. Here He said ﴿"We have come to you with a sign,"﴾ which indicates that there was one. How is the reconciliation? Al-Qaffal answered that the meaning of "sign" here is a reference to the genus of signs, as if He said: "We have come to you with clarification from God." That clarification may be one proof or many proofs.

As for His saying ﴿"And peace be upon those who follow guidance,"﴾ some said it is part of God's speech to them both, as if He said: ﴿"So say, 'Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord,'"﴾ and say to him: ﴿"And peace be upon those who follow guidance."﴾ Others said: rather, God's speech was complete at His saying ﴿"We have come to you with a sign from your Lord,"﴾ and His saying afterward ﴿"And peace be upon those who follow guidance"﴾ is a promise from them both to whoever believes and affirms that he will have safety from the punishments of this world and the next. Peace here means safety, as one says "ridā‘" and "ridā‘ah" (both meaning nursing). The lam and ʿalā here have the same meaning, as in His saying: ﴿"For them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode"﴾ (13:25), meaning "upon them." And He said: ﴿"Whoever does righteousness, it is for himself, and whoever does evil, it is against himself"﴾ (41:46). And in another place: ﴿"If you do good, you do good for yourselves; and if you do evil, it is against them"﴾ (17:7).

As for His saying ﴿"Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment is for whoever denies and turns away,"﴾ know that this verse is among the strongest indications that the punishment of a believer does not last forever. This is because the definite article in ﴿"the punishment"﴾ (al-ʿadhab) either indicates comprehensiveness of the genus or indicates the quiddity (the reality of the thing). On both readings, the restriction of this genus to whoever denies and turns away is implied. So it is necessary that for one who is not a denier and not one who turns away, this genus does not arise at all. The apparent meaning of this verse necessitates the certainty that God does not punish any of the believers for abandoning acting upon it at some times. So it must remain on its original basis of negating permanence, because a finite punishment, when it is followed by safety for an infinite duration, becomes like no punishment at all. Therefore, given the occurrence of that amount, it is proper to say that there is no punishment. Also, His saying ﴿"And peace be upon those who follow guidance,"﴾ and we have interpreted peace as safety, its apparent meaning necessitates that safety be attained by everyone who follows guidance. The one who knows God has followed guidance, so he must be a possessor of safety.

Here He said ﴿"We have come to you with a sign,"﴾ which indicates that there was one. How is the reconciliation? Al-Qaffal answered that the meaning of "sign" here is a reference to the genus of signs, as if He said: "We have come to you with clarification from God." That clarification may be one proof or many proofs.

As for His saying ﴿"And peace be upon those who follow guidance,"﴾ some said it is part of God's speech to them both, as if He said: ﴿"So say, 'Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord,'"﴾ and say to him: ﴿"And peace be upon those who follow guidance."﴾ Others said: rather, God's speech was complete at His saying ﴿"We have come to you with a sign from your Lord,"﴾ and His saying afterward ﴿"And peace be upon those who follow guidance"﴾ is a promise from them both to whoever believes and affirms that he will have safety from the punishments of this world and the next. Peace here means safety, as one says "ridā‘" and "ridā‘ah" (both meaning nursing). The lam and ʿalā here have the same meaning, as in His saying: ﴿"For them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode"﴾ (13:25), meaning "upon them." And He said: ﴿"Whoever does righteousness, it is for himself, and whoever does evil, it is against himself"﴾ (41:46). And in another place: ﴿"If you do good, you do good for yourselves; and if you do evil, it is against them"﴾ (17:7).

As for His saying ﴿"Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment is for whoever denies and turns away,"﴾ know that this verse is among the strongest indications that the punishment of a believer does not last forever. This is because the definite article in ﴿"the punishment"﴾ (al-ʿadhab) either indicates comprehensiveness of the genus or indicates the quiddity (the reality of the thing). On both readings, the restriction of this genus to whoever denies and turns away is implied. So it is necessary that for one who is not a denier and not one who turns away, this genus does not arise at all. The apparent meaning of this verse necessitates the certainty that God does not punish any of the believers for abandoning acting upon it at some times. So it must remain on its original basis of negating permanence, because a finite punishment, when it is followed by safety for an infinite duration, becomes like no punishment at all. Therefore, given the occurrence of that amount, it is proper to say that there is no punishment. Also, His saying ﴿"And peace be upon those who follow guidance,"﴾ and we have interpreted peace as safety, its apparent meaning necessitates that safety be attained by everyone who follows guidance. The one who knows God has followed guidance, so he must be a possessor of safety.

[Page 55]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿[Pharaoh] said, "Who then is your Lord, O Moses?" He said, "Our Lord is He who gave everything its form and then guided it." He said, "What then of the former generations?" He said, "Their knowledge is with my Lord, in a Record. My Lord neither errs nor forgets." He is the One who made the earth a cradle for you and threaded for you roads within it, and sent down water from the sky, and by it We brought forth pairs of various plants. Eat, and pasture your livestock. Surely in that are signs for people of intellect. From it We created you, into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you out once more.﴾

Know that when they (peace be upon them both) said, ﴿Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord,﴾ he said to them, ﴿Who then is your Lord, O Moses?﴾ In this there are several issues (masāʾil):

**The first issue:** Pharaoh was extremely powerful, of great dominion and with a large army. Yet when Moses (peace be upon him) called him to Allah, Moses did not occupy himself with violence or harm against him, but went out to him in debate, because if he had begun with harm he would have been attributed to ignorance and foolishness. So he disdained that and began with debate. This shows that foolishness without proof is something Pharaoh himself would not have approved of, despite his complete ignorance and disbelief. How then does it befit one who claims Islam and knowledge? Furthermore, when Pharaoh asked Moses (peace be upon him) this question, Moses accepted it and occupied himself with establishing evidence for the existence of the Creator. This indicates the invalidity of blind imitation (taqlīd). It also indicates the invalidity of the view of the Taʿlīmiyya (the Ismaili-style "instructionists"), who say: "We derive knowledge of God from the word of the Messenger," because Moses (peace be upon him) here acknowledged that knowledge of Allah must precede knowledge of the Messenger. It also refutes the view of the Ḥashwiyya (literalist traditionalists), who say: "We derive knowledge of God and religion from the Book and the Sunna."

**The second issue:** The verse indicates that it is permissible to relate the words of the falsifier (mubṭil), because Allah the Exalted related Pharaoh's words in denying God, and related the doubts of those who deny prophethood and the doubts of those who deny the Resurrection. However, you must, whenever you present a question, pair it with its answer, so that doubt does not remain, as Allah the Exalted did in these passages.

**The third issue:** The verse indicates that the one who is in the right must listen to the words of the falsifier and answer him without harm or alienation, as Moses (peace be upon him) did with Pharaoh here, and as Allah the Exalted commanded His Messenger in His saying: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good admonition﴾ [al-Naḥl: 125], and said: ﴿And if any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection until he hears the words of Allah﴾ [al-Tawba: 6].

**The fourth issue:** People have differed as to whether Pharaoh had knowledge of Allah the Exalted. It was said that he did have knowledge, but he used to display denial out of arrogance, tyranny, falsehood and slander. They argued for this with six points:

The first: His saying: ﴿You certainly know that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 102]. If the "tāʾ" in ʿalimta ("you know") is read with a fatḥa, then this is an address from Moses (peace be upon him) to Pharaoh, and this indicates that Pharaoh was knowing of this. Likewise His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls acknowledged them, out of injustice and arrogance﴾ [al-Naml: 14].

The second: He was rational, for otherwise he could not have been held accountable (mukallaf). Everyone who is rational knows by necessity that he came into existence after non-existence, and everyone who is like that is in need of a governor (mudabbir). These two necessary kinds of knowledge entail knowledge of the existence of the governor.

The third: Moses' saying here: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its form and then guided it.﴾ The word "alladhī" (who/which) requires that the attribute of knowledge be described by a known clause, so this clause must have been known to him.

The fourth: His saying in Surah al-Qaṣaṣ about Pharaoh and his people: ﴿And they thought that they would not be returned to Us﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 39]. This indicates that they knew the origin (mabda') but denied the return (maʿād).

The fifth: Pharaoh's rule did not extend beyond the Copts, nor did it reach al-Sham (Greater Syria). When Moses (peace be upon him) fled to Madyan, Shuʿayb said to him: ﴿Do not fear; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 25]. Given this, how could he believe that he is the Lord of the worlds?

The sixth: When he said: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 23], Moses (peace be upon him) said: ﴿The Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 24]. He said: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 27], meaning: I am asking him for the quiddity (māhiyya), and he is describing the attribute. So he did not dispute with Moses about existence, but asked him for the quiddity, and this indicates his acknowledgement of the basic existence.

Others have said that he was ignorant of his Lord. They agreed that a rational person cannot believe about himself that he is the creator of these heavens, earths, sun and moon, or that he created himself, because he knows by necessity his incapacity regarding them, and he knows by necessity that they existed before him. So he has necessary knowledge that he is neither their existent-maker nor their creator.

They differed about the manner of his ignorance of Allah the Exalted. It is possible that he was a dahrī (materialist who denies any originating agent at all). It is possible that he was a philosopher who held to a necessitating cause (ʿilla mūjiba). It is possible that he was one of the worshippers of the stars. And it is possible that he was among the Ḥulūliyya (those who hold incarnation) of the anthropomorphist (mujassima) type. As for his claim to lordship for himself, it means that they are obligated to obey him, submit to him, and not occupy themselves with obeying anyone else.

**The fifth issue:** He, glory be to Him, related in this surah that he said: ﴿Who then is your Lord, O Moses?﴾ and in Surah al-Shuʿarāʾ he said: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ So the question here is with "man" (who), which concerns the manner (kayfiyya), and in Surah al-Shuʿarāʾ it is with "mā" (what), which concerns the quiddity (māhiyya). These are two different questions, though the incident is one. The closer view is that the question of "man" precedes the question of "mā," because he used to say, "I am God and Lord." So he said: "Who then is your Lord?" When Moses established the proof for existence and realized that he could not contend with him in this station, given its clarity and manifestness, he turned to the second station, which is seeking the quiddity. This too alerts one that he had knowledge of Allah, because he abandoned dispute in this station, knowing its utmost clarity, and proceeded to the difficult station, since knowledge of the quiddity of Allah the Exalted is not attainable for human beings.

**The sixth issue:** He said ﴿Who then is your Lord﴾ and did not say "who then is your god," because he had established himself as lord in his saying: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child, and did you not remain among us for years of your life?﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 18]. He mentioned that in the manner of astonishment, as if he were saying to him: "I am your lord, so why do you claim another lord?" This statement resembles the statement of Nimrod. When Abraham (peace be upon him) said: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾ [al-Baqara: 258], Nimrod said to him: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾ [al-Baqara: 258]. The giving of life and causing of death that Abraham mentioned were not what Nimrod opposed him with, except in wording. Likewise here: when Moses claimed the lordship of Allah the Exalted, Pharaoh mentioned this statement, intending: "I am the lord, because I raised you." It is well known that the lordship Moses claimed for Allah, glory be to Him and Exalted, is different in meaning from this lordship, and there is no commonality between them except in wording.

* * *

**The seventh issue:** Know that Moses (peace be upon him) argued for the existence of the Creator from the conditions of created things, namely his saying: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its form and then guided it.﴾ This is the argument which Allah the Exalted mentioned to Muhammad (ﷺ) in His saying: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, and who determined and guided﴾ [al-Aʿlā: 1–3]. Abraham (peace be upon him) said: ﴿They are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds, who created me and it is He who guides me﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 77–78]. Moses (peace be upon him) relied in most matters on the proofs of Abraham (peace be upon him), and the explanation of this will come in Surah al-Shuʿarāʾ, if Allah the Exalted wills. Know that it seems that creation (khalq) means the assembling of forms and bodies, and guidance (hidāya) means the depositing of the perceptive and motive powers (quwā) into those bodies. On this understanding, creation precedes guidance; for this reason He said: ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 29]. So proportioning refers to the form, and breathing of the spirit is an indication of the depositing of the powers. He said: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 12], up to His saying: ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 14]. Thus it is clear that creation precedes guidance. And beginning to explain the wonders of Allah's wisdom in creation and guidance is embarking upon a sea with no shore. Let us mention from it some examples close to understanding:

The first: The natural philosopher says: heavy things fall and light things rise, and the heaviest of things is earth, then water, and the lightest is fire, then air. Therefore fire must be the highest of the elemental things, and earth the lowest. Then He, glory be to Him, reversed this order in the creation of man: the highest of things in him is the bone and hair, which are the driest parts of the body, and these stand in the position of earth. Beneath them He placed the brain, which stands in the position of water. Beneath it He placed the soul (nafs), which stands in the position of air. Beneath it He placed the innate heat (al-ḥarāra al-gharīziyya) in the heart, which stands in the position of fire. Thus He placed the position of earth in the upper body, and the position of fire in the lower body, so that it may be known that this is by the governance of the All-Powerful, the Wise, the Merciful, and not by the requirement of cause and nature.

The second: If you look at the wonders of the bee in building hexagonal hives, and at the wonders of the states of the bedbug and the mosquito in their guidance to what benefits themselves, you will know that this is not possible except by the inspiration of a governor who knows all that is knowable.

Third, He is the One who bestowed upon the creatures that by which their sustenance is maintained: food, drink, clothing and spouses. Then He guided them to the manner of benefiting from these. They extract iron from the mountains and pearls from the seas, they compound medicines and beneficial antidotes, and they combine different things to extract the pleasures of foods. Thus it is established that He, glorified is He, is the One who created all things. Then He gave them intellects by which they reach the manner of benefiting from them. This is not restricted to humans but is general across all animals: He gave the human a female human, the donkey a female donkey, and the camel a she-camel, then guided each to them so that procreation would endure. He guided the offspring to the mothers' teats. Moreover, this is not restricted to animals but is present in their organs: He created the hand with a particular structure and placed in it the power of grasping, He created the foot with a particular structure and placed in it the power of walking, and likewise the eye, the ear and all the organs. Then He linked some to others in ways from whose linkage a single whole results, namely the human being.

These things indicate the existence of the Creator, glorified is He, because the attribution of each body among these bodies with that quality, I mean composition, power and guidance, is either necessary or contingent. The first is false, because we observe those bodies after death detached from those compositions and powers, so this shows that it is contingent. And the contingent necessarily requires a determinant. That determinant is neither the human nor his parents, because doing that requires power over it and knowledge of what it contains of benefits and harms, and both matters are far from the human, for after the perfection of his intellect he is unable to alter a single hair, and after intense research into the books of anatomy, only a small amount of the benefits and purposes of the organs is known. Therefore there must be another existent who is in charge of their management and arrangement. That existent cannot be a body, because bodies are equal in corporeality, so the specialisation of that body with that influence must be contingent, and if it is contingent it requires another cause. Circularity and infinite regress are both impossible, so there must be an end to the chain of need in an existent that is an effective and governing agent, which is neither a body nor corporeal. Then the influence of that effector is either by essence or by choice. The first is impossible, because the one acting by essence does not distinguish one like from another like, and these bodies are equal in corporeality, so why did some of them become specialised with the celestial form, some with the elemental form, some with the vegetative form, and some with the animal form? Thus it is established that the effector and governor is powerful, and the powerful cannot produce such wondrous acts unless he is knowing. Furthermore, this governor, who is neither a body nor corporeal, must necessarily be necessary of existence in His essence and in His attributes, otherwise he would need another governor and infinite regress would follow, which is impossible. And if He is necessary of existence in His power and knowledge, then what is necessary in itself is not specialised with some possibilia rather than others, so He must be knowing of everything that can be known and powerful over everything that can be made subject to power. Thus it became evident, by this proof which Moses, peace be upon him, relied upon, and which the attribution of the world to a governor who is neither a body nor corporeal, and who is necessary of existence in His essence and attributes, knowing of all knowables and powerful over all powerables, points out in establishing it. That is Allah, glorified and exalted is He.

Eighth issue: Pharaoh addressed the two with his words ﴿So who is your Lord?﴾, then directed the address to one of them, namely Moses, peace be upon him, because he is the principal in prophethood and Aaron is his minister and follower. Or because Pharaoh, through his malice, knew of the speech impediment in the tongue of Moses, peace be upon him, so he wanted to make him speak rather than his brother, because of what he knew of his eloquence and of the impediment in Moses' tongue. This is indicated by his saying: ﴿Am I not better than this one who is despicable and can hardly express himself clearly?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 52].

* * *

Ninth issue: Regarding His saying ﴿who gave everything its creation, then guided﴾ there are two aspects:

One: there is inversion and displacement, meaning He gave His creatures everything they need and by which they are benefited.

The second: the intended meaning of "creation" is the form and shape suited to its benefit. It is as if He, glorified is He, said: He gave everything the form which suits its benefit and its welfare. It is also read as khalqahu (his creation), as an attribute of the genitive or of the genitive-annexed. The meaning is that everything Allah created He did not leave devoid of His bestowal and favour.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: What then is the state of the former generations?﴾ know that there are several aspects of the connection of this statement with what precedes it:

One: when Moses, peace be upon him, established for Pharaoh the matter of the origin and the return, Pharaoh said: if the establishment of the origin is at this level of clarity, then ﴿what is the state of the former generations?﴾ Did they affirm it and then abandon it? So when Moses, peace be upon him, argued with the decisive proof for establishing the Creator, Pharaoh attacked that proof by saying: if the matter is as strong as this proof which you mention, then the people of past generations must not have been heedless of it, so he opposed the proof with imitation.

Two: Moses, peace be upon him, first threatened with punishment in his saying: ﴿Indeed it has been revealed to us that the punishment is upon whoever denies and turns away﴾, so Pharaoh said: ﴿What then is the state of the former generations?﴾ For they denied, and yet they were not punished?

Three, and this is the most evident: when Pharaoh said: ﴿So who is your Lord, O Moses?﴾, Moses, peace be upon him, mentioned a manifest proof and a dazzling demonstration for this demand, saying: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation, then guided﴾. Pharaoh feared that he would expand upon the establishment of that argument, so that the truth of his claim and the corruption of Pharaoh's path would become apparent to the people. So he wanted to divert him from that discourse and occupy him with narratives, saying: ﴿What then is the state of the former generations?﴾ But Moses, peace be upon him, did not turn to that talk, rather he said: ﴿Their knowledge is with my Lord in a Book﴾, meaning my aim does not depend on their conditions, so I do not occupy myself with them. Then he returned to completing his first speech and presenting the dazzling proofs of Divine Oneness, saying: ﴿He who made for you the earth a cradle and threaded for you therein roads﴾. This aspect is the one relied upon for the soundness of this arrangement. Then there are issues here:

First issue: They differed regarding His saying ﴿Their knowledge is with my Lord in a Book﴾, for how can knowledge that is with the Lord be in a book? The verification is that the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, is His attribute, and an attribute of a thing subsists in it. As for an attribute of a thing being present in a book, that is not intelligible. So they gave two explanations:

The first: its meaning is that He, glorified is He, recorded those judgments in a book with Him, because what He wrote therein becomes manifest to the angels, so this would be an increase for them in inferring that He, exalted is He, is knowing of all knowables, free from forgetfulness and heedlessness. Someone may say: the phrase "in a Book" suggests that He, glorified and exalted is He, needs that book for that knowledge, and this, although it is not necessarily inevitable, at least suggests it at first, especially for the disbeliever. How then is it fitting to mention it with an obstinate person like Pharaoh at the time of the call?

The second explanation: that interpreting it as the persistence of those knowables in His knowledge, glorified is He, is like the persistence of what is written in a book, so the purpose of this statement is to emphasise that their secrets are known to Allah, exalted is He, such that nothing of them departs from His knowledge. This interpretation is reinforced by His saying afterwards: ﴿My Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾.

Second issue: They differed regarding His saying ﴿My Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾. Some said the meaning of the two expressions is one, namely nothing is hidden from Him and nothing escapes Him. This is the view of Mujahid. The majority hold a distinction between them, and they mentioned several aspects:

First, and the best of what was said is that of al-Qaffal: He does not err concerning things and their knowledge, and what He knows of that He does not forget. So the first expression indicates that He is knowing of all knowables, and the second, His saying "nor forgets", indicates the persistence of that knowledge forever, and it indicates the negation of change.

Second: Muqatil said: My Lord does not mistake that Book, nor does He forget what is in it.

Third: al-Hasan said: He does not mistake the time of resurrection, nor does He forget it.

Fourth: Abu 'Amr said: the root of error is absence, so the meaning is that He is not absent from anything, and nothing is absent from Him.

Fifth: Ibn Jarir said: He does not err in the disposition so as to believe what is not right to be right, and when He knows it, He does not forget it. These aspects are close in meaning, and the verified one is the first.

Third issue: When Pharaoh asked him about the God and said ﴿So who is your Lord, O Moses?﴾, and that was of the kind whose path is inference, he answered with what is correct in the most concise expression and the finest meaning. When he asked him about the state of the former generations, and that was of the kind whose path is reporting, and he had received no report about it, he entrusted it to the Knower of the Unseen. Know that when Moses, peace be upon him, mentioned the first proof, which is a general proof encompassing all created things, from humans and the rest of the animals, the kinds of plants and inanimate things, he then mentioned specific proofs, and they are three.

The first of them is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He who made for you the earth a cradle﴾. In this there are discussions:

First discussion: The people of Kufa read "mahdan" here and in al-Zukhruf, while the rest read "mihadan" in both. Abu 'Ubayda said: what I choose is mihadan, and mahd is the noun of the act, while others said: mahd is the noun and mihad is the plural, like farsh and firash. Abu 'Ubayda replied that firash is a noun and furush is a verbal form. Al-Mufaddal said both are verbal nouns of mahhada, when one prepares a bed for someone; it is said: mahhada mahdan and mihadan, and farasha farshan and firashan.

Second discussion: The author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿alladhi ja'ala﴾ is in the nominative because it is the predicate of an omitted subject, or because it is an attribute of "Rabbi", or it is in the accusative by way of praise. This is from its sources and its figurative usage. Know that it is necessary to be certain that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, for if we took it as the other two possibilities, it would follow that it is part of Moses' speech, and if it were so, the arrangement would be spoiled by His saying ﴿so We brought forth thereby pairs of various plants﴾, as will be explained, Allah willing.

Third discussion: The meaning of the earth being a cradle is that He, exalted is He, made it such that servants and others move about on it by sitting, standing, sleeping, cultivating, and all the forms of benefit. We have discussed this at length in Surat al-Baqarah in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He who made the earth for you a bed and the sky a canopy﴾ [al-Baqarah: 22].

The second of them is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and threaded for you therein roads﴾. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "salaka" derives from His saying ﴿What led you into Saqar?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 42] and ﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the guilty﴾, meaning He made for you roads therein and placed them between the mountains, the valleys and the deserts.

The third of them is His saying: ﴿and sent down from the sky water﴾, and the discussion of it has passed in Surat al-Baqarah.

These two necessary kinds of knowledge entail knowledge of the existence of the governor.

The third: Moses' saying here: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its form and then guided it.﴾ The word "alladhī" (who/which) requires that the attribute of knowledge be described by a known clause, so this clause must have been known to him.

The fourth: His saying in Surah al-Qaṣaṣ about Pharaoh and his people: ﴿And they thought that they would not be returned to Us﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 39]. This indicates that they knew the origin (mabda') but denied the return (maʿād).

The fifth: Pharaoh's rule did not extend beyond the Copts, nor did it reach al-Sham (Greater Syria). When Moses (peace be upon him) fled to Madyan, Shuʿayb said to him: ﴿Do not fear; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 25]. Given this, how could he believe that he is the Lord of the worlds?

The sixth: When he said: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 23], Moses (peace be upon him) said: ﴿The Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 24]. He said: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 27], meaning: I am asking him for the quiddity (māhiyya), and he is describing the attribute. So he did not dispute with Moses about existence, but asked him for the quiddity, and this indicates his acknowledgement of the basic existence.

Others have said that he was ignorant of his Lord. They agreed that a rational person cannot believe about himself that he is the creator of these heavens, earths, sun and moon, or that he created himself, because he knows by necessity his incapacity regarding them, and he knows by necessity that they existed before him. So he has necessary knowledge that he is neither their existent-maker nor their creator.

They differed about the manner of his ignorance of Allah the Exalted. It is possible that he was a dahrī (materialist who denies any originating agent at all). It is possible that he was a philosopher who held to a necessitating cause (ʿilla mūjiba). It is possible that he was one of the worshippers of the stars. And it is possible that he was among the Ḥulūliyya (those who hold incarnation) of the anthropomorphist (mujassima) type. As for his claim to lordship for himself, it means that they are obligated to obey him, submit to him, and not occupy themselves with obeying anyone else.

**The fifth issue:** He, glory be to Him, related in this surah that he said: ﴿Who then is your Lord, O Moses?﴾ and in Surah al-Shuʿarāʾ he said: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ So the question here is with "man" (who), which concerns the manner (kayfiyya), and in Surah al-Shuʿarāʾ it is with "mā" (what), which concerns the quiddity (māhiyya). These are two different questions, though the incident is one. The closer view is that the question of "man" precedes the question of "mā," because he used to say, "I am God and Lord." So he said: "Who then is your Lord?" When Moses established the proof for existence and realized that he could not contend with him in this station, given its clarity and manifestness, he turned to the second station, which is seeking the quiddity. This too alerts one that he had knowledge of Allah, because he abandoned dispute in this station, knowing its utmost clarity, and proceeded to the difficult station, since knowledge of the quiddity of Allah the Exalted is not attainable for human beings.

**The sixth issue:** He said ﴿Who then is your Lord﴾ and did not say "who then is your god," because he had established himself as lord in his saying: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child, and did you not remain among us for years of your life?﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 18]. He mentioned that in the manner of astonishment, as if he were saying to him: "I am your lord, so why do you claim another lord?" This statement resembles the statement of Nimrod. When Abraham (peace be upon him) said: ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾ [al-Baqara: 258], Nimrod said to him: ﴿I give life and cause death﴾ [al-Baqara: 258]. The giving of life and causing of death that Abraham mentioned were not what Nimrod opposed him with, except in wording. Likewise here: when Moses claimed the lordship of Allah the Exalted, Pharaoh mentioned this statement, intending: "I am the lord, because I raised you." It is well known that the lordship Moses claimed for Allah, glory be to Him and Exalted, is different in meaning from this lordship, and there is no commonality between them except in wording.
