Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verses 59–62:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: "Your appointment is the Day of Adornment, and that the people be gathered in the forenoon."﴾ ﴿Then Pharaoh withdrew, gathered his scheming, and came.﴾ ﴿Moses said to them: "Woe to you! Do not fabricate against Allah a lie, lest He destroy you with a punishment. Indeed, he has failed who fabricates."﴾ ﴿So they disputed their affair among themselves and secretly conferred.﴾ Know that in the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: It is possible that His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿He said: "Your appointment..."﴾ is the speech of Pharaoh, in which case he specified the time; and it is possible that it is the speech of Moses, peace be upon him. Al-Qadi said: The first is more apparent, because he is the one who demands the gathering, not Moses, peace be upon him. In my view, the more apparent is that it is the speech of Moses, peace be upon him, for several reasons:

The first of them: It is a response to Pharaoh's saying: ﴿Set up between us and you an appointment.﴾

The second: Specifying the Day of Adornment requires that everyone be informed of what is going to take place. Specifying it befits only the one who is in the right, who knows that the upper hand is his, not the one in falsehood, who knows that he has nothing but deception.

The third: His saying ﴿Your appointment﴾ is addressed to a plural. If we make it from Pharaoh to Moses and Aaron, it would necessarily mean either that it is an honorific plural, which does not befit Pharaoh's position with them, or that the least plural is two, which is not permissible. But if we make it from Moses, peace be upon him, to Pharaoh and his people, the sentence is sound.

The second issue: ﴿The Day of Adornment﴾ — some read it with a damma on the mim, and al-Hasan read it with a fatha. Al-Zajjaj said: If it is in the nominative, then it is the predicate of the subject, and the meaning is: the time of your appointment is the Day of Adornment. And whoever reads it in the accusative, then it is as an adverbial of time, meaning: your appointment takes place on the Day of Adornment. And His saying ﴿and that the people be gathered in the forenoon﴾ means: your appointment is the gathering of the people in the forenoon. So the position of ''an'' (أن) is nominative, and it may also be genitive by coordination with ''al-zinah'' (الزينة), as if he said: your appointment is on the Day of Adornment and on the day when the people are gathered in the forenoon. If it is said: Did you not say, in explaining His saying ﴿Set up between us and you an appointment﴾, that the sense is: set up a place of appointment which we will not break, a level place? How then does the answer correspond to it by mentioning a time? We say: It corresponds in meaning, even if it does not correspond in wording, because they must gather on the Day of Adornment at a specific place known for the gathering of people on that day. Thus by mentioning the time, the place is known.

The third issue: The exegetes mentioned several views concerning the Day of Adornment:

The first: It is a festival day for them on which they adorn themselves.

The second: Muqatil said: It is the day of Nawruz (the Persian New Year).

The third: Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: It is a market day for them.

The fourth: Ibn Abbas said: It is the day of 'Ashura. He said ''yuhsha'' (يُحْشَرَ) because they gather on that day by themselves, without anyone gathering them. It is also read ''wa-an tuhsha'' (وأنْ تُحْشَرَ) with the ya' and the ta', meaning: and that you, O Pharaoh, gather the people, and that he gather the day. It is also permissible that the pronoun in it refers to Pharaoh, mentioned in the third person, either according to the custom in which kings are addressed, or he addressed the people with His saying ﴿your appointment﴾ and made the pronoun of ''yuhsha'' refer to Pharaoh. He set that day as their appointment only so that the exaltation of the word of Allah, the manifestation of His religion, the humiliation of the disbeliever and the vanishing of falsehood would take place before the eyes of witnesses, in a general assembly, so that the account of that wondrous matter would be told often in every desert and settlement, and would spread among all the people of tents and cities.

[p. 64]

Al-Qadi said: He specified the day by His saying ﴿the Day of Adornment﴾, then specified a particular time within the day by His saying ﴿and that the people be gathered in the forenoon﴾.

As for His saying ﴿Then Pharaoh withdrew, gathered his scheming, and came﴾, know that ''tawalli'' (تَوَلّى) may mean turning away in opposition, and may mean departing. The apparent meaning here is that it means departing, namely leaving Moses, peace be upon him, at the appointed time at which they agreed to meet ''therein'' (فِيهِ). Muqatil said: ''Fa-tawalla'' means he turned away and persisted in his aversion from the truth. Included in His saying ﴿gathered his scheming﴾ are the magicians and all who gather for that, and included in it are the instruments and all that the magicians brought. ﴿Then came﴾: included in ''atā'' (أتى) is that he came to the place with the magicians, with the people, and with the instruments. Ibn Abbas said: They were seventy-two magicians, each of whom had a rope and a staff. It was also said: They were four hundred, and it was also said: more than that. Then a pavilion was set up for Pharaoh, and he sat in it, looking at them. The length of the pavilion was seventy cubits.

Then He, may He be exalted, showed that Moses, peace be upon him, before everything else, gave warning and caution about what they had said and undertaken, and so he said: ﴿Woe to you! Do not fabricate against Allah a lie﴾, by claiming that what I have brought is not true and that it is magic, so that you may oppose me. Al-Zajjaj said: With regard to the accusative of ''woyalkum'' (ويْلَكم), the meaning may be: Allah imposes upon them woe if they fabricate against Allah a lie. It may also be as a vocative, like His saying: ﴿O woe to me! Shall I bear a child while I am an old woman?﴾ [Hud: 72] and ﴿O woe to us! Who has raised us from our sleeping place?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52], and His saying ﴿lest He destroy you with a punishment﴾, meaning: He will punish you with a destroying punishment that uproots. Hamza, Asim and al-Kisa'i read the ya' of ''yushhitakum'' (يُسْحِتَكم) with a damma, from ''al-ishhat'' (الإسْحات), while the rest read it with a fatha, from ''al-suht'' (السُّحْت). ''Al-ishhat'' is the dialect of the people of Najd and the Banu Tamim, and ''al-suht'' is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. So it is as if He, may He be exalted, said: whoever fabricates against Allah a lie, two things befall him:

The first of them: The punishment of uprooting in this world, or the severe punishment in the Hereafter, and this is what is meant by His saying ﴿lest He destroy you with a punishment﴾.

The second: Failure and deprivation from the goal, and this is what is meant by His saying ﴿Indeed, he has failed who fabricates﴾.

Then He, glorified and exalted, showed that when Moses, peace be upon him, said that, they turned away from his words: ﴿So they disputed their affair among themselves.﴾ Concerning ''tanazu'' (تَنازَعُوا) there are two views:

The first: They conferred and consulted in order to settle upon one matter.

The second: Muqatil said: They disagreed among themselves. Then some of them said: Pharaoh and his people entered into the dispute; and some of them say: rather, it was the magicians alone, and the statement is open to interpretation, and there is nothing in the apparent wording that indicates a preference.

The exegetes mentioned several views concerning His saying ﴿and secretly conferred﴾:

The first: They conferred secretly from Pharaoh. On this assumption there are several views:

The first: Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: Their secret talk was: If Moses overcomes us, we will follow him.

The second: Qatada said: If he is a magician, we will overcome him; and if he is from heaven, then he has a matter [of his own].

The third: Wahb said: When he said ﴿Woe to you!﴾ and the verse, they said: This is not the speech of a magician.

The second view: They secretly conferred from Moses and Pharaoh, and their secret talk was their saying: ﴿Indeed, these two are magicians who want to drive you out of your land﴾, and this is the view of al-Suddi.

The third view: They secretly conferred from Moses and Aaron and from Pharaoh and his people as well, and their secret talk was: how the matter of the ropes and staffs should be arranged, and in what manner they should be displayed so that it would have more effect upon hearts and better reveal the flaws [of the other side]. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

He set that day as their appointment only so that the exaltation of the word of Allah, the manifestation of His religion, the humiliation of the disbeliever and the vanishing of falsehood would take place before the eyes of witnesses, in a general assembly, so that the account of that wondrous matter would be told often in every desert and settlement, and would spread among all the people of tents and cities.

[p. 64]

Al-Qadi said: He specified the day by His saying ﴿the Day of Adornment﴾, then specified a particular time within the day by His saying ﴿and that the people be gathered in the forenoon﴾.

As for His saying ﴿Then Pharaoh withdrew, gathered his scheming, and came﴾, know that ''tawalli'' (تَوَلّى) may mean turning away in opposition, and may mean departing. The apparent meaning here is that it means departing, namely leaving Moses, peace be upon him, at the appointed time at which they agreed to meet ''therein'' (فِيهِ). Muqatil said: ''Fa-tawalla'' means he turned away and persisted in his aversion from the truth. Included in His saying ﴿gathered his scheming﴾ are the magicians and all who gather for that, and included in it are the instruments and all that the magicians brought. ﴿Then came﴾: included in ''atā'' (أتى) is that he came to the place with the magicians, with the people, and with the instruments. Ibn Abbas said: They were seventy-two magicians, each of whom had a rope and a staff. It was also said: They were four hundred, and it was also said: more than that. Then a pavilion was set up for Pharaoh, and he sat in it, looking at them. The length of the pavilion was seventy cubits.

Then He, may He be exalted, showed that Moses, peace be upon him, before everything else, gave warning and caution about what they had said and undertaken, and so he said: ﴿Woe to you! Do not fabricate against Allah a lie﴾, by claiming that what I have brought is not true and that it is magic, so that you may oppose me. Al-Zajjaj said: With regard to the accusative of ''woyalkum'' (ويْلَكم), the meaning may be: Allah imposes upon them woe if they fabricate against Allah a lie. It may also be as a vocative, like His saying: ﴿O woe to me! Shall I bear a child while I am an old woman?﴾ [Hud: 72] and ﴿O woe to us! Who has raised us from our sleeping place?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52], and His saying ﴿lest He destroy you with a punishment﴾, meaning: He will punish you with a destroying punishment that uproots. Hamza, Asim and al-Kisa'i read the ya' of ''yushhitakum'' (يُسْحِتَكم) with a damma, from ''al-ishhat'' (الإسْحات), while the rest read it with a fatha, from ''al-suht'' (السُّحْت). ''Al-ishhat'' is the dialect of the people of Najd and the Banu Tamim, and ''al-suht'' is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. So it is as if He, may He be exalted, said: whoever fabricates against Allah a lie, two things befall him:

The first of them: The punishment of uprooting in this world, or the severe punishment in the Hereafter, and this is what is meant by His saying ﴿lest He destroy you with a punishment﴾.

The second: Failure and deprivation from the goal, and this is what is meant by His saying ﴿Indeed, he has failed who fabricates﴾.

Then He, glorified and exalted, showed that when Moses, peace be upon him, said that, they turned away from his words: ﴿So they disputed their affair among themselves.﴾ Concerning ''tanazu'' (تَنازَعُوا) there are two views:

The first: They conferred and consulted in order to settle upon one matter.

The second: Muqatil said: They disagreed among themselves. Then some of them said: Pharaoh and his people entered into the dispute; and some of them say: rather, it was the magicians alone, and the statement is open to interpretation, and there is nothing in the apparent wording that indicates a preference.

The exegetes mentioned several views concerning His saying ﴿and secretly conferred﴾:

The first: They conferred secretly from Pharaoh. On this assumption there are several views:

The first: Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: Their secret talk was: If Moses overcomes us, we will follow him.

The second: Qatada said: If he is a magician, we will overcome him; and if he is from heaven, then he has a matter [of his own].

The third: Wahb said: When he said ﴿Woe to you!﴾ and the verse, they said: This is not the speech of a magician.

The second view: They secretly conferred from Moses and Pharaoh, and their secret talk was their saying: ﴿Indeed, these two are magicians who want to drive you out of your land﴾, and this is the view of al-Suddi.

The third view: They secretly conferred from Moses and Aaron and from Pharaoh and his people as well, and their secret talk was: how the matter of the ropes and staffs should be arranged, and in what manner they should be displayed so that it would have more effect upon hearts and better reveal the flaws [of the other side]. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verses 59–62:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: "Your appointment is the Day of Adornment, and that the people be gathered in the forenoon."﴾ ﴿Then Pharaoh withdrew, gathered his scheming, and came.﴾ ﴿Moses said to them: "Woe to you! Do not fabricate against Allah a lie, lest He destroy you with a punishment. Indeed, he has failed who fabricates."﴾ ﴿So they disputed their affair among themselves and secretly conferred.﴾ Know that in the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: It is possible that His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿He said: "Your appointment..."﴾ is the speech of Pharaoh, in which case he specified the time; and it is possible that it is the speech of Moses, peace be upon him. Al-Qadi said: The first is more apparent, because he is the one who demands the gathering, not Moses, peace be upon him. In my view, the more apparent is that it is the speech of Moses, peace be upon him, for several reasons:

The first of them: It is a response to Pharaoh's saying: ﴿Set up between us and you an appointment.﴾

The second: Specifying the Day of Adornment requires that everyone be informed of what is going to take place. Specifying it befits only the one who is in the right, who knows that the upper hand is his, not the one in falsehood, who knows that he has nothing but deception.

The third: His saying ﴿Your appointment﴾ is addressed to a plural. If we make it from Pharaoh to Moses and Aaron, it would necessarily mean either that it is an honorific plural, which does not befit Pharaoh's position with them, or that the least plural is two, which is not permissible. But if we make it from Moses, peace be upon him, to Pharaoh and his people, the sentence is sound.

The second issue: ﴿The Day of Adornment﴾ — some read it with a damma on the mim, and al-Hasan read it with a fatha. Al-Zajjaj said: If it is in the nominative, then it is the predicate of the subject, and the meaning is: the time of your appointment is the Day of Adornment. And whoever reads it in the accusative, then it is as an adverbial of time, meaning: your appointment takes place on the Day of Adornment. And His saying ﴿and that the people be gathered in the forenoon﴾ means: your appointment is the gathering of the people in the forenoon. So the position of ''an'' (أن) is nominative, and it may also be genitive by coordination with ''al-zinah'' (الزينة), as if he said: your appointment is on the Day of Adornment and on the day when the people are gathered in the forenoon. If it is said: Did you not say, in explaining His saying ﴿Set up between us and you an appointment﴾, that the sense is: set up a place of appointment which we will not break, a level place? How then does the answer correspond to it by mentioning a time? We say: It corresponds in meaning, even if it does not correspond in wording, because they must gather on the Day of Adornment at a specific place known for the gathering of people on that day. Thus by mentioning the time, the place is known.

The third issue: The exegetes mentioned several views concerning the Day of Adornment:

The first: It is a festival day for them on which they adorn themselves.

The second: Muqatil said: It is the day of Nawruz (the Persian New Year).

The third: Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: It is a market day for them.

The fourth: Ibn Abbas said: It is the day of 'Ashura. He said ''yuhsha'' (يُحْشَرَ) because they gather on that day by themselves, without anyone gathering them. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verse 63 (part 1 of 2):

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They said: Indeed these two are certainly sorcerers who wish to drive you out of your land with their magic and to do away with your most excellent way of life.﴾ ﴿So gather your plan, then come in a row. And whoever prevails today will have succeeded.﴾ There are several issues concerning this verse:

Page 65

The first issue: The well-known recitation is ﴿inna hadhani la-sahiran﴾ (إنْ هَذانِ لَساحِرانِ). Some have abandoned this recitation and mentioned other readings:

The first: Abu 'Amr and 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited, "inna hadhayni la-sahiran" (إنَّ هَذَيْنِ لَساحِرانِ). They said: this is the recitation of 'Uthman, 'A'isha, Ibn al-Zubayr, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with them all. Abu 'Amr and 'Isa argued for this by what Hisham ibn 'Urwa narrated from his father, from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she was asked about His words: ﴿Indeed these two are sorcerers﴾ and about His words in al-Ma'ida: ﴿Indeed those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 69], and about His words: ﴿But those firm in knowledge among them and the believers believe in what has been revealed to you... and those who establish prayer and those who give zakah﴾ [an-Nisa': 162]. She said: "O nephew, this is an error of the scribe." It is also narrated from 'Uthman that he looked into the mushaf and said: "I see in it a lahn (grammatical error), and the Arabs will set it right with their tongues." And it is narrated from Abu 'Amr that he said: "I am truly ashamed to recite: ﴿Indeed these two are sorcerers﴾."

The second: Ibn Kathir recited "inna hadhanni" (إنْ هَذانِّ), with the "inna" lightened and the nun of "hadhan" doubled.

The third: Hafs, from 'Asim, recited "inna hadhani" (إنْ هَذانِ) with both nuns lightened.

The fourth: 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud recited: (wa-asarru al-najwa, anna hadhani sahirani) (وأسَرُّوا النَّجْوى، أنْ هَذانِ ساحِرانِ), with the alif of "anna" pronounced with fatha and its nun with sukun, and "sahirani" without the lam.

The fifth: From al-Akhfash: ﴿inna hadhani la-sahiran﴾ is a light (khafifah) form with the meaning of the heavy (thaqilah) form. It is the dialect of a people who raise the case endings with it and insert the lam to distinguish it from the "inna" that means "ma" (not).

The sixth: It is narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "ma hadhani illa sahiran" (ما هَذانِ إلّا ساحِرانِ). It is also narrated from him: [inna hadhani la-sahiran], and from al-Khalil the like of that. And from Ubayy also: [inna dhani la-sahiran] (إنْ ذانِ لَساحِرانِ). These are the irregular (shadh) recitations mentioned concerning this verse.

Know that the scholars of verification (al-muhaqqiqun) said: these recitations cannot be accepted as correct, because they are transmitted by way of individual reports (ahad), whereas the Qur'an must be transmitted by mass transmission (tawatur). For if we allowed the establishment of an addition to the Qur'an by way of individual reports, we could not be certain that what is with us is the whole Qur'an. For since it is permissible for these recitations, along with being from the Qur'an, not to have been transmitted by mass transmission, it is permissible for others too. Thus it is established that permitting these recitations to be from the Qur'an opens the door to permitting addition, subtraction and alteration in the Qur'an, and that removes the Qur'an from being a proof. Since that is false, what leads to it is also false. As for impugning the well-known recitation, it is worse than what came before, in several respects:

The first: Since the transmission of this recitation is in fame like the transmission of the whole Qur'an, if we judged it void, the same could be applied to the whole Qur'an, and that leads to discrediting mass transmission and discrediting the entire Qur'an, which is false. Once this is established, it is impossible for it to be set against an individual report transmitted from some of the Companions.

The second: The Muslims unanimously agreed that what lies between the two covers is the speech of Allah the Exalted, and the speech of Allah the Exalted cannot be a lahn (error) and a mistake. Thus the falsity of what is narrated from 'Uthman and 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with them both, that there is in it a lahn and a mistake, is established.

The third: Ibn al-Anbari said: The Companions are the imams and the exemplars. If they had found a lahn in the mushaf, they would not have delegated its correction to others after them, despite their warning against innovation and their encouragement to follow. Some of them even said: "Follow and do not innovate, for you have been sufficed." Thus it is established that the well-known recitation must be made correct. The grammarians differed concerning it and mentioned several explanations:

The first explanation, which is the strongest: this is a dialect of some of the Arabs. Some said it is the dialect of Bal-Harith ibn Ka'b; al-Zajjaj attributed it to Kinanah; Qutrub attributed it to Bal-Harith ibn Ka'b, Murad, Khath'am and some of Banu 'Udhrah; and Ibn Jinni attributed it also to some of Banu Rabi'ah. Al-Farra' cited in support of this dialect:

*So he lowered his gaze like the warrior, and had he found a passage, the warrior's fangs would have cracked (his jaws).*

Another cited:

*He gave us a striking blow between his two ears, which called him to the dust of the barren desert.*

Al-Farra' said: Some of Banu Asad related that he said: "This is the handwriting of my brother, I recognize it." Qutrub said: These people say: "ra'aytu rajulan" and "ishtaraytu thawban" (with the dual in alif). A man of Banu Dabbah, a pre-Islamic poet, said:

*I recognize from her the neck and the two eyes, and two nostrils resembling two gazelles.*

His saying "wa-manakhirayni" is according to the common dialect, and what is beyond that is according to the dialect of these people.

Another said:

*They flew above them, so fly above them, and tie tightly the two thongs of their girth.*

Another said:

*As if the grinding of his two fangs when he gnashes them is the cry of the two sand-grouse.*

Some said: al-Akhtaban is the male of the sand-grouse; so he made the two into one, and the proof remains in his saying "grinding of his fangs." He said: Yunus recited to me, from some of Banu al-Harith:

*As if the right hand of a ... and its ... is a flow of blood that will not cease to linger forever.*

They also recited:

*Indeed his father and his father's father have reached the furthest point in glory.*

Ibn Jinni said: We narrated from Qutrub:

*There, that you weep with a sturdy one, broad-hearted, long-armed.*

Then al-Farra' said: This, though rare, is more analogous, because what precedes the letter of the dual is fatha, so what follows should be alif; and if what follows were ya, it should be changed to alif because of the opening of what precedes it. Qutrub mentioned that they do this in flight toward the alif, which is the lightest of the letters of prolongation. This is the strongest explanation of this verse. It may also be said: the alif in this word is part of the root of the word, and a letter that is part of the root of a word may not be changed on account of the dual or the plural, for what is essential does not vanish through the accidental. So this argument requires that it not be permissible to say "inna hadhayni." But since we permit it, there is at least no reason not to permit with it the saying "inna hadhani."

The second explanation in answer: it may be said that "inna" here means "na'am" (yes). The poet said:

*And they say: "A gray hair has overtaken you," and you have grown old, so I said: "innah."*

That is, I said: "Yes." The "ha" in "innah" is the ha of pause, as in His words: ﴿My authority has gone from me﴾ [al-Haqqah: 29]. And Abu Dhu'ayb said:

*Gray has come upon the temples; "inna" from decay, the gray of the nape with the connected cheek-whisker.*

That is: "Yes, indeed, from decay." So "inna" became as if he had said: "Yes, these two are sorcerers." They raised an objection against this, saying: the lam does not enter the predicate, according to the preferred view, unless "inna" has entered the subject. But if "inna" has not entered the subject, the place of the lam is the subject, as one says: "la-Zayd a'lamu min 'Amr," and one does not say: "Zayd la-a'lamu min 'Amr." They answered this objection in two ways:

The first: We do not concede that the lam cannot properly enter the predicate, and the evidence for it is the saying:

*Umm al-Hulays is indeed an old woman, a decrepit one, who is content with the flesh of the neck-bone.*

Another said:

*My uncle, you are indeed, and whoever Jarir is his uncle, will attain glory and the maternal uncles will be honored.*

Qutrub recited:

*Did you not swear by Allah the Most High that your mounts are indeed among the best of mounts?*

And if "inna" is transmitted with kasra, the proof does not remain, except that Qutrub said: we heard it with the hamza opened. Also, the lam has been introduced into the predicate of "amsa" (to become). Ibn Jinni said: Abu 'Ali recited to us:

*They passed by swiftly and said, "How is your companion?" He to whom they addressed the question said, "In the evening he is indeed exhausted."*

Qutrub said: We also heard some Arabs say: "Ura-ka al-musalimiyya" and "Inni ra'aytuhu la-shaykhan," and "Zayd, by Allah, is indeed trusting in you." Kuthayyir said:

*And I have not ceased, since I came to know Layla, to be indeed like the bewildered one banished through every land.*

Another said:

*But I, from her love, am indeed a lovesick one.*

The objector said: These verses are among the irregularities, and they came thus out of necessity of poetry, and the speech of Allah the Exalted is far above necessity. This discussion is established only when we show that if the subject is not preceded by "inna," the lam must enter the subject and not the predicate. Its verification: the lam indicates the affirmation of the subject's being described by the predicate, and the lam indicates a state of the subject and an attribute of it, so it must enter the subject, because the cause that necessitates a ruling in a place must be specific to that place. It is not said: this is problematic in the case where "inna" enters the subject, for there the lam must enter the predicate although what you have mentioned is present in it. For we say that this is for the sake of necessity, since the word "inna" is for emphasis and the lam is for emphasis; so if we said "inna la-Zayda qa'imun," we would have placed one emphasizing particle upon another emphasizing particle, and that is impermissible. When it was impossible to introduce it upon the subject, we indeed placed it upon the predicate because of this necessity. As for when the particle "inna" does not enter the subject, this necessity is removed, so the lam must enter the subject. It is not said: if the negative particle may enter upon a negative particle, as in the saying:

*I have not seen, nor heard of, anything like today, a handsome, mangy man who pursued me.*

and the purpose of it is the emphasis of negation, why then is it not permissible to place an emphasizing particle upon an emphasizing particle, the purpose being the emphasis of affirmation? For we say: the difference between the two cases is that your saying "Zayd qa'im" indicates the ruling of Zayd's being described by standing; when you say "inna Zaydan qa'im," the word "inna" makes that ruling emphatic. So if you mentioned another emphasizer with the word "inna," it would become futile. But if you say "ra'aytu fulanan" (I saw so-and-so), this is for affirmation; when you introduce upon it the particle of negation, the particle of negation conveys the meaning of negation and does not convey emphasis, because it is independent in conveying the basic meaning, so how could it convey the additional meaning? But when you add to it another particle of negation, the second particle becomes an emphasis of the first, so it is not futile. This is the difference between the two cases. This is the extent of the explanation of this objection, and in my view it is weak, because all agree that when transmission and analogy conflict, transmission takes precedence; and because these causes are in the extreme of weakness, so how can the apparent transmission be repelled by them?

The second: In answer to their saying: the lam cannot properly enter the predicate unless the word "inna" has entered the subject, as Zajjaj mentioned. He said: if "inna" falls in the place of "na'am" and the lam is in its place, the sense being: "Na'am, these two for them are sorcerers," then the lam entered upon the subject and not upon the predicate. He said: I presented this view to Muhammad ibn Yazid and to Isma'il ibn Ishaq, and they approved it and said it is the best thing we have heard on this matter. Ibn Jinni said: This view is not correct, for several reasons:

The first reason: The principle is that the subject may be omitted only if it is a known and clear matter; otherwise, omitting it while ignorant of it would involve a kind of imposing the knowledge of the unseen upon the addressee. And if it is known, then through its being known it has been freed from being emphasized by the lam, because emphasis is needed only where knowledge of it is not present.

The second reason: Omission belongs to the category of brevity, and emphasis belongs to the category of elaboration, so combining them is not permissible; moreover, mentioning the emphasized and omitting the emphasizer is better to the intellect than the reverse.

The third reason: Our Basran companions refrained from emphasizing the omitted pronoun referring back to the subject in such a saying as: "Zayd, I struck" (Zayd darabtu), so they do not permit: "Zayd darabtu nafsahu" (Zayd, I struck himself), by making "nafs" an emphasis of the implicit ha' that is assumed in "darabtu," meaning "darabtuhu," because omission occurs only after verification and knowledge of it; and if it is so, it has been freed from its emphasis; so likewise here.

The fourth reason: All the grammarians have interpreted the saying of the poet:

*Umm al-Hulays is indeed an old woman, a decrepit one*

On the basis that the poet placed the lam (the emphatic lam, *lam al-ibtida'*) on the predicate (*khabar*, the predicate of the nominal sentence) out of poetic necessity (*darura*). Had what al-Zajjaj (d. 311 AH, grammarian and Qur'an scholar) held been permissible, the grammarians would not have departed from it, nor would they have interpreted the speech as a poetic necessity when they found a clear way to explain it.

It is possible to answer Ibn Jinni's objection by saying that the deletion of the subject (*mubtada'*, the topic of the nominal sentence) was acceptable only because the wording contains something that indicates it, namely his saying: "*hadhani*" (هَذانِ, "these two"). But if the emphasis (*ta'kid*) were deleted, there would be nothing in the wording to indicate it. Therefore, deleting the subject was more preferable than deleting the emphasis.

As for their refusal to emphasize the pronoun in the saying "Zayd, I struck himself" (*Zayd darabtu nafsahu*), that was only because attributing the verb to an explicit noun is preferable to attributing it to a pronoun. So when one says "Zayd, I struck himself," the word "*nafsahu*" (نَفْسَهُ, "himself") is an object (*maf'ul*), and therefore it cannot be made an emphasis of the pronoun. Thus, the emphasizing of a deleted element was prohibited here only for this reason, not because emphasizing a deleted element is absolutely prohibited.

As for his saying that the grammarians interpreted the verse of the poet:

*Umm al-Hulays la-'ajuzun shahraba*

as the poet having placed the lam on the predicate out of necessity, and that if what al-Zajjaj said were permissible the grammarians would not have departed from it, this objection is utterly baseless. The early scholars' oversight of this aspect does not necessitate its being false, for how often has an earlier scholar overlooked something that a later scholar grasped. This is the complete discussion in explaining this.

**The third answer:** The particle *inna* (إنَّ) is weak in its governing (*'amal*), because it governs by virtue of its resemblance to the verb. Therefore it must be weak in governing, and when it is weak, it is permissible for the subject to remain in its original case, which is the nominative (*raf'*).

*First premise:* It resembles the verb, and this resemblance exists both in form and in meaning. As for form, it is composed of three letters, its last letter is open (fatha), and it is specific to nouns just as verbs are. As for meaning, it conveys a meaning to the noun, namely affirming its being described by the predicate, just as when you say "Zayd stood" (*qama Zaydun*), your saying "stood" conveys a meaning to the noun.

*Second premise:* Since it resembles verbs, it must resemble them in governing. This is clear, based on the principle of concomitance (*dawaran*).

*Third premise:* It does not put the noun in the accusative and the predicate in the nominative. The argument is stated thus: when it becomes a governing particle, it either (1) puts both the subject and the predicate in the nominative, or (2) puts both in the accusative, or (3) puts the subject in the nominative and the predicate in the accusative, or (4) the reverse. The first is false, because the subject and predicate were both nominative before *inna* entered upon them; if they remained so after it entered upon them, no effect would appear for it at all. Moreover, it has been given the governing of the verb, and a verb does not put two nouns in the nominative, so there is no sense in the sharing.

The second is also false, because this too contradicts the governing of the verb, since a verb does not put something in the accusative while leaving unaffected what would put it in the nominative.

The third is also false, because it leads to equating the root (*asl*) with the branch (*far'*). For the verb's governing over the agent (*fa'il*) is first by the nominative, and over the object (*maf'ul*) by the accusative. If the accusative were made here in the same way, the root and the branch would be equated.

Since the three divisions are invalid, the fourth division is determined: that *inna* puts the noun in the accusative and raises the predicate. This indicates that these particles are foreign (*dakhila*) in governing, not original (*asila*), because placing the accusative element before the nominative in the matter of governing is a departure from the norm. This shows that the governing by these particles is not established by way of originality but by way of an incidental means.

*Fourth premise:* Since it has been established that its influence on the accusative of the noun is due to this resemblance, it must also be permissible for it to affect the nominative. This is because the noun's being a subject requires the nominative, and the entry of *inna* upon the subject does not remove from it the attribute of being a subject, since it serves to emphasize what was, not to remove what was. Having established this, we say: the attribute of being a subject requires the nominative, and the particle *inna* requires the accusative. But the first requirement is more worthy of being required for two reasons:

One: the attribute of being a subject is an original attribute of the subject, while the entry of *inna* upon it is an incidental attribute, and the original takes precedence over the incidental.

Two: the subject's attribute requiring the nominative is original, while the particle *inna* requiring the accusative is an incidental attribute, arising from its resemblance to the verb. So the first is more worthy.

Thus, from the totality of what we have established, it is proven that the nominative is preferable to the accusative. If preference is not achieved, then at least the permissibility is established. For this reason, when you bring the predicate of *inna* and then conjoin another noun to the first noun, it is permissible for that second noun to be either nominative or accusative.

**The fourth answer:** al-Farra' (d. 207 AH) said: The original of *hadhani* (هَذانِ) is *dha* (ذا), to which a *ha'* (هاء) was added, because *dha* is a deficient word, so it was completed with the *ha'* when pointing out. An *alif* was added for the dual, so it became *hadhani*. Two identical quiescent letters (*sakinan min jinsin wahid*) came together, so one had to be deleted. The original *alif* could not be deleted, because the root of the word is deficient, so it must not be made more deficient. Therefore the dual *alif* was deleted, since the *nun* indicates it. Hence *inna* did not govern it, because its governing applies to the dual *alif*.

Others said: The remaining *alif* is either the *alif* of the root or the *alif* of the dual. If the remaining one is the *alif* of the root, it is impermissible to delete it, because an external governing factor does not alter the essence of the word. If the remaining one is the *alif* of the dual, there is no doubt that they used it in place of the root *alif*, and the substitute of the root is necessarily a root. So this *alif* is a root, and it is impermissible to delete it. The sum of this returns to the first answer.

**The fifth answer:** al-Zajjaj related from the early grammarians that the *ha'* here is implied, and the sense is: "*innahu hadhani la-sahiran*" (إنَّهُ هَذانِ لَساحِرانِ, "indeed, it is these two who are indeed sorcerers"). This *ha'* is a pronoun referring to the matter and the affair (*al-amr wa-l-sha'n*). This is what has been said at this point.

As for the one who lightened it and read "*in hadhani la-sahiran*" (إنْ هَذانِ لَساحِرانِ), it is good, for what follows the light *in* is nominative, and the lam after it in the predicate is obligatory and required, although in the heavy *inna* it is permissible, so that the difference between the emphatic *inna* and the negative *in* may appear. The poet said:

*Wa-in Malikun lal-murtaja in tada'da'at*
*Raha al-harbi aw darat 'alayya khutub*

[Translation: "And if Malik is the one hoped for, if the millstone of war is shaken, or calamities turn against me."]

Another said:

*Inna al-qawma wal-hayya alladhi ana minhum*
*La-ahlu maqamatin wa-shaa'in wa-jamili*

[Translation: "Indeed, the people and the tribe of which I am one are the people of stations, of sheep and of camels."]

*Jamil* is the plural of *jamal* (camel). Then, among the Arabs, there are those who make *in* (in its deficient form) govern just as they make it govern in its complete form, by analogy with *kana* (كانَ), for it governs even when it is deficient, as in your saying "*lam yakun*" (لَمْ يَكُنْ), because the meaning of emphasis remains, even if the verbal resemblance disappears, since the consideration is for meaning. This dialect indicates that the consideration in the matter of governing is the meaning-based resemblance to the verb, which is the affirmation of emphasis, not the verbal resemblance. Just as the reliance in the matter of *kana* is on the meaning, not the wording, because it is a pure verb.

As for the apparent dialect, which is the abandonment of governing by the light *in*, it indicates that the verbal resemblance in the heavy *inna* is one of the two components of the cause concerning its governing. When it is lightened, the resemblance disappears, so it does not govern. This is unlike the quiescent *in*, which governs by its meaning, because it is a pure verb, and its wording is not considered.

Second matter: Allah, glorified and exalted, having mentioned what they concealed in their secret consultation, related what they openly declared, and the whole of it indicates an aversion (tanfir) from Musa, peace be upon him, and from following his religion:

The first of them is their saying: ﴿Indeed, these two are but sorcerers﴾. This is a disparagement from them of the miracles of Musa, peace be upon him, and then an exaggeration in turning people away from him, because every sound nature inclines toward aversion from magic and dislikes the sight of the sorcerer. And since a person knows that magic has no permanence, when they believed that he had magic they said: How can we follow him, for he has no lasting existence, nor does his religion, nor his doctrine.

The second: his saying: ﴿They wish to drive you out of your land﴾. This is at the utmost of aversion, because departing from one's place of origin and birth is severely hard on the hearts. This is what Allah, exalted, related of Pharaoh in his saying: ﴿Have you come to us to drive us out of our land with your magic, O Musa?﴾ It seems the sorcerers took up this doubt from Pharaoh and then repeated it.

The third: his saying: ﴿and do away with your ideal way of life﴾. This too has a strong effect on the heart, for when an enemy comes and takes control of all the positions and things one desires, that is at the utmost of hardship for the soul. So they mentioned these aspects to exaggerate in turning people away from Musa, encouraging the repelling of him and the nullifying of his affair. Here there are two discussions:

The first discussion: al-Farra' said: "al-Tariqah" (the way) means the noble men who serve as an example to others; it is said: "They are the way of their people," and it is also said of one individual: "He is the way of his people." Al-Zajjaj took the verse to be an instance of elision of the modified noun, meaning: "and do away with the people of your ideal way of life." On both interpretations, the meaning is that they were inciting the people, saying that Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both, wish to take away the nobles and chiefs of your people, who are the Children of Israel, in accordance with Musa's saying, peace be upon him: ﴿Send with us the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 17]. They were named "Children of Israel" because they were the most numerous of the people at that time in number and wealth. Among the exegetes is one who interpreted "the ideal way" as the religion: they named their religion "the ideal way," as in: ﴿every party rejoicing in what is with them﴾ [al-Rum: 32]. And among them is one who interpreted it as rank, position and leadership.

The second discussion: ﴿al-Muthla﴾ is feminine to agree with the feminine "tariqah" (way). They differed as to why the more excellent was named "al-amthal" (the best). Some of them said: al-amthal is the one most resembling the truth; it was said: al-amthal is the clearest and most manifest. Then, when Allah, exalted, related their exaggeration in turning people away from Musa and their encouragement to nullify his affair, He related their saying: ﴿So gather your plot, then come in a row﴾. Abu 'Amr read "ijma'u" with a connecting alif and an opened mim, meaning: do not leave any of your schemes without bringing it, the evidence for which is His saying: ﴿then he gathered his plot﴾. The rest read it with a cut alif and a kasra on the mim, and it has two meanings:

One of them: al-Farra' said: al-ijma' (resolve) is firm determination and resolve upon a matter; it is said: "I resolved (ajma'tu) upon the departure," like "azma'tu."

The second: it is in the sense of gathering. The discussion of this has passed at His saying: ﴿So resolve upon your affair with your partners﴾ [Yunus: 71]. Al-Zajjaj said: Let your resolve be all of you together like a hand, unified upon it, not differing. Then ﴿come in a row﴾. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Zajjaj mentioned two meanings:

One of them: that the saf (row) is the place of gathering, and the meaning is: come to the place where you gather for your festival and your prayer; or the meaning: come to one of the places of prayer, or the saf was a specific known name for a particular place of prayer, and so they were commanded to come to it.

The second: that saf is a verbal noun, and the meaning is: then come lined up together, so that it is more orderly for your affair and more awe-inspiring for your dignity. This is the view of the majority of exegetes. His saying: ﴿And he has indeed prospered today who has the upper hand﴾ is a parenthetical statement, meaning: whoever prevails has succeeded. They were, by this, acknowledging among themselves, in what they agreed upon, the display of what they were displaying of magic.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verses 66–68:

[Page 71]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "O Musa, either you throw, or we will be the first to throw."﴾ ﴿He said, "Rather, you throw." And suddenly their ropes and their staffs, because of their magic, appeared to him as though they were moving.﴾ ﴿So Musa sensed within himself a fear.﴾ ﴿We said, "Do not fear; indeed, it is you who are the superior.﴾ ﴿And throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow what they have crafted. What they have crafted is only the plot of a magician, and a magician does not succeed, wherever he goes."﴾

Know that when the mention of the appointed meeting, which is the Day of Adornment, had preceded, and also His saying, ﴿Then come forward in a row﴾ [Ta-Ha: 64], that made it unnecessary to say "so they assembled at this place." They said, "Either you throw," relying on what preceded it. His saying ﴿either you throw, or we will be the first to throw﴾ means: either you throw what is with you before us, or we throw what is with us before you. This offering of choice, together with their placing it first in speech, was a courtesy on their part and humility toward him. Therefore God, Exalted, granted them faith through his blessing. Then Musa, peace be upon him, met their courtesy with courtesy, and said, ﴿Rather, you throw.﴾ As for his saying ﴿Rather, you throw,﴾ there are two questions concerning it.

The first question: How is it permissible for Musa, peace be upon him, to say ﴿Rather, you throw,﴾ thereby commanding them to do what is magic and disbelief? For if they intended by it to deny Musa, peace be upon him, it would be disbelief. The answer is in several respects:

First: We do not grant that the act of throwing itself is disbelief and disobedience. For when they threw, and their aim was that the difference between that throwing and the miracle of the Messenger, peace be upon him, who is Musa, would become manifest, that throwing would be faith. Disbelief is only the intention to deny Musa, and he, peace be upon him, commanded only the throwing, not the intention to deny. So the question is resolved.

Second: That command was conditional, and the implied meaning is: "Throw what you are throwing, if you are truthful," as in His saying, ﴿So bring a surah like it, and call your witnesses besides God, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23], meaning, "if you are able."

Third: Since that was determined to be the way to remove doubt, it became permissible. This is like the one who has the truth, when he knows that in someone's heart there is a doubt, and that if he does not challenge him to mention it and state it in the strongest way he can, that doubt would remain in his heart and he would leave the religion because of it. Then it is permissible for the one with the truth to demand that he state it in the best possible manner, and his purpose in that is to answer it and remove its effect from his heart. So demanding that he mention the doubt for this purpose is permissible, and so it is here.

Fourth: That it is not a command at all, but its meaning is: "If you wish to do it, there is no physical hindrance to it, so that the truth may become manifest."

Fifth: There is no doubt that Musa, peace be upon him, was averse to that, and there is no doubt that he forbade them from it by his saying: ﴿Woe to you! Do not fabricate a lie against God, lest He destroy you with a punishment﴾ [Ta-Ha: 61]. If this is so, it is impossible that his saying should be a command to them to do that, because combining being a forbidder and a commander regarding the same act is impossible. So we know that his saying is not to be taken in its outward sense, and at that point the difficulty is removed.

The second question: Why did he place them first in throwing before himself, although placing the hearing of the doubt before the hearing of the proof is not permissible, so likewise placing the presentation of the doubt before the presentation of the proof must not be permissible, since it is possible that he might grasp the doubt and then not be free to grasp the proof afterward, and so he would remain then in disbelief and error? No one may say that this was because they had placed him before themselves, so he responded by placing them before himself, for such things are only fitting in matters concerning personal rights, whereas matters concerning proof and doubt are not permissible. The answer is that he, peace be upon him, had already displayed the miracle once, so there was no need for him to display it again, and the people had come only to oppose him. So he, peace be upon him, said: If I began by displaying the miracle first, I would be as a cause in their proceeding to display magic and to intend the nullification of the miracle, and that is not permissible. Rather, I entrust the matter to them, so that by their own choice they display that magic, and then I display the miracle that nullifies their magic. Thus, under this arrangement, it becomes a means of removing doubt, whereas under the first arrangement it would be a cause for the occurrence of doubt. So that was preferable.

[Page 72]

As for His saying ﴿And suddenly their ropes and their staffs, because of their magic, appeared to him as though they were moving,﴾ there are several issues:

First issue: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "They threw their ropes and their staffs, inclining from this side and inclining from that side, so it appeared to Musa, peace be upon him, that the whole earth was serpents, and that they were moving, and he was afraid. When it was said to him, ﴿And throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow what they have crafted,﴾ Musa threw his staff, and it was greater than their serpents. Then it began to grow larger until it filled the valley. Then it rose and ascended until it hung its tail at the edge of the dome. Then it descended and devoured everything they had done in both inclinations, while the people were looking at it, supposing nothing but that it was magic. Then it advanced toward Pharaoh to swallow him, opening its mouth eighty cubits wide, and he cried out to Musa, peace be upon him, so he took it, and behold, it was a staff as it had been. The magicians looked, and behold, it had left none of their ropes and staffs without devouring it. So the magicians knew that it was not magic, and they said: Where are our ropes and our staffs? Had it been magic, they would have remained. So they fell down prostrating and said: ﴿We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun﴾ [al-A'raf: 121–122]."

Second issue: They differed about the number of the magicians. Al-Qasim ibn Salam said: They were seventy thousand, each with a staff and a rope. Al-Suddi said: They were some thirty-odd thousand, each with a staff and a rope. Wahb said: They were fifteen thousand. Ibn Jurayj and Ikrimah said: They were nine hundred: three hundred from the Persians, three hundred from the Romans, and three hundred from Alexandria. Al-Kalbi said: They were seventy-two magicians, two of them from the Copts and seventy from the Children of Israel, whom Pharaoh had compelled to do that. Know that difference and variation occur in a large number of reports, and the apparent meaning of the Qur'an does not indicate any of them, and when reports conflict, they cancel each other out.

Third issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: In ﴿fa-idha﴾ this "idha" is the sudden "idha" (idha al-mufajaah). The verification concerning it is that it is the "idha" meaning "the time" which requires a verb to govern it and a clause to be added to it, but in some places it is restricted to governing a particular verb, which is the verb of suddenness, and the clause is initial and nothing else. So the sense of His saying ﴿fa-idha hibaluhum wa 'isiyyuhum﴾ is: "So Musa was suddenly confronted, at the time of the imagining of the movement of their ropes and staffs." This is an illustration, and the meaning is: upon his sudden encounter with their ropes and staffs imagined to him as moving. End quote.

Fourth issue: It is read "'usiyyuhum" with a ḍamma, which is the original form, and with a kasra it is an assimilation, like dulī and dilī, and qusī and qisī. It is read "tukhayyalu" with a taa' with a dot above, attributing the verb to the ropes and staffs, and it is read with a ya' with a dot below and a ḍamma, attributing the verb to the plotting and the magic. Al-Farra' said: that is, its movement is imagined to him.

Fifth issue: The pronoun in His saying ﴿yukhayyalu ilayhi﴾ refers to Musa, peace be upon him, and the meaning is that they reached in their magic the degree at which it became imagined to Musa, peace be upon him, that they were moving like the movement of something alive among serpents, not that they were in reality alive. It is said that they filled them with something which, when the sun falls upon it, makes it tremble and move. When they became numerous and joined one another, whoever saw them would think they were moving. As for what is related from Wahb, that they bewitched the eyes of the people and the eye of Musa, peace be upon him, until he imagined that, citing His saying, ﴿So when they threw, they bewitched the eyes of the people﴾ [al-A'raf: 116] and His saying, ﴿It is imagined to him, from their magic, that they are moving﴾, this is not permissible, because that time was the time of displaying the miracle and the proofs and removing doubt, and if he had come to a state where he could not distinguish the existent from the corrupt imagination, he would not have been able to display the miracle, and then the purpose would be spoiled.

[Page 73]

Therefore, the meaning is that he witnessed something which, were it not for his knowledge that there is no reality to that thing, he would have supposed that they were moving.

Second: That command was conditional, and the implied meaning is: "Throw what you are throwing, if you are truthful," as in His saying, ﴿So bring a surah like it, and call your witnesses besides God, if you are truthful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23], meaning, "if you are able."

Third: Since that was determined to be the way to remove doubt, it became permissible. This is like the one who has the truth, when he knows that in someone's heart there is a doubt, and that if he does not challenge him to mention it and state it in the strongest way he can, that doubt would remain in his heart and he would leave the religion because of it. Then it is permissible for the one with the truth to demand that he state it in the best possible manner, and his purpose in that is to answer it and remove its effect from his heart. So demanding that he mention the doubt for this purpose is permissible, and so it is here.

Fourth: That it is not a command at all, but its meaning is: "If you wish to do it, there is no physical hindrance to it, so that the truth may become manifest."

Fifth: There is no doubt that Musa, peace be upon him, was averse to that, and there is no doubt that he forbade them from it by his saying: ﴿Woe to you! Do not fabricate a lie against God, lest He destroy you with a punishment﴾ [Ta-Ha: 61]. If this is so, it is impossible that his saying should be a command to them to do that, because combining being a forbidder and a commander regarding the same act is impossible. So we know that his saying is not to be taken in its outward sense, and at that point the difficulty is removed.

The second question: Why did he place them first in throwing before himself, although placing the hearing of the doubt before the hearing of the proof is not permissible, so likewise placing the presentation of the doubt before the presentation of the proof must not be permissible, since it is possible that he might grasp the doubt and then not be free to grasp the proof afterward, and so he would remain then in disbelief and error? No one may say that this was because they had placed him before themselves, so he responded by placing them before himself, for such things are only fitting in matters concerning personal rights, whereas matters concerning proof and doubt are not permissible. The answer is that he, peace be upon him, had already displayed the miracle once, so there was no need for him to display it again, and the people had come only to oppose him. So he, peace be upon him, said: If I began by displaying the miracle first, I would be as a cause in their proceeding to display magic and to intend the nullification of the miracle, and that is not permissible. Rather, I entrust the matter to them, so that by their own choice they display that magic, and then I display the miracle that nullifies their magic. Thus, under this arrangement, it becomes a means of removing doubt, whereas under the first arrangement it would be a cause for the occurrence of doubt. So that was preferable.

[Page 72]

As for His saying ﴿And suddenly their ropes and their staffs, because of their magic, appeared to him as though they were moving,﴾ there are several issues:

First issue: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "They threw their ropes and their staffs, inclining from this side and inclining from that side, so it appeared to Musa, peace be upon him, that the whole earth was serpents, and that they were moving, and he was afraid. When it was said to him, ﴿And throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow what they have crafted,﴾ Musa threw his staff, and it was greater than their serpents. Then it began to grow larger until it filled the valley. Then it rose and ascended until it hung its tail at the edge of the dome. Then it descended and devoured everything they had done in both inclinations, while the people were looking at it, supposing nothing but that it was magic. Then it advanced toward Pharaoh to swallow him, opening its mouth eighty cubits wide, and he cried out to Musa, peace be upon him, so he took it, and behold, it was a staff as it had been. The magicians looked, and behold, it had left none of their ropes and staffs without devouring it. So the magicians knew that it was not magic, and they said: Where are our ropes and our staffs? Had it been magic, they would have remained. So they fell down prostrating and said: ﴿We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun﴾ [al-A'raf: 121–122]."

Second issue: They differed about the number of the magicians. Al-Qasim ibn Salam said: They were seventy thousand, each with a staff and a rope. Al-Suddi said: They were some thirty-odd thousand, each with a staff and a rope. Wahb said: They were fifteen thousand. Ibn Jurayj and Ikrimah said: They were nine hundred: three hundred from the Persians, three hundred from the Romans, and three hundred from Alexandria. Al-Kalbi said: They were seventy-two magicians, two of them from the Copts and seventy from the Children of Israel, whom Pharaoh had compelled to do that. Know that difference and variation occur in a large number of reports, and the apparent meaning of the Qur'an does not indicate any of them, and when reports conflict, they cancel each other out.

Third issue: The author of al-Kashshaf said: In ﴿fa-idha﴾ this "idha" is the sudden "idha" (idha al-mufajaah). The verification concerning it is that it is the "idha" meaning "the time" which requires a verb to govern it and a clause to be added to it, but in some places it is restricted to governing a particular verb, which is the verb of suddenness, and the clause is initial and nothing else. So the sense of His saying ﴿fa-idha hibaluhum wa 'isiyyuhum﴾ is: "So Musa was suddenly confronted, at the time of the imagining of the movement of their ropes and staffs." This is an illustration, and the meaning is: upon his sudden encounter with their ropes and staffs imagined to him as moving. End quote.

Fourth issue: It is read "'usiyyuhum" with a ḍamma, which is the original form, and with a kasra it is an assimilation, like dulī and dilī, and qusī and qisī. It is read "tukhayyalu" with a taa' with a dot above, attributing the verb to the ropes and staffs, and it is read with a ya' with a dot below and a ḍamma, attributing the verb to the plotting and the magic. Al-Farra' said: that is, its movement is imagined to him.

Fifth issue: The pronoun in His saying ﴿yukhayyalu ilayhi﴾ refers to Musa, peace be upon him, and the meaning is that they reached in their magic the degree at which it became imagined to Musa, peace be upon him, that they were moving like the movement of something alive among serpents, not that they were in reality alive. It is said that they filled them with something which, when the sun falls upon it, makes it tremble and move. When they became numerous and joined one another, whoever saw them would think they were moving. As for what is related from Wahb, that they bewitched the eyes of the people and the eye of Musa, peace be upon him, until he imagined that, citing His saying, ﴿So when they threw, they bewitched the eyes of the people﴾ [al-A'raf: 116] and His saying, ﴿It is imagined to him, from their magic, that they are moving﴾, this is not permissible, because that time was the time of displaying the miracle and the proofs and removing doubt, and if he had come to a state where he could not distinguish the existent from the corrupt imagination, he would not have been able to display the miracle, and then the purpose would be spoiled.

[Page 73]

Therefore, the meaning is that he witnessed something which, were it not for his knowledge that there is no reality to that thing, he would have supposed that they were moving.
