Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verse 69:

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So Moses sensed fear within himself﴾, al-Iijas (sensing, perceiving) is the perception of fear, meaning he found fear within himself. If it is said: there is no greater measure for removing fear than what Allah, exalted is He, did on behalf of Moses, peace be upon him. For He spoke to him first, and displayed to him the dazzling miracles such as the staff and the hand. Then He turned it back as it had been, after it had been like the greatest serpent. Then He gave him the eight requests, and mentioned the eight favours He had bestowed upon him before that. Then He said to him after all of that: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both, hearing and seeing﴾. With these many preliminaries, how did fear fall into his heart? The answer to it is from several aspects:

The first: that fear was only due to the weakness of heart with which the human being is created, even though Moses, peace be upon him, knew that they could not reach him and that Allah was his helper. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: he feared that doubt might enter people's minds regarding what they were seeing, so that they would think they had equalled Moses, peace be upon him, and that this would be confused for them. This interpretation is reinforced by His saying: ﴿Do not fear; indeed, you are the superior﴾. This is the view of Muqatil.

The third: he feared, when they began and his casting was delayed, that some of the people would leave before witnessing what he would cast, and so they would persist in the belief in falsehood.

The fourth: perhaps he, peace be upon him, had been commanded not to do anything except by revelation. When the descent of revelation concerning that matter was delayed at that time, he feared that revelation would not descend at that time, and he would remain in embarrassment.

The fifth: perhaps he, peace be upon him, feared that if he nullified the magic of those present, Pharaoh might have prepared other groups and would bring them, and he would then need once more to nullify their magic, and so on without any end appearing to him. At that point the matter would not be completed and the objective would not be achieved. Then Allah, exalted is He, removed that fear first in general and then in detail. As for the general, it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We said, "Do not fear; indeed, you are the superior"﴾. Its indication that his fear was due to a matter concerning the fact that his affair would not become apparent to the people is that Allah granted him security by His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are the superior﴾. In it there are kinds of emphasis:

The first: the mention of the word of emphasis, which is "inna" (indeed).

The second: the repetition of the pronoun.

The third: the definite article (lam al-ta'rif).

The fourth: the word "superiority" (al-uluww), which is manifest dominance. As for the detail, it is His saying: ﴿And throw what is in your right hand﴾. In this there is a question: why did He not say, "throw your staff"? The answer: it is permissible that this be a diminishing of it, meaning: do not be concerned with the multitude of their ropes and staves, and throw the single small thing in your right hand, for by the power of Allah, exalted is He, it will swallow them, despite its singleness and their multitude, its smallness and their greatness. It is also permissible that it be an magnifying of it, meaning: do not be impressed by these many bodies, for in your right hand there is something greater than all of them, and these, despite their multitude, are the least of things in its presence. So throw it, and it will swallow them by the permission of Allah, exalted is He, and annihilate them. As for His saying: ﴿talqaf﴾, meaning: when you throw it, it "will swallow what they have fabricated". The reading of the common readers is "talaqqaf" with the jussive and with shaddah, meaning: throw it and it will swallow them. Ibn 'Amir read "talaqqafu" with shaddah and a damma on the fa', on the sense of a circumstantial state, meaning: throw it while swallowing; or with the nominative, as a resumptive sentence. Hafs related from 'Asim with a sukun on the lam and lightening, meaning: it will take into its mouth, swallowing quickly. Both laqf and talaqquf return to this meaning. "Sana'u" here means "fabricated and forged". The Arabs say of falsehood: it is a fabricated speech and a invented speech. The correctness of His saying "talqaf" is that when he threw that and it became a serpent, it swallowed what they had fabricated. In His saying: ﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate﴾ there is an indication that he threw the staff and it became a serpent and swallowed what they had made. In the swallowing there is an indication that it swallowed all that they had thrown, and that is only possible with the greatness of its body and the intensity of its strength. It has been related of the magicians that at the moment of the swallowing they became certain that what Moses, peace be upon him, had brought was not within the capacity of human beings, for several reasons:

The first: the movement of the staff appeared in a manner that its like could not be produced by trickery.

The second: its size increased in a manner that could not be accomplished by trickery.

The third: the limbs appeared upon it, such as the eye, the nostrils, the mouth and others, and that cannot be accomplished by trickery.

The fourth: the swallowing of everything they had thrown, despite its multitude, and that cannot be accomplished by trickery.

The fifth: its return to being a small piece of wood as it had been, and none of that can be accomplished by trickery. Then Glorified and Exalted He made clear that what they had made was the plot of a magician. The meaning is that what is with you, O Moses, is a divine miracle, while what they have is false deceptions, so how could there be any conflict? It has been read "kaydu sahir" with nominative and accusative. Whoever reads it in the nominative does so on the basis that "ma" is a relative pronoun, and whoever reads it in the accusative does so on the basis that it is restrictive (kafiyah). It has been read "kaydu sihr" (the plot of magic), meaning "one possessing magic" or "those possessing magic", or they, because of their deep immersion in their magic, are as if they were magic itself in essence and substance, or "clear plot", because it is both magic and non-magic, as one says "the hundred for a dirham", and similarly "knowledge of fiqh" and "knowledge of grammar". Some questions remain:

The first question: why did He make "magician" singular and not plural? The answer: because the intention in this statement is the sense of the category, not the sense of number. Had it been plural, it would have been imagined that the intended meaning was a number. Do you not see His saying: ﴿and the magician does not prosper wherever he goes﴾, meaning this category.

The second question: why did He make it indefinite first and then definite second? The answer: it is as if He said: what they have brought is one type of magic, and all types of magic are of no benefit. There is no doubt that this statement in this form is more eloquent.

The third question: His saying: ﴿and the magician does not prosper wherever he goes﴾ indicates that the magician does not attain his aim through magic, whether good or bad, and that requires the complete negation of magic. The answer: the discussion of magic and its reality has already been treated in Surat al-Baqarah, so there is no need for repetition. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 20, verses 70–71:**

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate. They said, "We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses."﴾ ﴿[Pharaoh] said, "Have you believed in him before I give you permission? Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic. So I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will crucify you on the trunks of palm trees, and you will surely know whose punishment is more severe and more lasting."﴾

Know that in His words: ﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate﴾ there is an indication that [Moses] threw what was in his right hand, and it became a serpent that swallowed what they had made, and the matter became manifest. Thereupon they fell down prostrate. That is because they were at the highest level of the knowledge of magic. When they saw what Moses, peace be upon him, did, which was outside their craft, they knew that it was not magic at all. It is said that their leader said: "We used to overcome people with magic, and our instruments would remain with us if we were defeated. So if this is magic, where is what we threw?" They inferred from the change in the states of bodies the existence of the Creator, the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, and from its manifestation at the hand of Moses, peace be upon him, that he was a truthful messenger from Allah the Exalted. Therefore they repented, believed, and performed that which is the utmost in submission, which is prostration.

As for His words: ﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate﴾, the meaning is not that they were compelled to prostrate, for otherwise they would not have been praiseworthy. Rather, the interpretation of it is what al-Akhfash said: that because of the speed of their prostration, it was as if they had been thrown down. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "How wondrous is their matter! They threw down their ropes and staffs for disbelief and denial, then they threw down their heads after an hour for gratitude and prostration. How great is the difference between the two throwings!" It is related that they did not raise their heads until they saw Paradise and Hell and saw the reward of their people. It is related from Ikrimah: When they fell down prostrate, Allah showed them in their prostration their dwellings which they would come to in Paradise.

The judge [al-Qadi] said: "This is far-fetched, because if He had shown them directly, they would have become compelled, and that does not befit Him. Their words are: ﴿Indeed we have believed in our Lord that He may forgive us our sins﴾ [Ta-Ha: 73]." Its answer: Since it was permissible for Abraham, peace be upon him, despite being certain that he was forgiven, to say: ﴿And the one from whom I hope He will forgive my sin﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 82], why should the like not be permissible regarding the magicians?

Know that this story alerts to wondrous secrets concerning the matters of Lordship and the execution of the Divine decree and His destiny within the totality of created things. That is because the manifestation of those proofs was in the sight and hearing of all, so the manner of inference in them was clear and evident: that things came into being, and so they must have an influencer, and knowledge of this is necessary. That influencer is either creation itself or others. The first is manifestly false, because every sensible person knows by necessity from himself that he cannot create living beings and enlarge their bodies all at once, then reduce them again to what they were. These clear sciences, once they have settled in the intellect, yield certainty that there must be a manager of this world. So what can one say? Do you not see that those deniers were ignorant of the soundness of these premises? This is in the utmost remoteness, because we have shown that each of them is such that no sensible person can doubt it. Hence they knew their soundness, but they persisted in ignorance, disliked attaining knowledge and happiness for themselves, and loved attaining ignorance and wretchedness for themselves. I do not think any sensible person would ever be content with that for himself. So nothing remains but to say: intellect and proof are not sufficient; rather there must be a manager who creates these premises in the hearts and creates the awareness of how to arrange them and how to draw conclusions from them to the result, such that whenever He does that, the results arise in the hearts. This indicates that everything is by His decree and destiny, for there is no reliance upon intellects and hearts in their courses and their operations. Whoever casts off partisanship from his heart and looks at the states of his own self in the courses of his thoughts and views will grow more certain of what we have mentioned.

As for His words: ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses"﴾, know that the Ta'limiyya [Isma'ilis] argued by this verse and said: they believed in Allah whom they knew through Aaron and Moses, and that shows that knowledge of Allah is not obtained except from the Imam. This view is weak. Rather, in their words: ﴿We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses﴾ there are two benefits beyond what they mentioned:

The first benefit: Pharaoh claimed lordship in his words: ﴿I am your Lord, the Most High﴾ [an-Nazi'at: 24] and divinity in his words: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas: 38]. So if they had said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds," Pharaoh would have said: "They have believed in me, not in another." To cut off this accusation, they chose this expression. The evidence for this is that they mentioned Aaron before Moses, because Pharaoh claimed lordship over Moses on the basis that he had raised him, as in his words: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child?﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 18]. So when the people guarded against Pharaoh's insinuations, they necessarily mentioned Aaron before Moses, to sever this illusion.

The second benefit: When they witnessed that Allah the Exalted had singled out those two with those great miracles and noble ranks, they therefore said "the Lord of Aaron and Moses" for that reason. Then, when Pharaoh saw from them prostration and affirmation, he feared that this would become a cause for the rest of the people to follow them in believing in Allah the Exalted and His Messenger. So immediately he cast another doubt upon the Prophet, saying: ﴿Have you believed in him before I give you permission? Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic.﴾ This statement contains two doubts:

The first: his words: ﴿Have you believed in him before I give you permission?﴾ Its explanation: reliance upon the first impulse is not permissible; rather it requires investigation, debate, and the aid of reflections. Since you did none of that, but at once said "You have believed in him," this shows that your belief is not from insight but from some other cause.

The second: his words: ﴿Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic﴾, meaning: you are his students in magic, so you have agreed to display incapacity on your own part, to promote his affair and magnify his status. Then, after raising the doubt, he turned to threats, to deter them from belief and to deter others from following them in that. So he said: ﴿So I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides﴾. It is read "la-uqatti'anna" and "la-usallibanna" with the lighter form [i.e., without the shaddah]. Cutting on opposite sides means that the right hand and the left foot are cut off, because each of the two limbs is the opposite of the other: this is a hand and that is a foot, this is right and that is left. The phrase ﴿on opposite sides﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state, meaning: I will cut them off as differing ones, because when some of them differ from others, they are characterized by difference. Then he said: ﴿and I will crucify you on the trunks of palm trees﴾, so he likened the crucified person's being fixed in the trunk to the fixing of a thing placed within its container, and therefore he said: ﴿on the trunks of palm trees﴾. As for what is commonly said, that "fi" here means "ʿala" [on], it is weak. Then he said: ﴿and you will surely know whose punishment is more severe and more lasting.﴾ By his words "whose" he meant himself—may Allah curse him—because his words "whose" indicate that he meant himself and Moses, peace be upon him, as evidenced by his words: ﴿Have you believed in him?﴾. In this there is a display of his power and dominance, and of his habit of torturing people with various kinds of punishment, and of oppressing Moses, peace be upon him, along with mocking him, because Moses, peace be upon him, had never engaged in torture at all.

If it is said: Pharaoh, despite the recency of his witnessing the staff turn into a serpent with that greatness which you have explained, and you mentioned that it intended to swallow Pharaoh's palace, and the matter came to the point that he sought Moses's aid against the evil of that serpent—how, with the recency of that and his inability to repel it, is it conceivable that he would threaten the magicians and exaggerate in his warning to this degree, and mock Moses, peace be upon him, in his words: "whose punishment is more severe and more lasting"? We say: Why is it not permissible to say that he was in the utmost fear in his heart, but he displayed that boldness and audacity to sustain his prestige and to promote his affair? Whoever surveys the conditions of the people of the world knows that the helpless may do such things. And among what indicates the soundness of this is that every sensible person knows by necessity that the punishment of Allah is more severe than the punishment of human beings, yet he denied that. Also, he was certainly aware of his lie in his words: "Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic," because he knew that Moses, peace be upon him, had not associated with them at all, nor met them, and he knew from his magicians who each one's teacher was and how he had acquired that knowledge. Yet despite that, he kept saying these things. Thus it is established that his way in all of that is what we have mentioned.

Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "They were magicians at the beginning of the day, and martyrs at its end."

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 20, verses 70–71:**

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate. They said, "We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses."﴾ ﴿[Pharaoh] said, "Have you believed in him before I give you permission? Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic. So I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will crucify you on the trunks of palm trees, and you will surely know whose punishment is more severe and more lasting."﴾

Know that in His words: ﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate﴾ there is an indication that [Moses] threw what was in his right hand, and it became a serpent that swallowed what they had made, and the matter became manifest. Thereupon they fell down prostrate. That is because they were at the highest level of the knowledge of magic. When they saw what Moses, peace be upon him, did, which was outside their craft, they knew that it was not magic at all. It is said that their leader said: "We used to overcome people with magic, and our instruments would remain with us if we were defeated. So if this is magic, where is what we threw?" They inferred from the change in the states of bodies the existence of the Creator, the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, and from its manifestation at the hand of Moses, peace be upon him, that he was a truthful messenger from Allah the Exalted. Therefore they repented, believed, and performed that which is the utmost in submission, which is prostration.

As for His words: ﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate﴾, the meaning is not that they were compelled to prostrate, for otherwise they would not have been praiseworthy. Rather, the interpretation of it is what al-Akhfash said: that because of the speed of their prostration, it was as if they had been thrown down. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "How wondrous is their matter! They threw down their ropes and staffs for disbelief and denial, then they threw down their heads after an hour for gratitude and prostration. How great is the difference between the two throwings!" It is related that they did not raise their heads until they saw Paradise and Hell and saw the reward of their people. It is related from Ikrimah: When they fell down prostrate, Allah showed them in their prostration their dwellings which they would come to in Paradise.

The judge [al-Qadi] said: "This is far-fetched, because if He had shown them directly, they would have become compelled, and that does not befit Him. Their words are: ﴿Indeed we have believed in our Lord that He may forgive us our sins﴾ [Ta-Ha: 73]." Its answer: Since it was permissible for Abraham, peace be upon him, despite being certain that he was forgiven, to say: ﴿And the one from whom I hope He will forgive my sin﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 82], why should the like not be permissible regarding the magicians?

Know that this story alerts to wondrous secrets concerning the matters of Lordship and the execution of the Divine decree and His destiny within the totality of created things. That is because the manifestation of those proofs was in the sight and hearing of all, so the manner of inference in them was clear and evident: that things came into being, and so they must have an influencer, and knowledge of this is necessary. That influencer is either creation itself or others. The first is manifestly false, because every sensible person knows by necessity from himself that he cannot create living beings and enlarge their bodies all at once, then reduce them again to what they were. These clear sciences, once they have settled in the intellect, yield certainty that there must be a manager of this world. So what can one say? Do you not see that those deniers were ignorant of the soundness of these premises? This is in the utmost remoteness, because we have shown that each of them is such that no sensible person can doubt it. Hence they knew their soundness, but they persisted in ignorance, disliked attaining knowledge and happiness for themselves, and loved attaining ignorance and wretchedness for themselves. I do not think any sensible person would ever be content with that for himself. So nothing remains but to say: intellect and proof are not sufficient; rather there must be a manager who creates these premises in the hearts and creates the awareness of how to arrange them and how to draw conclusions from them to the result, such that whenever He does that, the results arise in the hearts. This indicates that everything is by His decree and destiny, for there is no reliance upon intellects and hearts in their courses and their operations. Whoever casts off partisanship from his heart and looks at the states of his own self in the courses of his thoughts and views will grow more certain of what we have mentioned.

As for His words: ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses"﴾, know that the Ta'limiyya [Isma'ilis] argued by this verse and said: they believed in Allah whom they knew through Aaron and Moses, and that shows that knowledge of Allah is not obtained except from the Imam. This view is weak. Rather, in their words: ﴿We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses﴾ there are two benefits beyond what they mentioned:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us, nor over Him who created us. So decree whatever you will decree. You can only decree concerning this worldly life.﴾ ﴿Indeed, we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins and the magic you compelled us to practise. And Allah is better and more enduring.﴾ ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell, in which he will neither die nor live.﴾ ﴿But whoever comes to Him as a believer who has done righteous deeds, for those are the high ranks,﴾ ﴿gardens of perpetual residence beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the reward of one who purifies himself.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, related Pharaoh's threat to those people, He related their response to it, which indicates that they had complete certainty and perfect insight into the fundamentals of the religion. They said: ﴿We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us﴾. This indicates that Pharaoh had demanded that they renounce faith, failing which he would do to them what he had threatened. They said ﴿We will never prefer you﴾ as an answer to what he had said, and they stated the reason: that what had come to them were clear proofs and evidences, while what Pharaoh mentions is purely worldly, and the benefits and harms of this world do not conflict with the benefits and harms of the Hereafter. As for His words ﴿nor over Him who created us﴾, there are two interpretations:

The first: the meaning is "We will never prefer you, O Pharaoh, over the clear proofs that have come to us, nor over Him who created us," that is, nor over obedience to Him who created us and worship of Him.

The second: it is permissible that it be in the genitive case as an oath. Know that when they realised that if they persisted in faith, Pharaoh would do what he had threatened, they said ﴿So decree whatever you will decree﴾, not in the sense that they had commanded him to do that, but they showed that this threat would not turn them at all from their faith or from what they had come to know of the truth in knowledge and in action. Then they explained what makes it easy for them to bear that, saying ﴿You can only decree concerning this worldly life﴾. It is also read: "This worldly life is decreed (tuqda)." Its justification is that "life" in the well-known reading is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and the adverbial use was extended by treating it as a direct object, like your saying "I fasted the day of Friday" (ṣumtu yawma l-jumʿa, ṣīma). The meaning is that your judgement and decree only take place in this worldly life, and whatever state it is in, it is perishing, whereas our aim is the happiness of the Hereafter, which is enduring. Reason requires bearing a perishing harm that leads to enduring happiness. Then they said: ﴿Indeed, we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins﴾. And since the most recent of their sins was what they had displayed of magic, they said ﴿and the magic you compelled us to practise﴾. They mentioned several aspects of that compulsion:

One: the kings of that time used to take some of their subjects and oblige them to learn magic. When one grew old, they would send young people to him to teach them, so that there would always be someone skilled in it at every time. They said this for that reason, meaning that we were compelled in learning first and in teaching second. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: the chiefs of the magicians were seventy-two, two of them Copts and the rest from the Children of Israel. They said to Pharaoh: "Show us Moses asleep." They saw him and found his staff guarding him. They said: "This is not a magician, for a magician's magic fails when he sleeps." But Pharaoh insisted that they confront him.

Third: al-Hasan said: the magicians were gathered from the cities to confront Moses, peace be upon him, and they were brought by summons, and they were compelled in attending, and perhaps they were also compelled in displaying magic.

Fourth: ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd said: the summons of the ruler is a compulsion. This is weak, because the summons of the ruler, if there is no fear accompanying it, is not compulsion. Then they said ﴿And Allah is better﴾ in reward for those who obey Him, ﴿and more enduring﴾ in punishment for those who disobey Him. This is an answer to His words: ﴿and you will know which of us is more severe in punishment and more enduring﴾. Al-Hasan said: Glory be to Allah! These people were disbelievers, and they were the most extreme of disbelievers, yet faith took root in their hearts in the blink of an eye, and so it did not seem great to them to say ﴿So decree whatever you will decree﴾ concerning the Essence of Allah, the Exalted. By Allah, one of you today accompanies the Qur'an for sixty years, and then he sells his religion for a paltry price.

Then they concluded this speech by describing the condition of believers and the condition of criminals on the plain of Resurrection. About the criminals they said: ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell, in which he will neither die nor live.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: the pronoun in His words ﴿Indeed (innahu)﴾ is the pronoun of the matter, meaning that the affair and the situation is such and such.

The second issue: the Muʿtazila used this verse to affirm definitively the threat against the people of major sins. They said: the person who commits a major sin is a criminal, and every criminal is due Hell, because of His words ﴿whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal﴾. The word "man" (whoever) in a conditional context indicates generality, as evidenced by the fact that it is permissible to make an exception of each one of them, and an exception removes from the speech what would have been included without it. Some of our theologians objected to this argument and said: We do not concede that the perpetrator of a major sin is a criminal. The proof of this is that He, may He be exalted, set the criminal in opposition to the believer, for He said in this same verse: ﴿But whoever comes to Him as a believer who has done righteous deeds﴾, and He said: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 29]. Also, He said: ﴿for him is Hell, in which he will neither die nor live﴾, and the believer who has committed a major sin, even if he is punished in the Fire, does not have this description. And in the sound report: "Those will come out of the Fire in whose heart is an atom's weight of faith."

Know that these objections are weak. As for his saying that Allah set the criminal in opposition to the believer, this is granted, but this only helps if it is established that the perpetrator of a major sin is a believer, whereas the position of the Muʿtazila is that he is not a believer. So this objector seems to have built his objection on his own school's position, and that is invalid. His second statement: that it is not fitting for the perpetrator of a major sin to be described as one for whom is Hell, in which he neither dies nor lives. We reply: We do not concede this, for the punishment of Hell is at the utmost severity. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 192]. As for the hadith, it is said: "The Qur'an is mutawatir (transmitted by multiple chains), so a single report (khabar al-wahid) does not oppose it." It may also be said: it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh) that the Qur'an may be specified by a single report. The opponent may answer: that yields only conjecture, so it is permissible to rely on it in practical matters, but this issue is not a practical matter; it is one of belief, so it is not permissible to resort to it here. If another person objects and says: We are agreed that this verse is conditional on the absence of repentance and on its punishment not being cancelled by the reward of his obedience, and the common element between the two cases is that there is nothing that cancels that punishment; but according to us, pardon cancels punishment, and according to us, the criminal for whom there is no pardon must enter Hell. Know that this objection is also weak. As for the condition of the absence of repentance, there is no need for it, because He said ﴿whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal﴾, meaning in the state of being a criminal, and the one who repents cannot be truly said to have come to his Lord in the state of being a criminal. As for the perpetrator of a minor sin, it is because he is not called a criminal, since "criminal" is a term of blame, so it is not permissible to apply it to the perpetrator of a minor sin. Rather, the correct objection is that we say: the generality of this threat is opposed by what comes after it, namely the generality of the promise in His words: ﴿But whoever comes to Him as a believer who has done righteous deeds, for those are the high ranks﴾. Our discussion concerns one who came with faith and righteous deeds and then, after that, committed some major sins. If it is said: the punishment for disobedience cancels the reward of obedience, we say: why is it not permissible to say that the reward of faith repels the punishment for disobedience? If they say: if that were so, it would be impermissible to curse him and to apply the prescribed punishment (ḥadd) to him. We say: As for cursing others, it is permissible according to us. As for applying the prescribed punishment to him, it may be a trial (miḥna), as in the case of the one who repents, and it may be for deterrence (tankīl). The Muʿtazila said: His words, may He be exalted, ﴿As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned, a deterrent from Allah﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 38]: Allah, the Exalted, explicitly states that applying the prescribed punishment for deterrence is obligatory, and whoever is like that cannot deserve praise and honour, and if that does not remain, the reward does not remain either, as we have said. This shows that the punishment for a major sin is more fitting to remove the reward of earlier acts of obedience than the punishment for a later major sin is to be repelled by them. This is the end of their argument on the issue of the threat. We say: the essence of the matter comes down to this: the text indicating that the prescribed punishment is applied for deterrence has become opposed to the texts indicating that he deserves reward. So why is preferring one of them over the other more appropriate than the reverse? This is because the believer is divided into thief and non-thief, and the thief is divided into believer and non-believer, so neither of the two has any superiority over the other in generality or specificity. When they conflict, they cancel each other out. Then we say: we do not concede that the word "man" is definitive in indicating generality; rather it is conjectural, and our issue is definitive, so it is not permissible to rely on what you have mentioned. The full discussion of this is in the book al-Mahsul fi l-Usul.

The third issue: the Mujassima (anthropomorphists) held fast to His words ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal﴾ and said: a body only comes to its Lord if the Lord is in a place. The reply: Allah, the Exalted, made their coming to the place of promise a coming to Allah metaphorically, like the saying of Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [al-Saffat: 99].

The fourth issue: a living body must either remain alive or become dead, so being empty of both descriptions is impossible. Its meaning in the verse is that he will be in Hell in the worst condition: he will not die a death that brings relief, nor live a life that gives enjoyment. Then He mentioned the condition of the believers, saying: ﴿But whoever comes to Him as a believer who has done righteous deeds, for those are the high ranks﴾. Know that His words ﴿who has done righteous deeds﴾ imply that he must have performed all the righteous deeds. By consensus this is neither required nor possible, so it should be understood as performing the obligatory duties. Then He mentioned that whoever comes with faith and righteous deeds will have the high ranks, and then He explained them, saying: ﴿gardens of perpetual residence beneath which rivers flow﴾. In the verse there is an indication that pardon is granted to the people of major sins, because He, may He be exalted, made the high ranks of Paradise for those who come to their Lord with faith and righteous deeds. So the other ranks, which are not high, must belong to others: they are none but the disobedient among the people of faith. As for His words ﴿That is the reward of one who purifies himself﴾, Ibn ʿAbbas said: He means one who says, "There is no god but Allah." I say: since this verse indicates that the high ranks are the reward of one who purifies himself, that is, who cleanses himself of sins, it follows by the ruling of that address that the ranks that are not high are not the reward of one who purifies himself; they belong to others who have committed acts of disobedience, and Allah, by His grace and mercy, has pardoned them. Know that the Qur'an does not state that Pharaoh did to those believing people what he had threatened them with, but this is established in the reports.

Then they concluded this speech by describing the condition of believers and the condition of criminals on the plain of Resurrection. About the criminals they said: ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell, in which he will neither die nor live.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: the pronoun in His words ﴿Indeed (innahu)﴾ is the pronoun of the matter, meaning that the affair and the situation is such and such.

They said: the person who commits a major sin is a criminal, and every criminal is due Hell, because of His words ﴿whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal﴾. The word "man" (whoever) in a conditional context indicates generality, as evidenced by the fact that it is permissible to make an exception of each one of them, and an exception removes from the speech what would have been included without it. Some of our theologians objected to this argument and said: We do not concede that the perpetrator of a major sin is a criminal. The proof of this is that He, may He be exalted, set the criminal in opposition to the believer, for He said in this same verse: ﴿But whoever comes to Him as a believer who has done righteous deeds﴾, and He said: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 29]. Also, He said: ﴿for him is Hell, in which he will neither die nor live﴾, and the believer who has committed a major sin, even if he is punished in the Fire, does not have this description. And in the sound report: "Those will come out of the Fire in whose heart is an atom's weight of faith."

Know that these objections are weak. As for his saying that Allah set the criminal in opposition to the believer, this is granted, but this only helps if it is established that the perpetrator of a major sin is a believer, whereas the position of the Muʿtazila is that he is not a believer. So this objector seems to have built his objection on his own school's position, and that is invalid. His second statement: that it is not fitting for the perpetrator of a major sin to be described as one for whom is Hell, in which he neither dies nor lives. We reply: We do not concede this, for the punishment of Hell is at the utmost severity. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 192]. As for the hadith, it is said: "The Qur'an is mutawatir (transmitted by multiple chains), so a single report (khabar al-wahid) does not oppose it." It may also be said: it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh) that the Qur'an may be specified by a single report. The opponent may answer: that yields only conjecture, so it is permissible to rely on it in practical matters, but this issue is not a practical matter; it is one of belief, so it is not permissible to resort to it here. If another person objects and says: We are agreed that this verse is conditional on the absence of repentance and on its punishment not being cancelled by the reward of his obedience, and the common element between the two cases is that there is nothing that cancels that punishment; but according to us, pardon cancels punishment, and according to us, the criminal for whom there is no pardon must enter Hell. Know that this objection is also weak. As for the condition of the absence of repentance, there is no need for it, because He said ﴿whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal﴾, meaning in the state of being a criminal, and the one who repents cannot be truly said to have come to his Lord in the state of being a criminal. As for the perpetrator of a minor sin, it is because he is not called a criminal, since "criminal" is a term of blame, so it is not permissible to apply it to the perpetrator of a minor sin. Rather, the correct objection is that we say: the generality of this threat is opposed by what comes after it, namely the generality of the promise in His words: ﴿But whoever comes to Him as a believer who has done righteous deeds, for those are the high ranks﴾. Our discussion concerns one who came with faith and righteous deeds and then, after that, committed some major sins. If it is said: the punishment for disobedience cancels the reward of obedience, we say: why is it not permissible to say that the reward of faith repels the punishment for disobedience? If they say: if that were so, it would be impermissible to curse him and to apply the prescribed punishment (ḥadd) to him. We say: As for cursing others, it is permissible according to us. As for applying the prescribed punishment to him, it may be a trial (miḥna), as in the case of the one who repents, and it may be for deterrence (tankīl). The Muʿtazila said: His words, may He be exalted, ﴿As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned, a deterrent from Allah﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 38]: Allah, the Exalted, explicitly states that applying the prescribed punishment for deterrence is obligatory, and whoever is like that cannot deserve praise and honour, and if that does not remain, the reward does not remain either, as we have said. This is the end of their argument on the issue of the threat. We say: the essence of the matter comes down to this: the text indicating that the prescribed punishment is applied for deterrence has become opposed to the texts indicating that he deserves reward. So why is preferring one of them over the other more appropriate than the reverse? This is because the believer is divided into thief and non-thief, and the thief is divided into believer and non-believer, so neither of the two has any superiority over the other in generality or specificity. When they conflict, they cancel each other out. Then we say: we do not concede that the word "man" is definitive in indicating generality; rather it is conjectural, and our issue is definitive, so it is not permissible to rely on what you have mentioned. The full discussion of this is in the book al-Mahsul fi l-Usul.

Its meaning in the verse is that he will be in Hell in the worst condition: he will not die a death that brings relief, nor live a life that gives enjoyment. Then He mentioned the condition of the believers, saying: ﴿But whoever comes to Him as a believer who has done righteous deeds, for those are the high ranks﴾. Know that His words ﴿who has done righteous deeds﴾ imply that he must have performed all the righteous deeds. By consensus this is neither required nor possible, so it should be understood as performing the obligatory duties. The Muʿtazila said: His words, may He be exalted, ﴿As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned, a deterrent from Allah﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 38]: Allah, the Exalted, explicitly states that applying the prescribed punishment for deterrence is obligatory, and whoever is like that cannot deserve praise and honour, and if that does not remain, the reward does not remain either, as we have said. This shows that the punishment for a major sin is more fitting to remove the reward of earlier acts of obedience than the punishment for a later major sin is to be repelled by them. This is the end of their argument on the issue of the threat. We say: the essence of the matter comes down to this: the text indicating that the prescribed punishment is applied for deterrence has become opposed to the texts indicating that he deserves reward. So why is preferring one of them over the other more appropriate than the reverse? This is because the believer is divided into thief and non-thief, and the thief is divided into believer and non-believer, so neither of the two has any superiority over the other in generality or specificity. When they conflict, they cancel each other out. Then we say: we do not concede that the word "man" is definitive in indicating generality; rather it is conjectural, and our issue is definitive, so it is not permissible to rely on what you have mentioned. The full discussion of this is in the book al-Mahsul fi l-Usul.

The third issue: the Mujassima (anthropomorphists) held fast to His words ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal﴾ and said: a body only comes to its Lord if the Lord is in a place. The reply: Allah, the Exalted, made their coming to the place of promise a coming to Allah metaphorically, like the saying of Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [al-Saffat: 99].

The fourth issue: a living body must either remain alive or become dead, so being empty of both descriptions is impossible. Its meaning in the verse is that he will be in Hell in the worst condition: he will not die a death that brings relief, nor live a life that gives enjoyment. Then He mentioned the condition of the believers, saying: ﴿But whoever comes to Him as a believer who has done righteous deeds, for those are the high ranks﴾. Know that His words ﴿who has done righteous deeds﴾ imply that he must have performed all the righteous deeds. By consensus this is neither required nor possible, so it should be understood as performing the obligatory duties. Then He mentioned that whoever comes with faith and righteous deeds will have the high ranks, and then He explained them, saying: ﴿gardens of perpetual residence beneath which rivers flow﴾. In the verse there is an indication that pardon is granted to the people of major sins, because He, may He be exalted, made the high ranks of Paradise for those who come to their Lord with faith and righteous deeds. So the other ranks, which are not high, must belong to others: they are none but the disobedient among the people of faith. As for His words ﴿That is the reward of one who purifies himself﴾, Ibn ʿAbbas said: He means one who says, "There is no god but Allah." I say: since this verse indicates that the high ranks are the reward of one who purifies himself, that is, who cleanses himself of sins, it follows by the ruling of that address that the ranks that are not high are not the reward of one who purifies himself; they belong to others who have committed acts of disobedience, and Allah, by His grace and mercy, has pardoned them. Know that the Qur'an does not state that Pharaoh did to those believing people what he had threatened them with, but this is established in the reports.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us, nor over Him who created us. So decree whatever you will decree. You can only decree concerning this worldly life.﴾ ﴿Indeed, we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins and the magic you compelled us to practise. That is the reward of one who purifies himself.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, related Pharaoh's threat to those people, He related their response to it, which indicates that they had complete certainty and perfect insight into the fundamentals of the religion. They said: ﴿We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us﴾. This indicates that Pharaoh had demanded that they renounce faith, failing which he would do to them what he had threatened. They said ﴿We will never prefer you﴾ as an answer to what he had said, and they stated the reason: that what had come to them were clear proofs and evidences, while what Pharaoh mentions is purely worldly, and the benefits and harms of this world do not conflict with the benefits and harms of the Hereafter. As for His words ﴿nor over Him who created us﴾, there are two interpretations:

The first: the meaning is "We will never prefer you, O Pharaoh, over the clear proofs that have come to us, nor over Him who created us," that is, nor over obedience to Him who created us and worship of Him.

The second: it is permissible that it be in the genitive case as an oath. Know that when they realised that if they persisted in faith, Pharaoh would do what he had threatened, they said ﴿So decree whatever you will decree﴾, not in the sense that they had commanded him to do that, but they showed that this threat would not turn them at all from their faith or from what they had come to know of the truth in knowledge and in action. Then they explained what makes it easy for them to bear that, saying ﴿You can only decree concerning this worldly life﴾. It is also read: "This worldly life is decreed (tuqda)." Its justification is that "life" in the well-known reading is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and the adverbial use was extended by treating it as a direct object, like your saying "I fasted the day of Friday" (ṣumtu yawma l-jumʿa, ṣīma). The meaning is that your judgement and decree only take place in this worldly life, and whatever state it is in, it is perishing, whereas our aim is the happiness of the Hereafter, which is enduring. Reason requires bearing a perishing harm that leads to enduring happiness. Then they said: ﴿Indeed, we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins﴾. And since the most recent of their sins was what they had displayed of magic, they said ﴿and the magic you compelled us to practise﴾. They mentioned several aspects of that compulsion:

One: the kings of that time used to take some of their subjects and oblige them to learn magic. When one grew old, they would send young people to him to teach them, so that there would always be someone skilled in it at every time. They said this for that reason, meaning that we were compelled in learning first and in teaching second. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Second: the chiefs of the magicians were seventy-two, two of them Copts and the rest from the Children of Israel. They said to Pharaoh: "Show us Moses asleep." They saw him and found his staff guarding him. They said: "This is not a magician, for a magician's magic fails when he sleeps." But Pharaoh insisted that they confront him.

Third: al-Hasan said: the magicians were gathered from the cities to confront Moses, peace be upon him, and they were brought by summons, and they were compelled in attending, and perhaps they were also compelled in displaying magic.

Fourth: ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd said: the summons of the ruler is a compulsion. This is weak, because the summons of the ruler, if there is no fear accompanying it, is not compulsion. Then they said ﴿And Allah is better﴾ in reward for those who obey Him, ﴿and more enduring﴾ in punishment for those who disobey Him. This is an answer to His words: ﴿and you will know which of us is more severe in punishment and more enduring﴾. Al-Hasan said: Glory be to Allah! These people were disbelievers, and they were the most extreme of disbelievers, yet faith took root in their hearts in the blink of an eye, and so it did not seem great to them to say ﴿So decree whatever you will decree﴾ concerning the Essence of Allah, the Exalted. By Allah, one of you today accompanies the Qur'an for sixty years, and then he sells his religion for a paltry price.

Then they concluded this speech by describing the condition of believers and the condition of criminals on the plain of Resurrection. About the criminals they said: ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell, in which he will neither die nor live.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: the pronoun in His words ﴿Indeed (innahu)﴾ is the pronoun of the matter, meaning that the affair and the situation is such and such.

The second issue: the Muʿtazila used this verse to affirm definitively the threat against the people of major sins. They said: the person who commits a major sin is a criminal, and every criminal is due Hell, because of His words ﴿whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal﴾. The word "man" (whoever) in a conditional context indicates generality, as evidenced by the fact that it is permissible to make an exception of each one of them, and an exception removes from the speech what would have been included without it. Some of our theologians objected to this argument and said: We do not concede that the perpetrator of a major sin is a criminal. The proof of this is that He, may He be exalted, set the criminal in opposition to the believer, for He said in this same verse: ﴿But whoever comes to Him as a believer who has done righteous deeds﴾, and He said: ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 29]. Also, He said: ﴿for him is Hell, in which he will neither die nor live﴾, and the believer who has committed a major sin, even if he is punished in the Fire, does not have this description. And in the sound report: "Those will come out of the Fire in whose heart is an atom's weight of faith."

Know that these objections are weak. As for his saying that Allah set the criminal in opposition to the believer, this is granted, but this only helps if it is established that the perpetrator of a major sin is a believer, whereas the position of the Muʿtazila is that he is not a believer. So this objector seems to have built his objection on his own school's position, and that is invalid. His second statement: that it is not fitting for the perpetrator of a major sin to be described as one for whom is Hell, in which he neither dies nor lives. We reply: We do not concede this, for the punishment of Hell is at the utmost severity. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 192]. As for the hadith, it is said: "The Qur'an is mutawatir (transmitted by multiple chains), so a single report (khabar al-wahid) does not oppose it." It may also be said: it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh) that the Qur'an may be specified by a single report. The opponent may answer: that yields only conjecture, so it is permissible to rely on it in practical matters, but this issue is not a practical matter; it is one of belief, so it is not permissible to resort to it here. If another person objects and says: We are agreed that this verse is conditional on the absence of repentance and on its punishment not being cancelled by the reward of his obedience, and the common element between the two cases is that there is nothing that cancels that punishment; but according to us, pardon cancels punishment, and according to us, the criminal for whom there is no pardon must enter Hell. Know that this objection is also weak. [Page 80]

**The Exalted said:** ﴿And We revealed to Moses: Travel by night with My servants, and strike for them a dry path through the sea; you will not fear being overtaken, nor will you be afraid.﴾ ﴿Then Pharaoh followed them with his hosts, and the sea covered them with what covered them.﴾ ﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray, and did not guide them.﴾

Know that in His words, ﴿And We revealed to Moses: Travel by night with My servants﴾, there is an indication that at that time the number of those who responded to Moses, peace be upon him, had grown. So God the Exalted willed to distinguish them from Pharaoh's group and to deliver them, so He revealed to him that he should travel with them by night. *Al-sura* (night travel) is the name for travelling at night, and *al-isra'* is similar to it. If it is asked, "What is the wisdom in their travelling by night?", we say there are several reasons:

The first: that their gathering should not be in view of the enemy, so that nothing prevents them from completing their purpose.

The second: so that it would be an obstacle to the pursuit of Pharaoh and his followers.

The third: so that when the two armies drew near, Moses' army would not see Pharaoh's army, and thus would not be frightened of them.

As for His words, ﴿strike for them a dry path through the sea﴾, there are two views:

The first: that is, make for them (*fa-ij'al lahum*), from the expression they use: "he struck (*darab*) a share (*sahman*) for him in his wealth," and "he struck (*darab*) the brick," meaning he made it.

The second: clarify for them a path through the sea by striking with the staff, namely that he strikes the sea with the staff until it splits, so the striking is transferred to the path. The sum is that by "striking the path" is meant making the path dry by striking. Then God the Exalted explained that all the causes of safety were present on that path:

The first: that it was dry (*yabasan*). It was read as *yabisan* and *yabsan*, with a fatha on the ya' and a sukun on the ba'. Whoever reads *yabisan* makes it refer to the path; whoever reads *yabasan* with a vowel on the ba' — *al-yabas* and *al-yabis* are one and the same thing, and the meaning is a path that is dry. Whoever reads *yabsan* with a sukun on the ba' — it is a lightened form of *al-yabs*, and what is meant is that there was no mud or dampness in it, let alone water.

The second: His words, ﴿you will not fear being overtaken, nor will you be afraid﴾, meaning you will not fear that Pharaoh will overtake you, for I will place a barrier between you and him by delaying him. Sibawayh said: His words ﴿you will not fear﴾ (*la takhafu*) are in the nominative case in two ways:

One: as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), like your saying: "not fearing and not dreading."

The second: as a nominal beginning (*ibtida'*), meaning "you do not fear." This is the view of al-Farra'. Al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj said the meaning is "you do not fear in it," like His words: ﴿And fear a day when no soul will avail another soul﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:48), meaning no soul will avail in it. Hamza read *la takhaf* (with a jussive), and in this there are two views:

One: that it is a prohibition.

The second: Abu 'Ali said: he made it the response to a conditional, meaning "if you strike, do not fear." On this reading they mentioned three possibilities concerning His words ﴿nor will you be afraid﴾:

One: that it is a new clause, as if it were said: "and you are not afraid," that is, it is part of your state that you are secure and do not dread.

The second: that the alif is not the alif converted from a ya' which is the final radical of the verb, but is an extra alif added for the sake of pausal vocalization, because of the verse-ending (*fasila*), like His words: ﴿and they led us astray from the way﴾ (al-Ahzab 33:67) and ﴿and you think about God with thoughts﴾ (al-Ahzab 33:10).

The third: that it is like the words of the poet:

*"An old woman of the 'Abshamiyya laughs at me, as if you had never seen before me a captive from Yemen."*

The third: His words ﴿nor will you be afraid﴾, and the meaning is that you do not fear the overtaking of Pharaoh, and you do not fear drowning in the water. As for His words, ﴿Then Pharaoh followed them with his hosts﴾, Abu Muslim said: the narrators of the language claim that *atba'ahum* and *tabi'ahum* are one and the same, and that is permissible. It is possible that the *ba'* is extra, and the meaning is: Pharaoh followed them with his hosts, like His words: ﴿Do not seize my beard or my head﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:94) and ﴿He carried his servant by night﴾ (al-Isra' 17:1). Al-Zajjaj said: it was read *fa-atba'ahum Fir'awnu* [*wa-junudahu*] — "and his hosts" — meaning "and with him were his hosts," and it was also read *bi-junudihi*, meaning he joined his hosts to them, and it is permissible that it means "with them."

As for His words, ﴿so the sea covered them﴾ (*fa-ghashiyahum*), the meaning is that it rose over them and covered them. And "what covered them" is an expression of magnitude, meaning that there covered them what no one knows the reality of except God the Exalted. It was also read: [*fa-ghashshahum min al-yammi ma ghashiyahum*], and the subject of *ghashshahum* is either God, glorified and exalted, or "what covered them," or Pharaoh, because he is the one who plunged his hosts into peril and caused their destruction.

As for His words, ﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray, and did not guide them﴾, al-Qadi (the judge) argued by it and said: If misguidance were created by God the Exalted, it would not be permissible to say "Pharaoh led his people astray," rather it would have to be said "God led them astray." Also, God the Exalted blamed him for that, so how could He be the creator of disbelief? For whoever blames another for something must himself not be the doer of that act, otherwise he would deserve that blame. His words, ﴿and did not guide them﴾, are a mockery of him, in his words: ﴿And I only guide you to the path of right conduct﴾ (Ghafir 40:29).

Let us mention the story and what it contains of discussions. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: When God the Exalted commanded Moses to lead his people across the sea — and Moses, peace be upon him, and the Children of Israel had borrowed jewellery and animals from the people of Pharaoh for a festival they were going out to — he set out with them by night, and they numbered six hundred thousand and three thousand and some more, none of them being sixty or twenty years old. Yusuf, peace be upon him, had charged them at his death that they should take his bones with them out of Egypt, but they did not take them out, so the people were perplexed until an old woman showed them the place of the bones, and they took them. Then Moses, peace be upon him, said to the old woman: "Ask for what you wish." She said: "I will be with you in Paradise."

Ibn 'Abbas also mentioned that "Muhammad ﷺ and Abu Bakr came upon a man of the Arabs and a woman who had nothing but a single she-goat, so they slaughtered it for them. Then he, peace be upon him, said: 'When you hear of a man who has appeared in Yathrib, go to him, for perhaps God will provide you with good from him.' When he heard of the appearance of the Messenger ﷺ, he came to him with his wife, and said: 'Do you recognise me?' He said: 'Yes, I recognised you.' Then he said to him: 'Ask for what you wish.' He said: 'Eighty ewes.' So he gave them to him and said: 'Indeed, the old woman of the Children of Israel was better than you.'"

Pharaoh set out in pursuit of Moses, peace be upon him, and at the head of his army were one thousand thousand and five hundred thousand, besides the two wings and the centre. When Moses reached the sea, he said: "Here I was commanded." Then Moses, peace be upon him, said to the sea: "Split apart!" but it refused. God revealed to him that he should strike the sea with his staff, so he struck it and it split. Moses, peace be upon him, said to them: "Enter into it." They said: "How, when its ground is moist?" So he called upon God, and the east wind blew over it and it dried. They said: "We fear drowning in some of us," so he made openings between them so that some could see others. Then they entered until they crossed the sea. Pharaoh then came to those paths, and his people said to him: "Moses has bewitched the sea, so it has become as you see." He was on a fine horse, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, came on a female horse with thirty-three angels, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, was in front of Pharaoh. The stallion saw the female horse of Gabriel and plunged into the sea with Pharaoh following its track. The angels called out to the people: "Catch up with the king!" until, when the last of them had entered and the first of them was about to come out, the sea closed over them and they drowned. The Children of Israel heard the sound of the sea rolling over them, and they said: "What is this, Moses?" He said: "God has drowned Pharaoh and his people." So they went back to look at them, and they said: "Moses, ask God to bring them out for us so that we may look at them." He prayed, and the sea cast them out onto the shore, and they took some of their weapons.

Ibn 'Abbas also mentioned that Gabriel, peace be upon him, said: "O Muhammad, if you had seen me as I pushed Pharaoh into the water and the mud, for fear that he might repent!" This is the meaning of His words: ﴿so the sea covered them with what covered them﴾.

There are discussions regarding the story:

**The first discussion:** It is narrated in reports that when Moses, peace be upon him, struck the sea with his staff, twelve dry paths emerged, ready to be traversed, and the water remained standing between one path and another like a great mountain (*tawd*, which is a mountain). Each tribe of the Children of Israel took one of these paths. Some said: rather, only one path emerged. The evidence for the first view is the reports, and from the Qur'an His words: ﴿so each division was like a great mountain﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:63). That cannot occur unless there were paths there, so that the water standing between the two paths is like a great mountain. The evidence for the second view is the apparent meaning of His words: ﴿strike for them a dry path through the sea﴾, which refers to one path, even though it is possible to take it as paths by considering the genus.

**The second discussion:** It is narrated that after Moses, peace be upon him, had shown them the path and clarified it for them, the Children of Israel were obstinate and said: "We want that some of us may see others," and this is far-fetched. That is because when the people saw Pharaoh's coming, they were in extreme fear, and a frightened person who finds a path of flight and escape, how could he be free for cold obstinacy?

**The third discussion:** Pharaoh was intelligent, indeed he was at the height of cunning, so how did he choose to throw himself into destruction? For he knew of himself that the splitting of the sea was not by his command. In view of this, they mentioned two possibilities:

One of them: that Gabriel, peace be upon him, was on a mare, and Pharaoh's horse followed her. One may say: this is far-fetched, for it is unlikely that the king's plunging into such places would precede the plunging of the whole army. What they mentioned is only complete if the matter were so. Also, if the matter were as they said, Pharaoh would be like one compelled in that entry, and that would increase his fear and move him to hold back from entering. Also, what need has Gabriel, peace be upon him, of this trick, when he could have seized him with his people and thrown him into the water from the outset? Rather, the better view is that he ordered the vanguard of his army to enter, and they entered and did not drown, so his supposition of safety prevailed. When all of them had entered, God the Exalted drowned them.

**The fourth discussion:** What is reported from Gabriel, peace be upon him, that he was pushing him into the water and the mud for fear that he would believe — this is far-fetched, because preventing belief is not fitting for angels and prophets, peace be upon them.

**The fifth discussion:** What is reported, that Moses, peace be upon him, spoke to the sea, saying to it: "Split apart for me so that I may cross over you," and the sea said: "No disobedient man passes over me." This is not impossible according to our principles, because with us, bodily structure (*al-bunyah*) is not a condition for life. According to the Mu'tazila (the Mu'tazilites), this is by way of the language of the state, not the language of speech. And God knows best.

The second: so that it would be an obstacle to the pursuit of Pharaoh and his followers.

The third: so that when the two armies drew near, Moses' army would not see Pharaoh's army, and thus would not be frightened of them.

As for His words, ﴿strike for them a dry path through the sea﴾, there are two views:

The first: that is, make for them (*fa-ij'al lahum*), from the expression they use: "he struck (*darab*) a share (*sahman*) for him in his wealth," and "he struck (*darab*) the brick," meaning he made it.

The second: clarify for them a path through the sea by striking with the staff, namely that he strikes the sea with the staff until it splits, so the striking is transferred to the path. The sum is that by "striking the path" is meant making the path dry by striking. Then God the Exalted explained that all the causes of safety were present on that path:

The first: that it was dry (*yabasan*). It was read as *yabisan* and *yabsan*, with a fatha on the ya' and a sukun on the ba'. Whoever reads *yabisan* makes it refer to the path; whoever reads *yabasan* with a vowel on the ba' — *al-yabas* and *al-yabis* are one and the same thing, and the meaning is a path that is dry. Whoever reads *yabsan* with a sukun on the ba' — it is a lightened form of *al-yabs*, and what is meant is that there was no mud or dampness in it, let alone water.

The second: His words, ﴿you will not fear being overtaken, nor will you be afraid﴾, meaning you will not fear that Pharaoh will overtake you, for I will place a barrier between you and him by delaying him. Sibawayh said: His words ﴿you will not fear﴾ (*la takhafu*) are in the nominative case in two ways:

One: as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), like your saying: "not fearing and not dreading."

The second: as a nominal beginning (*ibtida'*), meaning "you do not fear." This is the view of al-Farra'. Al-Akhfash and al-Zajjaj said the meaning is "you do not fear in it," like His words: ﴿And fear a day when no soul will avail another soul﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:48), meaning no soul will avail in it. Hamza read *la takhaf* (with a jussive), and in this there are two views:

One: that it is a prohibition.

The second: Abu 'Ali said: he made it the response to a conditional, meaning "if you strike, do not fear." On this reading they mentioned three possibilities concerning His words ﴿nor will you be afraid﴾:

One: that it is a new clause, as if it were said: "and you are not afraid," that is, it is part of your state that you are secure and do not dread.

The second: that the alif is not the alif converted from a ya' which is the final radical of the verb, but is an extra alif added for the sake of pausal vocalization, because of the verse-ending (*fasila*), like His words: ﴿and they led us astray from the way﴾ (al-Ahzab 33:67) and ﴿and you think about God with thoughts﴾ (al-Ahzab 33:10).

The third: that it is like the words of the poet:

*"An old woman of the 'Abshamiyya laughs at me, as if you had never seen before me a captive from Yemen."*

The third: His words ﴿nor will you be afraid﴾, and the meaning is that you do not fear the overtaking of Pharaoh, and you do not fear drowning in the water. As for His words, ﴿Then Pharaoh followed them with his hosts﴾, Abu Muslim said: the narrators of the language claim that *atba'ahum* and *tabi'ahum* are one and the same, and that is permissible. It is possible that the *ba'* is extra, and the meaning is: Pharaoh followed them with his hosts, like His words: ﴿Do not seize my beard or my head﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:94) and ﴿He carried his servant by night﴾ (al-Isra' 17:1). Al-Zajjaj said: it was read *fa-atba'ahum Fir'awnu* [*wa-junudahu*] — "and his hosts" — meaning "and with him were his hosts," and it was also read *bi-junudihi*, meaning he joined his hosts to them, and it is permissible that it means "with them."

As for His words, ﴿so the sea covered them﴾ (*fa-ghashiyahum*), the meaning is that it rose over them and covered them. And "what covered them" is an expression of magnitude, meaning that there covered them what no one knows the reality of except God the Exalted. It was also read: [*fa-ghashshahum min al-yammi ma ghashiyahum*], and the subject of *ghashshahum* is either God, glorified and exalted, or "what covered them," or Pharaoh, because he is the one who plunged his hosts into peril and caused their destruction.

As for His words, ﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray, and did not guide them﴾, al-Qadi (the judge) argued by it and said: If misguidance were created by God the Exalted, it would not be permissible to say "Pharaoh led his people astray," rather it would have to be said "God led them astray." Also, God the Exalted blamed him for that, so how could He be the creator of disbelief? For whoever blames another for something must himself not be the doer of that act, otherwise he would deserve that blame. His words, ﴿and did not guide them﴾, are a mockery of him, in his words: ﴿And I only guide you to the path of right conduct﴾ (Ghafir 40:29).

Let us mention the story and what it contains of discussions. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: When God the Exalted commanded Moses to lead his people across the sea — and Moses, peace be upon him, and the Children of Israel had borrowed jewellery and animals from the people of Pharaoh for a festival they were going out to — he set out with them by night, and they numbered six hundred thousand and three thousand and some more, none of them being sixty or twenty years old. Yusuf, peace be upon him, had charged them at his death that they should take his bones with them out of Egypt, but they did not take them out, so the people were perplexed until an old woman showed them the place of the bones, and they took them. Then Moses, peace be upon him, said to the old woman: "Ask for what you wish." She said: "I will be with you in Paradise."

Ibn 'Abbas also mentioned that "Muhammad ﷺ and Abu Bakr came upon a man of the Arabs and a woman who had nothing but a single she-goat, so they slaughtered it for them. Then he, peace be upon him, said: 'When you hear of a man who has appeared in Yathrib, go to him, for perhaps God will provide you with good from him.' When he heard of the appearance of the Messenger ﷺ, he came to him with his wife, and said: 'Do you recognise me?' He said: 'Yes, I recognised you.' Then he said to him: 'Ask for what you wish.' He said: 'Eighty ewes.' So he gave them to him and said: 'Indeed, the old woman of the Children of Israel was better than you.'"

Pharaoh set out in pursuit of Moses, peace be upon him, and at the head of his army were one thousand thousand and five hundred thousand, besides the two wings and the centre. When Moses reached the sea, he said: "Here I was commanded." Then Moses, peace be upon him, said to the sea: "Split apart!" but it refused. God revealed to him that he should strike the sea with his staff, so he struck it and it split. Moses, peace be upon him, said to them: "Enter into it." They said: "How, when its ground is moist?" So he called upon God, and the east wind blew over it and it dried. They said: "We fear drowning in some of us," so he made openings between them so that some could see others. Then they entered until they crossed the sea. Pharaoh then came to those paths, and his people said to him: "Moses has bewitched the sea, so it has become as you see." He was on a fine horse, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, came on a female horse with thirty-three angels, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, was in front of Pharaoh. The stallion saw the female horse of Gabriel and plunged into the sea with Pharaoh following its track. The angels called out to the people: "Catch up with the king!" until, when the last of them had entered and the first of them was about to come out, the sea closed over them and they drowned. The Children of Israel heard the sound of the sea rolling over them, and they said: "What is this, Moses?" He said: "God has drowned Pharaoh and his people." So they went back to look at them, and they said: "Moses, ask God to bring them out for us so that we may look at them." He prayed, and the sea cast them out onto the shore, and they took some of their weapons.

Ibn 'Abbas also mentioned that Gabriel, peace be upon him, said: "O Muhammad, if you had seen me as I pushed Pharaoh into the water and the mud, for fear that he might repent!" This is the meaning of His words: ﴿so the sea covered them with what covered them﴾.

There are discussions regarding the story:

**The first discussion:** It is narrated in reports that when Moses, peace be upon him, struck the sea with his staff, twelve dry paths emerged, ready to be traversed, and the water remained standing between one path and another like a great mountain (*tawd*, which is a mountain). Each tribe of the Children of Israel took one of these paths. Some said: rather, only one path emerged. The evidence for the first view is the reports, and from the Qur'an His words: ﴿so each division was like a great mountain﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:63). That cannot occur unless there were paths there, so that the water standing between the two paths is like a great mountain. The evidence for the second view is the apparent meaning of His words: ﴿strike for them a dry path through the sea﴾, which refers to one path, even though it is possible to take it as paths by considering the genus.

**The second discussion:** It is narrated that after Moses, peace be upon him, had shown them the path and clarified it for them, the Children of Israel were obstinate and said: "We want that some of us may see others," and this is far-fetched. That is because when the people saw Pharaoh's coming, they were in extreme fear, and a frightened person who finds a path of flight and escape, how could he be free for cold obstinacy?

**The third discussion:** Pharaoh was intelligent, indeed he was at the height of cunning, so how did he choose to throw himself into destruction? For he knew of himself that the splitting of the sea was not by his command. In view of this, they mentioned two possibilities:

One of them: that Gabriel, peace be upon him, was on a mare, and Pharaoh's horse followed her. One may say: this is far-fetched, for it is unlikely that the king's plunging into such places would precede the plunging of the whole army. What they mentioned is only complete if the matter were so. Also, if the matter were as they said, Pharaoh would be like one compelled in that entry, and that would increase his fear and move him to hold back from entering. Also, what need has Gabriel, peace be upon him, of this trick, when he could have seized him with his people and thrown him into the water from the outset? Rather, the better view is that he ordered the vanguard of his army to enter, and they entered and did not drown, so his supposition of safety prevailed. When all of them had entered, God the Exalted drowned them.

**The fourth discussion:** What is reported from Gabriel, peace be upon him, that he was pushing him into the water and the mud for fear that he would believe — this is far-fetched, because preventing belief is not fitting for angels and prophets, peace be upon them.

**The fifth discussion:** What is reported, that Moses, peace be upon him, spoke to the sea, saying to it: "Split apart for me so that I may cross over you," and the sea said: "No disobedient man passes over me." This is not impossible according to our principles, because with us, bodily structure (*al-bunyah*) is not a condition for life. According to the Mu'tazila (the Mu'tazilites), this is by way of the language of the state, not the language of speech. And God knows best.
