[p. 83]

The exalted God says: ﴿O Children of Israel, We had certainly delivered you from your enemy and made appointment with you at the right side of the mount and sent down upon you manna and quail.﴾ ﴿Eat from the good things We have provided you, but do not transgress therein, lest My anger descend upon you. And he on whom My anger descends has certainly fallen.﴾ ﴿And indeed, I am Forgiving toward one who repents, believes, does righteousness, and then remains guided.﴾

Know that when God bestowed upon the people of Moses, peace be upon him, various kinds of blessings, He reminded them of them. There is no doubt that removing harm must come before conferring benefit. There is also no doubt that conferring a religious benefit is greater, as a blessing, than conferring a worldly benefit. For this reason God began with His words: ﴿We delivered you from your enemy﴾, which indicates the removal of harm, for Pharaoh used to inflict upon them many kinds of oppression: killing, humiliation, expulsion, and exhausting labour in work. Then He followed with mention of the religious benefit, which is His words: ﴿And We made appointment with you at the right side of the mount﴾. The aspect of benefit in this is that at that time He sent down to them a Book containing the explanation of their religion and the exposition of their law. Then He completed the triad with mention of the worldly benefit, which is His words: ﴿And We sent down upon you manna and quail﴾, and ﴿Eat from the good things We have provided you﴾. Then He restrained them from disobedience by His words: ﴿but do not transgress therein, lest My anger descend upon you﴾. Then He made clear that whoever disobeys and then repents is accepted by God, by His words: ﴿And indeed, I am Forgiving toward one who repents﴾. This is the explanation of the purpose of the verse. Then here are some issues:

**First issue:** Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿قَدْ أنْجَيْتُكم وَوَعَدْتُكم﴾ (qad anjaytukum wa-wa'adtukum) up to His words ﴿from the good things We have provided you﴾, all with the *tā'* (first person singular), except His words ﴿And We sent down upon you the manna and quail﴾, which are with the *nūn* (first person plural). The rest read all of them with the *nūn*. Nāfi' and 'Āṣim read ﴿وَوَاعَدْناكم﴾ (wa-wā'adnākum), and Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿وَوَاعَدْتُكم﴾ (wa-wā'adtukum).

**Second issue:** al-Kalbī said: When Moses, peace be upon him, took the Children of Israel across the sea, they said to him: "Did you not promise us that you would bring us from our Lord a Book containing the obligations and rulings?" He said: "Yes." Then Moses hastened to his Lord to bring them the Book, and he promised them that he would come to them after forty nights from the day he set out. He said ﴿wa-wā'adnākum﴾ (We made appointment with you) only because he had made the promise to Moses that He would give him the Torah on their account. Muqātil said: He said "We made appointment with you" because the address was to him and to the seventy chosen men. And God knows best.

**Third issue:** The exegetes said: The mountain has no right side or left side, but what is meant is that Mount Sinai lies on the right of one who sets out from Egypt towards Syria. The word ﴿al-ayman﴾ (the right) is read in the genitive (*al-ayman*) by *jiwār* (attraction of case), like the expression *juḥru ḍabbin kharib* (the hole of a dried-up lizard). The people's benefit from this is either because God sent down the Torah to them, containing the explanation of their religion, or because when God spoke to Moses on the mount, great honour came to the people by reason of it.

**Fourth issue:** His words ﴿Eat﴾ (kulū) are not a command of obligation but a command of permission, like His words: ﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾ [al-Mā'idah 5:2].

**Fifth issue:** Regarding "the good things" (al-ṭayyibāt), there are two views:

The first: the delicacies, because the manna and quail are among the delicious foods.

The second, which is the view of al-Kalbī and Muqātil: the lawful, because it is something God sent down to them that no human hand had touched. It is permissible to combine the two aspects, for between the two meanings there is a shared meaning. The full discussion of this story has already passed in Sūrat al-Baqarah.

**Sixth issue:** Regarding His words ﴿but do not transgress therein﴾, there are several aspects:

The first: Ibn 'Abbās, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: "Do not transgress" means: let none of you wrong another by taking from his companion.

The second: Muqātil and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: Do not wrong yourselves therein by going beyond the bounds of what is permitted.

The third: al-Kalbī said: Do not disbelieve the blessing, that is, do not seek help with My blessing in opposing Me, nor turn away from gratitude, nor deviate from the lawful to the unlawful.

**Seventh issue:** al-A'mash and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿فَيَحُلَّ، وَمَن يَحْلُلْ﴾ (fa-yaḥull, wa-man yaḥlul), both with a *ḍamma* (u-vowel). Al-A'mash narrated from the companions of 'Abd Allāh (Ibn Mas'ūd) ﴿فَيَحِلَّ﴾ (fa-yaḥilla) with a *kasra* and ﴿وَمَن يَحْلُلْ﴾ (wa-man yaḥlul) with a *ḍamma*. The reading of the majority is with a *kasra* in both words. As for the one who reads with a *kasra*, its meaning is obligation, from *ḥalla al-dayn yaḥillu* when its payment became due, and from it is His words: ﴿until the offering reaches its place of sacrifice﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:196]. The one with a *ḍamma* means descent. His words ﴿فَقَدْ هَوَى﴾ (fa-qad hawā) mean: he has become wretched. It was also said: he has fallen into the abyss. It is said: *hawā yahwī hawiyyan* when one falls from a height to a lower place.

[p. 84]

**Eighth issue:** Know that God described Himself as Ghāfir (Forgiver), Ghafūr (Most Forgiving), and Ghaffār (Oft-Forgiving), and that He has *ghufrān* (forgiveness) and *maghfirah* (pardon), and He expressed this with the past, the present and the imperative forms. As for His describing Himself as Ghāfir, it is His words: ﴿Forgiver of sin﴾ [Ghāfir 40:3]. As for His being Ghafūr, it is His words: ﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving, Possessor of mercy﴾ [al-Kahf 18:58]. As for His being Ghaffār, it is His words: ﴿And indeed, I am Forgiving toward one who repents﴾. As for *ghufrān*, it is His words: ﴿Your forgiveness, our Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:285]. As for *maghfirah*, it is His words: ﴿And indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind﴾ [al-Ra'd 13:6]. As for the past form, it is His words concerning Dāwūd, peace be upon him: ﴿So We forgave him that﴾ [Ṣād 38:25]. As for the future form, it is His words: ﴿Indeed, God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisā' 4:48], and His words: ﴿Indeed, God forgives all sins﴾ [al-Zumar 39:53], and His words concerning Muḥammad (ﷺ): ﴿That God may forgive you﴾ [al-Fath 48:2]. As for the word *istighfār* (seeking forgiveness), it is His words: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin and for believing men and believing women﴾ [Muḥammad 47:19]. And concerning Nūḥ, peace be upon him: ﴿I said, "Seek forgiveness from your Lord; indeed, He is ever Forgiving"﴾ [Nūḥ 71:10]. And concerning the angels: ﴿and they seek forgiveness for those on earth﴾ [al-Shūrā 42:5]. Know that all the prophets, peace be upon them, sought forgiveness. As for Ādam, peace be upon him, he said: ﴿And if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-A'rāf 7:23]. As for Nūḥ, peace be upon him, he said: ﴿And unless You forgive me and have mercy upon me﴾ [Hūd 11:47]. As for Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, he said: ﴿And the one from whom I aspire that He will forgive me my error on the Day of Recompense﴾ [al-Shu'arā' 26:82], and he sought it for his father: ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord﴾ [Maryam 19:47]. As for Yūsuf, peace be upon him, he said to his brothers: ﴿No reproach upon you today; may God forgive you﴾ [Yūsuf 12:92]. As for Mūsā, peace be upon him, it is in the story of the Egyptian man: ﴿He said, "My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me"﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ 28:16]. As for Dāwūd, peace be upon him: ﴿So he asked forgiveness of his Lord﴾ [Ṣād 38:24]. As for Sulaymān, peace be upon him: ﴿My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom﴾ [Ṣād 38:35]. As for 'Īsā, peace be upon him: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ [al-Mā'idah 5:118]. As for Muḥammad (ﷺ), it is His words: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin and for believing men and believing women﴾. As for the community, it is His words: ﴿And those who came after them say, "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers"﴾ [al-Ḥashr 59:10].

Know that the extended discussion here is that we first explain the reality of forgiveness (*maghfirah*), then speak about God being Forgiver, Most Forgiving and Oft-Forgiving, then speak about whether His forgiveness is general, then explain how His forgiveness toward the prophets, peace be upon them, can be conceived when they have no sin. From this principle follows the argument of our companions (the Ash'arī school) in establishing pardon (*'afw*). Its formulation is that a sin is either minor or major, and either after repentance or before repentance. The first two categories, namely minor and major sins after repentance, would be unseemly for God to punish, and it is obligatory upon Him to overlook them. Abandoning what is unseemly is not called forgiveness. So it is necessary that forgiveness is realized only in the third category, which is what is sought. If it is said: This contradicts the explicit text of the verse, for it established forgiveness for one who combined four things: repentance, faith, righteous deed, and being guided. We reply: One who repents, believes, does righteous deeds, and then is guided, and then sins after that, is still a penitent, a believer, one who brings righteous deeds, and one who is guided, and yet he is a sinner. In that case our statement is sound. Here is a subtle point: a servant has three names: *al-ẓālim* (the wrongdoer), *al-ẓalūm* (the great wrongdoer), and *al-ẓallām* (the extremely great wrongdoer). *Al-ẓālim* is in His words: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself﴾ [Fāṭir 35:32]. *Al-ẓalūm* is in His words: ﴿Indeed, he was a great wrongdoer, ignorant﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 33:72]. *Al-ẓallām* applies when this is frequent from him. For God, in opposition to each of these names, there is a name. So it is as if He says: If you are a wrongdoer, I am Forgiving (*Ghāfir*); if you are a great wrongdoer, I am Most Forgiving (*Ghafūr*); and if you are an extremely great wrongdoer, I am Oft-Forgiving (*Ghaffār*): ﴿And indeed, I am Forgiving toward one who repents and believes﴾.

**Ninth issue:** The exegetes have differed greatly regarding His words ﴿then remains guided﴾ (thumma ihtadā), and the reason is that one who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds must necessarily be guided. So what is the meaning of His words ﴿then remains guided﴾ after mention of these things? The summarized views concerning it are three:

The first: What is meant by it is persistence upon that path, for one who is guided in the present does not have that sufficient for success in salvation unless he persists upon it in the future and dies upon it. This is confirmed by His words: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is God" and then remain steadfast﴾ [Fuṣṣilat 41:30]. The word *thumma* (then) in this verse denotes sequence in time, not a difference in rank, rather a difference in time. So it is as if He said: Bringing repentance, faith, and righteous deeds is something that may happen to anyone, and there is no difficulty in it; the difficulty lies only in persevering in it and continuing upon it.

[p. 85]

The second: What is meant by His words ﴿then remains guided﴾ is that he knows that this is by God's guidance and His enabling, and he remains seeking help from God in continuing it without shortcoming. This is from Ibn 'Abbās.

The third: What is meant by faith is belief founded upon proof, and the righteous deed is an allusion to the deeds of the limbs. After that remains what relates to purifying the heart from blameworthy character traits, which is called *al-ṭarīqah* (the path) in the language of the Ṣūfiyyah (Sufis), and then the unveiling of the realities of things to him, which is called *al-ḥaqīqah* (the reality) in the language of the Ṣūfiyyah. These two levels are what is meant by His words ﴿then remains guided﴾.

**Tenth issue:** Some said: Repentance from disbelief is obligatory first, then bringing faith second, and they argued for this from this verse, for God put repentance before faith. Our companions argued from this verse that righteous deed is not included in faith, because God conjoined the righteous deed to faith with *'aṭf* (conjunction), and the conjoined thing is different from the thing it is conjoined to.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verses 83–84:**

God Most High says: ﴿And what hastened you away from your people, O Musa?﴾ ﴿He said: "They are right behind me on my track, and I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased."﴾

Know that in His words, ﴿And what hastened you away from your people, O Musa?﴾, there is an indication that he had gone ahead of his people on the journey to the place. The intended meaning must be what He pointed out in His words, ﴿And We appointed for you the right side of the Mount﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:80] in this surah, and in other surahs, such as His words, ﴿And We appointed Musa for thirty nights﴾ [al-A'raf 7:142]. He means the appointed meeting (mīqāt) at the Mount. There are several questions regarding the verse.

The first question: His words, ﴿And what hastened you﴾, are an interrogative, and that is impossible for God. The answer: It is a denial in the form of a question, and there is no impossibility in this.

The second question: Musa, peace be upon him, is either said to have been forbidden from that advancing or not forbidden from it. If he was forbidden, then that advancing would be a disobedience, and it would follow that prophets commit disobedience. If we say he was not forbidden, then that denial would not be permissible from God Most High. The answer: Perhaps he, peace be upon him, had not found a text regarding that, and he advanced by his own ijtihad (independent judgment), but he erred in that ijtihad, and so he deserved reproach.

The third question: He said, ﴿and I hastened﴾, and hastening is blameworthy. The answer: It is praiseworthy in religion. God Most High said: ﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:133].

The fourth question: His words, ﴿that You may be pleased﴾, indicate that he, peace be upon him, did that only to obtain God's pleasure, and this is false for two reasons:

The first: it would entail that an attribute of God Most High is renewed. The second: that before that pleasure was attained, it would have to be said that God Most High was not pleased with Musa, because obtaining what is already obtained is impossible. And since He was not pleased with him, it would have to be that He was displeased with him, and that is not fitting for the condition of the prophets, peace be upon them. The answer: What is meant is obtaining the continuation of pleasure, just as His words, ﴿then he was guided﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:82], mean the continuation of guidance.

The fifth question: His words, ﴿And I hastened to You﴾, indicate that he went to the appointment before the time that God Most High had specified for him; otherwise, it would not be hastening. Then he thought that opposing God Most High's command was a cause of obtaining His pleasure, and that is not fitting even for the most ignorant of people, let alone the one whom God Most High addressed directly. The answer: As we mentioned, that was by ijtihad, and he erred in it.

The sixth question: His words, ﴿to You﴾, require that God be in a direction, because "ilā" (to) denotes the endpoint of a goal. The answer: We agree that God Most High was not on the mountain, so what is meant is "to the place of Your promise."

The seventh question: ﴿And what hastened you﴾ is a question about the cause of the hastening, so its fitting answer would have been for him to say: "I sought more of Your pleasure and yearned for Your speech." As for his words, ﴿They are right behind me on my track﴾, they do not match this, as you see. The answer has two aspects:

The first: God's question includes two things:

One of them: the denial of the hastening itself.

The second: a question about the cause of the advancing. So the more important of the two matters for Musa, peace be upon him, was this second, and he answered it first, saying: "Only a slight advance has occurred from me, and between me and those I preceded there is only a slight advance, of the kind by which a delegation goes ahead of its people." Then he followed it with the answer to the question about the hastening, saying: ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased.﴾

The second: when the awe of God Most High's rebuke came upon him, peace be upon him, he was distracted from the precise answer that fits the terms of the question. Know that in His words, ﴿And what hastened you away from your people, O Musa?﴾, there is an indication that God Most High commanded him to attend the appointed time together with specific people. They differed about who is meant by "the people." Some said: They are the seventy chiefs (nuqaba') whom God Most High had chosen to go out with him to the Mount, and Musa, peace be upon him, went ahead of them out of longing for his Lord. Others said: The people are all of the Children of Israel, and they are those whom Musa had left behind with Harun, and he had commanded him to appoint a successor among them until he himself returned with the seventy. So he said: ﴿They are right behind me on my track﴾, meaning: close to me, awaiting me. It is reported from Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub that "ithri" (with a kasra) is read, and from 'Isa ibn 'Umar that "uthri" (with a damma) is read, and also from him "ula" (with a short vowel, without the madd). And "al-athar" is more eloquent than "al-uthr." As for "al-uthr," it is attested in the phrase *firind al-sayf* (the watered pattern on a sword blade), and it is rare with the meaning of "athar."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verse 85–89 (part 1 of 2):

The words of the Exalted: ﴿He said, "Indeed, We have tried your people after you, and the Samiri has led them astray."﴾ ﴿So Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved. He said, "O my people, did your Lord not make you a good promise? Did the time seem long to you, or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you, so that you broke your promise to me?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We did not break our promise to you by our own will; but we were made to carry burdens of the ornaments of the people, so we threw them, and thus the Samiri cast."﴾ ﴿Then he brought forth for them a calf, a body with a lowing sound, and they said, "This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot."﴾ ﴿Do they not see that it returns no word to them and possesses for them neither harm nor benefit?﴾.

Know that when the Exalted said to Musa, ﴿And what hastened you away from your people?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 83], and Musa replied, ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased﴾ [Ta-Ha: 84], Allah informed him of what had happened among the people after he had left them, of what it would have been unlikely to happen had he been with them. He said: ﴿Indeed, We have tried your people after you, and the Samiri has led them astray.﴾ Here there are several issues:

The first issue: The Mu'tazilah said: it is not permissible that what is meant is that Allah created disbelief in them, for two reasons:

The first reason: the rational proofs indicating that it is not permissible for Allah to do that.

The second: He said, ﴿and the Samiri has led them astray.﴾ If Allah had created misguidance in them, the act of the Samiri would have had no effect in it, and His saying ﴿and the Samiri has led them astray﴾ would be void. Also, when Musa, peace be upon him, demanded from them the cause of that trial, he said: ﴿Did the time seem long to you, or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾ If that had occurred by the creation of Allah, the Exalted, they would have been able to say: the cause of it is that Allah created it in us, not what you mention, and the division made by Musa, peace be upon him, would be void. Also, He said: ﴿or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾ If that were by His creation, it would be impossible for Him to be angry with them for what He Himself created. Since that is void, it is necessary that His saying ﴿We have tried﴾ have another meaning; for fitnah may mean testing. It is said: "I tested the gold with fire" when one examines it with fire so that the good is distinguished from the bad. Here, Allah intensified the obligation upon them, because when the Samiri brought forth that calf for them, they became obligated to reason from the origination of the whole world and of bodies that it has a god who is not a body, and then they would know that the calf is not fit for divinity. So this worship was an intensification in obligation, and thus it was a trial. The intensification of obligation exists, as the Exalted said: ﴿Do people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2]. This is the end of the words of the Mu'tazilah. The Companions (al-Ash'ariyyah) said: there is no greater doubt in the sound coming from a calf made of gold than what is in the sun and the moon; the proof that negates the sun and the moon being a god is more fitting to negate that calf being a god. Then the origination of that calf is not an intensification of obligation, so it is not correct to interpret the verse as referring to it, and so it is necessary to interpret it as the creation of misguidance in them. As for their saying that misguidance was attributed to the Samiri, we say: is it not that all customary effects are attributed to their causes outwardly, even though the one who brings them into existence is Allah, the Exalted? So it is likewise here. Also, it has been read ﴿wa-aḍallahumu al-Sāmiriyyu﴾, meaning "and the most misguided of them was the Samiri," and on this reading there remains no argument for the Mu'tazilah. Then what cuts off the root of contention is holding to the distinction of the motive, as has been established in this book many times.

The second issue: The people here refers to those whom he had left with Harun, peace be upon him, on the shore of the sea, and they were six hundred thousand, of whom all were seduced by the calf except twelve thousand.

The third issue: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said in the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr: the Samiri was a non-Arab man from the people of Kirman who came to Egypt, and he was from a people who worshipped cows. What the majority hold is that he was from the great men of the Children of Israel, from a tribe called the Samirah. Al-Zajjaj said: 'Ata' related from Ibn 'Abbas: rather, he was a man from the Copts, a neighbor of Musa, peace be upon him, who had believed in him.

Page 88

The fourth issue: It is related in the story that they remained twenty nights after his departure and counted them as forty with their days, and said: "We have completed the period." Then the matter of the calf came after that. The reconciliation between this and his saying to Musa upon his arrival: ﴿Indeed, We have tried your people after you﴾ is in two ways:

The first: that He, the Exalted, informed of the anticipated trial using the wording of what exists and has occurred, according to His custom.

The second: that the Samiri began to plan the matter when Musa, peace be upon him, was absent, and he resolved to mislead them at the time of Musa's departure, peace be upon him, and it is as if he had decreed the trial to be existing.

The fifth issue: Musa, peace be upon him, returned only after completing the forty, namely the rest of Dhu al-Qa'dah and the ten of Dhu al-Hijjah.

* * *

The sixth issue: They mentioned several meanings for asaf (grief):

One of them: that it is the intensity of anger. On this interpretation, there is no repetition, since his saying "angry" (ghadban) indicates the basic anger, and his saying "asaf" indicates its completeness.

The second: most of them said sorrow and distress. It is said: "asifa ya'safu asafan" when he grieved, so he is "asif."

The third: some said that the asif is one who is enraged. They distinguished between rage (ightiyaz) and anger (ghadab) by saying that Allah, the Exalted, is not described as having ghayz (fury), but is described as having ghadab, since ghadab is the intention to harm the one who is angered, whereas ghayz is a change that befalls the one who is enraged, and that is not valid except of bodies, like laughing and weeping. Then, the Exalted related about Musa, peace be upon him, that he rebuked them after his return to them. The Mu'tazilah said: this indicates that what is meant by His saying ﴿Indeed, We have tried your people after you﴾ is not that He, the Exalted, created disbelief in them; otherwise He would not have rebuked them, rather Allah, the Exalted, should be rebuked. The Companions said: He has done that by His saying ﴿It is nothing but Your trial﴾ [al-A'raf: 155]. The totality of those rebukes consists of several matters:

One of them: His saying ﴿O my people, did your Lord not make you a good promise?﴾ and in this there are two questions:

The first question: His saying ﴿did your Lord not make you a promise?﴾ This statement would apply to them only if they had acknowledged another god besides the calf. But since they believed there was no god other than it, as Allah informed about them that they said, "This is your god and the god of Musa," how can this statement apply to them? The answer: they did acknowledge God, but they worshipped the calf according to the interpretation mentioned by the worshippers of idols.

The second question: What is meant by that good promise? The answer: they mentioned several meanings:

One of them: that what is meant is what He had promised them of sending down the Torah upon them, so that they might learn the laws and rulings, and that through it they would gain distinction among people; and this is what Allah mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And We promised you the right side of the Mount﴾.

The second: that the good promise is the true promise of reward for acts of obedience.

The third: the promise is the covenant, and this is the saying of Mujahid, and that covenant is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not transgress therein, lest My wrath descend upon you﴾ up to His saying ﴿then he was guided﴾. The evidence for this is His saying after that: ﴿Did the time seem long to you, or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾ So it is as if He said: "Have you forgotten that which Allah told you: ﴿And do not transgress therein﴾?"

The fourth: the good promise here may be a good promise in the benefits of religion and it may be in the benefits of this world. As for the benefits of religion, it is the promise of sending down the noble Book guiding to the laws and rulings, and the promise of attaining great reward in the Hereafter. As for the benefits of this world, it is that before the destruction of Pharaoh He had promised them their land and their homes, and He had indeed done that. The second: It is narrated that they knew the appointed term was forty nights, so they made each day correspond to a night and reduced it to twenty. The judge (al-Qadi) said: this is weak, because that could hardly be confused by anyone.

The second: what they promised him of remaining upon his religion until he returned to them from the Mount. At this, they said: ﴿We did not break our promise to you by our own will﴾. Regarding who the speaker of this answer is, there are two views:

The first: that they are those who did not worship the calf; so it is as if they said: "We did not break your promise by our own will," that is, by a matter we controlled. The second view: that this is the saying of the worshippers of the calf, and what is meant is that others cast doubt into our hearts, and the one who causes the cause is the doer of the effect, and the one who broke the promise is the one who cast the doubt, for he was like the owner over us. If it is said: how is it conceivable that about six hundred thousand rational, accountable people turned away from the true religion all at once to worship the calf, whose corruption is known by necessity; and then, when such a multitude had left the religion and manifested disbelief, how is it conceivable that they all returned from that religion at once merely because Musa, peace be upon him, returned alone to them? We say: this is not impossible regarding the simple-minded among people.

Whoever reads with lightening, its meaning is: "we carried with ourselves what we had borrowed from the people." As for whoever reads with intensification, there are several views:

One of them: that Musa, peace be upon him, made them carry it, that is, he commanded them to borrow the ornaments and to go out with them, so it is as if he obligated them to that.

The second: that he made us like a guarantor for them, until we return them to where Allah commands us.

Third: that God imposed that upon them in the sense that He obligated them to the ruling regarding spoils (maghnam). As for the awzar, they are burdens (al-athqal), and from this the sin was called wizr, because it is a weight. Then there are possibilities regarding it:

The first: because of their abundance, they were burdens.

The second: the spoils were forbidden to them, so it was obligatory upon them to guard them without benefit, so they were burdens.

The third: the intended meaning of the awzar is the sins, and the meaning is "We bore sins." It is related in a report that Harun (peace be upon him) said: "Indeed, it is impure, so purify yourselves from it." And al-Samiri said: "Indeed Musa (peace be upon him) was only detained as a punishment for the ornaments," so it is possible that they meant this statement. A person may say about a thing that he is obligated to return: "All of this is sin and wrongdoing."

Fourth: that ornament was something the Copts would adorn themselves with in their gatherings in which disbelief takes place. Undoubtedly they were described as being "burdens," just as the same is said about the instruments of sins.

As for His saying: ﴿So we threw it⦄, they mentioned regarding it several opinions concerning where they threw it:

The first opinion: they threw it into a pit in which Harun (peace be upon him) had commanded them to gather the ornaments, awaiting the return of Musa (peace be upon him).

The second opinion: they threw it in a place where al-Samiri had commanded them to do so.

The third opinion: in a place where fire was gathered, then they said: "Thus al-Samiri threw," meaning al-Samiri did the same as what we did.

As for His saying: ﴿Then he brought out for them a calf, a body that had a lowing⦄, they differed as to whether that body was alive or not.

The first view: No, because it is not permissible for a manifestation of a breach of custom (kharq al-'adah) to occur at the hand of one who is astray. Rather, al-Samiri fashioned a form in the shape of a calf and placed in it openings and holes such that the winds would enter it, and a sound would come out resembling the sound of a calf.

The second view: that it became alive and lowed as a calf lows, and they argued for it with several points:

The first: His saying: ﴿So I grasped a handful from the footprint of the Messenger⦄ [Ta-Ha: 96]. Had it not become alive, this statement would have no benefit.

The second: that He, Exalted, named it "calf," and "calf" is literally applied to a living animal, and He named it "body," and that term applies only to what is alive.

The third: He attributed lowing to it. They answered the argument of the first group by saying that the appearance of breaches of custom at the hand of one who claims divinity is permissible, because confusion does not arise; and here it is likewise, so it should not be impossible. 'Ikrimah related from Ibn 'Abbas that Harun (peace be upon him) passed by al-Samiri while he was making the calf, and said: "What are you making?" He said: "I make what benefits and does not harm; so pray for me." He said: "O Allah, give him what he asks." When Harun had gone, al-Samiri said: "O Allah, I ask You that it low," and it lowed. On this reading, that would be a miracle for the Prophet.

As for His saying: ﴿So they said: This is your god and the god of Musa⦄ [Ta-Ha: 88], there is a difficulty in it, namely: if the people were in such ignorance that they believed that this calf, made at that very hour, was the Creator of the heavens and the earth, then they were madmen and not accountable; and such madness over such a great gathering is impossible. And if they did not believe that, then how did they say: "This is your god and the god of Musa"? The answer: perhaps they were among the Hululis, so they permitted the indwelling of God, or the indwelling of one of His attributes, in that body. Though this too is most remote, because the appearance of lowing is not suitable to divinity. But perhaps the people were in extreme dullness and coarseness.

As for His saying: ﴿But he forgot⦄, there are several views:

The first: it is the speech of God, Exalted, as if He informed about al-Samiri that he forgot the reasoning proving the createdness of bodies, and that God does not dwell in anything, nor does anything dwell in Him. Then He, Glorified, explained the meaning by which one must reason, which is His saying: ﴿Do they not see that it does not return to them speech, nor does it possess for them any harm or benefit?⦄ That is, it did not occur to them that whoever does not speak, does not harm, and does not benefit, cannot be a god, and that there is no connection of the god to it in terms of being a dwelling-place or a place of dwelling.

The second view: that this is the statement of al-Samiri, who described Musa (peace be upon him) with it. The meaning is: "This is your god and the god of Musa," but Musa forgot that this was the god, so he went to seek Him in another place. This is the view of the majority.

The third view: "he forgot" refers to the time of the appointment for return. As for His saying: ﴿that it does not return to them speech, nor does it possess for them any harm or benefit⦄, this is an argument for its not being a god, since it does not speak, nor benefit, nor harm. This indicates that the god must necessarily be described by these attributes, just as His saying, exalted, in the story of Ibrahim (peace be upon him): ﴿Why do you worship what neither hears nor sees, and avails you nothing?⦄ [Maryam: 42]. And Musa (peace be upon him), for the most part, relied only on the proofs of Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

Two discussions remain here:

The first discussion: al-Zajjaj said: the preferred reading is "that it does not return" with raf', meaning "it does not return," like His saying: (And they thought there would be no trial, so they became blind and deaf) [al-Ma'idah: 71], meaning "there is not." It was also read with nasb, on the basis that this "an" is the one that governs the verbs.

The second discussion: this verse indicates the obligation of reflection in knowing God, Exalted. In another verse He said: ﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them nor guide them to a way?⦄ [al-A'raf: 148], which is close in meaning to His saying in condemning idol-worshippers: ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk?⦄ [al-A'raf: 195]. The purpose of this is not that if the calf spoke to them it would be a god, because a thing may be conditioned on many conditions, so the absence of one of them entails the absence of the conditioned thing, but the presence of one of them does not entail the presence of the conditioned thing.

Third: Some Jews said to 'Ali (peace be upon him): "Did you not bury your Prophet until you disagreed?" He said: "We differed only about his successor, and we did not differ about him. As for you, your feet had not dried from the water of the sea until you said to your Prophet: 'Make for us a god as they have gods.'"

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verse 85–89 (part 1 of 2):

The words of the Exalted: ﴿He said, "Indeed, We have tried your people after you, and the Samiri has led them astray."﴾ ﴿So Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved. He said, "O my people, did your Lord not make you a good promise? Did the time seem long to you, or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you, so that you broke your promise to me?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We did not break our promise to you by our own will; but we were made to carry burdens of the ornaments of the people, so we threw them, and thus the Samiri cast."﴾ ﴿Then he brought forth for them a calf, a body with a lowing sound, and they said, "This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot."﴾ ﴿Do they not see that it returns no word to them and possesses for them neither harm nor benefit?﴾.

Know that when the Exalted said to Musa, ﴿And what hastened you away from your people?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 83], and Musa replied, ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased﴾ [Ta-Ha: 84], Allah informed him of what had happened among the people after he had left them, of what it would have been unlikely to happen had he been with them. He said: ﴿Indeed, We have tried your people after you, and the Samiri has led them astray.﴾ Here there are several issues:

The first issue: The Mu'tazilah said: it is not permissible that what is meant is that Allah created disbelief in them, for two reasons:

The first reason: the rational proofs indicating that it is not permissible for Allah to do that.

The second: He said, ﴿and the Samiri has led them astray.﴾ If Allah had created misguidance in them, the act of the Samiri would have had no effect in it, and His saying ﴿and the Samiri has led them astray﴾ would be void. Also, when Musa, peace be upon him, demanded from them the cause of that trial, he said: ﴿Did the time seem long to you, or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾ If that had occurred by the creation of Allah, the Exalted, they would have been able to say: the cause of it is that Allah created it in us, not what you mention, and the division made by Musa, peace be upon him, would be void. Also, He said: ﴿or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾ If that were by His creation, it would be impossible for Him to be angry with them for what He Himself created. Since that is void, it is necessary that His saying ﴿We have tried﴾ have another meaning; for fitnah may mean testing. It is said: "I tested the gold with fire" when one examines it with fire so that the good is distinguished from the bad. Here, Allah intensified the obligation upon them, because when the Samiri brought forth that calf for them, they became obligated to reason from the origination of the whole world and of bodies that it has a god who is not a body, and then they would know that the calf is not fit for divinity. So this worship was an intensification in obligation, and thus it was a trial. The intensification of obligation exists, as the Exalted said: ﴿Do people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2]. This is the end of the words of the Mu'tazilah. The Companions (al-Ash'ariyyah) said: there is no greater doubt in the sound coming from a calf made of gold than what is in the sun and the moon; the proof that negates the sun and the moon being a god is more fitting to negate that calf being a god. Then the origination of that calf is not an intensification of obligation, so it is not correct to interpret the verse as referring to it, and so it is necessary to interpret it as the creation of misguidance in them. As for their saying that misguidance was attributed to the Samiri, we say: is it not that all customary effects are attributed to their causes outwardly, even though the one who brings them into existence is Allah, the Exalted? So it is likewise here. Also, it has been read ﴿wa-aḍallahumu al-Sāmiriyyu﴾, meaning "and the most misguided of them was the Samiri," and on this reading there remains no argument for the Mu'tazilah. Then what cuts off the root of contention is holding to the distinction of the motive, as has been established in this book many times.

The second issue: The people here refers to those whom he had left with Harun, peace be upon him, on the shore of the sea, and they were six hundred thousand, of whom all were seduced by the calf except twelve thousand.

The third issue: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said in the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr: the Samiri was a non-Arab man from the people of Kirman who came to Egypt, and he was from a people who worshipped cows. What the majority hold is that he was from the great men of the Children of Israel, from a tribe called the Samirah. Al-Zajjaj said: 'Ata' related from Ibn 'Abbas: rather, he was a man from the Copts, a neighbor of Musa, peace be upon him, who had believed in him.

The fourth issue: It is related in the story that they remained twenty nights after his departure and counted them as forty with their days, and said: "We have completed the period." The sixth issue: They mentioned several meanings for asaf (grief):

One of them: that it is the intensity of anger. On this interpretation, there is no repetition, since his saying "angry" (ghadban) indicates the basic anger, and his saying "asaf" indicates its completeness.

The second: most of them said sorrow and distress. It is said: "asifa ya'safu asafan" when he grieved, so he is "asif."

The third: some said that the asif is one who is enraged. They distinguished between rage (ightiyaz) and anger (ghadab) by saying that Allah, the Exalted, is not described as having ghayz (fury), but is described as having ghadab, since ghadab is the intention to harm the one who is angered, whereas ghayz is a change that befalls the one who is enraged, and that is not valid except of bodies, like laughing and weeping. Then, the Exalted related about Musa, peace be upon him, that he rebuked them after his return to them. The Mu'tazilah said: this indicates that what is meant by His saying ﴿Indeed, We have tried your people after you﴾ is not that He, the Exalted, created disbelief in them; otherwise He would not have rebuked them, rather Allah, the Exalted, should be rebuked. The Companions said: He has done that by His saying ﴿It is nothing but Your trial﴾ [al-A'raf: 155]. The totality of those rebukes consists of several matters:

Two discussions remain here:

It was also read with nasb, on the basis that this "an" is the one that governs the verbs.

The purpose of this is not that if the calf spoke to them it would be a god, because a thing may be conditioned on many conditions, so the absence of one of them entails the absence of the conditioned thing, but the presence of one of them does not entail the presence of the conditioned thing.

Third: Some Jews said to 'Ali (peace be upon him): "Did you not bury your Prophet until you disagreed?" He said: "We differed only about his successor, and we did not differ about him. As for you, your feet had not dried from the water of the sea until you said to your Prophet: 'Make for us a god as they have gods.'"

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verse 85–89 (part 1 of 2):

The words of the Exalted: ﴿He said, "Indeed, We have tried your people after you, and the Samiri has led them astray."﴾ ﴿So Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved. He said, "O my people, did your Lord not make you a good promise? Did the time seem long to you, or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you, so that you broke your promise to me?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We did not break our promise to you by our own will; but we were made to carry burdens of the ornaments of the people, so we threw them, and thus the Samiri cast."﴾ ﴿Then he brought forth for them a calf, a body with a lowing sound, and they said, "This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot."﴾ ﴿Do they not see that it returns no word to them and possesses for them neither harm nor benefit?﴾.

Know that when the Exalted said to Musa, ﴿And what hastened you away from your people?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 83], and Musa replied, ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased﴾ [Ta-Ha: 84], Allah informed him of what had happened among the people after he had left them, of what it would have been unlikely to happen had he been with them. He said: ﴿Indeed, We have tried your people after you, and the Samiri has led them astray.﴾ Here there are several issues:

The first issue: The Mu'tazilah said: it is not permissible that what is meant is that Allah created disbelief in them, for two reasons:

The first reason: the rational proofs indicating that it is not permissible for Allah to do that.

The second: He said, ﴿and the Samiri has led them astray.﴾ If Allah had created misguidance in them, the act of the Samiri would have had no effect in it, and His saying ﴿and the Samiri has led them astray﴾ would be void. Also, when Musa, peace be upon him, demanded from them the cause of that trial, he said: ﴿Did the time seem long to you, or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾ If that had occurred by the creation of Allah, the Exalted, they would have been able to say: the cause of it is that Allah created it in us, not what you mention, and the division made by Musa, peace be upon him, would be void. Also, He said: ﴿or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾ If that were by His creation, it would be impossible for Him to be angry with them for what He Himself created. Since that is void, it is necessary that His saying ﴿We have tried﴾ have another meaning; for fitnah may mean testing. It is said: "I tested the gold with fire" when one examines it with fire so that the good is distinguished from the bad. Here, Allah intensified the obligation upon them, because when the Samiri brought forth that calf for them, they became obligated to reason from the origination of the whole world and of bodies that it has a god who is not a body, and then they would know that the calf is not fit for divinity. So this worship was an intensification in obligation, and thus it was a trial. The intensification of obligation exists, as the Exalted said: ﴿Do people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2]. This is the end of the words of the Mu'tazilah. The Companions (al-Ash'ariyyah) said: there is no greater doubt in the sound coming from a calf made of gold than what is in the sun and the moon; the proof that negates the sun and the moon being a god is more fitting to negate that calf being a god. Then the origination of that calf is not an intensification of obligation, so it is not correct to interpret the verse as referring to it, and so it is necessary to interpret it as the creation of misguidance in them. As for their saying that misguidance was attributed to the Samiri, we say: is it not that all customary effects are attributed to their causes outwardly, even though the one who brings them into existence is Allah, the Exalted? So it is likewise here. Also, it has been read ﴿wa-aḍallahumu al-Sāmiriyyu﴾, meaning "and the most misguided of them was the Samiri," and on this reading there remains no argument for the Mu'tazilah. Then what cuts off the root of contention is holding to the distinction of the motive, as has been established in this book many times.

The second issue: The people here refers to those whom he had left with Harun, peace be upon him, on the shore of the sea, and they were six hundred thousand, of whom all were seduced by the calf except twelve thousand.

The third issue: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said in the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr: the Samiri was a non-Arab man from the people of Kirman who came to Egypt, and he was from a people who worshipped cows. What the majority hold is that he was from the great men of the Children of Israel, from a tribe called the Samirah. Al-Zajjaj said: 'Ata' related from Ibn 'Abbas: rather, he was a man from the Copts, a neighbor of Musa, peace be upon him, who had believed in him.

The fourth issue: It is related in the story that they remained twenty nights after his departure and counted them as forty with their days, and said: "We have completed the period." Then the matter of the calf came after that. The reconciliation between this and his saying to Musa upon his arrival: ﴿Indeed, We have tried your people after you﴾ is in two ways:

The first: that He, the Exalted, informed of the anticipated trial using the wording of what exists and has occurred, according to His custom.

The second: that the Samiri began to plan the matter when Musa, peace be upon him, was absent, and he resolved to mislead them at the time of Musa's departure, peace be upon him, and it is as if he had decreed the trial to be existing.

* * *

The sixth issue: They mentioned several meanings for asaf (grief):

One of them: that it is the intensity of anger. On this interpretation, there is no repetition, since his saying "angry" (ghadban) indicates the basic anger, and his saying "asaf" indicates its completeness.

The second: most of them said sorrow and distress. It is said: "asifa ya'safu asafan" when he grieved, so he is "asif."

The third: some said that the asif is one who is enraged. They distinguished between rage (ightiyaz) and anger (ghadab) by saying that Allah, the Exalted, is not described as having ghayz (fury), but is described as having ghadab, since ghadab is the intention to harm the one who is angered, whereas ghayz is a change that befalls the one who is enraged, and that is not valid except of bodies, like laughing and weeping. Then, the Exalted related about Musa, peace be upon him, that he rebuked them after his return to them. The Mu'tazilah said: this indicates that what is meant by His saying ﴿Indeed, We have tried your people after you﴾ is not that He, the Exalted, created disbelief in them; otherwise He would not have rebuked them, rather Allah, the Exalted, should be rebuked. The Companions said: He has done that by His saying ﴿It is nothing but Your trial﴾ [al-A'raf: 155]. The totality of those rebukes consists of several matters:

One of them: His saying ﴿O my people, did your Lord not make you a good promise?﴾ and in this there are two questions:

The first question: His saying ﴿did your Lord not make you a promise?﴾ This statement would apply to them only if they had acknowledged another god besides the calf. But since they believed there was no god other than it, as Allah informed about them that they said, "This is your god and the god of Musa," how can this statement apply to them? The answer: they did acknowledge God, but they worshipped the calf according to the interpretation mentioned by the worshippers of idols.

The second question: What is meant by that good promise? The answer: they mentioned several meanings:

One of them: that what is meant is what He had promised them of sending down the Torah upon them, so that they might learn the laws and rulings, and that through it they would gain distinction among people; and this is what Allah mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And We promised you the right side of the Mount﴾.

The second: that the good promise is the true promise of reward for acts of obedience.

The third: the promise is the covenant, and this is the saying of Mujahid, and that covenant is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not transgress therein, lest My wrath descend upon you﴾ up to His saying ﴿then he was guided﴾. The evidence for this is His saying after that: ﴿Did the time seem long to you, or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾ So it is as if He said: "Have you forgotten that which Allah told you: ﴿And do not transgress therein﴾?"

The fourth: the good promise here may be a good promise in the benefits of religion and it may be in the benefits of this world. As for the benefits of religion, it is the promise of sending down the noble Book guiding to the laws and rulings, and the promise of attaining great reward in the Hereafter. As for the benefits of this world, it is that before the destruction of Pharaoh He had promised them their land and their homes, and He had indeed done that. Then He said: ﴿Did the time seem long to you, or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾ So the meaning is: "Have you forgotten that covenant, or did you deliberately commit disobedience?" Know that the length of the period may bear several meanings:

One of them: "Did the time seem long to you regarding the blessings of Allah, the Exalted, such as His deliverance of you from Pharaoh and other countless blessings mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah?" This is like His saying: ﴿So the term seemed long to them, and their hearts hardened﴾ [al-Hadid: 16].

The second: It is narrated that they knew the appointed term was forty nights, so they made each day correspond to a night and reduced it to twenty. The judge (al-Qadi) said: this is weak, because that could hardly be confused by anyone.

The third: that Musa, peace be upon him, had promised them thirty nights, then Allah, the Exalted, added ten more to them, and that was the lengthening of the period. As for His saying ﴿or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾, this cannot be taken literally, because no one wishes that; but since disobedience necessitates that, and whoever wills a cause wills its effect by implication, the statement is correct. The scholars used this to argue that anger is among the attributes of acts and not among the attributes of essence, because an attribute of the essence of Allah, the Exalted, does not descend upon any of the bodies. As for His saying ﴿so you broke my promise﴾, this indicates a promise that existed from him, peace be upon him, with the people, and in it there are two views:

One of them: that what is meant is what they promised him of joining him and coming after his trail.

The second: what they promised him of remaining upon his religion until he returned to them from the Mount. At this, they said: ﴿We did not break our promise to you by our own will﴾. Regarding who the speaker of this answer is, there are two views:

The first: that they are those who did not worship the calf; so it is as if they said: "We did not break your promise by our own will," that is, by a matter we controlled. A man may attribute the act of his relative to himself, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And when We divided the sea for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 50], ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72], although the doer of that were their fathers and not them. So it is as if they said: the doubt grew strong upon the worshippers of the calf, and we were not able to prevent them from it, nor were we able to separate from them, for we feared that this would become a cause for division and an increase of trial.

The second view: that this is the saying of the worshippers of the calf, and what is meant is that others cast doubt into our hearts, and the one who causes the cause is the doer of the effect, and the one who broke the promise is the one who cast the doubt, for he was like the owner over us. If it is said: how is it conceivable that about six hundred thousand rational, accountable people turned away from the true religion all at once to worship the calf, whose corruption is known by necessity; and then, when such a multitude had left the religion and manifested disbelief, how is it conceivable that they all returned from that religion at once merely because Musa, peace be upon him, returned alone to them? We say: this is not impossible regarding the simple-minded among people.

Know that in "bi-mulkina" there are three readings: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma on the mim; Nafi' and 'Asim with a fatha on the mim; Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Ibn Kathir with a kasra. As for the kasra and the fatha, they are one and the same, and they are two dialects, like ratl and ratl. As for the damma, it means authority (sultan). Then the people explained that vague excuse, saying: ﴿but we were made to carry burdens of the ornaments of the people.﴾ Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr read "hamalna" (lightened), from carrying; and Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Hafs and Ibn 'Amir read "hummilna" (intensified). Whoever reads with lightening, its meaning is: "we carried with ourselves what we had borrowed from the people." As for whoever reads with intensification, there are several views:

One of them: that Musa, peace be upon him, made them carry it, that is, he commanded them to borrow the ornaments and to go out with them, so it is as if he obligated them to that.

The second: that he made us like a guarantor for them, until we return them to where Allah commands us.

Third: that God imposed that upon them in the sense that He obligated them to the ruling regarding spoils (maghnam). As for the awzar, they are burdens (al-athqal), and from this the sin was called wizr, because it is a weight. Then there are possibilities regarding it:

The first: because of their abundance, they were burdens.

The second: the spoils were forbidden to them, so it was obligatory upon them to guard them without benefit, so they were burdens.

The third: the intended meaning of the awzar is the sins, and the meaning is "We bore sins." It is related in a report that Harun (peace be upon him) said: "Indeed, it is impure, so purify yourselves from it." And al-Samiri said: "Indeed Musa (peace be upon him) was only detained as a punishment for the ornaments," so it is possible that they meant this statement. A person may say about a thing that he is obligated to return: "All of this is sin and wrongdoing."

Fourth: that ornament was something the Copts would adorn themselves with in their gatherings in which disbelief takes place. Undoubtedly they were described as being "burdens," just as the same is said about the instruments of sins.

As for His saying: ﴿So we threw it⦄, they mentioned regarding it several opinions concerning where they threw it:

The first opinion: they threw it into a pit in which Harun (peace be upon him) had commanded them to gather the ornaments, awaiting the return of Musa (peace be upon him).

The second opinion: they threw it in a place where al-Samiri had commanded them to do so.

The third opinion: in a place where fire was gathered, then they said: "Thus al-Samiri threw," meaning al-Samiri did the same as what we did.

As for His saying: ﴿Then he brought out for them a calf, a body that had a lowing⦄, they differed as to whether that body was alive or not.

The first view: No, because it is not permissible for a manifestation of a breach of custom (kharq al-'adah) to occur at the hand of one who is astray. Rather, al-Samiri fashioned a form in the shape of a calf and placed in it openings and holes such that the winds would enter it, and a sound would come out resembling the sound of a calf.

The second view: that it became alive and lowed as a calf lows, and they argued for it with several points:

The first: His saying: ﴿So I grasped a handful from the footprint of the Messenger⦄ [Ta-Ha: 96]. Had it not become alive, this statement would have no benefit.

The second: that He, Exalted, named it "calf," and "calf" is literally applied to a living animal, and He named it "body," and that term applies only to what is alive.

The third: He attributed lowing to it. They answered the argument of the first group by saying that the appearance of breaches of custom at the hand of one who claims divinity is permissible, because confusion does not arise; and here it is likewise, so it should not be impossible. 'Ikrimah related from Ibn 'Abbas that Harun (peace be upon him) passed by al-Samiri while he was making the calf, and said: "What are you making?" He said: "I make what benefits and does not harm; so pray for me." He said: "O Allah, give him what he asks." When Harun had gone, al-Samiri said: "O Allah, I ask You that it low," and it lowed. On this reading, that would be a miracle for the Prophet.

As for His saying: ﴿So they said: This is your god and the god of Musa⦄ [Ta-Ha: 88], there is a difficulty in it, namely: if the people were in such ignorance that they believed that this calf, made at that very hour, was the Creator of the heavens and the earth, then they were madmen and not accountable; and such madness over such a great gathering is impossible. And if they did not believe that, then how did they say: "This is your god and the god of Musa"? The answer: perhaps they were among the Hululis, so they permitted the indwelling of God, or the indwelling of one of His attributes, in that body. Though this too is most remote, because the appearance of lowing is not suitable to divinity. But perhaps the people were in extreme dullness and coarseness.

As for His saying: ﴿But he forgot⦄, there are several views:

The first: it is the speech of God, Exalted, as if He informed about al-Samiri that he forgot the reasoning proving the createdness of bodies, and that God does not dwell in anything, nor does anything dwell in Him. Then He, Glorified, explained the meaning by which one must reason, which is His saying: ﴿Do they not see that it does not return to them speech, nor does it possess for them any harm or benefit?⦄ That is, it did not occur to them that whoever does not speak, does not harm, and does not benefit, cannot be a god, and that there is no connection of the god to it in terms of being a dwelling-place or a place of dwelling.

The second view: that this is the statement of al-Samiri, who described Musa (peace be upon him) with it. The meaning is: "This is your god and the god of Musa," but Musa forgot that this was the god, so he went to seek Him in another place. This is the view of the majority.

The second: that the good promise is the true promise of reward for acts of obedience.

The third: the promise is the covenant, and this is the saying of Mujahid, and that covenant is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not transgress therein, lest My wrath descend upon you﴾ up to His saying ﴿then he was guided﴾. The evidence for this is His saying after that: ﴿Did the time seem long to you, or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾ So it is as if He said: "Have you forgotten that which Allah told you: ﴿And do not transgress therein﴾?"

The fourth: the good promise here may be a good promise in the benefits of religion and it may be in the benefits of this world. As for the benefits of religion, it is the promise of sending down the noble Book guiding to the laws and rulings, and the promise of attaining great reward in the Hereafter. As for the benefits of this world, it is that before the destruction of Pharaoh He had promised them their land and their homes, and He had indeed done that. Then He said: ﴿Did the time seem long to you, or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾ So the meaning is: "Have you forgotten that covenant, or did you deliberately commit disobedience?" Know that the length of the period may bear several meanings:

One of them: "Did the time seem long to you regarding the blessings of Allah, the Exalted, such as His deliverance of you from Pharaoh and other countless blessings mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah?" This is like His saying: ﴿So the term seemed long to them, and their hearts hardened﴾ [al-Hadid: 16].

The second: It is narrated that they knew the appointed term was forty nights, so they made each day correspond to a night and reduced it to twenty. The judge (al-Qadi) said: this is weak, because that could hardly be confused by anyone.

The third: that Musa, peace be upon him, had promised them thirty nights, then Allah, the Exalted, added ten more to them, and that was the lengthening of the period. As for His saying ﴿or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾, this cannot be taken literally, because no one wishes that; but since disobedience necessitates that, and whoever wills a cause wills its effect by implication, the statement is correct. The scholars used this to argue that anger is among the attributes of acts and not among the attributes of essence, because an attribute of the essence of Allah, the Exalted, does not descend upon any of the bodies. As for His saying ﴿so you broke my promise﴾, this indicates a promise that existed from him, peace be upon him, with the people, and in it there are two views:

One of them: that what is meant is what they promised him of joining him and coming after his trail.

The second: what they promised him of remaining upon his religion until he returned to them from the Mount. At this, they said: ﴿We did not break our promise to you by our own will﴾. Regarding who the speaker of this answer is, there are two views:

The first: that they are those who did not worship the calf; so it is as if they said: "We did not break your promise by our own will," that is, by a matter we controlled. A man may attribute the act of his relative to himself, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And when We divided the sea for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 50], ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72], although the doer of that were their fathers and not them. So it is as if they said: the doubt grew strong upon the worshippers of the calf, and we were not able to prevent them from it, nor were we able to separate from them, for we feared that this would become a cause for division and an increase of trial.

The second view: that this is the saying of the worshippers of the calf, and what is meant is that others cast doubt into our hearts, and the one who causes the cause is the doer of the effect, and the one who broke the promise is the one who cast the doubt, for he was like the owner over us. If it is said: how is it conceivable that about six hundred thousand rational, accountable people turned away from the true religion all at once to worship the calf, whose corruption is known by necessity; and then, when such a multitude had left the religion and manifested disbelief, how is it conceivable that they all returned from that religion at once merely because Musa, peace be upon him, returned alone to them? We say: this is not impossible regarding the simple-minded among people.

Know that in "bi-mulkina" there are three readings: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma on the mim; Nafi' and 'Asim with a fatha on the mim; Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Ibn Kathir with a kasra. As for the kasra and the fatha, they are one and the same, and they are two dialects, like ratl and ratl. As for the damma, it means authority (sultan). Then the people explained that vague excuse, saying: ﴿but we were made to carry burdens of the ornaments of the people.﴾ Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr read "hamalna" (lightened), from carrying; and Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Hafs and Ibn 'Amir read "hummilna" (intensified). Whoever reads with lightening, its meaning is: "we carried with ourselves what we had borrowed from the people." As for whoever reads with intensification, there are several views:

One of them: that Musa, peace be upon him, made them carry it, that is, he commanded them to borrow the ornaments and to go out with them, so it is as if he obligated them to that.

The second: that he made us like a guarantor for them, until we return them to where Allah commands us.

Third: that God imposed that upon them in the sense that He obligated them to the ruling regarding spoils (maghnam). As for the awzar, they are burdens (al-athqal), and from this the sin was called wizr, because it is a weight. Then there are possibilities regarding it:

The first: because of their abundance, they were burdens.

The second: the spoils were forbidden to them, so it was obligatory upon them to guard them without benefit, so they were burdens.

The third: the intended meaning of the awzar is the sins, and the meaning is "We bore sins." It is related in a report that Harun (peace be upon him) said: "Indeed, it is impure, so purify yourselves from it." And al-Samiri said: "Indeed Musa (peace be upon him) was only detained as a punishment for the ornaments," so it is possible that they meant this statement. A person may say about a thing that he is obligated to return: "All of this is sin and wrongdoing."

Fourth: that ornament was something the Copts would adorn themselves with in their gatherings in which disbelief takes place. Undoubtedly they were described as being "burdens," just as the same is said about the instruments of sins.
