As for His saying: ﴿So we threw it⦄, they mentioned regarding it several opinions concerning where they threw it:

The first opinion: they threw it into a pit in which Harun (peace be upon him) had commanded them to gather the ornaments, awaiting the return of Musa (peace be upon him).

The second opinion: they threw it in a place where al-Samiri had commanded them to do so.

The third opinion: in a place where fire was gathered, then they said: "Thus al-Samiri threw," meaning al-Samiri did the same as what we did.

As for His saying: ﴿Then he brought out for them a calf, a body that had a lowing⦄, they differed as to whether that body was alive or not.

The first view: No, because it is not permissible for a manifestation of a breach of custom (kharq al-'adah) to occur at the hand of one who is astray. Rather, al-Samiri fashioned a form in the shape of a calf and placed in it openings and holes such that the winds would enter it, and a sound would come out resembling the sound of a calf.

The second view: that it became alive and lowed as a calf lows, and they argued for it with several points:

The first: His saying: ﴿So I grasped a handful from the footprint of the Messenger⦄ [Ta-Ha: 96]. Had it not become alive, this statement would have no benefit.

The second: that He, Exalted, named it "calf," and "calf" is literally applied to a living animal, and He named it "body," and that term applies only to what is alive.

The third: He attributed lowing to it. They answered the argument of the first group by saying that the appearance of breaches of custom at the hand of one who claims divinity is permissible, because confusion does not arise; and here it is likewise, so it should not be impossible. 'Ikrimah related from Ibn 'Abbas that Harun (peace be upon him) passed by al-Samiri while he was making the calf, and said: "What are you making?" He said: "I make what benefits and does not harm; so pray for me." He said: "O Allah, give him what he asks." When Harun had gone, al-Samiri said: "O Allah, I ask You that it low," and it lowed. On this reading, that would be a miracle for the Prophet.

As for His saying: ﴿So they said: This is your god and the god of Musa⦄ [Ta-Ha: 88], there is a difficulty in it, namely: if the people were in such ignorance that they believed that this calf, made at that very hour, was the Creator of the heavens and the earth, then they were madmen and not accountable; and such madness over such a great gathering is impossible. And if they did not believe that, then how did they say: "This is your god and the god of Musa"? The answer: perhaps they were among the Hululis, so they permitted the indwelling of God, or the indwelling of one of His attributes, in that body. Though this too is most remote, because the appearance of lowing is not suitable to divinity. But perhaps the people were in extreme dullness and coarseness.

As for His saying: ﴿But he forgot⦄, there are several views:

The first: it is the speech of God, Exalted, as if He informed about al-Samiri that he forgot the reasoning proving the createdness of bodies, and that God does not dwell in anything, nor does anything dwell in Him. Then He, Glorified, explained the meaning by which one must reason, which is His saying: ﴿Do they not see that it does not return to them speech, nor does it possess for them any harm or benefit?⦄ That is, it did not occur to them that whoever does not speak, does not harm, and does not benefit, cannot be a god, and that there is no connection of the god to it in terms of being a dwelling-place or a place of dwelling.

The second view: that this is the statement of al-Samiri, who described Musa (peace be upon him) with it. The meaning is: "This is your god and the god of Musa," but Musa forgot that this was the god, so he went to seek Him in another place. This is the view of the majority.

The third view: "he forgot" refers to the time of the appointment for return. As for His saying: ﴿that it does not return to them speech, nor does it possess for them any harm or benefit⦄, this is an argument for its not being a god, since it does not speak, nor benefit, nor harm. This indicates that the god must necessarily be described by these attributes, just as His saying, exalted, in the story of Ibrahim (peace be upon him): ﴿Why do you worship what neither hears nor sees, and avails you nothing?⦄ [Maryam: 42]. And Musa (peace be upon him), for the most part, relied only on the proofs of Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

Two discussions remain here:

The first discussion: al-Zajjaj said: the preferred reading is "that it does not return" with raf', meaning "it does not return," like His saying: (And they thought there would be no trial, so they became blind and deaf) [al-Ma'idah: 71], meaning "there is not." It was also read with nasb, on the basis that this "an" is the one that governs the verbs.

The second discussion: this verse indicates the obligation of reflection in knowing God, Exalted. In another verse He said: ﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them nor guide them to a way?⦄ [al-A'raf: 148], which is close in meaning to His saying in condemning idol-worshippers: ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk?⦄ [al-A'raf: 195]. The purpose of this is not that if the calf spoke to them it would be a god, because a thing may be conditioned on many conditions, so the absence of one of them entails the absence of the conditioned thing, but the presence of one of them does not entail the presence of the conditioned thing.

Third: Some Jews said to 'Ali (peace be upon him): "Did you not bury your Prophet until you disagreed?" He said: "We differed only about his successor, and we did not differ about him. As for you, your feet had not dried from the water of the sea until you said to your Prophet: 'Make for us a god as they have gods.'"

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verse 85–89 (part 1 of 2):

The words of the Exalted: ﴿He said, "Indeed, We have tried your people after you, and the Samiri has led them astray."﴾ ﴿So Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved. He said, "O my people, did your Lord not make you a good promise? Did the time seem long to you, or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you, so that you broke your promise to me?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We did not break our promise to you by our own will; but we were made to carry burdens of the ornaments of the people, so we threw them, and thus the Samiri cast."﴾ ﴿Then he brought forth for them a calf, a body with a lowing sound, and they said, "This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot."﴾ ﴿Do they not see that it returns no word to them and possesses for them neither harm nor benefit?﴾.

Know that when the Exalted said to Musa, ﴿And what hastened you away from your people?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 83], and Musa replied, ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You might be pleased﴾ [Ta-Ha: 84], Allah informed him of what had happened among the people after he had left them, of what it would have been unlikely to happen had he been with them. He said: ﴿Indeed, We have tried your people after you, and the Samiri has led them astray.﴾ Here there are several issues:

The first issue: The Mu'tazilah said: it is not permissible that what is meant is that Allah created disbelief in them, for two reasons:

The first reason: the rational proofs indicating that it is not permissible for Allah to do that.

The second: He said, ﴿and the Samiri has led them astray.﴾ If Allah had created misguidance in them, the act of the Samiri would have had no effect in it, and His saying ﴿and the Samiri has led them astray﴾ would be void. Also, when Musa, peace be upon him, demanded from them the cause of that trial, he said: ﴿Did the time seem long to you, or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾ If that had occurred by the creation of Allah, the Exalted, they would have been able to say: the cause of it is that Allah created it in us, not what you mention, and the division made by Musa, peace be upon him, would be void. Also, He said: ﴿or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾ If that were by His creation, it would be impossible for Him to be angry with them for what He Himself created. Since that is void, it is necessary that His saying ﴿We have tried﴾ have another meaning; for fitnah may mean testing. It is said: "I tested the gold with fire" when one examines it with fire so that the good is distinguished from the bad. Here, Allah intensified the obligation upon them, because when the Samiri brought forth that calf for them, they became obligated to reason from the origination of the whole world and of bodies that it has a god who is not a body, and then they would know that the calf is not fit for divinity. So this worship was an intensification in obligation, and thus it was a trial. The intensification of obligation exists, as the Exalted said: ﴿Do people think that they will be left to say, "We believe," and they will not be tested?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2]. This is the end of the words of the Mu'tazilah. The Companions (al-Ash'ariyyah) said: there is no greater doubt in the sound coming from a calf made of gold than what is in the sun and the moon; the proof that negates the sun and the moon being a god is more fitting to negate that calf being a god. Then the origination of that calf is not an intensification of obligation, so it is not correct to interpret the verse as referring to it, and so it is necessary to interpret it as the creation of misguidance in them. As for their saying that misguidance was attributed to the Samiri, we say: is it not that all customary effects are attributed to their causes outwardly, even though the one who brings them into existence is Allah, the Exalted? So it is likewise here. Also, it has been read ﴿wa-aḍallahumu al-Sāmiriyyu﴾, meaning "and the most misguided of them was the Samiri," and on this reading there remains no argument for the Mu'tazilah. Then what cuts off the root of contention is holding to the distinction of the motive, as has been established in this book many times.

The second issue: The people here refers to those whom he had left with Harun, peace be upon him, on the shore of the sea, and they were six hundred thousand, of whom all were seduced by the calf except twelve thousand.

The third issue: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said in the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr: the Samiri was a non-Arab man from the people of Kirman who came to Egypt, and he was from a people who worshipped cows. What the majority hold is that he was from the great men of the Children of Israel, from a tribe called the Samirah. Al-Zajjaj said: 'Ata' related from Ibn 'Abbas: rather, he was a man from the Copts, a neighbor of Musa, peace be upon him, who had believed in him.

The fourth issue: It is related in the story that they remained twenty nights after his departure and counted them as forty with their days, and said: "We have completed the period." The sixth issue: They mentioned several meanings for asaf (grief):

The first: it is the speech of God, Exalted, as if He informed about al-Samiri that he forgot the reasoning proving the createdness of bodies, and that God does not dwell in anything, nor does anything dwell in Him. Then He, Glorified, explained the meaning by which one must reason, which is His saying: ﴿Do they not see that it does not return to them speech, nor does it possess for them any harm or benefit?⦄ That is, it did not occur to them that whoever does not speak, does not harm, and does not benefit, cannot be a god, and that there is no connection of the god to it in terms of being a dwelling-place or a place of dwelling.

The second view: that this is the statement of al-Samiri, who described Musa (peace be upon him) with it. The meaning is: "This is your god and the god of Musa," but Musa forgot that this was the god, so he went to seek Him in another place. This is the view of the majority.

The third view: "he forgot" refers to the time of the appointment for return. As for His saying: ﴿that it does not return to them speech, nor does it possess for them any harm or benefit⦄, this is an argument for its not being a god, since it does not speak, nor benefit, nor harm. This indicates that the god must necessarily be described by these attributes, just as His saying, exalted, in the story of Ibrahim (peace be upon him): ﴿Why do you worship what neither hears nor sees, and avails you nothing?⦄ [Maryam: 42]. And Musa (peace be upon him), for the most part, relied only on the proofs of Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

Two discussions remain here:

The first discussion: al-Zajjaj said: the preferred reading is "that it does not return" with raf', meaning "it does not return," like His saying: (And they thought there would be no trial, so they became blind and deaf) [al-Ma'idah: 71], meaning "there is not." It was also read with nasb, on the basis that this "an" is the one that governs the verbs.

The second discussion: this verse indicates the obligation of reflection in knowing God, Exalted. In another verse He said: ﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them nor guide them to a way?⦄ [al-A'raf: 148], which is close in meaning to His saying in condemning idol-worshippers: ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk?⦄ [al-A'raf: 195]. The purpose of this is not that if the calf spoke to them it would be a god, because a thing may be conditioned on many conditions, so the absence of one of them entails the absence of the conditioned thing, but the presence of one of them does not entail the presence of the conditioned thing.

Third: Some Jews said to 'Ali (peace be upon him): "Did you not bury your Prophet until you disagreed?" He said: "We differed only about his successor, and we did not differ about him. As for you, your feet had not dried from the water of the sea until you said to your Prophet: 'Make for us a god as they have gods.'"

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 20, verses 90–91:**

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And Harun had already said to them before: "O my people, you are only being tested by it, and indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command."﴾ ﴿They said: "We will not cease to be devoted to it until Musa returns to us."﴾

Know that Harun, peace be upon him, said this out of compassion, both for himself and for the creation. As for his compassion for himself, it is because he was commanded by God to enjoin good (al-amr bil-ma'ruf) and forbid evil (al-nahy 'an al-munkar), and he was commanded by his brother Musa, peace be upon him, through his words: ﴿Take my place among my people, reform, and do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾ [al-A'raf: 142]. So if he had not occupied himself with enjoining good and forbidding evil, he would have been opposing the command of God the Exalted and the command of Musa, peace be upon him, and that is not permissible.

God the Exalted revealed to Yusha' ibn Nun: "I will destroy forty thousand of your people, from their best, and sixty thousand from their worst." He said: "O Lord, these are the wicked, so what of the good?" He said: "They did not become angry for My anger."

Thabit al-Bunani said: Anas said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wakes up with a concern other than God the Exalted, has nothing to do with God. And whoever wakes up not caring about the Muslims, is not one of them." 

And from al-Sha'bi, from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The likeness of the believers in their mutual affection, their mercy, and their compassion is like the likeness of a body: when one of its limbs complains, the rest of the body responds to it with wakefulness and fever."

Abu 'Ali al-Hasan al-Ghuri said: I was in a certain place and I saw a small boat in which there were jars, with a label written on them "Latif." I said to the boatman: "What is this?" He said: "You are a meddling Sufi! These are the wines of al-Mu'tadid." I said to him: "Give me that mallet." He said to his servant: "Give it to him, so we can see what he does." So I took the mallet and climbed into the boat, and I kept breaking the jars one by one while the boatman shouted, until only one remained. I stopped. Then the owner of the ship came, seized me, and took me to al-Mu'tadid. His sword was already drawn before he spoke. When his gaze fell upon me, he said: "Who are you?" I said: "The muhtasib (market inspector)." He said: "Who appointed you to the hisba (the office of enjoining good and forbidding evil in public)?" I said: "The One who appointed you to the caliphate." He said: "Why did you break these jars?" I said: "Out of concern for you, since my hand could not reach to ward off what is harmful to you." He said: "Then why did you leave this one?" I said: "When I broke these jars, I broke them out of zeal for the religion of God. When I reached this one, I was impressed, so I stopped. Had I remained as I was, I would have broken it too." He said: "Go out, O shaykh, for I have appointed you muhtasib." I said: "I was doing it for God the Exalted, so I do not wish to be a police officer."

As for compassion toward the Muslims, it is because a person ought to be tender-hearted and compassionate toward his fellow human beings. And what greater compassion is there than to see a crowd rushing into the Fire and to prevent them from it?

From Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "God the Exalted says: 'Seek bounty from My merciful servants, and you will live under their protection, for I have placed My mercy in them. Do not seek it from those whose hearts are hard, for in them is My anger.'"

From 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa, who said: "I went out wanting to find the Prophet (ﷺ), and there were Abu Bakr and 'Umar with him. A child came and wept, so he (ﷺ) said to 'Umar: 'Take the child to you, for he is lost.' So 'Umar took him, and there was a woman wailing, uncovering her head in distress over her son. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Catch up with the woman,' and he called to her. She came and took her child, and began to weep while the child was in her lap. Then she turned and saw the Prophet (ﷺ), and became shy. Thereupon he (ﷺ) said: 'Do you see this woman as merciful toward her child?' They said: 'O Messenger of God, this is enough mercy.' He said: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, God is more merciful to the believers than this woman is to her child.'"

It is narrated: "While the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sitting with his companions, he looked at a young man at the door of the mosque and said: 'Whoever wishes to look at a man from the people of the Fire, let him look at this one.' The young man heard that and turned away, saying: 'My God and my Master, this is Your Messenger, testifying against me that I am one of the people of the Fire, and I know that he is truthful. If that is so, I ask You to make me a ransom for the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and to kindle the Fire with me until his oath is fulfilled, and do not kindle the Fire with anyone else.' Then Jibril, peace be upon him, descended and said: 'O Muhammad, give the young man good news that I have saved him from the Fire because of his affirmation of you, and his ransoming of your community with his own self, and his compassion for creation.'"

Having established this, know that enjoining good and compassion toward the Muslims are obligatory. Then Harun, peace be upon him, saw the people rushing into the Fire, and he did not care about their number nor their strength, but rather he declared the truth plainly, saying: ﴿O my people, you are only being tested by it﴾, and so on.

Here there is a subtle point. The Rafidah (a term for a Shi'i group that rejects the first caliphs) cling to his, peace be upon him, saying to 'Ali: "You are to me as Harun was to Musa." Yet Harun was not prevented by taqiyya (precautionary concealment of belief under threat) in such a gathering. Rather, he ascended the pulpit, declared the truth, and called the people to follow himself and forbade them from following others. So if the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) had been in error, it would have been obligatory upon 'Ali, peace be upon him, to do what Harun, peace be upon him, did: to ascend the pulpit without taqiyya or fear, and to say: ﴿Follow me and obey my command﴾. Since he did not do that, we know that the community was upon the correct path.

Know also that Harun, peace be upon him, followed in this admonition the best of methods, for he first restrained them from falsehood by his words: ﴿you are only being tested by it﴾. Then he called them, secondly, to the knowledge of God the Exalted by his words: ﴿and indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful﴾. Then he called them, thirdly, to the knowledge of prophethood by his words: ﴿so follow me﴾. Then he called them, fourthly, to the laws by his words: ﴿and obey my command﴾. This is the excellent order, for before everything there must be the removal of harm from the path, which is the removal of doubts; then the knowledge of God the Exalted is the foundation; then prophethood; then the law. Thus it is established that this order is in the best of forms.

He said: ﴿And indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful﴾, singling out this place with the name al-Rahman, because he was informing them that whenever they repented, God would accept their repentance, for He is the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. And from His mercy is that He delivered them from the calamities of Pharaoh.

Then, out of their ignorance, they met this excellent order of reasoning with blind imitation and denial. So they said: ﴿We will not cease to be devoted to it until Musa returns to us.﴾ It was as if they said: "We will not accept your argument, but we will accept the word of Musa." And the habit of the imitator is nothing other than that.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verses 92–95:

The Almighty said: ﴿Musa said, "O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me? Did you then disobey my command?" He said, "O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard or my head. Indeed I feared that you would say, 'You caused a division among the Children of Israel, and you did not observe my word.'"﴾

Know that those who object to the infallibility ('ismah, the protection of prophets from sin) of the prophets, peace be upon them, cling to this verse in several respects.

The first: Musa, peace be upon him, either commanded Harun to follow him or did not command him. If he commanded him, then either Harun followed him or did not follow him. If Harun followed him, then Musa's reproach of Harun was a sin and a wrongdoing, because reproaching someone who is not guilty is a sin. If Harun did not follow him, then Harun abandoned an obligation and so committed a sin. And if we say that Musa, peace be upon him, did not command him to follow, then his reproach to him for not following would be a sin. Thus it is established that under all possibilities, sin must be attributed either to Musa or to Harun.

The second: Musa's words, peace be upon him, ﴿Did you then disobey my command?﴾ are a rhetorical question expressing denial. It therefore follows that Harun had disobeyed him, and that this disobedience was blameworthy; otherwise Musa, peace be upon him, would have been lying, and that is a sin. So if Harun did this, he committed a sin.

The third: His saying, ﴿O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard or my head.﴾ This is a sin, because Harun, peace be upon him, had done what he was able to do of advice, admonition and rebuke. If Musa, peace be upon him, had investigated the incident, and after learning that Harun had done what he could, then seizing his head and beard would be a sin. And if he did so before learning the true situation, that too would be a sin.

The fourth: Harun, peace be upon him, said, ﴿Do not seize me by my beard or my head.﴾ If seizing his beard and head was permissible, then Harun's saying "do not seize" would be a prohibition against what was permissible for him to do, and that would be a sin. And if such seizing was not permissible, then Musa, peace be upon him, was committing a sin. These are subtle examples in this matter.

The answer to all of these: We have explained in the commentary on surah al-Baqarah, in the exegesis of His saying, ﴿So the Shaytan caused them to slip from it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], several kinds of clear proofs that it is impossible for prophets to commit sin. The essence of these objections is clinging to apparent meanings that are open to interpretation (ta'wil), and setting against them what is far from interpretation, by which an interpretation is not permissible if it is quickly reached. Once this premise is established, know that we have several answers to these objections:

The first: Although we differ over whether sin is permissible for the prophets, we agree that leaving what is preferable (tark al-awla) is permissible for them. If that is so, then the act that one of them did and the other prevented, namely Musa and Harun, peace be upon them, may have been such that one of them was preferable and the other was leaving the preferable. For this reason one did it and the other left it. If it is said that this interpretation is not permissible, because each of them was resolute in what he did, whether doing or abstaining, and doing or abstaining what is recommended is not something one is resolute about, we reply: restricting a general statement by evidence is not impossible. So we take that resoluteness in doing or abstaining to mean: do that, or leave it, if you intend what is most proper. This condition may be omitted when their mutual agreement to observe it is known and settled.

The second: Musa, peace be upon him, came while angry at his people, and he seized his brother's head and pulled him toward himself, just as a person does to himself in a similar way when angry. The angry, reflective man may bite his lips, twist his fingers, and grip his beard. So Musa, peace be upon him, treated his brother Harun as he would treat himself, because he was his brother and partner, and he did with him what a man does with himself in a state of thought and anger. As for his saying, ﴿Do not seize me by my beard or my head,﴾ it is not impossible that Harun, peace be upon him, feared that the Children of Israel, out of their ill opinion, would imagine that he was disapproving of him and not supporting him. Then he began to explain the story, saying, ﴿Indeed I feared that you would say, "You caused a division among the Children of Israel."﴾

The third: The Children of Israel had reached the extreme of ill opinion about Musa, peace be upon him, to the point that when Harun was absent from them for a time, they said to Musa, peace be upon him, "You killed him." When the Almighty appointed for Musa, peace be upon him, thirty nights and completed them with ten, and wrote for him on the tablets concerning everything, then he returned and saw what he saw among his people. He seized his brother's head to bring him near so that he might examine the circumstances of the event. Harun, peace be upon him, feared that something without basis would come to their hearts, so out of concern for Musa he said, "Do not seize me by my beard or my head," lest the people think what is unbecoming of you.

The fourth: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: Musa, peace be upon him, was a man of sharp temper, naturally inclined to vehemence, harshness and firmness in everything, extremely zealous for God, the Exalted, and His religion. When he saw his people worshipping a calf besides God, the Exalted, after they had seen the great signs, he could not restrain himself, and he threw down the tablets of the Torah, because the great astonishment overcame his mind, out of zeal and indignation for God, the Exalted. He reproached his brother and deputy over his people and turned upon him as an enemy who bares his teeth. Know that this answer is weak, because it is said: Suppose he was extremely angry; yet in that intense anger, did he remain rational and responsible or not? If he remained rational and responsible, then the questions remain in full. At most you have said that he came with intense anger, and that is among the sins, so you have added another difficulty. And if you say that in that anger he was neither rational nor responsible, this is something no Muslim would ever accept. These are the answers of those who do not permit minor sins (saghair). As for those who permit them, there is no doubt that the question falls away. And God knows best.

As for His saying, ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me?﴾ there are two views. The first: the word "from" (an) is redundant, and the meaning is "What prevented you from following me?" The second: the meaning is "What led you not to follow me?", so "prevented" (mana'aka) takes the place of "led" (da'aka).

Regarding "following" there are two views. One: "What prevented you from following me, by those who obeyed you, and joining me, and leaving your station among them?" This is the view of Ibn Abbas through the transmission of Ata. The second: "that you should follow me in my instruction, when I said to you: ﴿Take my place among my people, and act rightly, and do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾ [al-A'raf 7:142]. Why did you abandon fighting them and disciplining them?" This is the view of Muqatil.

Then He said: ﴿Did you then disobey my command?﴾ Its meaning is clear. This indicates that one who abandons what he was commanded is disobedient, and the disobedient deserves punishment, due to His saying: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Jinn 72:23], and His saying: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him to a Fire, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:14]. The two verses together indicate that the command is for obligation (wujub).

Harun, peace be upon him, then answered and said: ﴿O son of my mother.﴾ It has been said: he addressed him thus in order to turn him away from himself, so that he would leave him. It has also been said that he was his brother by the same mother. ﴿Do not seize me by my beard or my head.﴾

Know that there is nothing in the Qur'an indicating that he did that, for prohibiting something does not indicate that the one prohibited did what is prohibited, as in His saying: ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:1], and His saying: ﴿If you associate partners with Allah, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar 39:65]. What is stated is that he seized his brother's head, pulling him toward himself, and this alone does not indicate contempt for him. Rather, one may do that for various other purposes, as we have explained. Some people say that he seized his hair-lock (dhu'aba) with his right hand and his beard with his left, then said: ﴿Indeed I feared that you would say, "You caused a division among the Children of Israel, and you did not observe my word."﴾

Someone might say: Musa's words, peace be upon him, "What prevented you from not following me? Did you then disobey my command?" indicate that he had commanded him to do something. How then is it appropriate in reply to say: "I did not comply with your word only out of fear that you would say, 'and you did not observe my word'"? Could such speech be proper for a rational person?

The answer: Perhaps Musa, peace be upon him, commanded him to go to them on the condition that this would not lead to corruption among the people. When Musa said, "What prevented you from not following me?" Harun said: "Because you commanded me to follow you only when corruption did not occur. Had I come to you while corruption had occurred, I would not have been observing your word."

Imam Abu al-Qasim al-Ansari said: Guidance is more beneficial than mere indication (dalala). The sorcerers were outsiders to faith, and they had seen only a single sign, yet they believed, endured the severe punishment in this world, and did not turn back from faith. As for his people, they saw the staff turn into a serpent that swallowed everything the sorcerers had gathered, then return to being a staff. They saw the sorcerers acknowledge that this was not sorcery and that it was a divine matter. They saw the nine signs over a long period, then they saw the sea split into twelve paths, and that God, the Exalted, saved them from drowning and destroyed their enemies despite their great number. Then, although they had witnessed these signs, when they came out of the sea and saw a people worshipping cows, they said: "Make for us a god just as they have gods." And when they heard the lowing of a calf, they devoted themselves to its worship. This shows that the purpose is not achieved by proofs alone, but by guidance.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "Ya ibna umma" with a kasra on the mim and the possessive, and the kasra on the mim indicates the (suppressed) ya (of possession, "my"). The rest read it with a fatha, and its underlying form is "ya ibna umma" (with the final alif of the vowel-lengthening, as in the pause form of "umm-i" becoming "umma-h" ), i.e. the original is "Ya ibna ummah" ("O son of my mother"). And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verses 92–95:

The first: Musa, peace be upon him, either commanded Harun to follow him or did not command him. If he commanded him, then either Harun followed him or did not follow him. If Harun followed him, then Musa's reproach of Harun was a sin and a wrongdoing, because reproaching someone who is not guilty is a sin. If Harun did not follow him, then Harun abandoned an obligation and so committed a sin. And if we say that Musa, peace be upon him, did not command him to follow, then his reproach to him for not following would be a sin. Thus it is established that under all possibilities, sin must be attributed either to Musa or to Harun.

The second: Musa's words, peace be upon him, ﴿Did you then disobey my command?﴾ are a rhetorical question expressing denial. It therefore follows that Harun had disobeyed him, and that this disobedience was blameworthy; otherwise Musa, peace be upon him, would have been lying, and that is a sin. So if Harun did this, he committed a sin.

The third: His saying, ﴿O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard or my head.﴾ This is a sin, because Harun, peace be upon him, had done what he was able to do of advice, admonition and rebuke. If Musa, peace be upon him, had investigated the incident, and after learning that Harun had done what he could, then seizing his head and beard would be a sin. And if he did so before learning the true situation, that too would be a sin.

The fourth: Harun, peace be upon him, said, ﴿Do not seize me by my beard or my head.﴾ If seizing his beard and head was permissible, then Harun's saying "do not seize" would be a prohibition against what was permissible for him to do, and that would be a sin. And if such seizing was not permissible, then Musa, peace be upon him, was committing a sin. These are subtle examples in this matter.

The answer to all of these: We have explained in the commentary on surah al-Baqarah, in the exegesis of His saying, ﴿So the Shaytan caused them to slip from it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:36], several kinds of clear proofs that it is impossible for prophets to commit sin. The essence of these objections is clinging to apparent meanings that are open to interpretation (ta'wil), and setting against them what is far from interpretation, by which an interpretation is not permissible if it is quickly reached. Once this premise is established, know that we have several answers to these objections:

The first: Although we differ over whether sin is permissible for the prophets, we agree that leaving what is preferable (tark al-awla) is permissible for them. If that is so, then the act that one of them did and the other prevented, namely Musa and Harun, peace be upon them, may have been such that one of them was preferable and the other was leaving the preferable. For this reason one did it and the other left it. If it is said that this interpretation is not permissible, because each of them was resolute in what he did, whether doing or abstaining, and doing or abstaining what is recommended is not something one is resolute about, we reply: restricting a general statement by evidence is not impossible. So we take that resoluteness in doing or abstaining to mean: do that, or leave it, if you intend what is most proper. This condition may be omitted when their mutual agreement to observe it is known and settled.

The second: Musa, peace be upon him, came while angry at his people, and he seized his brother's head and pulled him toward himself, just as a person does to himself in a similar way when angry. The angry, reflective man may bite his lips, twist his fingers, and grip his beard. So Musa, peace be upon him, treated his brother Harun as he would treat himself, because he was his brother and partner, and he did with him what a man does with himself in a state of thought and anger. As for his saying, ﴿Do not seize me by my beard or my head,﴾ it is not impossible that Harun, peace be upon him, feared that the Children of Israel, out of their ill opinion, would imagine that he was disapproving of him and not supporting him. Then he began to explain the story, saying, ﴿Indeed I feared that you would say, "You caused a division among the Children of Israel."﴾

The third: The Children of Israel had reached the extreme of ill opinion about Musa, peace be upon him, to the point that when Harun was absent from them for a time, they said to Musa, peace be upon him, "You killed him." When the Almighty appointed for Musa, peace be upon him, thirty nights and completed them with ten, and wrote for him on the tablets concerning everything, then he returned and saw what he saw among his people. He seized his brother's head to bring him near so that he might examine the circumstances of the event. Harun, peace be upon him, feared that something without basis would come to their hearts, so out of concern for Musa he said, "Do not seize me by my beard or my head," lest the people think what is unbecoming of you.

The fourth: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: Musa, peace be upon him, was a man of sharp temper, naturally inclined to vehemence, harshness and firmness in everything, extremely zealous for God, the Exalted, and His religion. When he saw his people worshipping a calf besides God, the Exalted, after they had seen the great signs, he could not restrain himself, and he threw down the tablets of the Torah, because the great astonishment overcame his mind, out of zeal and indignation for God, the Exalted. He reproached his brother and deputy over his people and turned upon him as an enemy who bares his teeth. Know that this answer is weak, because it is said: Suppose he was extremely angry; yet in that intense anger, did he remain rational and responsible or not? If he remained rational and responsible, then the questions remain in full. At most you have said that he came with intense anger, and that is among the sins, so you have added another difficulty. And if you say that in that anger he was neither rational nor responsible, this is something no Muslim would ever accept. These are the answers of those who do not permit minor sins (saghair). As for those who permit them, there is no doubt that the question falls away. And God knows best.

As for His saying, ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me?﴾ there are two views. The first: the word "from" (an) is redundant, and the meaning is "What prevented you from following me?" The second: the meaning is "What led you not to follow me?", so "prevented" (mana'aka) takes the place of "led" (da'aka).

Regarding "following" there are two views. One: "What prevented you from following me, by those who obeyed you, and joining me, and leaving your station among them?" This is the view of Ibn Abbas through the transmission of Ata. The second: "that you should follow me in my instruction, when I said to you: ﴿Take my place among my people, and act rightly, and do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾ [al-A'raf 7:142]. Why did you abandon fighting them and disciplining them?" This is the view of Muqatil.

Then He said: ﴿Did you then disobey my command?﴾ Its meaning is clear. This indicates that one who abandons what he was commanded is disobedient, and the disobedient deserves punishment, due to His saying: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Jinn 72:23], and His saying: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him to a Fire, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:14]. The two verses together indicate that the command is for obligation (wujub).

Harun, peace be upon him, then answered and said: ﴿O son of my mother.﴾ It has been said: he addressed him thus in order to turn him away from himself, so that he would leave him. It has also been said that he was his brother by the same mother. ﴿Do not seize me by my beard or my head.﴾

Know that there is nothing in the Qur'an indicating that he did that, for prohibiting something does not indicate that the one prohibited did what is prohibited, as in His saying: ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:1], and His saying: ﴿If you associate partners with Allah, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar 39:65]. What is stated is that he seized his brother's head, pulling him toward himself, and this alone does not indicate contempt for him. Rather, one may do that for various other purposes, as we have explained. Some people say that he seized his hair-lock (dhu'aba) with his right hand and his beard with his left, then said: ﴿Indeed I feared that you would say, "You caused a division among the Children of Israel, and you did not observe my word."﴾

Someone might say: Musa's words, peace be upon him, "What prevented you from not following me? Did you then disobey my command?" indicate that he had commanded him to do something. How then is it appropriate in reply to say: "I did not comply with your word only out of fear that you would say, 'and you did not observe my word'"? Could such speech be proper for a rational person?

The answer: Perhaps Musa, peace be upon him, commanded him to go to them on the condition that this would not lead to corruption among the people. When Musa said, "What prevented you from not following me?" Harun said: "Because you commanded me to follow you only when corruption did not occur. Had I come to you while corruption had occurred, I would not have been observing your word."

Imam Abu al-Qasim al-Ansari said: Guidance is more beneficial than mere indication (dalala). The sorcerers were outsiders to faith, and they had seen only a single sign, yet they believed, endured the severe punishment in this world, and did not turn back from faith. As for his people, they saw the staff turn into a serpent that swallowed everything the sorcerers had gathered, then return to being a staff. They saw the sorcerers acknowledge that this was not sorcery and that it was a divine matter. They saw the nine signs over a long period, then they saw the sea split into twelve paths, and that God, the Exalted, saved them from drowning and destroyed their enemies despite their great number. Then, although they had witnessed these signs, when they came out of the sea and saw a people worshipping cows, they said: "Make for us a god just as they have gods." And when they heard the lowing of a calf, they devoted themselves to its worship. This shows that the purpose is not achieved by proofs alone, but by guidance.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "Ya ibna umma" with a kasra on the mim and the possessive, and the kasra on the mim indicates the (suppressed) ya (of possession, "my"). The rest read it with a fatha, and its underlying form is "ya ibna umma" (with the final alif of the vowel-lengthening, as in the pause form of "umm-i" becoming "umma-h" ), i.e. the original is "Ya ibna ummah" ("O son of my mother"). And God knows best.

Know that there is nothing in the Qur'an indicating that he did that, for prohibiting something does not indicate that the one prohibited did what is prohibited, as in His saying: ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:1], and His saying: ﴿If you associate partners with Allah, your deeds will surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar 39:65]. What is stated is that he seized his brother's head, pulling him toward himself, and this alone does not indicate contempt for him. Rather, one may do that for various other purposes, as we have explained. Some people say that he seized his hair-lock (dhu'aba) with his right hand and his beard with his left, then said: ﴿Indeed I feared that you would say, "You caused a division among the Children of Israel, and you did not observe my word."﴾

Someone might say: Musa's words, peace be upon him, "What prevented you from not following me? Did you then disobey my command?" indicate that he had commanded him to do something. How then is it appropriate in reply to say: "I did not comply with your word only out of fear that you would say, 'and you did not observe my word'"? Could such speech be proper for a rational person?

The answer: Perhaps Musa, peace be upon him, commanded him to go to them on the condition that this would not lead to corruption among the people. When Musa said, "What prevented you from not following me?" Harun said: "Because you commanded me to follow you only when corruption did not occur. Had I come to you while corruption had occurred, I would not have been observing your word."

Imam Abu al-Qasim al-Ansari said: Guidance is more beneficial than mere indication (dalala). The sorcerers were outsiders to faith, and they had seen only a single sign, yet they believed, endured the severe punishment in this world, and did not turn back from faith. As for his people, they saw the staff turn into a serpent that swallowed everything the sorcerers had gathered, then return to being a staff. They saw the sorcerers acknowledge that this was not sorcery and that it was a divine matter. They saw the nine signs over a long period, then they saw the sea split into twelve paths, and that God, the Exalted, saved them from drowning and destroyed their enemies despite their great number. Then, although they had witnessed these signs, when they came out of the sea and saw a people worshipping cows, they said: "Make for us a god just as they have gods." And when they heard the lowing of a calf, they devoted themselves to its worship. This shows that the purpose is not achieved by proofs alone, but by guidance.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "Ya ibna umma" with a kasra on the mim and the possessive, and the kasra on the mim indicates the (suppressed) ya (of possession, "my"). The rest read it with a fatha, and its underlying form is "ya ibna umma" (with the final alif of the vowel-lengthening, as in the pause form of "umm-i" becoming "umma-h" ), i.e. the original is "Ya ibna ummah" ("O son of my mother"). And God knows best.

[p. 96]

The Exalted said: ﴿He said, "What is your business, O Samiri?"﴾ ﴿He said, "I saw what they did not see, so I took a handful from the footprint of the Messenger and threw it away. Thus did my soul prompt me."﴾ ﴿He said, "Go, for it is yours in this life to say, 'No touching.' And you have an appointment that you will not be able to break. Look at your god, to which you remained devoted. We will surely burn it, then scatter it into the sea in scattering."﴾ ﴿Your god is only Allah, other than whom there is no god, Whose knowledge encompasses all things.﴾

Know that when Musa (peace be upon him) finished speaking with Harun (peace be upon him) and understood his excuse for the delay, he turned to the Samiri. It is possible that the Samiri had been present with Harun, so when Musa ended his speech with Harun, he began speaking with the Samiri. It is also possible that he had been far away and then the Samiri came later, or that Musa went to him in order to address him. So Musa (peace be upon him) said: ﴿What is your business, O Samiri?﴾ Al-khatb (business, matter) is a verbal noun; "khatabal-amr" means he sought the matter. So when one who is doing something is asked, "Ma khatbuka?" (What is your business?), the meaning is "What is your aim in it?" The purpose of the question is to denounce him and to magnify the seriousness of his action. Then the Samiri mentioned his excuse for that, saying: ﴿I saw what they did not see.﴾ On this there are two issues.

The first issue: it has been recited as (baṣirtu bimā lam yabṣirū bihi) with a kasra, and Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited (bimā lam tabṣurū) with a ta' with a dot above, while the rest recited it with a ya', meaning: "what the Children of Israel did not see."

The second issue: concerning seeing (al-ibṣār) there are two opinions. Abu 'Ubayda said: "I knew what they did not know," and from this comes their saying, "a man who is baṣīr" (meaning) "'ālim" (knowing). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Al-Zajjaj, in his explanation, said: "abṣartuhu" means "ra'aytuhu" (I saw him), and "baṣurtu bihi" means "ṣirtu bihi baṣīran 'ālimān" (I became one who sees with it, knowing). Others said: "I saw what they did not see," so his saying "baṣurtu bihi" means "abṣartuhu," and he meant that he saw the mount of Jibril (peace be upon him), so he took a handful of dust from the place of the hoofprint of his mount. Then he said: ﴿so I took a handful from the footprint of the Messenger and threw it away.﴾ On this there are several issues.

The first issue: al-Hasan recited "qubḍatan" with a damma on the qaf, and it is a noun for what is taken, like "ghurfa" and "ḍuffa." As for "qabḍa," it is the single act of grasping, and its application to what is grasped is a case of naming the object by the verbal noun, like "ḍarb al-amīr" (the ruler's striking). It was also recited "faqabaṣtu qabṣatan" with ḍād and ṣād: the ḍād is with the whole palm, and the ṣād with the tips of the fingers. Their parallels are "al-khaḍm" and "al-qaḍm": the kha' is with the whole mouth, and the qaf with its front part. Ibn Mas'ud recited "min athari faras al-Rasul" (from the trace of the Messenger's horse).

The second issue: most commentators said that by "the Messenger" is meant Jibril (peace be upon him), and by his "trace" is meant the dust he took from the place of his mount's hoof. Then they differed as to when he saw him. Most said: he only saw him on the day the sea was split. It is reported from 'Ali (peace be upon him) that when Jibril (peace be upon him) descended to take Musa (peace be upon him) to the Tur, the Samiri saw him among the people. They differed as to how the Samiri was singled out to see Jibril (peace be upon him) and recognize him among all the people. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said in the narration of al-Kalbi: he recognized him because he had seen him when he was young, and he was protected from being killed at the time when Pharaoh ordered the slaughter of the sons of the Children of Israel. A woman would give birth and put her child where the family of Pharaoh would not notice, and the angels would take the infants and raise them until they grew up and mingled with people. The Samiri was among those whom Jibril (peace be upon him) took, and he put his palm into his mouth and suckled honey and milk from it. He kept coming back to him until he recognized him, so when he saw him he recognized him. Ibn Juraij said: according to this, his saying "baṣurtu bimā lam yabṣurū bihi" means "ra'aytu mā lam yarawhu" (I saw what they did not see). As for the one who explained the word as "knowledge," that is also correct, and the meaning would be: "I knew that the dust of the mount of Jibril (peace be upon him) has the property of giving life." Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: there is no explicit statement in the Qur'an of what the commentators mentioned. So here there is another view, which is that by "the Messenger" is meant Musa (peace be upon him), and by his "trace" is meant his sunna (way) and his prescribed path that he was commanded to follow. A man may say: "So-and-so follows the trace of so-and-so," and "qabaḍa atharahu" when he follows his path. The meaning is: when Musa (peace be upon him) turned to the Samiri with blame and questioning about the matter that led him to mislead the people in the affair of the calf, he said: "I saw what they did not see," that is, I knew that what you are upon is not the truth. "I had taken a handful from your trace, O Messenger," that is, something of your sunna and religion, "so I threw it away," that is, I cast it aside. At that point Musa (peace be upon him) informed him of the punishment that he would have in this world and in the Hereafter. He used the form of speech about an absent person, as a man says to his leader while facing him: "What does the ruler say about such-and-such?" and "With what does the ruler command?" As for Musa (peace be upon him) calling him "Messenger" despite his denial and disbelief, this is according to the view of those whom Allah quoted as saying: ﴿And they said, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are surely mad!"﴾ [al-Hijr: 6], even though they did not believe in the sending down. Know that this view which Abu Muslim mentioned contains nothing but opposition to the commentators, yet it is closer to verification for several reasons.

The first: Jibril (peace be upon him) is not well known by the name "the Messenger," and no mention of him had preceded so that the definite article would be taken as referring to him. So the use of the word "the Messenger" to mean Jibril (peace be upon him) is as if it were an imposition of knowledge of the unseen. The second: it requires an elision, namely "a handful from the trace of the hoof of the Messenger's horse," and elision goes against the basic rule. The third: there must be a forced explanation of how the Samiri was singled out among all people to see and recognize Jibril (peace be upon him), and then how he knew that the dust of his mount's hoof had this effect. What they mentioned, that Jibril (peace be upon him) was the one who raised him, is far-fetched, because if the Samiri recognized Jibril at the time of his full mental maturity, he would certainly have known that Musa (peace be upon him) was a truthful Prophet, so how would he attempt to mislead? And if what he recognized was at the time of puberty, then what benefit is there in Jibril (peace be upon him) having raised him in childhood for the attainment of that knowledge? The fourth: if it were permissible for some of the disbelievers to have knowledge of dust of this nature, then someone could say: "Perhaps Musa (peace be upon him) had knowledge of something else resembling that, and because of it he brought the miracles." Its conclusion returns to the question posed by one who attacks the miracles and says: "Why is it not permissible to say that they, because of their knowledge of some medicines that have the property of producing that miracle, brought about that miracle?" And in that case the door of miracles would be entirely closed.

As for his saying: ﴿Thus did my soul prompt me,﴾ the meaning is: "I did what my soul called me to." The word "sawwalat" is derived from "su'āl" (asking/suggesting), so the meaning is: no one else called me to what I did; rather, I followed my own desire in it. Then, when Musa (peace be upon him) heard that from the Samiri, he answered him by clarifying his state in this world and the Hereafter, and clarifying the state of his god. As for his state in this world, it is his saying: ﴿Go, for it is yours in this life to say, "No touching."﴾ On this there are several views.

The first: the meaning is: "I do not touch and I am not touched." They said: whenever anyone touched him, the toucher and the touched would be struck with fever, so whenever anyone wanted to touch him he would cry out in fear of the fever and say, "No touching." The second: by his saying "No touching" is meant a prohibition against mixing with anyone or anyone mixing with him. Muqatil said: Musa (peace be upon him) expelled him from the quarter of the Children of Israel and said to him: "Go out, you and your family," so he went out as an outcast into the wilderness. Al-Wahidi objected to this, saying: a man who becomes shunned does not himself say "No touching"; rather, that is said to him. This objection is weak, because when a man remains an outcast and solitary, if he is asked, "How are you?" he may say, "No touching," meaning: no one touches me and I do not touch anyone. The meaning is: "I make you, O Samiri, so much an outcast that if you wanted to inform someone else about your state, you would say nothing but 'No touching.'" This view is better and closer to the arrangement of the speech than the first. The third: what Abu Muslim mentioned, namely that it is permissible to understand it as referring to touching women, so that it would be part of Allah's punishment of him: the cutting off of his offspring, so that he would have no child to keep him company, and Allah the Exalted would thus deprive him of the two adornments of this world that He mentioned in His saying: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world﴾ [al-Kahf: 46]. It was also recited "lā masāsa" on the pattern of "fajār," which is a proper name for a single instance of touching.

As for the explanation of his state in the Hereafter, it is his saying: ﴿And you have an appointment that you will not be able to break.﴾ The word "maw'id" is in the sense of "wa'd" (promise), meaning: this is your punishment in this world, and then there is a promise for you of the destination to the punishment of the Hereafter; so you are among those who lose both this world and the Hereafter, and that is the manifest loss. The people of Madina and Kufa recited "lan tukhlafahu" with a fatha on the lam, meaning: you will not be able to break that promise; that is, Allah will bring it to you and it will not be delayed from you. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Hasan recited it with a kasra on the lam, meaning: you will come to it, you will not be absent from it, and you will not fail to meet it. The fatha on the lam is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd, as if he were saying: "a true promise with no failure in it." It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud: "lan nukhlafahu" with a nun, as if Musa (peace be upon him) were relating the saying of Allah the Exalted in its own wording, as explained previously in His saying: ﴿that I may give you﴾ [Maryam: 19].

As for the explanation of the state of his god, it is his saying: ﴿Look at your god, to which you remained devoted.﴾ Al-Mufaddal said concerning "ẓaltu": it is read with a fatha and a kasra on the ẓā', and likewise ﴿then you would remain amazed﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 65]. Its origin is "ẓalilta," and the first lam was elided, because that happens when the second lam is silent, and the Arabs prefer to drop the first. Whoever recites the ẓā' with a kasra transfers the kasra of the dropped lam onto it; whoever recites it with a fatha leaves the ẓā' in its own state. They do the same with the doubled verb: they say "mastuhu" and "massastuhu." Then He said: ﴿We will surely burn it, then scatter it into the sea in scattering.﴾ On his saying ﴿We will surely burn it﴾ there are two views.

The first: what is meant is burning it with fire. This is one of the things that indicates that it had turned into flesh and blood, because gold cannot be burned with fire. Al-Suddi said: Musa (peace be upon him) commanded that the calf be slaughtered, so it was slaughtered and blood flowed from it; then it was burned, then its ashes were scattered. In Ibn Mas'ud's reading: "la-nadhbahannahu wa-la-nuḥarriqannahu" (we will surely slaughter it and surely burn it). The second: "la-nuḥarriqannahu" means "la-nabriduannahu" (we will surely file it down with a file). It is said: "ḥaraqahu yaḥruquhu" when he filed it down. This reading indicates that it had not turned into flesh or blood, for that cannot be filed down with a file. It is possible to say: it had become flesh, then it was slaughtered, then its bones were filed down with a file until they became in a state where they could be scattered.

The recitation of the common readers is with a damma on the nun and a shadda on the rā', and its meaning is "la-nuḥarriqannahu bil-nār" (we will surely burn it with fire). Abu Ja'far and Ibn Muhaysin recited "la-naḥruqannahu" with a fatha on the nun and a damma on the rā', without shadda, meaning "la-nabriduannahu" (we will surely file it down). Know that when Musa (peace be upon him) finished refuting what the Samiri had gone to, he returned to explaining the true religion and said: ﴿Your god is only﴾ that is, the one deserving worship and veneration: ﴿Allah, other than whom there is no god, Whose knowledge encompasses all things.﴾ Muqatil said: He knows who worships Him and who does not worship Him.

Abu Ja'far and Ibn Muhaysin recited "la-naḥruqannahu" with a fatha on the nun and a damma on the rā', without shadda, meaning "la-nabriduannahu" (we will surely file it down). Know that when Musa (peace be upon him) finished refuting what the Samiri had gone to, he returned to explaining the true religion and said: ﴿Your god is only﴾ that is, the one deserving worship and veneration: ﴿Allah, other than whom there is no god, Whose knowledge encompasses all things.﴾ Muqatil said: He knows who worships Him and who does not worship Him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verses 102–106:

Know that when He, glorified and exalted, had explained the story of Musa, peace be upon him, first with Pharaoh and then with the Samiri, He followed it with His saying: ﴿Thus do We relate to you﴾ from the other reports of the nations and their conditions, to magnify your status, to add to your miracles, and so that there may be more lessons and insight for those obligated by the religion. ﴿And We have indeed given you from Us a reminder﴾ means the Qur'an, as the Exalted said: ﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down﴾ [al-Anbiya: 50]; ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44]; ﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾ [Sad: 1]; ﴿No reminder comes to them﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 5]; ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down﴾ [al-Hijr: 6].

Then, in naming the Qur'an "the Reminder" there are several aspects. The first: it is a book containing mention of what people need of the affairs of their religion and their worldly life. The second: it mentions the kinds of the blessings and favours of Allah, the Exalted, and so it contains admonition and exhortation. The third: in it is mention and honour for you and for your people, as He said: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44]. Know that Allah, the Exalted, named all His books "a reminder," as He said: ﴿So ask the people of the Reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya: 7]. Just as He made clear His favour through this, He also made clear the severity of the threat against whoever turns away from it and does not believe in it, in several respects.

The first: His saying: ﴿Whoever turns away from it﴾, ﴿he will bear on the Day of Resurrection a burden﴾. The word "wizr" (burden) means a heavy punishment. He called it a burden by way of likeness to its heaviness upon the one punished and the difficulty of bearing it, which weighs on the one who carries it and breaks his back; or because it is the recompense of "wizr," which is sin. It is also read as "yuhammalu" (is made to carry). Then He, exalted, explained the description of that burden in two respects. The first: that he will be abiding and everlasting therein. The second: His saying: ﴿and evil will it be for them as a load on the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning: how evil is this burden as a load, i.e., as something carried. "Himlan" (as a load) is accusative as a specification (tamyiz).

The second: ﴿On the Day when the Horn is blown﴾. The purpose is to make clear that the Day of Resurrection is the Day when the Horn is blown. On this there are several issues.

The first issue: Abu 'Amr read "nanfukhu" with an open nun, like His saying "wa-nahshuru" (and We will gather). The others read "yunfakhu" in the passive form (the subject not named), and "nahshuru" with the nun, because the one who blows is an angel who has put the Horn to his mouth, while the one who gathers is Allah, the Exalted. It was also read as "yawma yanfukhu" with the yaʾ open, in the third person, and the pronoun refers to Allah, the Exalted, or to Israfil, peace be upon him. As for "yahshuru al-mujrimin" (He gathers the criminals), only al-Hasan read it so. It was also read "fi al-suwar" with an open waw, as the plural of "surah" (form).

The second issue: concerning "fi al-Sur" (in the Horn) there are two views. The first: that it is a horn into which one blows, by which people are called to the place of gathering. The second: that it is the plural of "surah" (form), and the blowing is the blowing of the spirit into them; the reading of those who read "al-suwar" with an open waw supports this. The first view is preferable, because of His saying: ﴿Then when the trumpet is sounded﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 8]. Allah, the Exalted, makes the matters of the Hereafter known to people by means of examples of what is witnessed in this world, and it is the custom of people to blow the trumpet at journeys and in armies.

The third issue: what is meant by this blowing is the second blast, because His saying after that: ﴿and We will gather the criminals that Day, blue-eyed﴾ is like an indication that the blowing into the Horn is like the cause of their gathering. This is like His saying: ﴿On the Day the Horn is blown, and you come forth in throngs﴾ [al-Naba: 18].

As for His saying: ﴿and We will gather the criminals that Day, blue-eyed﴾, there are issues concerning it:

The first issue: the Mu'tazila (a theological school) said: His saying "al-mujrimin" (the criminals) includes unbelievers and sinners, and so it indicates that there is no pardon for sinners. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: by "the criminals" He means those who took another god alongside Allah. This matter has already been discussed.

The second issue: they differed about what is meant by "al-zurqa" (blueness) in several ways. The first: al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: it means blue eyes and black faces, a blueness that disfigures their creation; and the Arabs regard that as an ill omen. If it is said: Did not Allah inform that they will be gathered blind? How can one be blind and blue-eyed? We say: perhaps they will be blind in one state and blue-eyed in another. The second: what is meant by blueness is blindness. Al-Kalbi said: "zurqan" means blind. Al-Zajjaj said: they will come out seeing at the first time and will become blind in the place of gathering, and the blackness of the eye, when it departs, turns blue. If it is said: How can one be blind when He said: ﴿It is only that He delays them to a Day when the eyes will stare fixedly﴾ [Ibrahim: 42], and the staring of the eye is impossible for one who is blind; and He said concerning them: ﴿Read your book﴾ [al-Isra: 14], and how can the blind read? The answer: their conditions may differ. The third: Abu Muslim said: what is meant by this blueness is the staring of their eyes, since the blue-eyed one is staring, because of the weakness of his sight he fixes his gaze upon a thing wishing to make it out, and this is the state of one who is afraid and anticipating what he dislikes; and it is like His saying: ﴿It is only that He delays them to a Day when the eyes will stare fixedly﴾. The fourth: "zurqan" means thirsty. Thalab related this from Ibn al-A'rabi, who said: because from the severity of thirst the blackness of their eyes changes until it turns blue. What supports this interpretation is His saying: ﴿and We will drive the criminals to Hell as a thirsty herd﴾ [Maryam: 86]. The fifth: Tha'lab related from Ibn al-A'rabi who said: "greedy for what they cannot attain."

The third attribute of the unbelievers on the Day of Resurrection is His saying: ﴿whispering among themselves: "You did not remain but ten [days]"﴾. On this there are issues:

The first issue: "yatakhafatun" means they speak secretly to one another. It is said: "khafata yakhfitu" and "khafata mukhafatatan," and "al-takhafut" is secret speaking, and it is like His saying: ﴿So you hear nothing but whispering﴾ [Ta-Ha: 108]. They whisper only because their hearts are filled with terror and dread, or because they have become in extreme weakness due to fear, so they cannot bear to speak aloud.

The second issue: they differed over whether the saying "in labithtum" (if you remained) refers to remaining in the world or in the grave. A group said: they meant remaining in the world; this is the view of al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Dahhak, and they argued for it by His saying: ﴿He will say: "How many years did you remain on the earth?" They will say: "We remained a day or part of a day; so ask those who count."﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 112–113]. If it is said: either it is said that they forgot the length of their stay in the world, or they did not forget it. The first is not permissible, for if that were allowed, one could remain fifty years in a city and then forget it. The second is not permissible either, because it would be a lie, and the people of the Hereafter do not lie, especially since this lie has no benefit. We say: there are several answers:

The first: perhaps when they are gathered at the beginning of the matter and witness those terrors, because of the intensity of their impact upon them they become distracted from the measure of their lifespan in the world, and they recall only a little. So they say: "Would that we had lived only those few days in the world, so that we would not fall into these terrors." A person at a severe terror may forget the most evident things. The full explanation of this is mentioned in Surah al-An'am in His saying: ﴿Then their trial will be only that they say: "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists"﴾ [al-An'am: 23].

The second: they know the measure of their lifespan in the world, but when they compared their lifespans in the world with the lifespans of the Hereafter they found them to be extremely few. So some of them said: "We remained in the world only ten days," and the wisest of them said: "Rather, we remained only one day," meaning: the measure of our stay in the world, compared with our stay in the Hereafter, is like ten days, rather like one day, rather like nothing. And the reason the ten and the one are singled out is that a small amount in such contexts is only expressed by ten or one.

The third: when they witnessed the hardships they recalled the days of blessing and joy and grieved over them, so they described them as short, because days of joy are brief.

The fourth: the days of the world have passed while the days of the Hereafter are yet to come, and what has gone, however long its duration, is little compared with what is to come, however short its duration; how much more so when the matter is reversed.

For these reasons Allah, the Exalted, preferred the view of the one who went to the extreme of minimizing, when He said: ﴿when the best of them in conduct says: "You did not remain but a day"﴾.

The second view: that what is meant is remaining in the grave. Supporting this is His saying: ﴿And on the Day the Hour is established, the criminals will swear that they remained but an hour. Thus were they deluded﴾ [al-Rum: 55], and ﴿But those who were given knowledge and faith will say: "You remained in the Book of Allah until the Day of Resurrection"﴾ [al-Rum: 56]. As for one who permits lying to the people of the Resurrection, there is no difficulty for him regarding the verse. As for one who does not permit it, he says: when Allah, the Exalted, revived them in the grave and punished them, then caused them to die, then resurrected them on the Day of Resurrection, they did not know how long their stay in the grave had been; so it occurred to some of them that it was about ten days, and others said it was one day. Then when they fell into punishment a second time, they wished for the time of death, which is the time of deliverance, because of the severity of the torment they had encountered.

The third issue: most scholars hold that His saying: ﴿if you remained but ten﴾ means ten days, so the statement of the one who said: ﴿if you remained but a day﴾ is less. Muqatil said: ﴿if you remained but ten﴾ means ten hours, like His saying: ﴿As if, on the Day they see it, they had not remained except an evening or its morning﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 46]. On this interpretation the day would be the longer. And Allah knows best.

Know that by this statement, glorified and exalted is He, He made clear the greatest of the bewilderment they suffered, by which they were driven to this kind of whispering.
