So they say: "Would that we had lived only those few days in the world, so that we would not fall into these terrors." A person at a severe terror may forget the most evident things. The full explanation of this is mentioned in Surah al-An'am in His saying: ﴿Then their trial will be only that they say: "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists"﴾ [al-An'am: 23].

The second: they know the measure of their lifespan in the world, but when they compared their lifespans in the world with the lifespans of the Hereafter they found them to be extremely few. So some of them said: "We remained in the world only ten days," and the wisest of them said: "Rather, we remained only one day," meaning: the measure of our stay in the world, compared with our stay in the Hereafter, is like ten days, rather like one day, rather like nothing. And the reason the ten and the one are singled out is that a small amount in such contexts is only expressed by ten or one.

The third: when they witnessed the hardships they recalled the days of blessing and joy and grieved over them, so they described them as short, because days of joy are brief.

The fourth: the days of the world have passed while the days of the Hereafter are yet to come, and what has gone, however long its duration, is little compared with what is to come, however short its duration; how much more so when the matter is reversed.

For these reasons Allah, the Exalted, preferred the view of the one who went to the extreme of minimizing, when He said: ﴿when the best of them in conduct says: "You did not remain but a day"﴾.

The second view: that what is meant is remaining in the grave. Supporting this is His saying: ﴿And on the Day the Hour is established, the criminals will swear that they remained but an hour. Thus were they deluded﴾ [al-Rum: 55], and ﴿But those who were given knowledge and faith will say: "You remained in the Book of Allah until the Day of Resurrection"﴾ [al-Rum: 56]. As for one who permits lying to the people of the Resurrection, there is no difficulty for him regarding the verse. As for one who does not permit it, he says: when Allah, the Exalted, revived them in the grave and punished them, then caused them to die, then resurrected them on the Day of Resurrection, they did not know how long their stay in the grave had been; so it occurred to some of them that it was about ten days, and others said it was one day. Then when they fell into punishment a second time, they wished for the time of death, which is the time of deliverance, because of the severity of the torment they had encountered.

The third issue: most scholars hold that His saying: ﴿if you remained but ten﴾ means ten days, so the statement of the one who said: ﴿if you remained but a day﴾ is less. Muqatil said: ﴿if you remained but ten﴾ means ten hours, like His saying: ﴿As if, on the Day they see it, they had not remained except an evening or its morning﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 46]. On this interpretation the day would be the longer. And Allah knows best.

Know that by this statement, glorified and exalted is He, He made clear the greatest of the bewilderment they suffered, by which they were driven to this kind of whispering.

﴿And they ask you about the mountains. Say: My Lord will blow them away with a blast.﴾ ﴿And He will leave them a level plain,﴾ ﴿in which you will see no crookedness or unevenness.﴾ ﴿On that Day they will follow the Summoner, from whom there is no deviation. Voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful, and you will hear nothing but a murmur.﴾ ﴿On that Day, intercession will not benefit anyone except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted and whose words He approves.﴾ ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, but they cannot encompass Him in knowledge.﴾ ﴿Faces will be humbled before the Living, the Self-Subsisting. And he who bears wrongdoing will be lost.﴾ ﴿But whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer will fear neither injustice nor diminution.﴾.

Know that when He, exalted is He, described the matter of the Day of Resurrection, He related the question of those who did not believe in the Gathering (al-ḥashr), so He said: ﴿And they ask you about the mountains.﴾ There are several explanations of this question. The first: His saying ﴿they whisper among themselves﴾ is a description by God, exalted is He, of all the criminals in this respect, so it is as if they said: How can that be, when the mountains stand in the way and prevent this whispering? The second: al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it was revealed concerning the polytheists of Mecca who said: O Muḥammad, what will the mountains be like on the Day of Resurrection? Their question was in the manner of mockery. The third: perhaps his people said: O Muḥammad, you claim that the world will come to an end. If what you say were true, it would have to begin first with deficiency and then end in annihilation, but the conditions of the world remain as they were at the beginning, so how can what you say about the ruin of the world be true? This is a doubt which Galen (Jālīnūs) relied upon to argue that the heavens do not perish. He said: because if they perished, they would begin with deterioration first, until their deterioration reached annihilation; since no deterioration appears in them, we know that the claim of annihilation is false. Then God, exalted is He, commanded His Messenger to answer this question, and He added to the answer other matters explaining the conditions of the Resurrection and its terrors.

The first attribute: His saying ﴿So say: My Lord will blow them away with a blast.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: He said ﴿So say﴾ with the fāʾ of consequence (fāʾ al-taʿqīb, the fāʾ indicating immediate sequence), because their aim in this question was to challenge the Gathering and the Resurrection. Therefore He commanded him to answer with the fāʾ of immediate sequence, since delaying clarification in such a fundamental matter of belief (masʾalah uṣūliyyah) is not permissible, whereas in legal details (furūʿiyyah) it is permissible. For this reason He said ﴿qul﴾ without the particle of sequence there.

The second issue: the pronoun in His saying ﴿will blow them away﴾ refers to the mountains, and nasf means scattering, that is, the mountains will become like scattered dust, dispersed by dispersal. When the mountains disappear, the obstacles disappear, and thus the truth of His saying ﴿they whisper﴾ becomes known. Al-Khalīl said: ﴿yanfusuhā﴾ means He will remove them and make them fly away. As for the pronoun in His saying ﴿fa-yadharuhā﴾, it refers to the earth, and it dispenses with mentioning it beforehand, as is the custom of people in referring to it by a pronoun, as when they say: "Nobody is more generous upon it than so-and-so," and God, exalted is He, said: ﴿He left upon its back no creature﴾ [Fāṭir: 45]. He said ﴿He will leave them a level plain﴾ only to make clear that this blowing does not remove the evenness, lest it be supposed that when the mountains moved from one place to another they became an obstacle there. All of this applies when the aim of their question was to object to the manner of the whispering. But if the purpose of the question was what we mentioned, namely that there is no deterioration in them at present, and therefore their affair must not end in annihilation, then the answer would be: the annihilation of a thing may be an annihilation that occurs gradually (tawlīdiyyan), in which case deterioration must precede annihilation; and it may be an annihilation that occurs all at once, and here deterioration need not precede annihilation. God, exalted is He, made clear that He disperses the compositions of this corporeal world all at once by His power and will, so there is no need here for deterioration to precede annihilation.

The third issue: God, exalted is He, described the earth at that time with attributes. The first: that it is a qāʿ, which is a low-lying place, and it was said that it is a pool of standing water. The second: ṣafṣaf, which is ground with no vegetation on it. Abū Muslim said: qāʿ is the smooth, level earth, and likewise ṣafṣaf. The third: His saying ﴿in which you will see no crookedness or unevenness﴾. The author of al-Kashshāf (al-Zamakhsharī) said: they distinguished between ʿiwaj and ʿawaj: ʿiwaj with a kasra is used for meanings, and ʿawaj with a fatḥa for concrete things. If it is said: the earth is a concrete thing, so how is the word with kasra in its ʿayn correct for it? We say: the choice of this word has a wonderful effect in describing the earth as even and free of bending. For if you were to take a piece of land and level it, and you exaggerated in levelling it, then when you compare it to geometric measurements, you will find in it kinds of crookedness beyond the range of sight. He said: that degree of bending, being so fine, was assigned to the category of meanings, so it was said of it: ʿiwaj with a kasra. Know that this verse indicates that on that day the earth will be a true sphere, because a polygonal surface must have its surfaces joined to one another not in a straight line but at angles, and that would be refuted by the apparent meaning of the verse. The fourth: amt is a slight protrusion; it is said: "He stretched his rope until there was no amt in it." From these four attributes it is established that on that day the earth will be smooth, free of elevation, depression, and all kinds of deviation and bending.

The second attribute of the Day of Resurrection is His saying ﴿On that Day they will follow the Summoner, from whom there is no deviation.﴾ Regarding the Summoner there are two views. The first: that this Summoner is the blast in the Trumpet (al-ṣūr). His saying ﴿from whom there is no deviation﴾ means that He does not turn away from anyone in His summons, but gathers all. The second: that he is an angel standing upon the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis, calling out and saying: "O decayed bones, scattered joints, torn flesh! Rise up to your Lord for reckoning and recompense." So they hear the voice of the Summoner and follow it. It is said that this is Isrāfīl, peace be upon him, placing his foot upon the rock. If it is asked: is this summons before the revivification or after it? We say: if the purpose of the summons is to inform them, then it must be after the revivification, because calling out to the dead is pointless. But if the purpose is not to inform them, rather the aim is another aim, such as being a kindness (luṭf) to the angels and a benefit to them, then that is permissible before the revivification.

**The third attribute:** His saying: ﴿And voices will be hushed before the Most Merciful, so you will hear nothing but a whisper﴾. On this verse there are several interpretations.

First: the voices will be hushed from the intensity of terror, humbled and subdued, so you will hear nothing but *hams* (a whisper), which is the hidden remembrance. Abu Muslim said: Humans and jinn both know that they have no owner other than Him, so no voice will be heard from them that exceeds a whisper, which is the faintest of sounds, nearly speech understood only by the movement of the lips because of its weakness. It is fitting that one whom Allah holds to account should lower his gaze, weaken his voice, falter in his speech, and have prolonged anguish.

Second: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, and Ibn Zayd said: *al-hams* is the sound of footsteps. The meaning, then, is that you will hear nothing but the shuffling of feet and their movement toward the place of gathering.

[Page 103]

**The fourth attribute:** His saying: ﴿On that Day, intercession will not avail except for one whom the Most Merciful permits and whose words He approves﴾. The author of *al-Kashshaf* (*al-Kashshaf*, the Qur'an commentary of al-Zamakhshari) said: The word *man* (whoever) may be in the nominative or the accusative. In the nominative, it is a *badal* (apposition, substitution) for *al-shafa'ah* (intercession), with an omitted genitive (the phrase is elliptical), meaning: intercession will not avail except the intercession of one whom the Most Merciful permits. In the accusative, it is the object.

I say: The second possibility is preferable for several reasons. First: the first possibility requires supplying a pronoun and changing the *i'rab* (the grammatical case-endings), whereas the second does not require this. Second: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿intercession will not avail﴾ refers to those who intercede with it, and the exception returns to them. It is as if He said: intercession will not benefit any of creation except a person who is approved. Third: it is known by necessity that the rank of an intercessor is a great rank, which is attained only by one whom Allah has permitted to hold it and who is acceptable in His sight. If we interpret the verse this way, it becomes like clarifying what is already clear. But if we interpret the verse as referring to the one for whom intercession is made, that would not be clarifying what is clear, so that interpretation is preferable.

Having established this, we say: The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school of theology) said: The *fasiq* (grave sinner) is not approved in the sight of Allah, exalted is He, so the Messenger must not intercede on his behalf, because this verse indicates that the one for whom intercession is made must be approved in the sight of Allah.

Know that this verse is among the strongest proofs for the establishment of intercession on behalf of sinners, because His saying ﴿and whose words He approves﴾ is satisfied if Allah, exalted is He, approves one of his statements. The *fasiq* has indeed been approved by Allah, exalted is He, in one of his statements, namely the testimony that there is no god but Allah. Therefore intercession must benefit him, since the exception from a negation is an affirmation.

If it is said: He, exalted is He, made an exception from that negation on two conditions: first, that permission be granted; second, that He approves of his statement. Suppose that the *fasiq* meets one of the two conditions, namely that He approves of his statement. But why do you say that permission was granted for him? This is the very point in question. We reply: This condition, that He approved of his statement, is sufficient for the exception to apply, as shown by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they do not intercede except for those with whom He is pleased﴾ [al-Anbiya': 28]. There He was satisfied with this condition alone. This verse indicates that permission is necessary. From the combination of both it becomes clear that when He approves a person's statement, permission for intercession is attained; and when both conditions are met, the exception applies and the purpose is accomplished.

* * *

**The fifth attribute:** His saying: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, while they cannot encompass Him in knowledge﴾. On this there are several issues.

And for one who says that His saying ﴿whom the Most Merciful permits﴾ refers to the intercessor, the pronoun refers to him as well. The meaning is: the intercession of the angels and prophets will not avail except for one whom the Most Merciful permits to be interceded for by the angels and prophets. Then He said: ﴿He knows what is before them﴾, meaning what is before the angels, as He said in the Verse of the Throne. This is the view of al-Kalbi and Muqatil, and in it there is a rebuke to those who worship the angels so that they may intercede for them. Muqatil said: He knows what was before He created the angels and what they did after their creation.

First: al-Kalbi said: ﴿what is before them﴾ refers to the matters of the Hereafter, and ﴿what is behind them﴾ refers to the matters of this world. Third: al-Dahhak said: He knows what has passed and what remains, and when the Resurrection will occur.

The first: He, exalted is He, made clear that He knows what is before the servants and what is behind them, then said ﴿and they cannot encompass Him in knowledge﴾, meaning the servants cannot encompass in knowledge what is before them and what is behind them.

The sixth attribute is His saying: ﴿And faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Sustainer; and he who carries wrongdoing will have failed﴾. Its meaning is that on that Day faces will be humbled, that is, they will be abased, and sovereignty and dominance will belong to God, the Exalted, alone, with none other. The word *al-ʿānī* (the captive) is derived from the root of *ʿanw* (humbling), and it is said: *ʿanā yaʿnū ʿanāʾan* when he became a captive. [Page 105]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an, and We have varied in it some of the threats, that perhaps they may fear Allah, or it may produce for them a reminder﴾ ﴿So exalted is Allah, the King, the Truth. And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you, and say, "My Lord, increase me in knowledge."﴾

Know that His saying ﴿And thus﴾ is a conjunction with His saying ﴿Thus do We relate﴾. That is, "And in the same manner, We continue, and upon its method, We have sent down the whole Qur'an." Then He described the Qur'an with two matters:

The first: that it is in Arabic, so that the Arabs may understand it, and thus recognize its inimitability (i'jaz), its composition (nazm), and its departure from the genre of human speech.

The second: His saying ﴿and We have varied in it some of the threats﴾, meaning We repeated it and explained it in detail. The clarification of obligatory duties (fara'id) and prohibitions (mahaarim) falls under "threats," because a threat is an act that has consequences. Its repetition therefore necessitates the clarification of the rulings. For this reason He said ﴿that perhaps they may fear Allah﴾, and what is meant is guarding against what is forbidden and abandoning what is obligatory. The meaning of the word la'alla (perhaps) has already been explained in Surat al-Baqarah in His saying: ﴿And those before you, that perhaps you may fear Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:21].

As for His saying ﴿or it may produce for them a reminder﴾, there are two interpretations. The first: the meaning is that We have only sent down the Qur'an so that they may become God-fearing, that is, guarded against what is not fitting, or so that the Qur'an may produce for them a reminder that calls them to acts of obedience and to doing what is fitting. Regarding this, there are questions:

The first question: How can the Qur'an be the cause of producing a reminder? The answer: When the reminder occurs upon its recitation, the reminder is attributed to it.

The second question: Why is the reminder attributed to the Qur'an, while God-fearing (taqwa) is not attributed to it? The answer: God-fearing is an expression for not doing what is ugly, and that is a continuation of the original state of non-existence, so it is not permissible to attribute it to the Qur'an. As for the occurrence of a reminder, it is a matter that came into being after it had not existed, so it is permissible to attribute it to the Qur'an.

The third question: The word aw (or) denotes alternation, and there is no alternation between God-fearing and the occurrence of a reminder; rather, God-fearing is not valid except together with a reminder. So what is the meaning of the word aw? The answer: This is like their saying, "Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin," meaning, "Do not be free of both of them." Likewise here.

The second interpretation: It may be said that We have sent down the Qur'an so that they may fear Allah. If that does not happen, then at least the Qur'an produces for them a reminder, honor, and good repute. Under both assumptions, its sending down is a source of God-fearing.

Then, when He, may He be exalted, magnified the matter of the Qur'an, He followed it by magnifying Himself, saying: ﴿So exalted is Allah, the King, the Truth﴾, as an alert to what His creation must do by way of glorifying Him. He was described as "the Truth" because His dominion does not cease and does not change, and it is not derived from anyone else, nor is anyone other than Him more entitled to it. For this reason He is described with that. The word ta'ala (exalted) is of the form tafa'ala from al-'uluww (loftiness). It has been established that His loftiness, His greatness, and His lordship share a single meaning, namely, His being characterized by the attributes of majesty (jalal). Imaginations cannot contain Him, intellects cannot determine Him, and He is free of benefits and harms. Thus, He, may He be exalted, sent down the Qur'an only so that they may guard against what is not fitting and hasten to what is fitting. He is also free of being perfected by their acts of obedience and of being harmed by their disobedience. Acts of obedience occur only through His granting success (tawfiq) and facilitation, while acts of disobedience occur as an act of justice from Him, and each is made easy for what he was created for.

As for His saying ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: Regarding its connection to what precedes it, there are two views. The first view: Abu Muslim said: From His saying ﴿And they ask you about the mountains﴾ up to here, the speech is complete and ends. Then His saying ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾ is a new address. It is as if He had said: "And they ask you, and do not hasten with the Qur'an." The second view: It is reported that he, peace be upon him, feared that some of it might escape him, so he would recite along with the angel. Therefore he was commanded to be silent while the angel recited, and then to take up the recitation after the angel finished. It is as if He, may He be exalted, explained how the Qur'an benefits those who are responsible (mukallafun), and clarified that He, glorified be He, is exalted above everything that is not fitting, and that He is characterized by beneficence and mercy. Whoever is so must protect His Messenger from forgetfulness and oblivion in the matter of revelation. Since safety from forgetfulness and oblivion was achieved, He said: ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾.

[Page 106]

The second issue: His saying ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾ may mean: do not hasten in reciting it to yourself; it may mean: do not hasten in conveying it to others; it may mean: do not hasten in believing its apparent meaning; and it may mean: do not hasten in informing others of what its apparent meaning requires. As for His saying ﴿before its revelation is completed to you﴾, it may mean: before its completion (tamam) is revealed to you; it may mean: before its clarification (bayan) is revealed to you, because these two matters cannot be achieved except through revelation. It is well known that he, peace be upon him, was not forbidden from reciting it in order that he might memorize and convey it. Therefore, what is meant is that he should neither urge himself nor urge others to it until its completion or its clarification, or both, becomes clear through revelation, because it is obligatory to suspend judgment on the meaning of a speech until it is finished, lest there follow after it an exception, a condition, or other specifiers (mukhassisat). This is the verification (tahqiq) in explaining the verse.

Let us mention the statements of the exegetes:

One: This is like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾ [al-Qiyamah 75:16]. He, peace be upon him, was eager to take the Qur'an from Jibril, peace be upon him, and he would hasten to recite it before Jibril had finished, fearing forgetfulness. So it was said to him: "Do not hasten until his revelation is completed, so that your taking of it will be with steadiness and tranquility, and Allah will increase you in understanding and knowledge." This is the statement of Muqatil and al-Suddi, and 'Ata reported it from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Two: "Do not hasten with the Qur'an, so that you recite it to your companions before the explanation of its meanings is revealed to you." This is the statement of Mujahid and Qatadah.

Three: al-Dahhak said: "The people of Makkah and the bishop of Najran said: 'O Muhammad, inform us about such and such, and we have set you a term of three days.' The revelation was delayed for him, and the word spread that the Jews had overcome Muhammad. So Allah, may He be exalted, sent down this verse: ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾" — that is, with its descent before its revelation is completed to you from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) to Israfil, and from him to Jibril, and from him to you — ﴿And say, "My Lord, increase me in knowledge."﴾

Four: al-Hasan reported that "a woman came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'My husband slapped my face.' He said: 'Between you both is retaliation (qisas).' Then the saying ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾ was revealed, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ refrained from retaliation until the revelation of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Men are in charge of women﴾ [an-Nisa' 4:34]." This is far-fetched, and reliance is on the first explanation.

As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And say, "My Lord, increase me in knowledge."﴾, the meaning is that He, glorified and exalted, commanded him to turn to Allah, glorified be He, to increase knowledge, which becomes manifest through the completion of the Qur'an or the clarification of what was revealed to him.

The third issue: If the hastening that he was forbidden from was done by revelation, then how was he forbidden from it? The answer: Perhaps he did it by his own ijtihad (independent reasoning), and leaving it was preferable, so for this reason he was forbidden from it.

As for His words, ﴿and We found in him no resolve﴾, there are several inquiries.

The first inquiry: the verb "wajada" (found) may mean "knew," as in "and We found in him no resolve," or it may be the opposite of "non-existence," as if He said, "and We found no resolve in him."

The second inquiry: "'azm" means determination and firmness. The words ﴿and We found in him no resolve﴾ may mean: We found in him no resolve to persist in disobedience, which is closer to praise; or it may mean: We found in him no resolve to abandon disobedience; or We found in him no resolve to guard and be cautious against heedlessness; or We found in him no resolve to take precaution in the manner of exercising independent reasoning (ijtihad), if we say that he, peace be upon him, erred only through ijtihad.

As for His words, ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis, who refused﴾, this contains several issues.

The first: whether the addressees were all the angels or some of them.

The second: what is the meaning of prostration.

The third: whether Iblis was among the angels or not. If he was not, how is the exception valid, and by what means did he become commanded to prostrate?

The fourth: whether this indicates that Adam is superior to Muhammad (ﷺ) or not.

The fifth: how his refusal, described in the words "he refused," entailed disbelief, and whether he was a disbeliever from the beginning or became one because of that refusal.

Know that these issues have been discussed thoroughly in Surat al-Baqarah.

As for His words, ﴿So We said, "O Adam, indeed this is an enemy to you and to your wife, so let him not expel you both from the Garden, lest you be made wretched"﴾, there are several questions.

The first: what is the cause of that enmity? The answer has several aspects. The first: Iblis was envious, so when he saw the traces of Allah's blessings upon Adam, peace be upon him, he envied him and thus became his enemy. The second: Adam was a young man who was knowledgeable, as in His words, ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ (al-Baqarah: 31), whereas Iblis was an old man who was ignorant, because he asserted his own superiority by the nobility of his origin, and that is ignorance; and an ignorant old man is always an enemy of a knowledgeable young man. The third: Iblis was created from fire, while Adam was created from water and earth, so there is enmity between their origins, and that enmity remained.

The second question: why did He say, ﴿so let him not expel you both from the Garden﴾, when the one who expelled them from the Garden is Allah, the Exalted? The answer: since it was by his whispering that he did what resulted in the expulsion, the attribution is valid.

The third question: why was the act of wretchedness attributed to Adam alone, and not to Eve, although both shared in the act? The answer has two aspects. The first: included within the wretchedness of the man, who is the guardian of his household and their commander, is their wretchedness, just as included within his happiness is their happiness. So the statement was specifically attributed to him rather than to her, while preserving the observance of the verse-ending rhyme (fasila). The second: by wretchedness is meant toil in seeking sustenance, and that falls upon the man rather than the woman. It is related that a red ox was sent down to Adam, and he would plough with it and wipe the sweat from his brow.

As for His words, ﴿Indeed, it is granted to you that you will not hunger therein, nor be naked﴾ and ﴿And that you will not thirst therein, nor be exposed to the sun﴾, there are several issues.

If it is objected that (an) does not enter upon (anna), since one does not say (an anna Zaydan muntaliqun), and the (wāw) substitutes for (anna) and stands in its place, why then was it inserted before it? We answer: the (wāw) was not established to always be a substitute for (anna); rather, it is a substitute for any governing particle. Since it is not a particle established solely for emphasis, there is no barrier to combining them, just as the combination of (an) and (anna) is barred.

The second issue: satiety, quenching of thirst, clothing, and sheltering in shade are the pivots upon which human affairs revolve. So Allah, the Exalted, mentioned that these things are attained for him in the Garden without need for earning or seeking. He mentioned them in the form of negation, against their opposites, which are hunger, nakedness, thirst, and the sun, so that some kinds of the wretchedness against which He warned him would reach his hearing, until he would be thorough in avoiding the cause that brings him into it. All these things are, as it were, an explanation of the wretchedness mentioned in His words, ﴿lest you be made wretched﴾.

The Exalted said: ﴿And We had already made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot, and We found in him no resolve.﴾ ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis, who refused.﴾ ﴿So We said, "O Adam, indeed this is an enemy to you and to your wife, so let him not expel you both from the Garden, lest you be made wretched.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is granted to you that you will not hunger therein, nor be naked.﴾ ﴿And that you will not thirst therein, nor be exposed to the sun.﴾

Know that this is the sixth occurrence of the story of Adam, peace be upon him, in the Qur'an. The first is in Surat al-Baqarah, then in al-A'raf, then in al-Hijr, then in al-Isra', then in al-Kahf, and then here. Know also that there are several views on how this verse relates to what precedes it.

The first: when the Exalted said, ﴿Thus do We relate to you the news of what has passed﴾ (Ta-Ha: 99), and then He magnified the matter of the Qur'an and emphasised it, He mentioned this story as a fulfilment of the promise in His words, ﴿Thus do We relate to you the news of what has passed.﴾

The second: when He said, ﴿And We have diversified therein the warnings, that they may fear Allah or it may produce for them a remembrance﴾ (Ta-Ha: 113), He followed it with the story of Adam, peace be upon him, as if He said: The obedience of the children of Adam to Satan, and their neglect of guarding themselves against his whisperings, is an ancient matter. For We had already made a covenant with Adam before, meaning before these people to whom We have diversified the warnings and whom We have admonished thoroughly, when We said, ﴿Indeed, this is an enemy to you and to your wife.﴾ Yet despite that, he forgot and abandoned that covenant. So the human failure to guard against Satan is an ancient matter.

The third: when He said to Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿And say, "My Lord, increase me in knowledge"﴾ (Ta-Ha: 114), He mentioned after it the story of Adam, peace be upon him. For after Allah had made the covenant with him and had strongly reaffirmed it and warned him against the enemy, he forgot. This shows the weakness of human strength in guarding (against error), and so one needs at that point to seek help from one's Lord, that He grant him success in acquiring knowledge and preserve him from heedlessness and forgetfulness.

The fourth: when it was said to Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you﴾ (Ta-Ha: 114), this indicates that he was striving in matters of religion beyond what was obligatory. Then, when He described him with excess, He described Adam with negligence in that matter, for he was lax and did not guard himself until he forgot. Thus He described the first with negligence and the other with excess, so that it would be known that a human being is never free of some kind of lapse.

The fifth: when it was said to Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿And do not hasten﴾, his heart was constricted and he said to himself: "If I had not proceeded to what is not fitting, I would not have been forbidden from it." So it was said to him: "If you did what you were forbidden, you did it out of your eagerness for worship and your keenness to preserve the performance of the revelation. Your father Adam proceeded to what was not fitting out of laxity and abandoned guarding himself, so your situation is better than his."

As for His words, ﴿And We had already made a covenant with Adam before﴾, there is no doubt that the meaning of "covenant" here is a command from Allah, the Exalted, or a prohibition from Him, just as it is said of the commands and instructions of kings: "The king signalled to him and charged him." The exegetes said: "We charged him not to eat from the tree and not to approach it."

As for His words, ﴿before﴾, there are several views. The first: before these people to whom We have diversified the warnings in the Qur'an. The second: Ibn 'Abbas said: before he ate from the tree, We had charged him not to eat from it. The third: meaning before Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an; this is the view of al-Hasan.

As for His words, ﴿but he forgot﴾, we have discussed it thoroughly in Surat al-Baqarah, and we repeat here a little of it. Regarding forgetting, there are two views. The first: what is meant is its opposite, remembrance; he was rebuked for neglecting to guard himself and for not being meticulous in retention until forgetfulness arose from it. Al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, used to say: "By Allah, he never disobeyed except through forgetfulness." The second: the meaning of forgetting is abandoning, that he abandoned what he had been charged with, namely guarding himself from the tree, and ate from its fruit. It is read as (fa-nussiya), meaning, "Satan made him forget." On this reading, one may say that he proceeded to the disobedience without interpretation, or that he proceeded to it with an interpretation. The discussion of this has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah.

As for His words, ﴿and We found in him no resolve﴾, there are several inquiries.

The first inquiry: the verb "wajada" (found) may mean "knew," as in "and We found in him no resolve," or it may be the opposite of "non-existence," as if He said, "and We found no resolve in him."

The second inquiry: "'azm" means determination and firmness. The words ﴿and We found in him no resolve﴾ may mean: We found in him no resolve to persist in disobedience, which is closer to praise; or it may mean: We found in him no resolve to abandon disobedience; or We found in him no resolve to guard and be cautious against heedlessness; or We found in him no resolve to take precaution in the manner of exercising independent reasoning (ijtihad), if we say that he, peace be upon him, erred only through ijtihad.

As for His words, ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis, who refused﴾, this contains several issues.

The first: whether the addressees were all the angels or some of them.

The second: what is the meaning of prostration.

The third: whether Iblis was among the angels or not. If he was not, how is the exception valid, and by what means did he become commanded to prostrate?

The fourth: whether this indicates that Adam is superior to Muhammad (ﷺ) or not.

The fifth: how his refusal, described in the words "he refused," entailed disbelief, and whether he was a disbeliever from the beginning or became one because of that refusal.

Know that these issues have been discussed thoroughly in Surat al-Baqarah.

As for His words, ﴿So We said, "O Adam, indeed this is an enemy to you and to your wife, so let him not expel you both from the Garden, lest you be made wretched"﴾, there are several questions.

The first: what is the cause of that enmity? The answer has several aspects. The first: Iblis was envious, so when he saw the traces of Allah's blessings upon Adam, peace be upon him, he envied him and thus became his enemy. The second: Adam was a young man who was knowledgeable, as in His words, ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ (al-Baqarah: 31), whereas Iblis was an old man who was ignorant, because he asserted his own superiority by the nobility of his origin, and that is ignorance; and an ignorant old man is always an enemy of a knowledgeable young man. The third: Iblis was created from fire, while Adam was created from water and earth, so there is enmity between their origins, and that enmity remained.

The second question: why did He say, ﴿so let him not expel you both from the Garden﴾, when the one who expelled them from the Garden is Allah, the Exalted? The answer: since it was by his whispering that he did what resulted in the expulsion, the attribution is valid.

The third question: why was the act of wretchedness attributed to Adam alone, and not to Eve, although both shared in the act? The answer has two aspects. The first: included within the wretchedness of the man, who is the guardian of his household and their commander, is their wretchedness, just as included within his happiness is their happiness. So the statement was specifically attributed to him rather than to her, while preserving the observance of the verse-ending rhyme (fasila). The second: by wretchedness is meant toil in seeking sustenance, and that falls upon the man rather than the woman. It is related that a red ox was sent down to Adam, and he would plough with it and wipe the sweat from his brow.

As for His words, ﴿Indeed, it is granted to you that you will not hunger therein, nor be naked﴾ and ﴿And that you will not thirst therein, nor be exposed to the sun﴾, there are several issues.

The first issue: it is read as (wa-annaka) both with a fatha and with a kasra. The reading with a fatha is in coordination with (an la taju'a fīhā), "that you will not hunger therein." If it is objected that (an) does not enter upon (anna), since one does not say (an anna Zaydan muntaliqun), and the (wāw) substitutes for (anna) and stands in its place, why then was it inserted before it? We answer: the (wāw) was not established to always be a substitute for (anna); rather, it is a substitute for any governing particle. Since it is not a particle established solely for emphasis, there is no barrier to combining them, just as the combination of (an) and (anna) is barred.

The second issue: satiety, quenching of thirst, clothing, and sheltering in shade are the pivots upon which human affairs revolve. So Allah, the Exalted, mentioned that these things are attained for him in the Garden without need for earning or seeking. He mentioned them in the form of negation, against their opposites, which are hunger, nakedness, thirst, and the sun, so that some kinds of the wretchedness against which He warned him would reach his hearing, until he would be thorough in avoiding the cause that brings him into it. All these things are, as it were, an explanation of the wretchedness mentioned in His words, ﴿lest you be made wretched﴾.

[p. 108]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verse 120:

[Page 109]
His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying: "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?"﴾ ﴿So they both ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves from the Garden. And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he erred.﴾ ﴿Then his Lord chose him, turned to him in forgiveness, and guided him.﴾

Know that He, glorified is He, made clear that He honoured Adam, peace be upon him, by making him the one before whom the angels prostrated. He also made clear that He informed him of the intensity of Iblis's enmity towards him and towards his wife, and that because of his enmity he calls them to disobedience, which, once committed, causes all those blessings to vanish entirely. Then, despite this, there occurred from him and from Eve the undertaking of the slip that occurred. And what is astonishing is what is related from Abu Umamah al-Bahili, who said: "If the dreams of the children of Adam up to the Hour were placed in one pan of a scale, and the dream of Adam were placed in the other, his dream would outweigh their dreams." But striving against the decree of God, exalted is He, is impossible. Know also that the event of Adam is wondrous, because God, exalted is He, encouraged him to seek enduring comfort and a well-ordered livelihood by His saying: ﴿So let him not expel you both from the Garden, for then you will be distressed.﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is for you that you will not hunger therein nor go naked.﴾ ﴿And that you will not thirst therein nor be exposed to the sun.﴾ Iblis also encouraged him to seek enduring comfort by his saying: ﴿Shall I direct you to the tree of eternity?﴾ and to seek a well-ordered livelihood by his saying: ﴿and a kingdom that does not decay.﴾ So the thing towards which God encouraged Adam was the very thing towards which Iblis encouraged him, except that God conditioned it upon guarding against that tree, while Iblis conditioned it upon undertaking to approach it. Then, Adam, peace be upon him, despite his perfect intellect and knowledge that God, exalted is He, is his Lord, his helper and his nourisher, had been informed that Iblis is his enemy, since he refused to prostrate to him and exposed himself to the curse because of his enmity. How, in this one event and single purpose, did he accept the words of Iblis while knowing his complete enmity towards him, and turn away from the word of God, exalted is He, while knowing that He is the helper and the nourisher? Whoever reflects upon this matter will have his wonder prolonged, and will come to know in the end that this story is like an admonition that there is no repeller of God's decree and no preventer of it, and that the proof, even if it is in the utmost clarity and the highest strength, does not yield benefit by it except when God, exalted is He, decrees and determines that.

As for His saying: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him﴾, it has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah how he whispered and with what he whispered. If it is said: why did "whispered" take the preposition "li" (to/for) in His saying ﴿Then Satan whispered to them both﴾ at one point, and "ila" (to) at another? We say: His saying ﴿whispered to him﴾ means "for his sake," and His saying ﴿whispered to him﴾ means he conveyed the whispering to him, like the saying "he spoke to him" (haddatha lahu) and "he confided to him" (asarra ilayhi). Then He made clear that this whispering was by enticing him in two matters:

The first: His saying: ﴿shall I direct you to the tree of eternity?﴾ He attributed the tree to eternity (al-khuld), which is endless existence, because whoever eats from it becomes immortal according to his claim. The second: His saying: ﴿and a kingdom that does not decay﴾, meaning whoever eats from this tree, his kingdom will endure. Al-Qadi said: It is not apparent that Adam accepted this from him. Rather, if this whispering occurred while Adam, peace be upon him, was a prophet, it would be impossible for Adam, peace be upon him, to have accepted it from him, because there must be an interval between the state of obligation and the state of recompense by death. And in meaning, since Adam was a prophet, it was impossible that he would not know this. We say: We do not concede that there must be an occurrence of this interval between the state of obligation and the state of recompense. Why is it not permissible to say: there is no need for an interval at all? And if there must be one, then the occurrence of the interval by a swoon or a light sleep suffices. Then, if there must be an occurrence of the interval by death, why do you say that a prophet must know this? Do not some among you say that Moses, peace be upon him, only asked for the vision because he did not know its impossibility for God, exalted is He? If that ignorance is permissible, why is this ignorance not permissible? Furthermore, what is the proof that Adam was a prophet at that time, since our doctrine is that the event of the slip occurred before his mission and not after it? Moreover, what indicates that Adam, peace be upon him, accepted this is His saying, exalted is He, immediately after mentioning the whispering: ﴿So they both ate from it﴾, and this sequence indicates causation, like the saying: "Ma'iz committed fornication, so he was stoned," and "The Messenger of God forgot

[Page 110]
so he prostrated." For this "fa" indicates that the stoning is as the effect of the fornication, and the prostration as the effect of the forgetfulness. So likewise here, the eating must be as the consequence of hearing His saying: ﴿shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?﴾ and this causation would only occur if Adam had accepted that from him, for if he had rejected his words, he would not have proceeded to eat on the basis of his words. Thus it is established that Adam, peace be upon him, accepted that from Iblis. Then, He, glorified is He, made clear that when they both ate, their private parts became apparent to them. Ibn 'Abbas said: they were stripped of the light with which God had clothed them, until their private parts became visible. And the reason He said "their private parts" (sawatuhuma) in the plural is as He said: ﴿your hearts have inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4]. If it is said: was the appearance of their private parts like a recompense for their disobedience? We say: There is no doubt that this was like something conditioned upon that eating, but it may be that it was not a punishment for it, rather it was only consequent upon it for another benefit.

[Al-Razi, *Mafatih al-Ghayb*, commentary on verses 121–122 of Surah Ta-Ha (20)]

Regarding His saying ﴿And they began to stitch together over themselves from the leaves of the Garden﴾, there are several discussions (*abhath*, sing. *bahth*, "section").

**The first discussion:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: *taffaqa yaf'alu kadhā* is like *ja'ala yaf'alu*, *akhadha*, and *anshā'a*. Its rule regarding the predicate is the same as that of *kāda* (to be about to): the predicate is a present-tense verb. The distance between them is short. *Ṭafiqa* indicates the beginning of an action, while *kāda* indicates its approach and nearness.

**The second discussion:** It has been read as *yakhiṣṣifāni* (with intensive and repeated form), from *khaṣafa al-na'l* (to stitch the sandal), which means to sew onto it the *khiṣāf* (patches). That is, they stuck the leaf over their private parts for covering. It was the leaf of the fig tree.

As for His saying ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he went astray﴾, some people have held on to this as evidence that a major sin (*kabīrah*, a grave sin) proceeded from him, for two reasons:

The first: *al-'āṣī* (the disobedient) is a term of blame, so it applies only to the one who commits a major sin, based on His saying the Exalted: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him to a Fire, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Nisa': 14]. And there is no meaning for "the one who commits a major sin" except one who does an act for which he is punished.

The second: *al-ghawāya* and *al-ḍalāla* (going astray and error) are synonymous terms, and *al-ghayy* is the opposite of *al-rushd* (right guidance). A term like this applies only to the sinner who is immersed in his sin.

Some people answered the first argument by saying: disobedience (*al-ma'ṣiyah*) is the violation of a command, and a command may concern an obligation (*wājib*) or a recommended act (*mandūb*, a recommended act that is not obligatory). They say: "I advised him regarding his child's matter in such-and-such, and he disobeyed me," and "I ordered him to take the medicine, and he disobeyed me." If the matter is like this, there is no barrier to applying the name of disobedience to Adam, not because he abandoned an obligation, but because he abandoned a recommended act.

The one who presented the argument answered this objection by saying: we have shown that the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates that the disobedient one deserves punishment, and custom indicates that it is a term of blame. Therefore the name "disobedient" must be restricted to one who abandons an obligation. Also, if the one who abandons a recommended act were called disobedient, then all the prophets would have to be described as disobedient at all times, because they never cease to abandon recommended acts.

If it is said: describing the one who abandons a recommended act as disobedient is metaphorical, and metaphor is not consistently applied. We reply: once you concede that it is metaphorical, the default is that it is not.

As for his statement, "I advised him regarding his child's matter in such-and-such, and he disobeyed me," and "I ordered him to take the medicine, and he disobeyed me," we reply: we do not accept that this usage is transmitted from the Arabs. Even if we accept it, they use it only when they are certain regarding the one seeking counsel that he must do that act, and that it is not permissible to neglect that act. In that case, the sense of command is present even if the obligation itself is not. This indicates that the word "disobedience" may not be used except when a command is established. However, we have all agreed that a command from Allah the Exalted entails obligation. So it follows that the application of the word "disobedience" to Adam, peace be upon him, was only because he abandoned an obligation.

Some people conceded that the verse indicates that disobedience proceeded from him, but they claimed that the disobedience was a minor sin (*ṣaghīrah*) and not a major sin. This is the view of the majority of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), and it is also weak, because we have shown that the name "disobedient" is a term of blame, and because the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates that he deserves punishment, which does not befit a minor sin.

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani answered by saying that he disobeyed in matters of worldly benefit, not in matters connected with the religious obligations. The same applies to "went astray." This too is far-fetched, because worldly benefits are permissible, and one who does them is not described as disobedient, which is a term of blame. Nor is it said: ﴿So he made them fall by deception﴾ [al-A'raf: 22].

[Page 111]

As for the argument based on His saying the Exalted, ﴿and so he went astray﴾, they answered it in several ways:

The first: He lost the bliss of the Garden. This is because when he ate from that tree, in order that his kingdom might be eternal, then when he ate, it vanished. So when his striving failed and did not succeed, it was said that he went astray. The real meaning is that *al-ghayy* is the opposite of *al-rushd*, and *al-rushd* is to reach something by means of another thing that leads to the intended goal. So whoever reaches something by means of another thing, and then obtains the opposite of his intended goal, that is *ghayy*.

The second: Some said: *ghawā* means he became sated from excessive eating. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: this, even if it is valid according to the dialect of those who change a kasrah-ended *ya'* preceded by... into an *alif*, so that they say *fanā* and *baqā* for *faniya* and *baqiya*, and they are the Banu Tayy, is nonetheless a vile interpretation. Know that the better view in my opinion, and the one that most cuts off contention, is to say: this incident occurred before prophethood, and we have explained that in Surah al-Baqarah.

Here is a discussion that must be addressed: although the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates that Adam disobeyed and went astray, no one may say that Adam was a disobedient, misguided person. Several matters support our statement:

The first: Al-Utbi said: it is said of a man who cut a garment and sewed it that he cut it and sewed it, but it is not said that he is a *khā'iṭ* (tailor) or *khayyāṭ* (professional seamster) until he repeatedly does that act and is known for it. It is known that this slip did not proceed from Adam, peace be upon him, except once, so it is necessary that this name may not be applied to him.

The second: On the assumption that this incident occurred before prophethood, it is not permissible, after Allah accepted his repentance and honored him with messengership and prophethood, to apply this name to him, just as one does not say of a person who has embraced Islam after disbelief that he is a disbeliever in the sense that he was one. Indeed, even on the assumption that this incident occurred after prophethood, it would still not be permissible to say that, because he, peace be upon him, repented of it. Just as a Muslim man who drank wine or committed fornication and then repented and his repentance was good is not called afterward a wine-drinker or fornicator, so it is here.

The third: Our saying "disobedient" and "misguided" gives the false impression that he was disobedient in most matters and misguided concerning the knowledge of Allah the Exalted. These two words did not occur in the Qur'an unrestricted, but were tied to the story in which he disobeyed. So it is as if He said: "He disobeyed in such-and-such," and this does not create the false impression mentioned above.

The fourth: What is permitted for Allah the Exalted is not permitted for anyone else. Just as a master may, upon his slaves' and children's disobedience, use speech that is not permitted for anyone other than the master regarding his slave and child.

As for His saying, ﴿Then his Lord chose him, turned to him [in forgiveness], and guided him﴾, the meaning is: then He chose him, so He turned to him, i.e., returned to him with pardon and forgiveness, and guided him to his right course until he returned to remorse and seeking forgiveness, and Allah accepted that from him.

It was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "If the weeping of the people of the world were gathered together with the weeping of Dawud, his weeping would be greater. And if all of that were gathered together with the weeping of Nuh, the weeping of Nuh would be greater. He was named Nuh only because of his lamenting (*nawh*) over himself. And if all of that were gathered together with the weeping of Adam, the weeping of Adam over his sin would be greater."

Wahb said: when his weeping increased, Allah the Exalted revealed to him and commanded him to say: "There is no god but You; glory be to You, and praise be to You. I have done evil and wronged myself, so forgive me, for You are the best of forgivers." Adam, peace be upon him, said it, and then [Allah] said: Say, "There is no god but You; glory be to You, and praise be to You. I have done evil and wronged myself, so have mercy on me, for You are the most merciful of the merciful." Then He said: Say, "There is no god but You; glory be to You, and praise be to You. I have done evil and wronged myself, so accept my repentance, for You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful."

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: these are the words which Adam, peace be upon him, received from his Lord.

[Al-Razi, *Mafatih al-Ghayb*, commentary on verses 121–122 of Surah Ta-Ha (20)]

[Page 111]

As for the argument based on His saying the Exalted, ﴿and so he went astray﴾, they answered it in several ways:

The first: He lost the bliss of the Garden. This is because when he ate from that tree, in order that his kingdom might be eternal, then when he ate, it vanished. So when his striving failed and did not succeed, it was said that he went astray. The real meaning is that *al-ghayy* is the opposite of *al-rushd*, and *al-rushd* is to reach something by means of another thing that leads to the intended goal. So whoever reaches something by means of another thing, and then obtains the opposite of his intended goal, that is *ghayy*.

The second: Some said: *ghawā* means he became sated from excessive eating. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: this, even if it is valid according to the dialect of those who change a kasrah-ended *ya'* preceded by... into an *alif*, so that they say *fanā* and *baqā* for *faniya* and *baqiya*, and they are the Banu Tayy, is nonetheless a vile interpretation. Know that the better view in my opinion, and the one that most cuts off contention, is to say: this incident occurred before prophethood, and we have explained that in Surah al-Baqarah.

Here is a discussion that must be addressed: although the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates that Adam disobeyed and went astray, no one may say that Adam was a disobedient, misguided person. Several matters support our statement:

The first: Al-Utbi said: it is said of a man who cut a garment and sewed it that he cut it and sewed it, but it is not said that he is a *khā'iṭ* (tailor) or *khayyāṭ* (professional seamster) until he repeatedly does that act and is known for it. It is known that this slip did not proceed from Adam, peace be upon him, except once, so it is necessary that this name may not be applied to him.

The second: On the assumption that this incident occurred before prophethood, it is not permissible, after Allah accepted his repentance and honored him with messengership and prophethood, to apply this name to him, just as one does not say of a person who has embraced Islam after disbelief that he is a disbeliever in the sense that he was one. Indeed, even on the assumption that this incident occurred after prophethood, it would still not be permissible to say that, because he, peace be upon him, repented of it. Just as a Muslim man who drank wine or committed fornication and then repented and his repentance was good is not called afterward a wine-drinker or fornicator, so it is here.

The third: Our saying "disobedient" and "misguided" gives the false impression that he was disobedient in most matters and misguided concerning the knowledge of Allah the Exalted. These two words did not occur in the Qur'an unrestricted, but were tied to the story in which he disobeyed. So it is as if He said: "He disobeyed in such-and-such," and this does not create the false impression mentioned above.

The fourth: What is permitted for Allah the Exalted is not permitted for anyone else. Just as a master may, upon his slaves' and children's disobedience, use speech that is not permitted for anyone other than the master regarding his slave and child.

As for His saying, ﴿Then his Lord chose him, turned to him [in forgiveness], and guided him﴾, the meaning is: then He chose him, so He turned to him, i.e., returned to him with pardon and forgiveness, and guided him to his right course until he returned to remorse and seeking forgiveness, and Allah accepted that from him.

It was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "If the weeping of the people of the world were gathered together with the weeping of Dawud, his weeping would be greater. And if all of that were gathered together with the weeping of Nuh, the weeping of Nuh would be greater. He was named Nuh only because of his lamenting (*nawh*) over himself. And if all of that were gathered together with the weeping of Adam, the weeping of Adam over his sin would be greater."

Wahb said: when his weeping increased, Allah the Exalted revealed to him and commanded him to say: "There is no god but You; glory be to You, and praise be to You. I have done evil and wronged myself, so forgive me, for You are the best of forgivers." Adam, peace be upon him, said it, and then [Allah] said: Say, "There is no god but You; glory be to You, and praise be to You. I have done evil and wronged myself, so have mercy on me, for You are the most merciful of the merciful." Then He said: Say, "There is no god but You; glory be to You, and praise be to You. I have done evil and wronged myself, so accept my repentance, for You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful."

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: these are the words which Adam, peace be upon him, received from his Lord.

[Page 112]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He said, "Go down from it, all of you, as enemies to one another. But when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will not go astray, nor will he be distressed. But whoever turns away from My remembrance, indeed he will have a constricted life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind." He will say, "My Lord, why have You gathered me blind, while I was [once] seeing?" He will say, "Thus Our verses came to you, but you forgot them; and likewise today you are forgotten." And thus We recompense those who transgress and do not believe in the verses of their Lord. And the punishment of the Hereafter is severer and more enduring.﴾

Know that there is a question concerning the beginning of this verse. The statement ﴿Go down﴾ is either addressed to two persons or to more than two. If it is addressed to two persons, how does He then say ﴿when guidance comes to you from Me﴾, which is plural address? And if it is addressed to more than two, how does He say ﴿Go down﴾? The scholars have given several answers.

The first: Abu Muslim said: the address is to Adam together with his offspring, and to Iblis together with his offspring. Because the two are two kinds, the statement ﴿Go down﴾ is correct; and because each of the two kinds contains multitudes, the statement ﴿when guidance comes to you﴾ is correct.

The second: the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshaf, the Qur'an commentary of al-Zamakhshari) said: since Adam and Eve, peace be upon them, were the origin of mankind and the two sources from which it branched out, they were treated as if they were mankind themselves; so they were addressed in the manner of addressing people, and He said ﴿when guidance comes to you﴾ in the plural form.

As for His statement ﴿as enemies to one another﴾, al-Qadi said: to give this apparent meaning its due, it suffices that Iblis and the devils are enemies to humans and humans are enemies to them. When the enmity of one of the two groups toward the other is added to that, there is no obstacle to its entering the speech. And His statement ﴿when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance﴾ indicates that the intended ones are the offspring. The scholars have differed about what is meant by "guidance." Some said: the messengers. Others said: reflection and proofs. Others said: the Qur'an. The verified view is that guidance is an expression for indication, so all of that is included. And in His statement ﴿will not go astray, nor will he be distressed﴾ there is an indication that what is meant by the guidance whose following Allah has guaranteed is the following of the proofs, and following them is not complete except by reasoning with them and acting upon them. Whoever is in this condition, Allah the Exalted has guaranteed him that he will not go astray and will not be distressed. And concerning this there are three aspects:

The first: he will not go astray in this world, nor be distressed in the Hereafter.
The second: he will not go astray and will not be distressed in the Hereafter, because Allah the Exalted guides him to Paradise and establishes him therein.
The third: he will not go astray and will not be distressed in this world.

If it is said: one who follows the guidance of Allah may nevertheless be afflicted with distress in this world, we reply: what is meant is that he will not go astray in religion, and will not be distressed because of religion. If distress arises from another cause, there is no harm.

When Allah the Exalted had promised those who follow guidance, He followed it with a threat concerning those who turn away, saying: ﴿But whoever turns away from My remembrance﴾. The "remembrance" (dhikr) applies to the Qur'an and to the rest of Allah's books, as its explanation has preceded; and it may be understood to mean the proofs.

As for His statement ﴿indeed he will have a constricted life﴾: "ḍankan" (constricted) originally means narrowness and hardship, and it is a verbal noun which is then used as a descriptive, so one says "a constricted dwelling" and "a constricted life." It is as if He said: a life possessing constriction. Know that this constriction threatened is either in this world, or in the grave, or in the Hereafter, or in religion, or in all of that or most of it.

As for the first: a group of exegetes held this view, because the Muslim, through his reliance upon Allah, lives in this world a good life, as He said: ﴿We will surely give him a good life﴾ [al-Nahl: 97]. The disbeliever in Allah is greedy for this world, always seeking more, so his life is constricted and his state is dark.

And [also] among the disbelievers are those upon whom Allah has imposed humiliation and destitution because of their disbelief. He the Exalted said: ﴿Humiliation and destitution were stamped upon them, and they returned with anger from Allah. That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61]. And He said: ﴿Had they established the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 66]. And He the Exalted said: ﴿Had the people of the towns believed and been mindful of Allah, We would have opened for them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 96]. And He said: ﴿Seek forgiveness of your Lord; indeed He is Ever-Forgiving. He will send down the sky upon you in abundant rain, and provide you with wealth and children﴾ [Nuh: 10–12]. And He said: ﴿And if they had remained upon the way, We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾ [al-Jinn: 16].

As for the second, which is the constriction of the grave, this is the view of ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, and ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas. Abu Hurayrah traced it back to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed the punishment of the grave is for the disbeliever," and he said, "By Him in whose hand my soul is, indeed ninety-nine dragons will be set upon him in his grave." Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the verse was revealed concerning al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzza al-Makhzumi. And what is meant is the squeezing of the grave, in which his ribs will be interlocked.

As for the third, which is the narrowness in the Hereafter in Hell: their food therein will be ḍarīʿ (a thorny plant) and zaqqum (a tree of Hell), and their drink will be ḥamīm (boiling water) and ghislin (the pus of the people of Hell). They will neither die therein nor live. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Kalbi.

As for the fourth, which is the narrowness in matters of religion: Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the constricted life is that the doors of goodness are closed to him, so he is not guided to anything of them. al-Shibli was asked about his (ʿalayhi al-salam) statement: "When you see the people of affliction, ask Allah for well-being." He said: the people of affliction are the people of heedlessness of Allah the Exalted, so their punishment is that Allah returns them to themselves. And what constriction is narrower and more severe than that a person be returned to himself? It is related from ʿAta' that he said: the constricted life is the life of the disbeliever, because he is not certain of reward and punishment.

As for the fifth, which is that what is meant is constriction in all of that or most of it: it is narrated from ʿAli, peace be upon him, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The punishment for disobedience is threefold: constriction of livelihood, hardship in adversity, and that he cannot obtain his sustenance except through disobedience to Allah the Exalted."

As for His statement ﴿and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾, there are several aspects:

The first: this is like His statement ﴿and We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, mute, and deaf﴾ [al-Isra': 97]. And just as "zurqa" (blue-eyed, i.e., with a bluish cast) was explained as blindness, it is said: he will be gathered seeing, but when he is driven to the place of gathering he becomes blind. The discussion of this and about it has already passed under His statement ﴿zurqan﴾.

The second: Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and Muqatil said: it means blind to the proof. This is also the narration of Saʿid ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. al-Qadi said: this view is weak, because on the Day of Resurrection Allah must make them know the falsity of what they were upon, until the truth becomes distinguished for them from falsehood. Someone in this condition is described as such only metaphorically, and what is meant is that he was like that before that. And His statement ﴿while I was [once] seeing﴾ does not fit with this, for he was not like that in the state of this world.

I say: what reinforces this objection is that He the Exalted gave as the reason for that blindness the fact that the responsible person forgot the proofs in this world. If the blindness occurring in the Hereafter were the consequence of that forgetting, it would bring no harm to the responsible person because of it, just as it brought him no harm in this world because of it. Know that the verification of the answer to this objection is derived from another matter, namely that the ignorant souls in this world, separated from their bodies while still in their ignorance, remain in that ignorance in the Hereafter, and that this ignorance becomes there a cause of the greatest spiritual pains. Between this method and the method of al-Qadi, which is based on the principles of the Mu'tazila (a school of rationalist theology), there is a great distance.

The third: al-Jubba'i said: what is meant by His gathering him blind is that he will not be guided on the Day of Resurrection to any path from which he gains good; rather he will remain standing, bewildered, like a blind man who is not guided to anything.

As for His statement ﴿He will say, "My Lord, why have You gathered me blind, while I was [once] seeing?" He will say, "Thus Our verses came to you, but you forgot them; and likewise today you are forgotten."﴾ There are two aspects to the explanation of this answer:

The first: He the Exalted only sent this blindness upon him as a recompense for his abandoning the following of guidance and turning away from it.

The second: the human souls, when they separate from their bodies ignorant and astray from connection with the spiritual realities, remain in that state after separation, and the spiritual pains are magnified. For this reason Allah the Exalted gave as the cause of the occurrence of blindness in the Hereafter the turning away from the proofs in this world. As for the one who interpreted the constricted life as constriction in this world, he said: He the Exalted made clear that whoever turns away from His remembrance in this world, for him is a constricted life in this world and blindness in the Hereafter.

As for His statement ﴿And thus We recompense those who transgress and do not believe in the verses of their Lord﴾: the scholars have differed concerning it. Some said: he associated partners with Allah and disbelieved. Others said: he transgressed by disobeying Allah. He the Exalted has clarified what is meant by that in His statement ﴿and do not believe in the verses of their Lord﴾, because that is like an explanation of His statement "transgressed." And He made clear that He recompenses one in this condition with what has been mentioned before, namely the constricted life and blindness. Then He made clear after that that the punishment of the Hereafter is severer and more enduring. As for "severer," it is because of its magnitude; and as for "more enduring," it is because it is not cut off.
