**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 20, verses 128–131:**

God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Has it not guided them how many generations We destroyed before them, among whose dwellings they walk? Indeed in that are signs for people of intellect (ulî al-nuhâ)﴾ ﴿And were it not for a word that had preceded from your Lord, it would have been inevitable, and a specified term﴾ ﴿So be patient over what they say, and glorify your Lord with His praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting, and during the hours of the night glorify Him, and at the ends of the day, that you may be pleased﴾.

Know that when God, exalted is He, explained how the one who turns away from His remembrance will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection, He followed this with what the responsible person (al-mukallaf) should take as a lesson from the circumstances in this world concerning those who denied the messengers. So He said: ﴿Has it not guided them﴾. The commonly read recitation is أفَلَمْ يَهْدِ with the yâ' marked with a dot below (بِالياءِ المُعْجَمَةِ مِن تَحْتُ), and its subject (fâ'il) is His words: ﴿how many generations We destroyed﴾. Al-Qaffal said: He made the great number of those whom He destroyed from the generations a clarification for them, just as He made the like of that an admonition and a deterrent for them.

Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read أفَلَمْ نَهْدِ لَهُمْ with the nûn. Al-Zajjaj said: This means, "Have We not made clear to them a clarification by which they would be guided, if they had reflected and contemplated?"

As for His words ﴿how many we destroyed﴾, the intended meaning is to emphasize the great number of those whom God, exalted is He, destroyed from the past generations. By His words ﴿among whose dwellings they walk﴾ He means that the Quraysh witness those great signs which indicate the blessings they had enjoyed and the various kinds of destruction that befell them. There is a lesson in witnessing these things that is not found otherwise. He explained that in those signs there are signs for ulî al-nuhâ, that is, for people of intellect. The more accurate view is that al-nuhâ (intellect/restraint) has a distinction over ʿaql (reason), and the term al-nuhâ is used only of one who has a reason by which he restrains himself from ugly deeds. Just as our saying ulû al-ʿazm (people of resolve) has a distinction over ulû al-ḥazm (people of firm judgment), so some have said: "They are the people of scrupulousness (al-waraʿ) and of piety (al-taqwâ)."

Then God, exalted is He, explained the reason why punishment is not sent down immediately upon those who denied and disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ). So He said: ﴿And were it not for a word that had preceded from your Lord, it would have been inevitable, and a specified term﴾. There is an inversion (taqdîm wa-taʾkhîr) in this, and the sense is: "And were it not for a word that had preceded from your Lord and a specified term, it would have been inevitable." There is no doubt that the "word" is God's informing His angels, and His writing in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfûẓ), that his community (peace be upon him), even if they deny, will be delayed, and will not be treated as others are treated with total annihilation (al-istiʾṣāl). They differed regarding the reason why this was not done to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). Some said: Because He knew that among them there would be one who believes. Others said: He knew that among their offspring there would be one who believes, and if He had sent punishment upon them, destruction would have engulfed them all. Others said: The wisdom in this is hidden, and none knows it but Him. The People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) said: He has, by the judgment of sovereignty (bi-ḥukm al-mâlikiyya), the right to single out whomever He wills with His grace and whomever He wills with His punishment, without any cause. For if His act were for a cause, then if that cause were eternal, the act would have to be eternal, and if it were originated, it would require another cause, and this would lead to an infinite regress (al-tasalsul). Therefore the people of verification (ahl al-taḥqîq) said: Everything He does is without a cause.

As for the "specified term," there are two views. The first: "And were it not for a specified term in this world for that punishment, which is the day of Badr." The second: "And were it not for a specified term in the Hereafter for that punishment." This second view is closer. The meaning would be: "And were it not for a word that includes the postponement of the punishment until the Hereafter, as in His words ﴿Nay, the Hour is their appointed time﴾ [al-Qamar: 46], the punishment would have been inevitable for them for what they undertake of denying the Messenger and harming him."

Then, when God, exalted is He, informed His Prophet that He would not destroy anyone before the fulfilment of his term, He commanded him to be patient over what they say. There is no doubt that what is intended is that he should be patient over what they say that he dislikes. This may be the saying of some of them: "He is a sorcerer, or a madman, or a poet," and so on. It may also mean their denial of him regarding what he claims of prophethood. And it may also mean their refusal to accept from him. For all of that is something that grieves him and harms him. So God, exalted is He, encouraged him to be patient and urged him to persist in calling to God, exalted is He, and conveying what he had been entrusted with of the message, and not to let what they undertake divert him from that.

Then al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: This verse is abrogated (mansûkha) by the verse of fighting (âyat al-qitâl). [Note: naskh (abrogation) means that a later ruling removes the effect of an earlier one.] Then He said: ﴿and glorify your Lord with His praise﴾, and this is similar to His words: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqara: 45]. There are several issues in this:

The first issue: ﴿with the praise of your Lord﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥâl), meaning: "while you are praising your Lord for having granted you success in glorifying Him and having helped you in it."

The second issue: He commanded glorification after patience only because the remembrance of God, exalted is He, brings consolation and rest, since there is no rest for the believers except in meeting God, exalted is He.

The third issue: They differed about tasbîḥ (glorification) in two ways. Most of them held that what is intended by it is prayer (al-ṣalâ), and these differed in three ways. The first: the verse indicates that the five daily prayers are neither more nor fewer. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: The five prayers are included in it. Before the rising of the sun is the Fajr prayer, and before its setting is the Dhuhr and ʿAṣr prayers, since both are before sunset. "And during the hours of the night, glorify Him" is Maghrib and the final ʿIshâʾ. His words "and at the ends of the day" serve as an emphasis for the two prayers falling at the two ends of the day, which are the Fajr prayer and the Maghrib prayer, just as the middle prayer (al-ṣalât al-wusṭâ) was singled out for emphasis in His words: ﴿and the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqara: 238].

The second view: The verse indicates the five daily prayers plus an addition. As for its indication of the five prayers, it is because the time is either before the rising of the sun or before its setting, so night and day are included in these two expressions, and thus the times of the obligatory prayers are included in them. What remains is His words: "during the hours of the night glorify Him, and at the ends of the day," and "the ends of the day" are for the voluntary prayers (al-nawâfil).

The third view: It indicates fewer than five. The first view is stronger and more deserving of consideration.

All of this applies if we take tasbîḥ as prayer. Abu Muslim said: It is not far-fetched to take it as declaring God free of imperfection (al-tanzîh) and exalting Him (al-ijlâl), and the meaning would be: "Occupy yourself with declaring God, exalted is He, free of imperfection during these times." This view is closer to the apparent meaning and to what was mentioned earlier. That is because He first made him patient over what they say, namely their denial of him and their manifesting of polytheism and disbelief, and what befits that is to command him to declare God free of what they say, so that he would always manifest that and call to it. Therefore He said what encompasses all times.

The fourth issue: The best remembrance is that which is done at night, because gathering of the heart is greater in it. This is due to the stillness of people, the calm of their movements, and the idling of the senses from motion and from work. For this reason, the Glorified and Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the rising at night is firmer in tread and more upright in speech﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 6], and He said: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter...﴾ [al-Zumar: 9]. Also, because night is the time of quiet and rest, when it is devoted to worship it is harder on the souls and more exhausting for the body, so it is more deserving of reward and grace.

The fifth issue: Someone may say: The day has two ends, so how did He say "the ends of the day" (aṭrâf al-nahâr)? Rather, the better expression would have been as He said: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day﴾ [Hud: 114]?

The answer: Some people said: The minimum of a plural is two, so the question falls away. Others said: It was put in the plural because it recurs in every day and returns.

As for His words ﴿that you may be pleased (laʿallaka tarḍâ)﴾, there are several views. The first: This is like a great king saying: "O so-and-so, busy yourself with the service, perhaps you will benefit from it." The meaning is: "I will bring you to a high rank of blessing." This is an allusion to His words: ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be pleased﴾ [al-Ḍuḥâ: 5], and His words: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ [al-Isrâ: 79]. The second: "that you may be pleased with what you receive of reward." The third: "that you may be pleased with what you receive of intercession." Al-Kisa'i and ʿAsim read لَعَلَّكَ تُرْضى with a ḍamma on the tâʾ (taʾ), and the meaning does not differ, because when God, exalted is He, causes him to be pleased, then He is pleased with him, and when He is pleased with him, then He has caused him to be pleased.

The second issue: He commanded glorification after patience only because the remembrance of God, exalted is He, brings consolation and rest, since there is no rest for the believers except in meeting God, exalted is He.

The third issue: They differed about tasbîḥ (glorification) in two ways. Most of them held that what is intended by it is prayer (al-ṣalâ), and these differed in three ways. The first: the verse indicates that the five daily prayers are neither more nor fewer. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: The five prayers are included in it. Before the rising of the sun is the Fajr prayer, and before its setting is the Dhuhr and ʿAṣr prayers, since both are before sunset. "And during the hours of the night, glorify Him" is Maghrib and the final ʿIshâʾ. His words "and at the ends of the day" serve as an emphasis for the two prayers falling at the two ends of the day, which are the Fajr prayer and the Maghrib prayer, just as the middle prayer (al-ṣalât al-wusṭâ) was singled out for emphasis in His words: ﴿and the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqara: 238].

The second view: The verse indicates the five daily prayers plus an addition. As for its indication of the five prayers, it is because the time is either before the rising of the sun or before its setting, so night and day are included in these two expressions, and thus the times of the obligatory prayers are included in them. What remains is His words: "during the hours of the night glorify Him, and at the ends of the day," and "the ends of the day" are for the voluntary prayers (al-nawâfil).

The third view: It indicates fewer than five. So His words "before the rising of the sun" refer to Fajr, "before its setting" refer to ʿAṣr, and "during the hours of the night" refer to Maghrib and ʿAtama (ʿIshâʾ), leaving Dhuhr outside. The first view is stronger and more deserving of consideration.

All of this applies if we take tasbîḥ as prayer. Abu Muslim said: It is not far-fetched to take it as declaring God free of imperfection (al-tanzîh) and exalting Him (al-ijlâl), and the meaning would be: "Occupy yourself with declaring God, exalted is He, free of imperfection during these times." This view is closer to the apparent meaning and to what was mentioned earlier. That is because He first made him patient over what they say, namely their denial of him and their manifesting of polytheism and disbelief, and what befits that is to command him to declare God free of what they say, so that he would always manifest that and call to it. Therefore He said what encompasses all times.

The fourth issue: The best remembrance is that which is done at night, because gathering of the heart is greater in it. This is due to the stillness of people, the calm of their movements, and the idling of the senses from motion and from work. For this reason, the Glorified and Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the rising at night is firmer in tread and more upright in speech﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 6], and He said: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter...﴾ [al-Zumar: 9]. Also, because night is the time of quiet and rest, when it is devoted to worship it is harder on the souls and more exhausting for the body, so it is more deserving of reward and grace.

The fifth issue: Someone may say: The day has two ends, so how did He say "the ends of the day" (aṭrâf al-nahâr)? Rather, the better expression would have been as He said: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day﴾ [Hud: 114]?

The answer: Some people said: The minimum of a plural is two, so the question falls away. Others said: It was put in the plural because it recurs in every day and returns.

As for His words ﴿that you may be pleased (laʿallaka tarḍâ)﴾, there are several views. The first: This is like a great king saying: "O so-and-so, busy yourself with the service, perhaps you will benefit from it." The meaning is: "I will bring you to a high rank of blessing." This is an allusion to His words: ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be pleased﴾ [al-Ḍuḥâ: 5], and His words: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ [al-Isrâ: 79]. The second: "that you may be pleased with what you receive of reward." The third: "that you may be pleased with what you receive of intercession." Al-Kisa'i and ʿAsim read لَعَلَّكَ تُرْضى with a ḍamma on the tâʾ (taʾ), and the meaning does not differ, because when God, exalted is He, causes him to be pleased, then He is pleased with him, and when He is pleased with him, then He has caused him to be pleased.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 20, verses 128–131:**

God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Has it not guided them how many generations We destroyed before them, among whose dwellings they walk? Indeed in that are signs for people of intellect (ulî al-nuhâ)﴾ ﴿And were it not for a word that had preceded from your Lord, it would have been inevitable, and a specified term﴾ ﴿So be patient over what they say, and glorify your Lord with His praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting, and during the hours of the night glorify Him, and at the ends of the day, that you may be pleased﴾.

Know that when God, exalted is He, explained how the one who turns away from His remembrance will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection, He followed this with what the responsible person (al-mukallaf) should take as a lesson from the circumstances in this world concerning those who denied the messengers. So He said: ﴿Has it not guided them﴾. The commonly read recitation is أفَلَمْ يَهْدِ with the yâ' marked with a dot below (بِالياءِ المُعْجَمَةِ مِن تَحْتُ), and its subject (fâ'il) is His words: ﴿how many generations We destroyed﴾. Al-Qaffal said: He made the great number of those whom He destroyed from the generations a clarification for them, just as He made the like of that an admonition and a deterrent for them.

Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read أفَلَمْ نَهْدِ لَهُمْ with the nûn. Al-Zajjaj said: This means, "Have We not made clear to them a clarification by which they would be guided, if they had reflected and contemplated?"

As for His words ﴿how many we destroyed﴾, the intended meaning is to emphasize the great number of those whom God, exalted is He, destroyed from the past generations. By His words ﴿among whose dwellings they walk﴾ He means that the Quraysh witness those great signs which indicate the blessings they had enjoyed and the various kinds of destruction that befell them. There is a lesson in witnessing these things that is not found otherwise. He explained that in those signs there are signs for ulî al-nuhâ, that is, for people of intellect. The more accurate view is that al-nuhâ (intellect/restraint) has a distinction over ʿaql (reason), and the term al-nuhâ is used only of one who has a reason by which he restrains himself from ugly deeds. Just as our saying ulû al-ʿazm (people of resolve) has a distinction over ulû al-ḥazm (people of firm judgment), so some have said: "They are the people of scrupulousness (al-waraʿ) and of piety (al-taqwâ)."

Then God, exalted is He, explained the reason why punishment is not sent down immediately upon those who denied and disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ). So He said: ﴿And were it not for a word that had preceded from your Lord, it would have been inevitable, and a specified term﴾. There is an inversion (taqdîm wa-taʾkhîr) in this, and the sense is: "And were it not for a word that had preceded from your Lord and a specified term, it would have been inevitable." There is no doubt that the "word" is God's informing His angels, and His writing in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfûẓ), that his community (peace be upon him), even if they deny, will be delayed, and will not be treated as others are treated with total annihilation (al-istiʾṣāl). They differed regarding the reason why this was not done to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). Some said: Because He knew that among them there would be one who believes. Others said: He knew that among their offspring there would be one who believes, and if He had sent punishment upon them, destruction would have engulfed them all. Others said: The wisdom in this is hidden, and none knows it but Him. The People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) said: He has, by the judgment of sovereignty (bi-ḥukm al-mâlikiyya), the right to single out whomever He wills with His grace and whomever He wills with His punishment, without any cause. For if His act were for a cause, then if that cause were eternal, the act would have to be eternal, and if it were originated, it would require another cause, and this would lead to an infinite regress (al-tasalsul). Therefore the people of verification (ahl al-taḥqîq) said: Everything He does is without a cause.

As for the "specified term," there are two views. The first: "And were it not for a specified term in this world for that punishment, which is the day of Badr." The second: "And were it not for a specified term in the Hereafter for that punishment." This second view is closer. The meaning would be: "And were it not for a word that includes the postponement of the punishment until the Hereafter, as in His words ﴿Nay, the Hour is their appointed time﴾ [al-Qamar: 46], the punishment would have been inevitable for them for what they undertake of denying the Messenger and harming him."

Then, when God, exalted is He, informed His Prophet that He would not destroy anyone before the fulfilment of his term, He commanded him to be patient over what they say. There is no doubt that what is intended is that he should be patient over what they say that he dislikes. This may be the saying of some of them: "He is a sorcerer, or a madman, or a poet," and so on. It may also mean their denial of him regarding what he claims of prophethood. And it may also mean their refusal to accept from him. For all of that is something that grieves him and harms him. So God, exalted is He, encouraged him to be patient and urged him to persist in calling to God, exalted is He, and conveying what he had been entrusted with of the message, and not to let what they undertake divert him from that.

Then al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: This verse is abrogated (mansûkha) by the verse of fighting (âyat al-qitâl). [Note: naskh (abrogation) means that a later ruling removes the effect of an earlier one.] Then He said: ﴿and glorify your Lord with His praise﴾, and this is similar to His words: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾ [al-Baqara: 45]. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verses 132–135 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And do not extend your eyes toward what We have given enjoyment to some pairs of them, the splendour of the worldly life, that We may test them therein. But the provision of your Lord is better and more enduring.﴾ ﴿And enjoin prayer upon your family, and be steadfast in it. We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you. And the good end is for righteousness.﴾ ﴿And they say, "Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?" Has there not come to them the clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your verses before we are humiliated and disgraced?"﴾ ﴿Say, "Each is waiting, so wait. You will soon know who are the companions of the even path and who is rightly guided."﴾

Know that when Allah had made His Messenger, peace be upon him, patient regarding what they say, and had commanded him to turn instead to glorification (tasbih), He followed that with His prohibition against extending his eyes toward what He had given enjoyment to those people. So He said: ﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾, and in this there are issues.

The first issue: Regarding His saying ﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾ there are two aspects. The first: what is meant is the gaze of the eye. Those who say this state: extending the gaze (mad al-nazar) means prolonging it, and not turning it back, out of admiration for the thing looked upon and wonder at it, as the onlookers of Qarun did when they said: ﴿Oh, would that we had the like of what Qarun has been given. Indeed, he is one of great fortune﴾ [Al-Qasas: 79], until those who had knowledge and faith confronted them with their words: ﴿Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better for one who believes and does righteousness﴾ [Al-Qasas: 80]. And in this is that a gaze which is not extended is pardoned, as when a person looks at something once and then lowers his gaze. Since looking at adornments is almost inherent in human nature, it was said: ﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾, meaning: do not do what you are accustomed to do. The pious have been strict regarding the obligation of lowering the gaze from the buildings of the oppressors and the equipment of the corrupt, in clothing, mounts and other things, because they have made these things for the eyes of onlookers; so whoever looks at them fulfils their purpose and is, as it were, strengthening them in acquiring them.

The second aspect: Abu Muslim said: what is forbidden by His saying ﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾ is not looking, but grief; that is, do not grieve over what has escaped you of the worldly portion they have attained.

The second issue: Abu Rafi' said: "A guest came to the Prophet ﷺ, so he sent me to a Jew to sell or borrow against something. He said, 'By Allah, I will not do that except against a pledge.' I informed him of his words, and he commanded me to take his coat of mail to him. Then the saying of Allah the Exalted was revealed: ﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾." And he, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed Allah does not look at your forms nor at your wealth, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds."

Abu al-Darda' said: The world is the home of one who has no home, and the wealth of one who has no wealth, and for it gathers one who has no intellect. Al-Hasan said: Were it not for the foolishness of people, the world would have been ruined. It is reported from Isa son of Maryam, peace be upon him, that he said: Do not take the world as a lord lest it take you as its slaves. It is reported from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr that whenever he saw what was with the rulers, he would recite this verse and say: "The prayer, may Allah have mercy on you."

As for His saying ﴿what We have given enjoyment to﴾ [i.e.] We made them delight in it. Imti' (enjoyment) is delighting in what is perceived of beautiful sights, what is heard of melodious sounds, what is smelled of pleasant fragrances, and other things such as garments and marriages. It is said: amta'ahu imta'an and matta'ahu tamtee'an, and the tafil form implies intensity. As for His saying ﴿pairs of them﴾, meaning kinds and similar ones among the disbelievers; it derives from pairing things together, which is similarity. This is because they are alike in going astray from the right course. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: kinds of them. Al-Kalbi and al-Zajjaj said: men of them.

As for His saying ﴿the splendour of the worldly life﴾, there are four possibilities regarding its case. The first: it is in the accusative of dispraise, or in the accusative of specification, or as a second object implied by the meaning of "matta'na" as "a'taina", or as a substitute for the place of the prepositional phrase, or as a substitute for "azwajan" on the assumption of "dhawi" (possessors of). If it is asked: what is the meaning of zahra for those who vowelise it with a fatha? We say: zahra has the same meaning, namely adornment and radiance, as in "al-jahra" in the recitation "Show us Allah openly (jahratan)". It may also be the plural of "zahir", describing them as the splendour of this world, for the brightness of their complexions and the radiance of their faces, in contrast to the pallor of complexion and austerity of clothing found among the righteous.

As for His saying ﴿that We may test them therein﴾, they have mentioned several aspects regarding it. The first: that We may punish them thereby, as in His saying: ﴿So let not their wealth nor their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them thereby in the life of this world﴾ [At-Tawbah: 55]. The second: Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: a misguidance from Me for them. The third: al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: a tightening of the obligation upon them, because turning away from the world when it is present and turning to Allah is harder than that when it is absent. For this reason the return of the poor to the service of Allah the Exalted and their supplication to Him is greater than the supplication of the rich. Also, those who are given the world have various kinds of obligations which would not have been binding upon them without it. Also, one who is capable of sins finds avoidance of sins harder for him than one who is poor and incapable. For these reasons, increase in worldly things is a tightening of the obligation.

Then He said to His Messenger: ﴿But the provision of your Lord is better and more enduring.﴾ The more apparent meaning is that what you seek, which you find of reward, is better than what they seek, and more enduring, because it lasts and does not cease, whereas that is not the case with what they have been given of the world. It may also be that what is meant is that what you have been given of the little of the world, when you combine it with obedience, is better for you in terms of its end and more enduring. So He mentioned provision in the world and described it by the goodness of its outcome when one is content with it and patient with it. It may also be that what is meant is what he was given of prophethood and lofty ranks.

As for His saying ﴿And enjoin prayer upon your family﴾, some understood it as his relatives, and some understood it as all the people of his religion, and this is closer. It is like His saying: ﴿And he used to enjoin his family to prayer and zakat﴾ [Maryam: 55]. Although it may be that what is meant is those who share his dwelling, since drawing attention to prayer and commanding it at its times is possible for them and not for the rest of the community; that is, just as We commanded you to pray, so you command your people to it. As for His saying ﴿and be steadfast in it﴾, what is meant is: as you command them, so maintain it by action, for admonition by the tongue of action is more complete than by the tongue of speech. "After the revelation of this verse, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to go to Fatimah and Ali, peace be upon them both, every morning and say: 'The prayer,' and he did this for months."

Then Allah the Exalted explained that He commands them with this only for their benefit, and that He is exalted above benefits, by His saying: ﴿We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you.﴾ And in this there are aspects. The first: Abu Muslim said: the meaning is that Allah only wants from him and from them worship, and does not want from him that He should provide for him, as masters want tribute from slaves. It is like His saying: ﴿I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me. I do not want from them any provision, nor do I want that they should feed Me﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 56–57]. The second: "We do not ask you for provision" for yourself nor for your family; rather, We provide for you and provide for your family, so empty your mind for the affairs of the Hereafter. Its meaning is the saying of people: whoever is in the service of Allah, Allah will be in his service. The third: the meaning is that when We commanded you to pray, it was not because We benefit from your prayer; so He expressed this meaning by His saying: "We do not ask you for provision," but rather We provide for you in the world with forms of blessings and in the Hereafter with reward. Abdullah ibn Salam said: "When distress or hardship came upon the family of the Prophet ﷺ, he would command them to pray, and recite this verse."

Know that there is no concession in this verse for abandoning earning a livelihood, for He, the Exalted, said in describing the righteous: ﴿men whom neither commerce nor trade diverts from the remembrance of Allah﴾ [An-Nur: 37]. As for His saying "and the good end is for righteousness", what is meant is that the good outcome is for the people of taqwa, meaning the taqwa of Allah the Exalted.

Then, after this instruction, He, glory be to Him, related their doubt, as if it were part of the completion of His saying: ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾; and it is their saying: ﴿Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?﴾ By this speech they were deceived into thinking that He imposes faith upon them without a sign. In another place they said: ﴿Let him bring us a sign, as the former messengers were sent﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 5]. Allah the Exalted answered this with His saying: ﴿Has there not come to them the clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ And in this there are aspects. The first: that what is in the Qur'an agrees with what is in their books, although the Messenger ﷺ did not occupy himself with study and learning, and had never seen a teacher at all; so this would be a report of the unseen, and thus a miracle. The second: the clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures is what they contain of glad tidings concerning Muhammad ﷺ, his prophethood and his mission. The third: Ibn Jarir and al-Qaffal mentioned that the meaning of ﴿Has there not come to them the clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ is: the news of the nations whom We destroyed when they asked for signs and disbelieved in them, how We hastened punishment upon them; so what would secure them that their condition in asking for signs would not be like the condition of those? This clarification has come to them in the Qur'an, and for this reason He described the Qur'an as ﴿the clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures﴾. Know that He mentioned the pronoun referring to "clear evidence" because it carries the sense of proof and argument. Then He explained that Allah the Exalted removed from them every excuse and pretext regarding the obligation, and so He said: ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger?"﴾ The meaning is that they would have had the right to say this, and it would have been an excuse for them. But now, since We have sent you and made clear through your tongue to them what is upon them and what is for them, they have no argument at all; rather the argument is against them. The phrase ﴿before it﴾ may mean before the sending of the Messenger, or before the clear signs he displayed. If it is asked: what is the meaning of His saying "And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said", while the one destroyed cannot speak? We say: the meaning is that they would have had the right to say this on the Day of Resurrection; and for this reason He said: ﴿before we are humiliated and disgraced﴾, and that is appropriate only for the punishment of the Hereafter. It is reported that Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Three will argue before Allah the Exalted on the Day of Resurrection: the one who died in the interval (fatra) says: 'No messenger came to me, otherwise I would have been the most obedient of Your creation to You,' and he recited His saying: ﴿Why did You not send to us a messenger?﴾; and the one whose mind was overcome says: 'You did not make for me a mind by which I might benefit'; and the child says: 'I was young and did not understand.' Then a fire is raised for them, and it is said to them: 'Enter it.' Whoever was in Allah's knowledge to be wretched enters it, and whoever was in His knowledge to be happy remains. Then Allah the Exalted says to them: 'You disobeyed today; so how would you have fared had My messengers come to you?'" The judge (al-Qadi) criticised the report and said: it is not fitting to punish one who does not understand.

* * *

Know that in this verse there are issues:

The first issue: al-Jubba'i said: this verse indicates the obligation of performing lutf (grace), for the meaning is that it is obligatory for Him to do for the responsible persons that by which they would believe if He had done it; and if He had not done it, they would have had the right to say: "Why did You not do that for us so that we would believe? Why did You not send to us a messenger so that we would follow Your verses?" And if it is known that they would not believe even if He sent the messenger to them, there would be no argument in that; so it is established that it is an argument for them only when it is known that they would believe at His hand if they obeyed Him.

Indeed, he is one of great fortune﴾ [Al-Qasas: 79], until those who had knowledge and faith confronted them with their words: ﴿Woe to you! And in this is that a gaze which is not extended is pardoned, as when a person looks at something once and then lowers his gaze. Since looking at adornments is almost inherent in human nature, it was said: ﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾, meaning: do not do what you are accustomed to do. The pious have been strict regarding the obligation of lowering the gaze from the buildings of the oppressors and the equipment of the corrupt, in clothing, mounts and other things, because they have made these things for the eyes of onlookers; so whoever looks at them fulfils their purpose and is, as it were, strengthening them in acquiring them.

The second aspect: Abu Muslim said: what is forbidden by His saying ﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾ is not looking, but grief; that is, do not grieve over what has escaped you of the worldly portion they have attained.

The second issue: Abu Rafi' said: "A guest came to the Prophet ﷺ, so he sent me to a Jew to sell or borrow against something. He said, 'By Allah, I will not do that except against a pledge.' And he, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed Allah does not look at your forms nor at your wealth, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds."

Abu al-Darda' said: The world is the home of one who has no home, and the wealth of one who has no wealth, and for it gathers one who has no intellect. Al-Hasan said: Were it not for the foolishness of people, the world would have been ruined. It is reported from Isa son of Maryam, peace be upon him, that he said: Do not take the world as a lord lest it take you as its slaves. It is said: amta'ahu imta'an and matta'ahu tamtee'an, and the tafil form implies intensity. As for His saying ﴿pairs of them﴾, meaning kinds and similar ones among the disbelievers; it derives from pairing things together, which is similarity. This is because they are alike in going astray from the right course. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: kinds of them. Al-Kalbi and al-Zajjaj said: men of them.

As for His saying ﴿the splendour of the worldly life﴾, there are four possibilities regarding its case. It may also be that what is meant is what he was given of prophethood and lofty ranks.

This clarification has come to them in the Qur'an, and for this reason He described the Qur'an as ﴿the clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures﴾. Then He explained that Allah the Exalted removed from them every excuse and pretext regarding the obligation, and so He said: ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger?"﴾ The meaning is that they would have had the right to say this, and it would have been an excuse for them. It is reported that Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Three will argue before Allah the Exalted on the Day of Resurrection: the one who died in the interval (fatra) says: 'No messenger came to me, otherwise I would have been the most obedient of Your creation to You,' and he recited His saying: ﴿Why did You not send to us a messenger?﴾; and the one whose mind was overcome says: 'You did not make for me a mind by which I might benefit'; and the child says: 'I was young and did not understand.' * * *

Know that in this verse there are issues:

The first issue: al-Jubba'i said: this verse indicates the obligation of performing lutf (grace), for the meaning is that it is obligatory for Him to do for the responsible persons that by which they would believe if He had done it; and if He had not done it, they would have had the right to say: "Why did You not do that for us so that we would believe? Why did You not send to us a messenger so that we would follow Your verses?" And if it is known that they would not believe even if He sent the messenger to them, there would be no argument in that; so it is established that it is an argument for them only when it is known that they would believe at His hand if they obeyed Him.

The second issue: al-Ka'bi said: His saying "Why did You not send to us a messenger?" is the clearest proof that He accepts the argument of His servants, and that His saying "He is not questioned about what He does" [Al-Anbiya': 23] is not as the people of compulsion (jabr) supposed, that what is injustice from us would be justice from Him; rather its interpretation is that nothing but justice proceeds from Him. Since it is established that He accepts argument, then if they had not been able to do what they were commanded, they would have had the greatest argument in it.

Third issue: Our companions (the Ash'ari scholars) said: The verse indicates that obligation (wujub) is not realized except through the Sharia, for if punishment were established before the coming of the Sharia, punishment would be occurring before the coming of the Sharia.

Then, Glorified is He concluded the surah with a kind of warning, saying: ﴿Say: Each is waiting, so wait﴾. That is, each of us and of you is awaiting the outcome of his affair. This waiting may be before death, either because of the command to fight (jihad) or because of the rise of power and might. It may be at death, for each of the two adversaries awaits the death of the other. It may be after death, which is the manifestation of the matter of reward and punishment, for in the Hereafter the righteous is distinguished from the wrongdoer by what appears upon the righteous of the various forms of Allah's honor, and upon the wrongdoer of the various forms of his humiliation. ﴿So you will know﴾ at that time ﴿who are the companions of the even path and who has been guided﴾ to it. It is not meant in the sense of doubt and uncertainty, but rather in the manner of threat and rebuke toward the disbelievers. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 20, verses 132–135 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And do not extend your eyes toward what We have given enjoyment to some pairs of them, the splendour of the worldly life, that We may test them therein. But the provision of your Lord is better and more enduring.﴾ ﴿And enjoin prayer upon your family, and be steadfast in it. We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you. And the good end is for righteousness.﴾ ﴿And they say, "Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?" Has there not come to them the clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your verses before we are humiliated and disgraced?"﴾ ﴿Say, "Each is waiting, so wait. You will soon know who are the companions of the even path and who is rightly guided."﴾

Know that when Allah had made His Messenger, peace be upon him, patient regarding what they say, and had commanded him to turn instead to glorification (tasbih), He followed that with His prohibition against extending his eyes toward what He had given enjoyment to those people. So He said: ﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾, and in this there are issues.

The first issue: Regarding His saying ﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾ there are two aspects. The first: what is meant is the gaze of the eye. Those who say this state: extending the gaze (mad al-nazar) means prolonging it, and not turning it back, out of admiration for the thing looked upon and wonder at it, as the onlookers of Qarun did when they said: ﴿Oh, would that we had the like of what Qarun has been given. Indeed, he is one of great fortune﴾ [Al-Qasas: 79], until those who had knowledge and faith confronted them with their words: ﴿Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better for one who believes and does righteousness﴾ [Al-Qasas: 80]. And in this is that a gaze which is not extended is pardoned, as when a person looks at something once and then lowers his gaze. Since looking at adornments is almost inherent in human nature, it was said: ﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾, meaning: do not do what you are accustomed to do. The pious have been strict regarding the obligation of lowering the gaze from the buildings of the oppressors and the equipment of the corrupt, in clothing, mounts and other things, because they have made these things for the eyes of onlookers; so whoever looks at them fulfils their purpose and is, as it were, strengthening them in acquiring them.

The second aspect: Abu Muslim said: what is forbidden by His saying ﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾ is not looking, but grief; that is, do not grieve over what has escaped you of the worldly portion they have attained.

The second issue: Abu Rafi' said: "A guest came to the Prophet ﷺ, so he sent me to a Jew to sell or borrow against something. He said, 'By Allah, I will not do that except against a pledge.' I informed him of his words, and he commanded me to take his coat of mail to him. Then the saying of Allah the Exalted was revealed: ﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾." And he, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed Allah does not look at your forms nor at your wealth, but He looks at your hearts and your deeds."

Abu al-Darda' said: The world is the home of one who has no home, and the wealth of one who has no wealth, and for it gathers one who has no intellect. Al-Hasan said: Were it not for the foolishness of people, the world would have been ruined. It is reported from Isa son of Maryam, peace be upon him, that he said: Do not take the world as a lord lest it take you as its slaves. It is reported from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr that whenever he saw what was with the rulers, he would recite this verse and say: "The prayer, may Allah have mercy on you."

As for His saying ﴿what We have given enjoyment to﴾ [i.e.] We made them delight in it. Imti' (enjoyment) is delighting in what is perceived of beautiful sights, what is heard of melodious sounds, what is smelled of pleasant fragrances, and other things such as garments and marriages. It is said: amta'ahu imta'an and matta'ahu tamtee'an, and the tafil form implies intensity. As for His saying ﴿pairs of them﴾, meaning kinds and similar ones among the disbelievers; it derives from pairing things together, which is similarity. This is because they are alike in going astray from the right course. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: kinds of them. Al-Kalbi and al-Zajjaj said: men of them.

As for His saying ﴿the splendour of the worldly life﴾, there are four possibilities regarding its case. The first: it is in the accusative of dispraise, or in the accusative of specification, or as a second object implied by the meaning of "matta'na" as "a'taina", or as a substitute for the place of the prepositional phrase, or as a substitute for "azwajan" on the assumption of "dhawi" (possessors of). If it is asked: what is the meaning of zahra for those who vowelise it with a fatha? We say: zahra has the same meaning, namely adornment and radiance, as in "al-jahra" in the recitation "Show us Allah openly (jahratan)". It may also be the plural of "zahir", describing them as the splendour of this world, for the brightness of their complexions and the radiance of their faces, in contrast to the pallor of complexion and austerity of clothing found among the righteous.

As for His saying ﴿that We may test them therein﴾, they have mentioned several aspects regarding it. The first: that We may punish them thereby, as in His saying: ﴿So let not their wealth nor their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them thereby in the life of this world﴾ [At-Tawbah: 55]. The second: Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: a misguidance from Me for them. The third: al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: a tightening of the obligation upon them, because turning away from the world when it is present and turning to Allah is harder than that when it is absent. For this reason the return of the poor to the service of Allah the Exalted and their supplication to Him is greater than the supplication of the rich. Also, those who are given the world have various kinds of obligations which would not have been binding upon them without it. Also, one who is capable of sins finds avoidance of sins harder for him than one who is poor and incapable. For these reasons, increase in worldly things is a tightening of the obligation.

Then He said to His Messenger: ﴿But the provision of your Lord is better and more enduring.﴾ The more apparent meaning is that what you seek, which you find of reward, is better than what they seek, and more enduring, because it lasts and does not cease, whereas that is not the case with what they have been given of the world. It may also be that what is meant is that what you have been given of the little of the world, when you combine it with obedience, is better for you in terms of its end and more enduring. So He mentioned provision in the world and described it by the goodness of its outcome when one is content with it and patient with it. It may also be that what is meant is what he was given of prophethood and lofty ranks.

As for His saying ﴿And enjoin prayer upon your family﴾, some understood it as his relatives, and some understood it as all the people of his religion, and this is closer. It is like His saying: ﴿And he used to enjoin his family to prayer and zakat﴾ [Maryam: 55]. Although it may be that what is meant is those who share his dwelling, since drawing attention to prayer and commanding it at its times is possible for them and not for the rest of the community; that is, just as We commanded you to pray, so you command your people to it. As for His saying ﴿and be steadfast in it﴾, what is meant is: as you command them, so maintain it by action, for admonition by the tongue of action is more complete than by the tongue of speech. "After the revelation of this verse, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to go to Fatimah and Ali, peace be upon them both, every morning and say: 'The prayer,' and he did this for months."

Then Allah the Exalted explained that He commands them with this only for their benefit, and that He is exalted above benefits, by His saying: ﴿We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you.﴾ And in this there are aspects. The first: Abu Muslim said: the meaning is that Allah only wants from him and from them worship, and does not want from him that He should provide for him, as masters want tribute from slaves. It is like His saying: ﴿I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me. I do not want from them any provision, nor do I want that they should feed Me﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 56–57]. The second: "We do not ask you for provision" for yourself nor for your family; rather, We provide for you and provide for your family, so empty your mind for the affairs of the Hereafter. Its meaning is the saying of people: whoever is in the service of Allah, Allah will be in his service. The third: the meaning is that when We commanded you to pray, it was not because We benefit from your prayer; so He expressed this meaning by His saying: "We do not ask you for provision," but rather We provide for you in the world with forms of blessings and in the Hereafter with reward. Abdullah ibn Salam said: "When distress or hardship came upon the family of the Prophet ﷺ, he would command them to pray, and recite this verse."

Know that there is no concession in this verse for abandoning earning a livelihood, for He, the Exalted, said in describing the righteous: ﴿men whom neither commerce nor trade diverts from the remembrance of Allah﴾ [An-Nur: 37]. As for His saying "and the good end is for righteousness", what is meant is that the good outcome is for the people of taqwa, meaning the taqwa of Allah the Exalted.

Then, after this instruction, He, glory be to Him, related their doubt, as if it were part of the completion of His saying: ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾; and it is their saying: ﴿Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?﴾ By this speech they were deceived into thinking that He imposes faith upon them without a sign. In another place they said: ﴿Let him bring us a sign, as the former messengers were sent﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 5]. Allah the Exalted answered this with His saying: ﴿Has there not come to them the clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ And in this there are aspects. The first: that what is in the Qur'an agrees with what is in their books, although the Messenger ﷺ did not occupy himself with study and learning, and had never seen a teacher at all; so this would be a report of the unseen, and thus a miracle. The second: the clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures is what they contain of glad tidings concerning Muhammad ﷺ, his prophethood and his mission. The third: Ibn Jarir and al-Qaffal mentioned that the meaning of ﴿Has there not come to them the clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ is: the news of the nations whom We destroyed when they asked for signs and disbelieved in them, how We hastened punishment upon them; so what would secure them that their condition in asking for signs would not be like the condition of those? This clarification has come to them in the Qur'an, and for this reason He described the Qur'an as ﴿the clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures﴾. Know that He mentioned the pronoun referring to "clear evidence" because it carries the sense of proof and argument. Then He explained that Allah the Exalted removed from them every excuse and pretext regarding the obligation, and so He said: ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger?"﴾ The meaning is that they would have had the right to say this, and it would have been an excuse for them. But now, since We have sent you and made clear through your tongue to them what is upon them and what is for them, they have no argument at all; rather the argument is against them. The phrase ﴿before it﴾ may mean before the sending of the Messenger, or before the clear signs he displayed. If it is asked: what is the meaning of His saying "And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said", while the one destroyed cannot speak? We say: the meaning is that they would have had the right to say this on the Day of Resurrection; and for this reason He said: ﴿before we are humiliated and disgraced﴾, and that is appropriate only for the punishment of the Hereafter. It is reported that Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Three will argue before Allah the Exalted on the Day of Resurrection: the one who died in the interval (fatra) says: 'No messenger came to me, otherwise I would have been the most obedient of Your creation to You,' and he recited His saying: ﴿Why did You not send to us a messenger?﴾; and the one whose mind was overcome says: 'You did not make for me a mind by which I might benefit'; and the child says: 'I was young and did not understand.' Then a fire is raised for them, and it is said to them: 'Enter it.' Whoever was in Allah's knowledge to be wretched enters it, and whoever was in His knowledge to be happy remains. Then Allah the Exalted says to them: 'You disobeyed today; so how would you have fared had My messengers come to you?'" The judge (al-Qadi) criticised the report and said: it is not fitting to punish one who does not understand.
